Death toll rises to 39 after migrant boat capsizes off Senegal
The death toll in Senegal’s boat capsize has risen to 39 after new bodies were discovered Monday, according to the country’s emergency services
DAKAR, Senegal -- The death toll from the capsize off Senegal of a boat carrying migrants rose to 39 following the discovery of more bodies on Monday, the country’s emergency services said.
The boat, which left Saint-Louis in northern Senegal and was headed to the Spanish coast, overturned on Sunday, offshore from the town of Kébémer, north of the capital Dakar.
The Ministry of Interior said Sunday at least 21 people had died and rescuers were looking for possible survivors. It did not say how many people were on the boat, but several passengers are still believed to be missing.
Only one passenger was rescued alive.
The boat was following a well-traveled migration route for thousands of young Senegalese seeking better economic conditions. They travel on uncovered wooden canoes for around 800 miles on the Atlantic Ocean to reach Europe. Young people face high unemployment and poverty as the country struggles with an economic crisis.
Senegal’s President Bassirou Diomaye Faye offered condolences and vowed to clamp down on networks behind the dangerous crossings.

Nebraska rushed Medicaid work rules. Then a cancer patient was told he'd lost coverage
Eli McCreary of Omaha, Neb., said he had recently been diagnosed with kidney cancer when he got a call from a local hospital run by CHI Health. He said he was informed that he wasn't insured anymore under Medicaid — and that the hospital would cancel his appointments unless he paid out-of-pocket.
McCreary, who was 64 at the time, said he phoned a call center for help. He said he was told his benefits under Medicaid, the government health program for people with low incomes or disabilities, now required that he have a job.
"You're required to do work to stay on," McCreary said a representative told him. "And you haven't fulfilled your work requirement."
For decades, McCreary said, he has battled drug addiction. A substance use treatment program discharged him in March, and in June he was diagnosed with cancer in his right kidney, according to documents reviewed by KFF Health News. He also has diabetes and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.
"I don't understand what job I can get," McCreary said. "I can't walk. I can hardly breathe. I can't move around. What job am I going to get?"
McCreary said he canceled a CT scan and other tests at the hospital, which is part of CommonSpirit Health, the nation's largest Catholic health system. He also delayed a cancer-related appointment with a physician who travels back and forth to Omaha. "I missed my window of opportunity with him for another month," he said.
Taylor Miller, a spokesperson for CHI Health, declined to answer questions about McCreary's experience. In an emailed statement, she said that "CHI Health is committed to helping patients understand their health care coverage and access to care, including available financial assistance resources."
Determined to be the first state to enforce Medicaid work requirements under President Trump's signature One Big Beautiful Bill Act, Nebraska launched the new rules May 1 — eight months before most states are set to do the same. With their newly elected majorities in Congress, Democrats have said they plan to repeal the changes to Medicaid in their first 100 hours in office in January. But it is unclear if they will be successful, because Trump could veto it.
Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen said in December that state officials "certainly appreciate President Trump and his whole administration for delivering this key reform." Pillen spoke alongside a videoed-in Mehmet Oz, the Trump administration official overseeing Medicare and Medicaid.
"We're excited to be able to be the first to make it happen," the Republican governor said.
Laura Strimple, a spokesperson for the governor, didn't respond to requests for comment. Jeff Powell, a spokesperson for Nebraska's Department of Health and Human Services, said its rollout "has been very successful." He pointed to state data showing 86% of affected applicants met the requirement or qualified for an exclusion and 93% of existing enrollees kept their coverage.
Health clinics and organizations advocating for poor and working-class Nebraskans say the rollout has been rife with problems — many due to poor training and inadequate staffing.
The high price of cutting benefits
About 70,000 adult Medicaid recipients in Nebraska are subject to the work requirements. They must prove they're working or participating in a similar activity for 80 hours a month, unless they qualify for an exemption. State officials and consultants advising them have said the May 1 date was challenging to meet.
To deploy the law's Medicaid coverage restrictions, Nebraska budgeted millions of dollars for government contractors, according to state documents KFF Health News obtained via a public records request. Documents from Nebraska's health department outline $8.2 million in contractor costs to enact Medicaid changes, including work requirements and more frequent checks for whether people still qualify.
Nebraska operates the information technology system that determines who in the state qualifies for Medicaid, unlike most states, which outsource the work to companies under contracts often worth hundreds of millions of dollars. But Nebraska's health department nonetheless relies on the private sector to help administer its Medicaid program.
The $8.2 million in costs span two years. They stem from two companies that Nebraska uses to increase agency staffing: Public Consulting Group, based in Boston, and Atlanta-based Covendis, which supplies information technology staffers.
One of the companies has praised Nebraska's implementation of work requirements. A post on Public Consulting Group's website quotes senior consultant Latanya Michaux.
"I really cannot brag enough about how well Nebraska handled this requirement," Michaux said, crediting the firm's "incredible relationship" with the state.
Covendis executives did not respond to requests for comment. Powell said the health department "uses contracted staff when hiring a state employee is either uneconomical or impractical because of time constraints, or when the role requires highly specialized skill sets."
Advocates who work with Medicaid enrollees in Nebraska say that participants are confused and don't know whether the rules apply to them. These advocates say enrollees also have gotten inaccurate information. In December, Pillen said the state "won't be adding workforce" to implement the work requirements, a decision those advocates have criticized. Pillen in July also instituted a government-wide hiring freeze.
Nebraska listed at least half a dozen contractors costing more than $250,000 each, including one person whose compensation exceeds $1.8 million, the documents show. Nebraska submitted the records to federal Medicaid regulators as part of a routine process to secure federal money. Powell said the funding requests "may not reflect actual expenditures."
Sarah Maresh, a program director with the social justice advocacy nonprofit Nebraska Appleseed, said the amounts were "shocking."
"When you put in complicated policies like this, there are large corporations making money behind the scenes," Maresh said. "This just further confirms that it's happening in Nebraska quietly."
Confusion and longer wait times
The Medicaid work requirements in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and other changes shepherded by Republicans will curtail insurance gains that came from the Affordable Care Act, also known as Obamacare. The GOP tax and spending law, which the Congressional Budget Office estimated would reduce federal Medicaid spending by more than $900 billion over a decade, adds reporting requirements and restrictions that make it harder for people to stay enrolled.
As of early July, most denials related to the work requirements among Nebraska adults applying for Medicaid were due to unsubmitted paperwork, according to internal documents from Nebraska's health department that KFF Health News obtained through a public records request. The state wrote this was "expected."
State data shows that average wait times at a Nebraska health department call center nearly doubled between May and July, going from about 13 minutes to 26 minutes, before declining in August. In interviews, advocates for Medicaid enrollees said they've encountered people who have waited on the phone for hours.
Nebraska received more than 101,000 calls in August, a 66% jump from May.
"If people are working, they just don't have time to be sitting on the phone to go through all of this stuff," said Kenny McMorris, CEO of the Charles Drew Health Center, a federally qualified health center in North Omaha. He said roughly half of Charles Drew's 13,385 patients are on Medicaid, and of those, 42% are subject to the work requirements.
"You can leverage the technology, but you still got to have people there to help," McMorris said.
Then there are experiences the official data may not catch, like what happened to McCreary — saddled with figuring out what happened with his Medicaid benefits amid a health crisis, and whether it was even true that he had to work to keep them.
McCreary had heard about the Medicaid work requirements but didn't know they might apply to him. Powell confirmed McCreary was eligible for Medicaid because of the ACA — putting him in the population subject to work requirements.
His ordeal underscores the fallout from being caught in confusing government systems and silos that aren't obvious to the public.
"This cancer ain't going to stop just because I ain't got insurance," he said. "It's going to keep working on me."
When he received the call from the hospital about his coverage, "I was really in despair," McCreary said. Eventually, he said, he called for help.
Nebraska's health department runs AccessNebraska, a call center for help with safety net benefits such as Medicaid and the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, commonly known as food stamps. But the number McCreary recalls dialing ended up not being AccessNebraska — it was for a different call center, one for SNAP accounts that Nebraska outsources to a private company. Powell said the state has no record of McCreary calling the health department.
McCreary said the worker didn't have a good explanation for why the Medicaid work requirements would apply to him. Before his health deteriorated, McCreary worked as a driver for an asphalt services company. He said he worked "until I couldn't do the job anymore."
"I really had hoped to work longer," he said. "I kind of enjoyed that job."
Attorneys and policy professionals who work with people on Medicaid and other public benefit programs said that McCreary's substance use treatment, lasting four months starting in November 2025, and other health conditions should have exempted him.
The federal law outlines categories of exemptions, such as being too sick to work. People who are considered too ill include those who have a serious medical condition or a substance use disorder.
Nebraska's health department said it sent tens of thousands of letters, text messages and emails to inform enrollees about the new requirements. According to state documents, Nebraska said it would "implement enhancements" to its computer system and online portal, including allowing people to submit documents online and having "clear, plain-language" enrollee notices. McCreary, however, doesn't have an account on Nebraska Medicaid's online portal, preferring to handle things over the phone or in person.
He also said it's possible he missed letters from Nebraska Medicaid about his coverage.
"I don't know if it's my fault or not," McCreary said.
The Cornhusker State's experience could be a harbinger of things to come. Next year, work requirements will apply to millions of adult Medicaid enrollees in more than 40 states.
The nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office has estimated the policy will lead to 5.3 million more people being uninsured in the U.S. by 2034.
"We definitely had fun"
The One Big Beautiful Bill Act's Medicaid changes are the most complicated in years — changes that government benefit experts say will strain and exacerbate long-standing problems with state technology systems for health benefits.
"It's already a shaky system, and now you've added more burdens on top of that," said Gelila Selassie, director of health advocacy for the nonprofit Justice in Aging.
Nebraska and federal officials, as well as consultants advising the state, detailed the difficulties and successes with the state's May 1 launch during an August panel discussion at a national conference in Oregon.
"They said, 'We're going to go live May 1.' To which CMS said, 'Oh, my God!'" Brent Weaver, an official who specializes in Medicaid IT at the U.S. Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, said about Nebraska.
Nebraska officials knew "they weren't as agile as they probably would have liked to have been," Weaver said, "but they didn't let that stop them."
"If they fail, we looked at it as a failure," he added in comments that broadly praised the state's approach.
CMS did not answer questions from KFF Health News about Nebraska's rollout and Weaver's remarks.
In Nebraska, a group of 60 people held hours-long meetings three days a week that were "very exhausting," Michaux, of Public Consulting Group, said during a different session at the conference.
"Our calendars were cleared, and that was the focus," Michaux said.
Because CMS had not yet issued regulations outlining key details such as how people could get exemptions — it would do so June 1 — Nebraska officials said they had to rely on the law's broad language to make initial decisions.
"We had to get comfortable being uncomfortable," Jacob Kawamoto, a deputy director at Nebraska's Medicaid division, said at the conference.
Public Consulting Group said it worked with the state to develop new guidance and "process guides" — materials for Nebraska eligibility workers with instructions on how to process Medicaid applications or renewals. Training materials for Nebraska caseworkers reviewed by KFF Health News refer to those guides.
"The training was very robust, and the process guides were very robust," Michaux said.
Maresh disagreed with that characterization. "There are gaps" in the state's training materials, she said, and caseworkers "are confused" about work requirements.
Public Consulting Group also helped the state institute changes to Nebraska's Medicaid IT system, according to the company. "We are preparing for future updates and enhancements," Michaux said.
In response to questions, Public Consulting Group spokesperson Alyssa Brown said the company "has supported Nebraska Medicaid via a broad range of consulting services since 2019, including work on federal and state compliance initiatives." She said Michaux "discussed" the process guides at the conference but Nebraska developed them. Similarly, Brown said the company did not develop training.
Federal taxpayers will largely bear the costs of implementing the One Big Beautiful Bill Act's Medicaid policies in Nebraska and elsewhere. Congress allocated $200 million in one-time funding to states. Under federal regulations, the U.S. government picks up most of the tab for state IT system changes, paying as much as 90% of the cost.
"Even though it was not so easy," Michaux said at the conference, "we definitely had fun standing up the Medicaid work requirement program."
Public Consulting Group's employees, Brown told KFF Health News, are "passionate about public service and helping our clients improve the lives of the people they serve."
Dropping Medicaid enrollment
As of August, roughly 1,100 Nebraskans had been denied benefits because of Medicaid work requirements. Most denials were because people did not respond to requests for information.
Nebraska's total Medicaid enrollment has declined by roughly 4,600 people since May, a drop of 1.4%, according to an August report.
As for McCreary, the Nebraska health department's Powell maintained he experienced "no lapses in coverage" and said he was disenrolled from Medicaid after turning 65. Despite what McCreary said he was told, Powell said Medicaid work requirements weren't the reason: He aged out of Medicaid and into Medicare before they could be applied to him.
Selassie, from the nonprofit Justice in Aging, said McCreary's care shouldn't have been disrupted.
McCreary is now enrolled in Medicare, and Medicaid covers some of his health costs. He was able to reschedule his canceled appointments.
"The cancer has grown so much," he said.
He had surgery in early November to remove his right kidney.
KFF Health News correspondent Samantha Liss contributed to this report.
KFF Health News is a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF — the independent source for health policy research, polling, and journalism.

CHICAGO — If one word could describe research presented at this year’s American Heart Association scientific sessions, it might be “neutral.”
The meeting began with two blockbuster disappointments, hinted at in top-line results released weeks or months ago but detailed with unvarnished specificity Saturday morning. The ZEUS trial targeting inflammation showed no difference between the treatment and placebo arms. The HORIZON trial taking aim at lipoprotein(a) also revealed nearly identical results, whether participants were on or off the drug.
In other words, neutral.

The sound of firecrackers filling the air is not far away as Deepavali draws closer. But the excitement of bursting firecrackers comes with a word of caution from ophthalmologists as they warn that a moment of carelessness can cause eye injuries ranging from minor abrasions to severe ocular trauma.
M. Elangovan, director, Regional Institute of Ophthalmology and Government Ophthalmic Hospital (RIO-GOH), Chennai, said that there are different types of crackers. “Bursting types (explosive crackers) will produce irregular, small and forcible particles in all directions and are the most dangerous. These particles can travel at such a velocity that they could hit or penetrate any soft surface. Then, there is direct heat injury caused by crackers such as sparklers that can cause scar formations in the cornea or conjunctiva due to the heat generated. Sudden and close exposure to bright light-emitting crackers can also cause bleaching or temporary blackout due to the impact on the rod and cone cells in the retina,” he explained.

Social media users are spreading seven rules that U.S. President Donald Trump has allegedly proposed to limit privileges for lawmakers in Congress.
The alleged rules, according to many Facebook posts, included proposals like removing pensions for Congress members and requiring lawmakers to participate in the same government-run social services many Americans use, like Medicare for health care insurance and Social Security for retirement paychecks. Here's how the claim usually went, per the aforementioned posts:
I'm in agreement From Fox News. I wonder how loud it'll get if Trump could pull this off. It will be interesting.
President Trump is asking everyone to share this, in three days, most people in the United States will have seen the message. This is an idea that should be passed around, regardless of political party.
The TRUMP Rules:
1. Tenure / No Pension. A Congressman/woman collects a salary while in office and receives no pay when they're out of office. And no more perks go with them.
2. Congress (past, present, & future) participates in Social Security. All funds in the Congressional retirement fund move to the Social Security system immediately. All future funds flow into the Social Security system, and Congress participates with the American people. It may not be used for any other purpose.
3. Congress must purchase their own retirement plan, just as ALL Americans do.
4. Congress will no longer vote themselves a pay raise. Congressional pay will rise at the ok same rate as the COLA for monthly Social Security recipients minus 1% if having a budget balance deficit.
5. Congress loses their current care system and participates in the same health care system (Medicare) as the American people.
6. Congress must equally abide by all laws they impose on the American people (i.e. NO MORE INSIDER TRADING!!!).
7. All contracts with past and present Congressmen/women are void. The American people did not make this contract with Congressmen/women. Congress made all these contracts by and for themselves.
Serving in Congress is an honor and privilege, NOT a career.
The Founding Fathers envisioned citizen legislators should serve their term(s), then go home and go back to work … not get all kinds of freebies. Term limits of 2 terms and treat them like a regular citizen!
You will need to copy and paste.
I AGREE SO I'M SHARING!
Meanwhile, Snopes readers asked about similar posts and searched the website using the keywords "Trump rules."
The above text is a copypasta — a copy-and-pasted internet hoax common on Facebook. As Snopes has previously reported, variants of this particular copypasta have spread online since at least 2009, when a version of the rules listed above were labeled "The 28th Amendment" and attributed to business magnate Warren Buffet.
Internet users circulated it as the "Congressional Reform Act of 2017" during Trump's first term and the "Congressional Reform Act of 2025" in 2025, during his second term.
Fox News, which the copypasta cited as its source, has not reported on "The TRUMP Rules" as of this writing, per a search of the news outlet's website. As of this writing, Trump has also not posted about this particular copypasta online, according to two databases that track his social media output. The White House web page for news releases did not reference these supposed rules. Finally, a search for "The TRUMP Rules" on Google returned no credible and relevant results treating the list as a legitimate proposal.
Thus, we have rated this claim false.
The so-called reforms listed in the act also include a mixture of rules that already exist and proposals that would actually change existing policy. Here's a breakdown of what these supposed reforms would and would not change:
Do Congress members receive pensions?
Congress members, like most federal employees, are eligible for a pension. Here's the pension eligibility requirements, per the Congressional Research Service:
Members of Congress are eligible for a pension at the age of 62 if they have completed at least 5 years of service. Members are eligible for a pension at age 50 if they have completed 20 years of service, or at any age after completing 25 years of service. The amount of the pension depends on length of service (as measured in months) and the average of the highest three years of salary. By law, the starting amount of a Member's retirement annuity may not exceed 80% of his or her final salary.
Do Congress members pay into Social Security? Do they pay into their own retirement plans?
Per our previous reporting, Congress members have paid into Social Security since 1984, when they first became eligible for Social Security benefits.
Congress members first elected in 1984 or later are covered automatically under the Federal Employees' Retirement System, which other government workers use, and can decline coverage.
Aside from Social Security, lawmakers elected before 1984 can be covered under the Civil Service Retirement System, a separate pension plan, CSRS Offset, which is a mix of CSRS and Social Security, or Social Security alone. Lawmakers also pay into these plans — how much they pay and which plans they pay into differs based on when they were elected.
Can Congress members approve a pay raise for themselves?
Congress members can vote for a pay raise as dictated by the Constitution, but the raise doesn't take effect until the next election due to the 27th Amendment. Technically, a law passed in 1989 grants Congress an automatic cost-of-living pay raise, but lawmakers have blocked those pay increases from taking effect for years. Rank-and-file members of Congress, who receive $174,000 annually as of this writing, have not increased their pay since 2009.
Do Congress members have their own health care system? Do they participate in Medicare?
Under the Affordable Care Act of 2010, commonly known as Obamacare, lawmakers must give up the insurance coverage previously provided to them via the Federal Employees Health Benefits Program and buy health insurance through a plan or exchange created under the act. The Office of Personnel Management has also dictated that members of Congress must purchase through DC Health Link, a program offered under the ACA.
Members of Congress also pay into Medicare and are eligible for it, just like any American.
Are Congress members allowed to participate in insider trading?
Congress members are allowed to trade stock, but legally, they're not supposed to conduct insider trading. The Stop Trading on Congressional Knowledge Act of 2012 — known as the STOCK Act — prohibits members of Congress from using "any nonpublic information derived from the individual's position ... or gained from performance of the individual's duties, for personal benefit."
Critics argue the STOCK Act failed to stop insider trading, however, and no member of Congress has been prosecuted for insider trading under the STOCK Act as of this writing — although policy experts have said there's been "persistent credible allegations" of insider trading since the act passed.

Breast cancer begins long before the lump: why diet and lifestyle matter
While genetic predisposition is one factor, a majority of breast cancers develop in women with no family history: metabolic health and physical inactivity play a role too, and it is important for women to know about these factors
Students seen taking part in a ‘Pink Umbrella’ walk to create awareness on breast cancer. Image used for representational purposes only
| Photo Credit: VELANKANNI RAJ B
Last month, celebrated as Breast Cancer Awareness Month, reminded us, as it does every year, about the importance of mammograms, early diagnosis, and advances in treatment. These messages save lives and deserve continued attention. However, there is another conversation that often receives far less attention: the role of food, physical activity, obesity, diabetes, physical activity, and metabolic health in breast cancer.
In my oncology clinic, patients are often surprised when I bring up these topics. They say, “Doctor, I knew breast cancer was related to family history. I didn’t know that lifestyle diseases such as diabetes and obesity had anything to do with it.”

On Nov. 6, after Republicans lost the House and Senate in the 2026 midterm elections, purported footage of U.S. Sen. Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., spread in which he was unresponsive when a reporter asked for his reaction to the GOP's losses and whether he thought "Republicans would get anything done in the lame-duck session."
In the clip, McConnell, seated in a wheelchair, stared ahead, blinking a few times while someone (possibly an aide) spoke to the reporter off-camera. McConnell briefly glanced at the reporter.
Posts on X (archived), Facebook and YouTube sharing the video questioned the state of McConnell's health. (The senator had been hospitalized for several months earlier in 2026.)
The footage, which appeared on Newsmax show "Frontline" on Nov. 6, is authentic and was taken by Newsmax reporter Kilmeny Duchardt on Capitol Hill. There is no visible manipulation with artificial intelligence or other digital editing tools. As such, we rate this claim as true.
Snopes reached out to McConnell's staff to learn more about his health and his reaction in the video. We will update this post if we learn more.
On Nov. 6, "Frontline" host Carl Higbie shared the clip of McConnell on his show. The footage is available on Newsmax as well as YouTube.
Off screen, someone interrupted Duchardt, who said, "OK, no problem," suggesting she was interacting with the senator's aide.
Higbie reacted to the video saying, "That can't be legal, he's a vegetable!" He asked Theo Wold, a former assistant attorney general under President Donald Trump, for his reaction. Wold said:
This isn't just an ideological conflict for the soul of the Republican Party now, it is a generational one. We are tired of the geriatric gerontocracy ruling the conservative movement … the idea that [Republican Sen. Thom Tillis] and these folks now want to negotiate on things like amnesty with the Democrats. Look, you can't negotiate with a tiger when your face is inside of its mouth, OK? And what we need now are fighters who are not wheelchair-bound, but who can actually stand on their own two feet.
Over the years, Snopes readers have frequently asked us if the senator is dead or dying. Snopes has reported on many rumors about McConnell's health, including investigating a claim the U.S. government paid for his polio treatment.

The US military has published a Request for Information on a federal procurement website signaling interest in deploying a “proliferated cislunar constellation” consisting of an unspecified number of satellites performing an undisclosed mission in the vicinity of the Moon.
The announcement follows statements in recent months from the Space Force’s acquisitions chief for advanced programs, Maj. Gen. Stephen Purdy, that the military was getting serious about extending its reach to the Moon. The Space Force’s most distant satellites today are in geostationary orbit, some 22,000 miles (36,000 kilometers) over the equator, collecting routine surveillance and missile warning data.
Most recently, Purdy spoke of a shift in Pentagon leadership’s thinking about the Moon following an executive order signed by President Donald Trump last December. The order set out the Trump administration’s space policy. One section of the order deals with the US government’s ability to detect, characterize, and counter threats to US space interests from low-Earth orbit to cislunar space, the term of art for the region of space around the Moon.
Fighting for the Moon
“I’ve got the Secretary of War and the Chairman of the Joint Chiefs full on stating in public: ‘This is a warfighting domain,’” Purdy said at Space Systems Command’s Industry Days event in October, according to a report in Air & Space Forces Magazine. “And so, I would ask you all, please jump on my cislunar bandwagon because I need some more friends here, along with our deep, passionate crew that have been working on this for years.”
Officials have emphasized the military’s role at the Moon is to protect US interests there as the United States and China ramp up their lunar programs, with a series of robotic missions culminating in crewed lunar landings in the next few years. Some US officials foresee a competition for real estate and resources at the Moon, where there are a finite number of safe landing zones that can access the Moon’s water ice at the south pole.

The spiritual triumph of ‘light over darkness’ is celebrated during Diwali, which people mark by lighting traditional lamps, decorating homes and gathering with family and friends

Starting Tuesday, Mexican schools will ban cellphones from classrooms as part of a federal government effort to limit children's and teenagers' use of electronic devices, following similar measures taken by over a hundred countries in the last decade.
The initiative, spearheaded by Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum, has been supported by experts who see it as an opportunity to reduce young Mexicans' exposure to technology and the resulting attention deficit, stress and anxiety.
Mexican authorities are also preparing to implement regulations this month that will require digital platforms to remove posts containing hate speech, abuse, sexual violence, harassment, cyberbullying and other illegal content.
However, the cellphone ban, which will take effect on November 3, is already facing resistance in some parts of the country. Some parents fear being unable to communicate with their children amid ongoing violence, from which children and adolescents are not spared.
According to the civil society coalition Network for Children's Rights in Mexico (REDIM), in the first half of this year, one in 10 Mexicans between the ages of 0 and 17 were victims of crimes involving organised crime.
“I don't think parents will accept not giving their children a means of digital communication, especially when those children … are spending so much time at home instead of at school,” said Francisco Ortiz, state representative of the National Union of Parents in Sinaloa, accusing the government of ignoring parents and approving regulations that “go against parental authority, against the rights of parents.”
The decree issued by Sheinbaum prohibits the use of cellphones and electronic devices inside elementary and middle schools throughout the school day, and only allows their use for educational purposes under the guidance of teachers or for personal emergencies, disability and health needs. Students can take their phones with them on the way to school.
Benigno Gomez, a father from Reynosa in the northern state of Tamaulipas, said that while he understood the educational authorities' need to reduce students' time on cellphones, he found it “a little difficult” that they weren't allowed to have a cellphone to deal with a potential risk situation.
Mexican authorities have not commented on these concerns and have instead focused on the harm caused by cellphones.
During a recent address to the Chamber of Deputies, Mexico's Secretary of Public Education, Mario Delgado, stated that the Sheinbaum administration seeks to “prevent addiction to digital platforms and the disorders they cause in minors.”
Parents seek reassurance
Just as the sun was beginning to rise, the residents of Escuinapa, the capital of the municipality of the same name located in southern Sinaloa, awoke on the morning of October 22 to alarming news. A bus that regularly travels through the small town -- which relies on mango and shrimp production -- was shot at by a man on a motorcycle.
More than a dozen high school students were on board. A video recorded by one of the passengers circulated on social media, showing children on the floor and others hiding among the seats while one teenager asks another, “Do you have any credit (on your cellphone)?”
In the attack, only the bus driver was injured, suffering cuts from shards of glass shattered by the gunfire.
Upon learning of the shooting, one Escuinapa resident immediately called her teenage daughter, who had left early for high school in a car driven by her aunt.
“Just hearing my daughter's voice and knowing she was OK calmed me down,” said the woman, who asked to remain anonymous for fear of the criminals plaguing her community -- admitting that she didn't hesitate to interrupt her daughter's class to check on her.
The mother expressed doubts that parents will comply with the cellphone ban, fearing that violence could now reach schools in Escuinapa, and insisted that “the safety of our children comes first.”
In defence of the regulation
For Israel Sanchez, president of the National Union of Parents, the Mexican government's decision represents progress after years of struggle by the civil organisation, which brings together hundreds of parents from public and private schools, mostly Catholic.
Sanchez argued that authorities must undertake an awareness campaign for parents and provide training for teachers to achieve the effective implementation of the regulation.
Lucía Magis-Weinberg, a neurodevelopmental researcher at the University of Washington who has studied the effects of technology on children and adolescents for years, said Mexico is joining the international movement to regulate cellphones at a very opportune moment.
Magis-Weinberg acknowledged the benefits of technology for socialisation and accessing information but said it is “a double-edged sword.”
Regulations are needed to avoid cognitive damage, digital conflicts, and the risks of platforms that “are designed to maintain, to maximise our attention.”
The ban on cellphones in schools is already in place in 114 countries, according to UNESCO data. In Europe, restrictions have gained increasing traction, especially in France, where the ban was extended to secondary schools in August. Controls have also been implemented in some countries in Latin America, such as Ecuador, Brazil, Chile, Bolivia and Costa Rica. In the United States, bans are only maintained in some states.

The story so far: The Sample Registration System (SRS) Statistical Report of 2021, released by the Office of the Registrar General of India recently, showed that India has maintained its Total Fertility Rate (TFR) at 2.0 — the same as reported in 2020. While the national average for TFR has remained the same, there is a wide regional variation in TFR data for States and Union Territories (UTs) reported independently.
The highest TFR was recorded in Bihar at 3.0 and the lowest was reported for West Bengal and Delhi at 1.4. The data went on to reveal that in the decade between 2009-11 and 2019-21, TFR has been on an overall decline, in States, and nationally, albeit at different rates.

2026 అక్టోబర్ చివరలో జరిగిన ఇజ్రాయెల్ ఎన్నికల్లో ప్రధానమంత్రి బెంజమిన్ నెతన్యాహు పార్టీ, దాని మిత్రపక్షాలు మొత్తం 53 సీట్లు గెలుచుకున్నాయి. అయితే, ప్రభుత్వాన్ని ఏర్పాటు చేయడానికి అవసరమైన 61 సీట్లను సాధించలేకపోయాయి. ప్రతిపక్ష పార్టీలు 48 సీట్లు గెలుచుకోగా, అరబ్ పార్టీలకు 19 సీట్లు వచ్చాయి. ఎన్నికల తర్వాత, కొత్త ప్రభుత్వాన్ని ఎవరు ఏర్పాటు చేయగలరో నిర్ణయించేందుకు అధ్యక్షుడు ఐజాక్ హెర్జోగ్ వివిధ పార్టీల నాయకులతో చర్చలు ప్రారంభించారు.
ఈ నేపథ్యంలో, ఇజ్రాయెల్ పార్లమెంటులో ముస్లిం ఎంపీలు అందరూ కలిసి నమాజ్ చేస్తున్నారంటూ ఒక వీడియో (ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ) సోషల్ మీడియాలో షేర్ చేస్తున్నారు. ఈ పోస్టులో చేస్తున్న వాదనలో నిజమెంతుందో ఇప్పుడు పరిశీలిద్దాం.
క్లెయిమ్: ఇజ్రాయెల్ పార్లమెంటులో ముస్లిం ఎంపీలు అందరూ కలిసి నమాజ్ చేస్తున్న వీడియో.
ఫ్యాక్ట్: ఈ వీడియో జోర్డాన్ రాజధాని అమ్మాన్లోని జోర్డాన్ పార్లమెంటులో 2026 నవంబర్ 3న ఎంపీలు మధ్యాహ్నం (దుహర్) నమాజ్ చేస్తున్న దృశ్యాలను చూపిస్తుంది. ఇజ్రాయెల్ పార్లమెంటులో ముస్లిం ఎంపీలు నమాజ్ చేసినట్లు ఎలాంటి వార్తలు లేవు. కాబట్టి, ఈ పోస్టులో చేసిన వాదన తప్పు.
మొదట, ఇజ్రాయెల్ పార్లమెంటు (క్నెసెట్)లో ఇటీవల ఇలాంటి ఘటన ఏదైనా జరిగిందా అని వెతికితే, ఈ ఘటన జరిగినట్టు ఎలాంటి విశ్వసనీయ వార్తా కథనాలు మాకు లభించలేదు. అంతేకాకుండా, ఇజ్రాయెల్ పార్లమెంటు అధికారిక వెబ్సైట్ ప్రకారం, కొత్తగా ఎన్నికైన క్నెసెట్ తొలి సమావేశం 10 నవంబర్ 2026న జరగనుంది. ఈ సమావేశంలో కొత్తగా ఎన్నికైన ఎంపీలు ప్రమాణ స్వీకారం చేయడంతో పాటు, పార్లమెంటు స్పీకర్ను ఎన్నుకోనున్నారు.
తర్వాత, వైరల్ వీడియో యొక్క కీ ఫ్రేమ్లను రివర్స్ ఇమేజ్ సెర్చ్ చేయగా, అవే దృశ్యాలతో కూడిన వీడియోలు BBC News Arabic (ఇక్కడ), జోర్డాన్కు చెందిన మీడియా సంస్థలు (ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ) ప్రచురించినట్లు గుర్తించాం. ఈ కథనాల ప్రకారం, 3 నవంబర్ 2026న జోర్డాన్ రాజధాని అమ్మాన్లోని ప్రతినిధుల సభ (జోర్డాన్ పార్లమెంటు) లో ఎంపీలు మధ్యాహ్నం (దుహర్) నమాజ్ చేస్తున్న దృశ్యాలు ఇవి.
ఈ కథనాల ప్రకారం, పార్లమెంటు శాశ్వత బ్యూరో సభ్యులను ఎన్నుకునేందుకు నిర్ణయించిన సమావేశానికి ముందు ఎంపీ డా. అహ్మద్ అల్-రఖబ్ నమాజ్కు నాయకత్వం వహించారు. కొన్ని మీడియా సంస్థలు ప్రచురించిన పూర్తి వీడియోలో ఆయన నమాజ్కు నాయకత్వం వహిస్తున్న దృశ్యాలను కూడా చూడవచ్చు.
అంతేకాకుండా, వైరల్ వీడియోలో కనిపిస్తున్న జోర్డాన్ జాతీయ చిహ్నం (ఇక్కడ ), అలాగే జోర్డాన్ పార్లమెంటు లోపలి భాగానికి సంబంధించిన దృశ్యాలు (ఇక్కడ) కూడా ఈ వీడియో జోర్డాన్ పార్లమెంటుకు చెందినదేనని స్పష్టం చేస్తున్నాయి.
చివరిగా, జోర్డాన్ పార్లమెంటులో ఎంపీలు నమాజ్ చేస్తున్న వీడియోను, ఇజ్రాయెల్ పార్లమెంటులో ముస్లిం ఎంపీలు నమాజ్ చేస్తున్నారని తప్పుగా షేర్ చేస్తున్నారు.

Why a US-Russia showdown left Morocco celebrating
- Published
Morocco has welcomed the end of a decades-long UN peacekeeping mission in Western Sahara, after a diplomatic showdown between the US and Russia left the Security Council unable to agree on its future.
The council failed on Friday to renew the mandate of the UN Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara (Minurso) after Russia vetoed a US-backed proposal. A rival Russian draft to extend the mission also failed to secure enough votes.
The decision raises questions about the future of Africa's longest territorial dispute and the fragile ceasefire between Morocco, which claims Western Sahara, and the Polisario Front which has been fighting for the territory's independence for more than 50 years.
Here is what you need to know.
Why is Western Sahara disputed?
Western Sahara, on Africa's north-west coast, was a Spanish colony until 1975. It has significant phosphate reserves and valuable fishing grounds along its Atlantic coast.
As Spain prepared to withdraw, both Morocco and Mauritania claimed the territory.
The International Court of Justice found historical ties of allegiance but no territorial sovereignty that overrode the Sahrawi people's right to self-determination.
Morocco's then King Hassan II responded by organising the Green March. On 6 November 1975 about 350,000 Moroccan civilians entered the territory in a mass demonstration intended to put pressure on Spain.
Days later, Spain signed the Madrid Accords with Morocco and Mauritania, agreeing to transfer administrative control. Morocco took the northern two-thirds and Mauritania the southern third. The agreement did not settle the question of sovereignty.
The Polisario Front, an independence movement founded in 1973, opposed the deal. It saw it as replacing Spanish colonial rule with Moroccan and Mauritanian control.
Mauritania renounced its claim in 1979, but Morocco continued fighting Polisario.
Algeria became Polisario's main regional ally, providing military support and hosting its leadership and thousands of Sahrawi refugees in camps near the city of Tindouf.
The North African country says its position is based on the right to self-determination, while Morocco sees Western Sahara as an integral part of its territory.
Morocco and Algeria fought a brief border war in 1963 over disagreements about territory inherited from French colonial rule. Their relationship has remained tense, with Western Sahara at the centre of their dispute.
What was the UN's mission role?
After 16 years of fighting, Morocco and Polisario agreed to a UN-brokered ceasefire in 1991, with the territory divided by a sand wall, or berm, to keep the rival forces apart.
The UN established Minurso to monitor the ceasefire and organise a referendum on the territory's future. Sahrawis were meant to choose between independence and integration with Morocco.
The vote was scheduled for 1992 but never took place. The two sides could not agree on who would be eligible to participate, with disputes over voter identification becoming a major obstacle.
In 2007, Morocco put forward a proposal for autonomy, which would see Sahrawis managing their internal affairs, while Rabat retained control over defence and foreign relations.
The Polisario Front and Algeria rejected the plan, insisting on a referendum that included independence as an option.
Years of UN-sponsored negotiations failed to produce a breakthrough.
The ceasefire broke down in November 2020, when Polisario said it was resuming armed struggle.
But following a long diplomatic campaign by Morocco, the UN Security Council voted in 2025 in favour of a resolution backing the autonomy plan as the "most feasible" solution for the disputed territory.
While most Sahrawis live in the part of Western Sahara controlled by Morocco, tens of thousands are estimated to be in refugee camps in Algeria.
What happened at the UN?
The US proposed extending Minurso's mandate for another year, but its draft went beyond the usual renewal.
It would have removed the word "referendum" from the mission's name and made Morocco's autonomy proposal the sole basis for further negotiations.
The draft received the support of 11 of the Security Council's 15 members, including France and the UK but Russia vetoed it, arguing that it was too favourable to Morocco.
Russia then proposed extending Minurso's mandate without changing its terms. That draft also failed, receiving only two votes in favour.
Minurso's mandate expired at the end of Saturday, 31 October. The UN said the following day that the mission had entered a liquidation period, with a reduced team overseeing the transfer of military equipment and other assets.
UN Secretary-General António Guterres said the Sahrawi people's right to self-determination must be respected and warned of the risk of renewed hostilities.
The Polisario Front condemned the US proposal. Its representative, Sidi Omar, thanked Russia for vetoing it, saying it would "torpedo the foundations of the UN peace process" and threaten regional and international peace.
Morocco, meanwhile, said the mission's personnel and equipment should leave the territory in the coming days, arguing that Western Sahara issue should no longer be considered by the Security Council.
Minurso had 155 military personnel and was expected to cost $62m (£46m) in the financial year beginning in June, according to a UN report.
Why is Morocco celebrating the end of the UN mission?
Morocco's royal palace welcomed the failure to renew Minurso's mandate.
In Laayoune, the territory's largest city, footage showed people celebrating, waving Moroccan flags and displaying portraits of King Mohammed VI.
"The decision is an opportunity for Rabat to challenge what it sees as an international mechanism that has failed to resolve the dispute," Issam Laaroussi, a Moroccan expert in international relations, tells the BBC.
He said Morocco would now have more room to push its autonomy proposal and shift negotiations away from a referendum on independence towards autonomy under Moroccan sovereignty.
The decision does not, however, change Western Sahara's legal status or amount to international recognition of Moroccan sovereignty.
Western Sahara remains on the UN list of non-self-governing territories, while the African Union officially recognises its independence, as the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic (SADR).
But the decision comes after several countries backed the position of Morocco, which in recent years has made securing international support for its claim a central part of its foreign policy.
In 2020, the US recognised Moroccan sovereignty over Western Sahara as part of an agreement to establish diplomatic relations between Morocco and Israel.
France also backed Morocco's autonomy plan as the basis for resolving the dispute in 2024.
Morocco rejoined the African Union in 2017, more than three decades after leaving its predecessor, the Organisation of African Unity, in protest at the SADR's admission.
Since returning, Rabat has sought to build support for its position from within the organisation. At least 10 African countries have opened diplomatic missions in the territory in support of Rabat.
"Morocco is not necessarily seeking to abandon the UN process, but to change the framework for negotiations and draw greater support from regional organisations," says Laaroussi.
Addressing a special joint session of parliament on Monday, House of Representatives Speaker Ahmed Touizi hailed the end of Minurso as a victory for the country's diplomacy.
He said the country should now move from "managing the dispute to implementing its autonomy plan under Moroccan sovereignty, while pressing ahead with development projects in the territory."
Could this lead to a renewed war?
The fear is that Minurso's departure could lead to renewed fighting.
The mission has monitored military developments and helped reduce the risk of escalation.
Aid organisation Oxfam warned that losing its monitoring and de-escalation role could undermine stability, with serious consequences for civilians.
Laaroussi admits that the mission's departure could create security gaps.
"Minurso's departure does not create the original conflict, because the conflict is already there, but it could aggravate an already fragile security environment," he says.
The UN decision has also fuelled nationalist rhetoric online.
Several Moroccan users have shared AI-generated images of themselves in military uniform, declaring their readiness to fight for Morocco's sovereignty over Western Sahara.
In Morocco, Western Sahara is widely regarded as a national cause. Political parties that are often divided on other issues are united in supporting the country's claim to sovereignty over the territory.
Foreign Minister Nasser Bourita has said the end of the mission does not mean the end of the ceasefire, and that Rabat remains committed to it "within respect of its security and sovereignty."
Polisario has not said what it will do next.
Any resumption of fighting could well draw in Algeria, as tensions with Morocco remain high.
According to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI), both countries significantly increased military spending last year, with SIPRI citing their dispute over Western Sahara as a key driver.
Algeria spent an estimated $25.4bn, more than four time Morocco's $6.3bn.

The 2026 festive season began in muted fashion, but the performance of some of the key new-age tech stocks in the pre-festive quarter (Q2 FY27) shows that even in this environment businesses are able to extract and expand profits, and grow their topline. When we see the financial performance of ecommerce, fintech and logistics stocks, it’s clear companies entered this period with a lot more confidence and absorbed some of these headwinds. Pretty much each one of them improved on their profitability metrics and their topline. As Inc42 reported in October, early data from the festive season sales indicated that Indian consumers kept shopping, but with more abandon. Online sales slipped from last year, card spending and smartphone sales weakened, and surveys suggest urban households are trimming discretionary budgets too. Rising household costs, uncertainty over jobs and incomes, and discounts that no longer feel compelling have made shoppers wary of big-ticket purchases. Consumers are still browsing for products, but in the current climate, conversion rates have fallen for premium products, which usually see a big uptick. A lot of this has to do with the macroeconomic factors, rising energy prices and logistics costs, and lingering grave geopolitical concerns that have dented consumer confidence and spending. In Q2, logistics tech players expanded capacity ahead of the festive shopping rush, with higher volumes offering an opportunity to improve operating leverage. Ecommerce companies capitalised on seasonal demand, even as the pressure to balance growth with profitability persisted. Meanwhile, fintech companies, particularly those with a big UPI focus, faced a different equation: the prospect of merchant discount rates (MDR) on select UPI transactions. While MDR itself is yet to come into effect, the fintech ecosystem’s quarter was defined by swelling toplines, which bodes well for the next quarter where MDR is likely to become a real factor. Profitability broadened across the listed new-age tech universe, with nine of the 11 large tech stocks (with a market cap of over ₹10,000 Cr) across these key sectors reporting a net profit in Q2 FY27. The combined bottomline of these companies improved by around ₹1,100–1,400 Cr year-on-year (YoY), depending on how exceptional items in the base quarter are treated, according to market data. More importantly, EBITDA grew faster than revenue at all nine profitable companies, suggesting that operating leverage is beginning to show up in reported performance. But a significant profit pool remained concentrated in a handful of companies, while businesses such as Swiggy and Meesho continue to report losses despite improving operating metrics. Atul Thakkar, executive director at Anand Rathi Investment Banking, believes the market is moving towards rewarding earnings delivery rather than growth narratives. “Over the next 12–18 months, we expect earnings delivery, rather than growth narratives, to be the main driver of returns in this space,” he said, This distinction is particularly relevant when the three major segments, fintech, logistics and ecommerce are assessed separately. Fintech has delivered the strongest operating performance, logistics has shown some of the clearest margin improvement, and ecommerce has produced a wide range of outcomes. But how did the profitability story unfolded across these three sectors? Logistics Tech Shifts Into High Gear It was largely a capacity-building quarter for logistics companies, with the full benefit of festive demand expected to play out in Q3. Yet, the results already point to improving operating leverage, as shipment volumes grew faster than revenue at the larger third-party logistics (3PL) players. Shadowfax’s revenue rose 57%, while express and hyperlocal orders grew nearly 70%. Adjusted EBITDA increased sharply, with margins expanding to 5%. Delhivery reported a similar divergence: express shipments grew 32%, against 22% growth in express revenue. Its adjusted EBITDA margin also improved, while first-half operating cash flow more than doubled. The gap between volume and revenue growth suggests that incremental shipments are not translating into proportionate revenue. Profitability, therefore, will depend on whether higher volumes can offset pricing pressure and rising costs across fuel, wages and last-mile delivery. Delhivery’s return to profitability also needs context: the year-ago quarter included acquisition-related integration costs linked to Ecom Express. Its adjusted EBITDA and cash generation offer a more useful measure of underlying progress. Shiprocket, meanwhile, turned profitable, reporting a net profit of ₹60 Lakh against a loss of ₹20.3 Cr a year ago. Revenue grew 35%, while adjusted EBITDA more than tripled. Its core business continued to expand, with transactions growing 31% and adjusted EBITDA margin improving to 12.8%. The results point to improving economics, although the reported profit remains modest. Across the sector, technology and network utilisation are central to the margin story. Shadowfax is deploying AI-led route optimisation and expanding its seller platform, while Delhivery is investing in automation and autonomous material-handling systems. These initiatives could improve productivity, but their returns will depend on execution and the ability to absorb peak-season volumes without adding costs at the same pace. The festive quarter will be the real test. Stronger volumes should support operating leverage, but sustained margin expansion will require better network utilisation, disciplined pricing and control over fulfilment costs. Logistics is showing clearer signs of improving economics, though the gap between shipment growth and revenue realisation remains a key risk. Fintech’s Profit Engines Roar Fintech was the strongest performer in Q2 FY27, with all the major companies in the segment reporting profits. Moreover, EBITDA growth outpaced revenue growth at each, pointing to improving operating leverage. The gains, however, are coming from deeper monetisation of existing customers rather than payment volumes alone. Paytm is increasingly diversifying beyond payments, with financial services distribution contributing about a third of its revenue. Its merchant subscription base and financial services business continue to expand, reducing its dependence on payment processing. Meanwhile, Pine Labs is extracting more value from its merchant network through subscriptions, affordability products and transaction-linked services. PB Fintech’s growing renewal book offers a similar advantage: recurring insurance revenue is expanding faster than its core insurance business, making growth less dependent on fresh policy acquisition. The bigger question for fintech is whether these operating gains can withstand regulatory changes. The proposed UPI MDR framework could create an additional revenue stream, but the benefit to payment companies will depend on how the pool is shared between banks and other ecosystem participants. With implementation postponed beyond the festive period, it remains an opportunity rather than an earnings driver for now. Insurance distribution faces a more direct overhang. The proposed changes to commission structures and expense limits could alter the economics of online intermediaries such as PB Fintech. Its growing renewal revenue offers some cushion, but the impact on new-policy distribution remains uncertain. “While fintech companies have demonstrated an ability to improve monetisation and operating leverage, the regulatory environment remains a key determinant of how sustainable these gains will be. For this segment, regulation is a bigger variable than execution,” said Thakkar. Ecommerce’s Profitability Divide Widens Ecommerce delivered the widest divergence in Q2 FY27. While revenue growth remained strong across quick commerce, ecommerce and consumer brands, profitability varied sharply, reflecting differences in scale, cost structures and monetisation. For example, Meesho saw its net loss narrow to 68%, while marketplace contribution margin improved to 6% of NMV from 3.3% a year ago. However, newer initiatives remain loss-making and are yet to establish meaningful scale. Consumer brands delivered a more consistent earnings performance. Nykaa’s profit more than tripled, supported by margin expansion and growth across beauty and fashion. Lenskart also reported strong profit growth, with expansion across its India and international businesses. Higher store productivity, rising volumes and operating cash flow suggest that growth is being supported by better utilisation of the existing network, alongside store additions. Input-cost inflation remains another pressure point for consumer brands. Passing on higher costs through pricing could protect margins but risks weighing on demand and average order values. Gross margins, customer retention and acquisition costs will be as important as revenue growth in assessing the durability of earnings. Why Profits Are Just Half The Story As these sectors continue to mature, operating leverage is becoming more important than headline growth. However, profitability remains concentrated, with a handful of companies accounting for a substantial share of the sector’s earnings. The ownership shift is also worth watching. Foreign investors have reduced exposure to several listed new-age tech companies, while domestic institutions have increased participation. But domestic ownership is no guarantee against corrections when earnings or regulatory developments disappoint. According to market analysts, retail investors are likely to increasingly favour companies that are not only profitable but also generate revenue from multiple products within their existing customer base and use operating cash flow to fund expansion. We can see this in the aggressive diversification across the industry, particularly in fintech and logistics tech. This wave favours established fintech businesses, asset-light logistics networks and ecommerce companies where the seller-customer flywheel is up and running. Post the festive season spike, even if it may be a relatively smaller spike compared to previous years, the cash generation and regulatory resilience of these companies will be worth watching. That could very well mark the next phase of maturity. MARKETS WATCH: NEW ISSUES, POST-IPO JOURNEY & MORE Inside Razorpay’s ₹6,000 Cr IPO: As Razorpay gears up for its ₹6,000 Cr IPO, the proposed UPI merchant discount rate and its AI ambitions could shape its valuation. But can these growth levers convince public market investors to look beyond its thin margins? Honasa’s Profit Up 87%: The Mamaearth parent reported an 87% YoY jump in Q2 FY27 net profit to ₹73.2 Cr, while revenue rose 36% to ₹731.2 Cr. Growth across focus categories, offline channels and younger brands helped drive the company’s quarterly performance. Go Digit PAT Dips: Go Digit’s net profit declined 31.1% YoY to ₹142.4 Cr in Q2 FY27 despite a marginal 1.7% rise in insurance revenue to ₹2,720.5 Cr. Higher insurance service expenses and claims weighed on profitability, even as motor insurance revenue grew. RateGain Profit Rises 47%:The travel-focused SaaS company’s profit rose 46.5% YoY to ₹74.7 Cr in Q2 FY27, driven by operating revenue zooming 152.6% YoY to ₹745.4 Cr. This came on the back of the consolidation of travel marketing platform Sojern, which RateGain acquired for $250 Mn last year. Moneyview Revenue Grows 41%: The fintech company’s consolidated net profit surged 417.6% YoY to ₹200.7 Cr in Q2 FY27, while operating revenue grew 41% to ₹1,120.2 Cr. The fintech reported a managed AUM of ₹23,892 Cr, with its shares gaining 5.7% following the earnings announcement.

Deadly flash floods hit northern Iraq on Saturday as severe thunderstorms swept across the region, including in neighbouring Iran. The city of Erbil, in Iraq, was particularly badly hit, with extensive damage to homes and businesses. Streets were inundated as torrential rain fell over a short period.
Rainfall exceeded forecasts, with an estimated 80mm falling in the city, compared with expectations of 30mm. Two people were killed in the floods.
In Europe, Storm Bruna is forecast to bring strong winds to Portugal this week, particularly along the west coast. Gusts are expected to reach 50mph (80km/h), with heavy rain and thunderstorms also expected. The total rainfall could reach 200mm by the end of the week. The storm has already affected the Canary Islands, where Tenerife recorded a gust of 80mph on Saturday night.
Japan experienced a cold and snowy end to last week, with further snowfall expected in Hokkaido and parts of the mountains in the main island Honshu.
Temperatures in Japan are forecast to fall below the seasonal average early this week, with Sapporo, the capital of Hokkaido prefecture, expected to plunge to 10C below average. Maximum temperatures in the city are likely to be about 4-6C on Monday and Wednesday, while Tuesday’s high is forecast to be about 0C. Minimum temperatures could fall to -6C by Wednesday, and -8C in other western parts of Hokkaido on Tuesday.
Ski resorts are preparing for visitors after snowfall began on Friday. Total snowfall is expected to reach 30-50cm around Kiroro and Niesko, with about 20-30cm in Furano, Rusutsu and Sapporo.
Other resorts could receive up to 20cm of snow by Wednesday. Strong winds accompanied the snow on Friday and over the weekend, with gusts of about 75mph in Kiroko and Niesko.
During the strong El Niño, sea surface temperatures in the equatorial Pacific were about 3.5C above the climatological average at their peak in late October. As a result, Peru has been experiencing air temperatures 5-10C above the seasonal average. The unusually warm conditions expected to continue into next week.

Many people are not big fans of game publisher EA right now for good reason, but for those who remember a better time in the 1990s, there’s a little good news. Twenty-five classic games from that EA era have been lightly remastered and updated, then placed for sale on Steam and GOG, including several Wing Commander games and nearly the entire Ultima series.
Below is the full list of remastered or re-released games:
- Road Rash: 30th Anniversary Edition
- Wing Commander: 35th Anniversary Edition
- Wing Commander II: Vengeance of the Kilrathi: 35th Anniversary Edition
- Wing Commander III: Heart of the Tiger: 30th Anniversary Edition
- Wing Commander IV: The Price of Freedom: 30th Anniversary Edition

- Ultima I: The First Age of Darkness

- Ultima VI: The False Prophet
- Ultima VII: The Complete Edition
- Ultima VIII: Gold Edition
- Ultima IX: Ascension
- Ultima Underworld I
- Ultima Underworld II
The story behind seven remasters
In a lengthy blog post published this week, Jim Vessella, a senior producer at EA, described the efforts that went into remastering Wing Commander I-IV and Prophecy, Privateer 2, and Road Rash.
It’s a long, detailed story that’s worth reading yourself, but here’s a top-level summary. After working on the mostly widely acclaimed Command & Conquer: Remastered Collection in 2019, Vessella writes that he learned about and visited a room at EA’s Redwood Shores campus that contained a large archive of poorly labeled or sorted physical media from ages past.
In his free time, and with the help of others, he began cataloging this archive and discovered, among other things, that it contained virtually the entirety of the original masters of Wing Commander III and Wing Commander IV‘s full-motion-video cutscenes.
The story that ensues involves building a small team of contractors, poring through the footage 17 hours a day on swing shifts to label and digitize it, and then coordinating with several key community members—particularly Matt Wells, who has made community enhancement patches for some of the Wing Commander games—to put together remasters of those games.

Desperate families flee hometowns as shuttered schools leave students packed in crowded classrooms
Across the U.S., many students are experiencing disruptions as school buildings close and consolidate due to declining enrollment and reduced funding

Thousands of American students began this academic year at unfamiliar schools after their campuses were shut down.
Starting a new school year can be nerve-wracking under any circumstances, but for these pupils, it came with the added challenge of adjusting to an entirely new school after their previous ones closed.
An increasing number of cash-strapped school districts around the country have resorted to closing campuses to save money, as U.S. birth rates continue a multidecade slide and state and federal education funding dries up.
New research shows student enrollment has fallen much faster than schools are closing, suggesting more painful financial choices lie ahead. The Associated Press is covering school closures in partnership with The Hechinger Report and Big Local News at Stanford University. These are some takeaways from their reporting.
A total of 1,156 U.S. schools closed during the last academic year, the highest number since the pandemic, according to an analysis of federal data by Big Local News at Stanford University. The Vallejo City Unified School District, a working-class district near San Francisco, serves half as many students as it did two decades earlier.
District leaders have closed five campuses since 2025, a quarter of the district's schools. They've also placed up to a third of all staff positions on the chopping block to help plug a staggering $36 million deficit. In Vallejo, a city still struggling to bounce back from the closure of a naval base in the 1990s, school enrollment has tumbled from nearly 18,000 in the fall of 2006 to about 9,300, the district says.
School districts nationwide, including large systems in Cleveland, Houston and Philadelphia, are facing similar closures. The enrollment and financial situation is unlikely to improve, said Lydia Rainey, research principal at the Center on Reinventing Public Education.
“States aren’t about to open the coffers and swoop in with additional funds to save schools,” she said. Nationwide, public school enrollment fell by more than 1.4 million students, roughly 3%, between fall 2019 and 2024, according to an Associated Press analysis of federal education data collected by Stanford University economist Thomas Dee and sociologist Jaymes Pyne.
The total number of schools has declined, too, but only to about pre-pandemic levels, the researchers found, suggesting closures are lagging behind enrollment declines. Lower birth rates are the primary reason for enrollment decline, but a federal crackdown on immigration and the post-pandemic expansion of private school vouchers and homeschool options have contributed.
Bellwether and WestEd, two research groups, recently estimated declining enrollment could cause schools to lose $11.5 billion in state revenue annually by 2030-2031, potentially prompting widespread layoffs, cuts to academic programs and school closures. Research shows closing schools rarely yields the financial relief districts hope for.
Busing students to their reassigned schools, severance for pink-slipped staff and security for empty facilities often eat up any savings. School closures can also set students back academically and make it harder to attract teachers, who may worry the jobs aren't stable. Closing schools can trigger a downward spiral, too, as frustrated families flee to charter or private schools or other districts.
In Vallejo, some parents said they chose to homeschool this fall or were planning to sell their homes and move to neighboring districts. “Families are literally packing up their kids and moving away,” said Vallejo mom Kimberly Núñez-Brandão, whose daughter's elementary school closed.
She recently attended curriculum night for her daughter's new school, Glen Cove Elementary, and shared her shock at learning Penny's new fifth-grade teacher had 32 students in his first class. “They already overwhelmed teachers with 30-plus students,” she said.
“Who’s winning here?” Rubén Aurelio, superintendent for Vallejo schools, acknowledged cuts and closures can be hard for families but said they are necessary to correct for school districts and budgets designed for a different reality.
“We’re not just closing schools to close schools,” Aurelio said. “We’re right-sizing a district that was built for significantly more kids. And if we’re going to actually improve outcomes for the kids we still have, we need to concentrate resources.”
The already painful cost-cutting measure may push even more families into competing charter networks, neighboring districts or private alternatives, further eroding the funding schools get per enrolled student. So along with cutting budgets, Vallejo is renovating older campuses, hoping to draw younger parents who can't afford to start a family in San Francisco.
The superintendent said he also plans to open a Tagalog-language school soon, targeting Filipino families from across the Bay Area. Marisa de la Torre, a managing director of the UChicago Consortium on School Research, said instability created by school closures may last for a while. Studies from the University of Chicago show that academically, displaced students often suffer long-term drops in reading and math.
That's especially true when students end up at low-performing schools. “It takes a while to recover, if they recover at all,” she said. Núñez-Brandão isn't sure she wants to stick around long enough to find out. Weeks into the new school year, Penny still struggled to adjust to Glen Cove.
She started to make new friends and said she feels comfortable on campus. She also liked her teacher, a first-year educator who'd joined Vallejo's teacher residency program, launched last year to attract new educators and improve retention. But with 32 kids in the class, she said it's hard to concentrate.
On a Tuesday in October, Núñez-Brandão received a note in the Glen Cove parent portal: Penny's teacher resigned, effective immediately. The school will rely on a long-term substitute for now, the district said. The Associated Press' education coverage receives financial support from multiple private foundations.

In particular there was unhappiness about how Tuchel told them to approach the closing stages of the game after Anthony Gordon had given them a 55th-minute advantage.
Enzo Fernandez struck an equaliser with five minutes left, before Lautaro Martinez headed in a stoppage-time winner.
As reported by BBC Sport at the time, a number of senior England players held misgivings at Tuchel's instructions for the closing stages of the Argentina loss, believing the approach was too negative and defensive.
Hindsight, of course, is 20/20. England appeared to retreat in the closing stages of the last-16 tie against Mexico earlier in the tournament - but successfully defended a 3-2 lead to reach the quarter-finals to trigger scenes of joy at the iconic Azteca Stadium.
Nevertheless, certain players felt let down by the team's apparent pragmatism during the closing stages of the loss to Argentina amid a sense that going for the South Americans' jugular would have provided greater success.
What was said at the review meeting
Inevitably, the game against Argentina emerged as a key theme at the squad discussion.
It is understood that Tuchel pointed to the quality of the opposition as a key factor on why they eventually succumbed to two late Argentina goals.
There is, of course, merit to that argument. Lionel Messi was in the opposition team after all.
That said, it was not an argument the players in the meeting were prepared to universally accept.
There is a strongly held view within the England squad that their team, man-for-man, was superior to Argentina, who had 38-year-old Nicolas Otamendi on the field for the closing 18 minutes of the game.
All players were afforded an opportunity to air their personal views during the meeting.
As you would expect, captain Harry Kane was strong and forthright with his views.
Jude Bellingham, too, is said to have been particularly candid in expressing his belief that this current crop of England players were more than capable of continuing to take the game to Argentina.
Bellingham's contribution to the meeting is said to have underlined his growing influence within the England squad, with many believing the Real Madrid midfielder will become the team's captain once Kane is no longer in the picture.
If the air needed to be cleared after the World Cup then it appears those honest discussions at the end of September did the trick.
Barring the 3-2 defeat by Spain at Wembley in their first Nations League fixture in September, England have bounced back from the loss to Argentina emphatically - scoring 12 goals without conceding in three fixtures against the Czech Republic and Croatia.
Similarly, the fluctuating relationship between Bellingham and Tuchel seems to have improved, too.
"It was a bit of an up and down [relationship] of course but we are in a good place," Tuchel said last week.
"I love to be his coach. He's a top player, a very influential player and I think it goes both ways."
We will get a clearer idea of how 'Tuchel 2.0' is progressing in the next few days when England host Croatia on Thursday and travel to Madrid to face world champions Spain on Sunday.
