- The claim that Democrats won the 2026 U.S. midterm elections in all the states that don't require people to show ID to vote is true.
- According to the National Conference of State Legislatures, 14 states and Washington, D.C., do not require voters to show ID at the polls.
- Election results from The Associated Press showed that Democrats won a Senate seat, more than half of a state's U.S. House seats — or both — in those 14 states.
- However, there was no evidence that Democrats won races only in states that had no voter ID requirements. Democrats won Senate seats or the majority of a state's House races in several states with ID requirements. Conversely, Republicans won some individual races in states that do not require ID on polling day.
- Snopes based our assessment of this claim on midterm election projections from the AP. Though many news outlets "call" races on election night, results are not official until a state's elections officials have certified them.
Following the 2026 U.S. midterm elections, a claim circulated that Democrats won all the U.S. states that do not require people to show ID to vote.
For example, one X user wrote (archived):
Fun Midterms fact:
- Dems won all of the states that do not require voter ID at the polls. 100%.
- States that GOP won such as Florida, Alabama, Wyoming etc., require voter ID
- GOP won none of the no-ID states such as California, New York, Illinois, etc. Zero.
The claim also circulated on Facebook (archived). Days before the election, the Australian TV journalist James Morrow made a similar claim, saying, "So, are people going to start to put two and two together and say, gosh, why do all these Democrats keep running in cities where you don't need ID?"
It's unclear what the social media posts mean by "winning a state." For the purposes of this fact check, we've defined "winning a state" as winning a Senate seat, more than half of a state's U.S. House seats, or both.
The claim that Democrats won all the U.S. states that don't require voters to show ID at the polls is true, though election results from The Associated Press showed that Democrats also won a Senate seat or more than half of a state's House seats in several states that do require voters to show ID. Conversely, Republicans won individual races in states that do not require ID on polling day.
According to the National Conference of State Legislatures, which collates legislation from all the states on various topics, 14 states and Washington, D.C., do not impose any ID requirements on voters at the polls. Democrats won Senate seats or made up more than half of the state's representatives (or both) in all 14 of those states. (Washington, D.C., does not elect a senator and has a non-voting representative in the House.)
However, Democrats also won Senate seats or made up more than half of the state's representatives in several states that do require voters to show ID at the polls. Democrats won a majority in the Senate and House in three states that require voters to show ID, meaning there was no evidence to suggest that Democrats could win only in states with no voter ID requirements at the polls.
It's worth noting that we based our assessment of this claim on midterm election projections from the AP. Though many news outlets "call" races on election night, results are not official until a state's elections officials have certified them.
The breakdown
According to the NCSL, these 14 states don't ask voters to show any ID at the polls: California, Hawaii, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Minnesota, Nevada, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Oregon, Pennsylvania and Vermont.
The remaining 36 states have laws that request or require voters to show some form of ID at the polls. Some of these states specifically require photo ID.
While it's true Democrats won Senate seats or made up more than half of the state's representatives in all 14 states without voter ID requirements, that's only half the story.
Democrats also won a Senate seat or made up more than half of the state's representatives in several that do require voter ID: Arizona, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Georgia, Iowa, Kansas, Michigan, New Hampshire, North Carolina, Ohio, Rhode Island, South Carolina, Texas, Virginia and Washington.
In Iowa, for example, Democrat Josh Turek flipped Republican Sen. Joni Ernst's seat. Democrats also won three of the state's four races for the House.
According to Iowa's secretary of state, voters must show "an Iowa driver's license or non-operator ID, U.S. passport, U.S. military ID or veteran's ID, tribal ID/document, or Iowa voter ID" at the polls. Iowa elections officials also require photo ID if someone is registering to vote on Election Day.
Michigan, New Hampshire and Rhode Island all require voters to show photo ID at the polls. Democrats won a majority of the seats in the House and a Senate seat in these three states.
Because the claim that Democrats "won" all the states that don't require voter ID is true, the claim that Republicans only won states that did require voter ID is also true.
Republican candidates didn't win any Senate seats in states with no voter ID requirements. However, they did win a minority of the available House seats in nine of the 14 states with no voter ID at the requirements.
For example, Republicans won six out of 17 House seats in Pennsylvania and six out of 26 in New York, which are both states that don't require any form of voter ID at the polls.
Democratic wins in 'no ID' states not a sign of fraud
There is no evidence tying Democrat wins in states that don't require voter ID at the polls to election fraud theories such as noncitizen voting. Snopes reported in advance of the midterm elections that noncitizens rarely vote in U.S. elections.
Based on accounts from elections officials, we found that existing protections throughout the registration process would make it extremely difficult for bad actors to register enough ineligible voters to sway elections. We also found that existing protections already work to ensure that only eligible voters can register and cast a ballot.
According to the Fair Elections Center, a nonpartisan voting rights and election reform organization, all the 14 states that do not require voter ID at the polls require voters to submit either a state driver's license number, state ID number or part of their Social Security number when registering to vote.
There was also no evidence to suggest that Democrats could win only in states that did not have voter ID requirements at the polls.
For further reading, follow Snopes' coverage of the 2026 U.S. midterm elections.

Indian investors who held Apple, Amazon, Tesla, and NVIDIA, shares allege they logged into their Stockal accounts to find those investments replaced with shares of a thinly traded Chinese microcap. Nearly 30 investors say their portfolios were altered without consent on October 15. Their established US stock holdings were allegedly liquidated and the proceeds used to buy Nasdaq-listed Zhibao Technology shares. One investor told Moneycontrol that securities worth $3.1 Mn, or around ₹29 Cr, were sold within two minutes, followed by purchases of 30.5 Lakh Zhibao shares within 15 minutes. Another reported that holdings worth $335,768 were sold and 3 Lakh Zhibao shares purchased. Media reports put investor-reported losses above ₹100 Cr. Inc42 has not independently verified this aggregate or authenticated the investors’ account details and alleged transactions. An FIR has reportedly been registered in Bengaluru. The dispute now centres on how the accounts were accessed, whether safeguards failed, and who bears responsibility across Stockal, its parent Borderless Investing, and US brokerage partner DriveWealth. How The Trades Unfolded Founded in 2016 by Sitashwa Srivastava and Vinay Bharathwaj, Stockal enables Indians to invest overseas through US stocks, exchange-traded funds, and curated portfolios. It has raised over $15 Mn from investors like ScaleX Partners, Arc Ventures, July Ventures, HDFC Securities, and Cadenza Ventures. The startup partners with DriveWealth to facilitate US stock investments. Bharathwaj left Borderless in 2022 and is currently the founder and CEO of “AI-first money intelligence and advisory platform” Cruise Money, as per his LinkedIn profile. Investors allege the October 15 transactions replaced holdings in companies including Alphabet and AMD with Zhibao shares, leaving them exposed to a thinly traded microcap. Borderless said DriveWealth notified it on October 16, India time, of suspicious trading across 13 accounts. Its assessment indicated an unauthorised third party had accessed 26 accounts using valid login credentials. In 13 accounts, large-cap US equities were liquidated to acquire thinly traded microcap securities. Borderless said it restricted access shortly after receiving the notification. An investor told Moneycontrol that Borderless contacted him on October 18, acknowledged suspicious activity, and said DriveWealth had restricted transactions in his account. Zhibao’s subsequent decline deepened investors’ reported losses. Against an average purchase price of around $1.05 cited in investor accounts, the shares closed at $0.42 on October 23 — a fall of approximately 60%. Differing Accounts Of Access In an October 30 letter to an investor, DriveWealth reportedly said the unauthorised access occurred through the Stockal interface and attributed responsibility for associated security lapses to Stockal. It reportedly said it froze the account on Stockal’s instructions. Responding to Inc42’s questions, DriveWealth said, “The Stockal incident is unrelated to DriveWealth’s systems. It occurred on Stockal’s app, not our platform. DriveWealth does not have a customer-facing app through which trades are placed, and our systems and client data were not affected by this incident.” Borderless’s public statement offered a possible explanation – social engineering involving information exposed in another company’s data breach several weeks earlier. It stressed that this connection remained unverified and under investigation. Borderless said its investigation found no evidence of a breach or compromise of its platform, interface, infrastructure, or internal systems. It also said no funds were withdrawn from affected accounts, based on findings available so far. This distinction leaves the disputed trades themselves central to investors’ concerns – their allegation concerns changes to their holdings without consent, irrespective of whether money left the accounts. Safeguards Under The Spotlight The precise access method remains under investigation. However, the incident raises questions about whether possession of valid credentials could have been sufficient to execute the disputed trades. Yash Kadakia, founder and CTO of cybersecurity firm Security Brigade, told Inc42 that stolen credentials are a common entry point, but platforms cannot shift responsibility entirely to customers when compromised passwords enable financial transactions. He said layered safeguards should include two-factor authentication, SIM binding, device and geographical checks, and separate transaction-level authentication. Behavioural monitoring is also critical. Multiple accounts accessed from one IP address, or similar trading patterns across accounts within a short period, should trigger scrutiny, he said. Such monitoring could explain DriveWealth’s detection of suspicious activity, Kadakia suggested, although the actual detection mechanism remains unclear. He added that implementation and enforcement remain challenges despite stronger SEBI cybersecurity requirements for regulated entities. Borderless Sets Out Its Position Borderless said it had engaged independent cybersecurity specialists, introduced additional authentication and account-protection measures, and found no evidence of a wider threat to its platform, products, or other customer accounts. It maintained that unauthorised trading identified so far was restricted to 13 accounts. The company said it had been engaging affected customers and working with DriveWealth to reconstruct events, examine disputed transactions, and explore avenues for a fair resolution. However, it said assistance should not be construed as an admission of liability, negligence, wrongdoing, or responsibility. It said it was cooperating with authorities and regulators. Borderless also maintained it had provided substantive responses to media enquiries before publication and cautioned that its public account could change as the investigation progressed. Inc42 has separately sought answers on the transactions, investigation, and investor concerns. The story will be updated upon receiving a response. Who Bears The Responsibility? The controversy has also drawn attention to Stockal’s former partnership with HDFC Securities. Launched in 2019 through globalinvesting.in, their operational association ended in July 2024. HDFC Securities has clarified that it is not named among the accused in the FIR and said it would cooperate with regulators and law enforcement authorities. While HDFC Securities has clarified its position, questions about the disputed trades remain unresolved. How were the accounts accessed, why were the transactions not intercepted, and what recourse do affected investors have to restore their holdings or recover losses? Cross-border investing divides responsibilities across the customer interface, trade execution, and custody of securities. Establishing each intermediary’s obligations and the safeguards applied will be central to determining accountability. For affected investors, the immediate issue remains whether the investigation will explain the disputed trades and deliver a resolution. For now, neither the source of the alleged compromise nor responsibility for the claimed losses has been conclusively established. Edited by Vinaykumar Rai

Kimi Antonelli was 10 when his father Marco first realised the boy sitting on his lap, operating the steering and gears, might have an exceptional talent as a racing driver.
The pair were at the Adria circuit in north-east Italy, Marco with his Lamborghini sports car team, Kimi competing in a karting race.
It was the end of the day and Marco, a former driver himself, asked his son: "Do you want to try the Lamborghini?"
Of course he did.
Marco strapped himself and Kimi into the car, belts extended around both. Dad was in charge of the throttle and brake, his son would control the rest.
"I couldn't see the track because he was in front of me with a helmet on," Marco tells BBC Sport. "I could only see beside me the marker panels before each corner - 100m, 50m.
"We started to drive, step by step, faster, faster, faster. In the end, I pushed like I was alone and I arrived at the braking point at the end of the straight, 320km/h, braked very hard and at the limit.
"The car had a lot of oversteer. Kimi controlled the oversteer perfectly, then I went on the throttle, Kimi finished the oversteer, changed gear, and went.
"I said: 'OK, stop, because it has now become dangerous.' But when I saw the video, 10 years old, on my leg, oversteer, everything perfect, I said: 'Maybe he has something special.'"
And now Kimi, who turned 20 only in August, has dominated F1 in only his second season, and become the youngest world champion in the sport's history.
This is the story of a boy his dad says was "born in a garage".
"Kimi from 15 days old was in the garage and heard the sound of the engine and the smell of the exhaust," says Marco, who worked with his wife Veronica on their racing team business.
It was the Christmas holidays when Kimi was about three, and Marco had brought home a simulator he had bought for his guests to try out at the Bologna Motor Show.
"Each evening, Kimi wanted to drive," Marco remembers.
Just like seven years later in the Lamborghini, Kimi would sit on Marco's leg, the controls divided in the same way.
"I remember one night I started to fall asleep because I had been at work very early and we had a crash because I didn't brake when we arrived at the end of the straight," Marco says.
"And Kimi said: 'Dad, dad, no sleep, no sleep. I have to drive.'"
Marco Antonelli did not originally want his son to become a racing driver, because of his own struggles during his career.
"Sometimes you are fast but not in the right position to become a professional driver," he says.
In the 1990s, Marco Antonelli was on the cusp of becoming a works driver in the DTM touring car series, then a huge hit with audiences across Europe.
He tested for Alfa Romeo, but then the team boss left and the opportunity evaporated. Another chance came up with BMW, alongside Roberto Ravaglia and Steve Soper - stars at the time. Again, the same thing happened.
"I suffered a lot for it," Marco says. "And, of course, I was scared that my son [would] relive the same situation. At the beginning, I was very stressed about the passion my son had for motorsport."
Kimi tried a go-kart for the first time when he was five, and immediately showed an awareness of racing lines, braking points and car control.
The Antonellis were what Marco describes as "a normal family". They could not possibly afford to pay for Kimi to take part in all the categories on the way to Formula 1.
Marco decided he could fund Kimi through karting and a year of the basic single-seater category, Formula 4. After that, he figured he might be able to put him in one of his GT cars and become professional that way.
But Kimi immediately started to impress. Whatever category he entered, he was quick, and won.
By the time Kimi was 11, his name was buzzing around motor racing circles. Mercedes heard about him, and their driver academy scout Gwen Lagrue flew to Italy to check him out.
It was a season in which Antonelli had ended up driving a kart with less power than those of his rivals. Marco had told Kimi this would be good for him - he should think not about the result, but about how to improve, always push hard.
"Gwen was impressed about this condition of power and driving in this category that Kimi did," Marco says. "And maybe they understood that Kimi was a different child."
Now Kimi was a member of the Mercedes driver academy, Marco could stop worrying about money, and start focusing on helping his son achieve his full potential.
Mercedes were not the only big names in F1 who had noticed Antonelli's promise.
"When he was in karting, you could already see he was one of the stand-out talents," says four-time world champion Max Verstappen, the only other teenager to win an F1 race.
At 15, Antonelli was ready to move up to cars, and, as a final preparation, did a couple of races in a karting category with gears. On his debut, with minimal pre-event testing, he took pole position. After that, he went to the world final, and stuck it on pole again.
This was the end of 2021, after which Antonelli moved full-time into cars. Through 2022, he swept the board in various championships in Formula 4, and the same happened in Formula Regional in 2023.
1 of 4
By now, Mercedes team boss Toto Wolff was already thinking that Antonelli would be his next F1 driver, potentially a replacement for Lewis Hamilton. With the seven-time champion approaching 40, Wolff was planning on taking control of that generational transition.
So when it came time to negotiate a new contract with Hamilton in 2023, Wolff played hardball. Hamilton wanted to sign for at least two firm years, Wolff only one. In the end, they compromised on a contract for 2024 with an option for 2025.
Hamilton, unimpressed, decided to look at his options, and signed to join Ferrari in 2025, telling Wolff in late January 2024, before the start of that season.
Wolff immediately phoned Marco Antonelli, to tell him the "very big news".
"'We put Kimi in Formula 1,'" Marco remembers Wolff saying. "'What do you think?'
"I said: 'Oh, [it] is a difficult question you ask me. Of course I'm happy that you think about Kimi but are you sure he's ready?'"
Mercedes were at a management away day. Wolff called his senior engineers together to tell them about Hamilton's decision.
"We were reviewing options and trying to come to a fairly rapid conclusion," says trackside engineering director Andrew Shovlin.
"We were all keen to just go with Kimi, which we knew was a bit of a risk. But it was quite exciting and we thought, based on his career to date, he had a good chance of being very good. It seemed like a good challenge."
Antonelli had not even driven an F1 car when Wolff made the call. Mercedes put together a testing programme for him, 20-odd days in cars a couple of years old at tracks all over the world to prepare him for his F1 debut in 2025.
Shovlin and the engineers were immediately impressed.
"It was how rapidly he would get up to speed," Shovlin says. "What you normally see with drivers is they're just incrementally going a little bit quicker, braking a bit later.
"If you compare with other drivers we've seen in an F1 car for the first time, the best I'd ever seen until then was George [Russell]. You suddenly saw someone who was quite similar.
"With Kimi, he took a couple of runs to work out how the car behaved and then he'd be more or less on the limit.
"The other thing you can see is the fidelity of the car control, how they can sit with it right on the edge of breaking away from them on entry to a corner, but they can just control it in that condition.
"Equally, when you looked at the mistakes he was making, they were often errors of judgement or lack of experience. They weren't run-out-of-talent mistakes."
Antonelli made one of these at the 2024 Italian Grand Prix. Wolff decided to give him his first experience of an F1 weekend in first practice at his home race at Monza.
It was a spectacular debut - for both good and bad reasons.
Antonelli set the fastest time on his first lap. Then he went for another. He was flying, miles quicker than anyone up to that point, but then he crashed heavily at the final corner, Parabolica.
"No-one on earth could have got the car around the corner at the speed he was attempting," Shovlin says. "He clearly got into his head that he would try and do something special and it was an error of judgment."
Wolff took Antonelli aside, told him it was OK, and not to worry about it. But the crash had a significant impact on Antonelli.
Wolff was very clear in public about managing expectations of Antonelli going into his debut season.
"I conditioned myself so strong that I said: 'There's going to be moments of brilliance and moments where you want to tear your hair out'," Wolff says.
There were stand-out moments, including pole for the sprint in Miami.
But the middle part of the season, through Europe, was a disappointment. A change to the rear suspension design made the car nervous and rocked his confidence. His pace was not impressive, and he made too many mistakes.
"We expected more highlights from him," Shovlin says.
Marco Antonelli explains: "Mercedes needed to have a good result after a period that was not like the Hamilton era. And, of course, needed two cars that always take points.
"Kimi felt this necessity. The crash in Monza was very tough for him to forget. It created on him a big pressure."
Wolff said the "moments of brilliance were there" but then there was "a spell of nine races that was really not good".
"Me, personally, I never doubted," says Wolff. "Other people doubted. In the team and externally."
A year on from his practice debut, Antonelli crashed again in Monza practice.
"This was the point where I said: 'Kimi, you've got to turn this around. This is just not good enough'," says Wolff. "He said: 'I know.'"
Marco Antonelli says he and his son talked a lot during this period and that Kimi "understood that everything can change".
"The period was bad but you can see light at the end of the tunnel," he says. "And step by step he started to take confidence."
Once F1 had left Europe in the autumn of last year, there was a shift.
"Suddenly, we felt like we were making really good progress," says Shovlin.
"There were signs towards the end of the year. I'm not saying any of us thought we'd see what we've seen so far this year, but that we had a decent F1 driver."
Antonelli has been rather more than that this year. He took the season by storm, and established a consistent supremacy over Russell.
In the best car in the field, Antonelli took six poles and six wins in the first 11 races, establishing a 50-point lead in the championship.
Mercedes lost their dominant form in the second half of the season in the face of challenges from first McLaren and then Red Bull.
But Antonelli remained a consistent threat at the front, and he killed off his Monza ghosts in the Italian Grand Prix with a stunning victory after an engine penalty led to him starting 19th on the grid.
He put in a drive of clinical excellence and, with help from a safety car, chased down and caught Russell in the final laps to take a win that will go down in folklore.
The extent of his turnaround in form has shocked almost everyone.
"We were all surprised," Wolff says. "My thoughts were always that he needed to make the experience of knowing all the tracks, the pressure of performing on such a high level under the spotlight of the media, the constant public feedback, whether you're doing well or not, the situations everyone wanted to be close to him.
"There wasn't one single defining factor where I would have said that made it difficult for him, but this year, he knew exactly what to expect. What was really nice to see is that the self-confidence, without feeling any entitlement, has shone."
Marco points to his son's "very strong" mentality.
"In F4 and Freca, he started with not good results, and he was able to remake everything and, at the end, work hard and win the championship," he says.
"We talk about F1. I don't know what the spark is in his brain, but Kimi in the past did the same."
Verstappen says: "For me, there was never any doubt that he would make the jump the year after and already be a lot more consistently competitive.
"It's normal in the progression of a driver. In your rookie season, it can be quite tough, but at the moment, of course, he's doing an amazing job."
Kimi pays tribute to his father, describing him as his "rock", while Wolff also praises the driver's "typical Italian family".
"They are caring, they are loving," Wolff says. "Kimi's character, he's gentle, he has empathy, he has charisma, he has the right amount of intelligence for being a racing driver."
Mercedes have been talking to Antonelli about managing his emotions, which have flared at times this season, such as in the sprint in Canada, when the racing between the two Mercedes drivers came close to boiling over.
Shovlin says: "He just says: 'I'm young, I'm Italian, what do you expect?'"
The remark reveals Antonelli's sense of humour, but also a maturity and self-awareness that might not always be expected in someone so young.
Wolff says: "He has all that. He's actually not [fitting the stereotype of] a typical emotional Italian. He's so clear [in] what he needs to do in a car. I don't see lots of emotion. I see full focus, full concentration. I see, 'OK, this is a problem, let's analyse it, and move on.'
"You see him in a debrief afterwards. You couldn't really say whether there was a bad or a good session. It's all very balanced and stable."
Antonelli took advice on this when he met tennis legend Roger Federer at Wimbledon this summer.
"We chatted about my races," Antonelli says. "About when he used to play, and about life in general.
"About pressure, he just told me to focus on one race at a time, just focus on what you can control, and also to control the emotions, especially the ones that can make you do mistakes."
Federer's words echoed something Marco has always impressed on his son.
"In our family, we use this concept in normal life as well," he says.
"We have to live every day our best day. You work hard every day to arrive at the end of the project you have."
Back in February 2024, Wolff followed up his phone call to Marco with a meeting in Milan.
"Toto said 'Of course it will be difficult, but I think after one year of experience, we can do very well with Kimi in F1'," Marco says.
"The project was 2025 experience, 2026 start to achieve results. I think we overachieved."

The Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK)-led government in Tamil Nadu, which completed six months in office on Monday (November 9, 2026), appears to be largely enjoying the goodwill of people, even though concerns are being raised about the regime’s tendency to be directionless.
Though Chief Minister C. Joseph Vijay, on his very first day in office, had declared that he had inherited an “empty coffer,” the government has been continuing with all the major welfare measures. The “precarious” financial condition did not come in the way of his government carrying out some other steps such as the extension of the breakfast scheme for school students, the provision of gold rings to babies born at government hospitals, the distribution of eight-gram gold coins and silk saris to eligible women, and the expansion of free travel for women on buses of the State Transport Corporations.
Reports of a “marked reduction“ in corruption regarding government appointments, transfers, and public services have impressed many observers including former Union Minister P. Chidambaram and UN diplomat-turned-political writer R. Kannan.
‘Transparency, strongest asset’
In an interview with this newspaper a couple of months ago, Mr. Chidambaram stated: “I also understand that sanctions for the appointment of teachers in [government-aided] schools and colleges have been sent by post.”
According to Mr. Kannan, “transparency remains the Vijay administration’s strongest asset.” The ruling party’s national spokesperson, Americai V. Narayanan, says: “He [Mr. Vijay] does not do things to please others or earn applause. He does them because he genuinely believes in them. In politics, where symbolism often outweighs conviction, that distinction matters.”
Areas of criticism
Notwithstanding the general perception about the government‘s integrity, the two Dravidian majors — the Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK) and the All India Anna Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (AIADMK) — have been unsparing. One of the areas of their attack is on the power front, where the current regime had, ironically, begun with the increase in the quantum of free power to 200 units bimonthly to domestic consumers subject to the overall consumption not exceeding 500 units. The regime’s plans for power purchase on a short-term basis at a higher cost has raised questions about the government’s competence.
DMK president M.K. Stalin and AIADMK’s Amma Peravai secretary R.B. Udhayakumar wondered when Keralam could buy electricity at lower price, why Tamil Nadu has not been able to procure at comparable rates. Besides, even the lower price has triggered a controversy in the neighbouring State.
It is not only on the power front where the government is found on a weak wicket but also on many other policy matters. On the issue of wooing industrial investment, the Opposition’s attack has not been firmly rebutted by the government. As for the TVK regime’s project of building a new Secretariat complex, there has not been any categorical statement from the Chief Minister on the controversy triggered by it, though his Ministerial colleagues, at times, make different observations.
Govt. appears directionless: Kannan
“The new government often appears directionless, evidenced by hasty decision-making and conspicuous silence on controversial issues,“ Mr. Kannan observes. He adds that moving forward, the priority must shift from perpetual campaigning to effective governance.
A senior citizen, who calls himself a “well wisher“ of the ruling party, points out that “a structured, periodic forum for district and block-level leaders would help. Without it, the party could pay a price in the forthcoming local body elections.”
Even as the TVK government faces a host of challenges in sustained governance, it is also expected to fulfil its key electoral promises such as the increase in the monthly assistance for women to ₹2,500.

If the vote to impeach Hegseth passes in the House, the Senate must then vote to either acquit or convict Hegseth on the articles of impeachment. Under the Constitution, convicting and removing a public official from office requires a two-thirds majority in the Senate.
Shortly after Election Day, a rumor spread that U.S. Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., planned to force a vote to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth in response to the Democrats' outsize victories in the 2026 midterms — which were widely seen as a rebuke of President Donald Trump's policies, particularly his war in Iran.
The rumor circulated on X and Facebook. Snopes readers searched the website for information on a possible Hegseth impeachment trial.
In short, the claim is true. It originated with a CNN article titled "Republicans quickly turn against Pete Hegseth after midterms rout." Here's what the story said about Massie (emphasis ours): 
House Republicans are expected to vote to directly repudiate the defense secretary in a matter of days. Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky, the famously anti-Trump GOP lawmaker, told CNN he plans to trigger a vote to impeach Hegseth when Congress returns next week — and multiple GOP sources said they expect it to pass.
Massie then referenced CNN's reporting in a Nov. 4 X post (archived) that confirmed he planned to reintroduce articles of impeachment against Hegseth. (Massie previously forced a vote on impeaching Hegseth in September, which failed.)
"There is one contingency in which I won't reintroduce the articles of impeachment: Hegseth resigns," Massie said on his official X account, which has a gray checkmark badge verifying that it authentically represents a government official.
Snopes has not independently verified CNN's report that at least some Republicans believe Massie's impeachment articles against Hegseth will pass.
The House passes impeachment articles through a simple majority. The Senate must then vote on whether to convict Hegseth on those articles of impeachment before he would be removed from office — and the Constitution requires a two-thirds majority vote in the Senate to convict.
Congress has never successfully removed a Cabinet member from office under the impeachment process.
After several news outlets reported that Hegseth did not intend to step down and that Trump was showing support for him — at least publicly — Massie said in a Nov. 5 X post that his impeachment resolution was a "much gentler version of what's coming when Dem's control Congress."
(While Democrats won majorities in both congressional chambers, they won't actually take control of the Senate and House of Representatives until the new members are sworn in in January.)
Following Massie's Nov. 5 post, Hegseth shared a video that same day calling Massie a "disgruntled, defeated congressman" who, alongside Democratic allies, "dropped sham articles of impeachment against yours truly" (at 4:12).
In the video, Hegseth compared the impeachment efforts against him to lawmakers' previous attempts to impeach Trump.
"It's all about the politics of personal destruction," he said. "Didn't work against President Trump, and it won't work with me."

Nvidia said on Sunday it “is initiating an independent investigation in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort”.
The Republican-led foreign affairs and intelligence committees of the US Congress asked Huang to testify next week at a closed-door briefing on Nvidia’s “security protocols against foreign adversary espionage” in response to a New York Times report in October alleging he had a close relationship with a Chinese businesswoman who passed information to Beijing.
Alice Huang or Huang Le, of no relation to the Nvidia CEO, is an executive at a Singapore-based datacenter company called Megaspeed. She had previously been suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips to China, prompting American officials to surveil and monitor her.
Those officials have determined that she was acting as a Chinese intelligence asset, passing commercial information to Beijing, the New York Times reported, citing unnamed sources.
The company’s board said in a statement on that, while it has no reason to believe that either US national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, its inquiry will examine all available information.
“The Board prioritizes US national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders,” the company said. “The Board has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team and will provide further updates as appropriate.”
Huang fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it, it added.
Axios reported on Sunday, citing a draft email by Huang to employees, that Huang admitted to having a romantic relationship with a suspected Chinese spy and took full responsibility for his actions.
“I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did,” Huang said in the draft email also seen by Reuters.
Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the Axios report.
The Times reported on Sunday that a memo drafted by US secretary of state Marco Rubio circulated among top policymakers in the Trump administration last spring, citing intelligence that the businesswoman who had a relationship with Nvidia’s chief executive was a spy for China’s ministry of state security. Despite those concerns, Huang and his wife, Lori Huang, were invited to a state dinner at the White House in September for Xi Jinping, China’s president, and seated at the top table with Donald Trump and Xi.
Nvidia’s powerful chips serve as a cornerstone of the AI boom, placing Jensen Huang into one of the most influential leadership positions in the industry. In that position, he has developed a close partnership with Trump as the US government attempts to defend its position as a leader in AI development.
However, national security concerns have prompted strict US export controls, effectively barring the company from selling its top-tier processors to customers in China.
US officials have cited threats to the US supply chain and fears over national security risks as a rationale for the restrictions. Scott Bessent, the US treasury secretary, has also suggested that China could be sanctioned for theft of US data and intellectual property.
The Trump administration has imposed restrictions on exports of advanced AI chips to China as a matter of national security. Megaspeed’s Alice Huang was suspected to have been helping the government get around those restrictions.
The investigation also follows a rough few days on Wall Street for AI tech firms, particularly Nvidia. A sell-off of tech stocks that began earlier this month and gained steam with disappointing earnings led to a total decline of nearly $1tn in value off the tech-heavy Nasdaq exchange in one week and erased about $2tn in a month.
A drop of 3.1% for Nvidia, previously worth about $5tn, whose chips have made it the poster child of the AI frenzy, was the heaviest force pulling the S&P 500 downward recently.
Robert Mackey, Nick Robins-Early and Blake Montgomery contributed reporting

Hajra Begum rolls a potato in her hands, checking its skin for cuts, soft spots and signs of rot. After a day harvesting in her family’s field in Chorwan, a remote mountain village in Gurez, Indian-administered Kashmir, she is sorting the crop for winter storage. Some of the potatoes will feed her family through the cold months; others will be saved for planting in spring.
“It should be perfect for planting,” she says. “If you keep a bad potato, you will waste the whole next year.”
Begum, 40, is preparing to lower the potatoes into a khraw, a traditional underground storage pit lined with straw and sealed against the cold. For generations, khraws have kept potatoes, turnips and cabbages through Himalayan winters, when heavy snowfall cuts villages off from the Kashmir valley and temperatures fall below -20C (-4F) – cold enough to crack pipes and freeze diesel.
But the practice is slowly dying out. As roads have improved and young people have left for work and education, fewer families maintain the pits. Their decline threatens not only a traditional way of storing food but also the local potato varieties themselves and the knowledge of which ones store well, resist rot and produce reliable harvests.
“When I was young, almost every family had three or four pits,” Begum says. “Now, down in the main valley, they have abandoned the practice altogether. Only a handful of families still use them. The rest buy from the market or subsidised ones from the government.”
Begum learned from her mother how to tell potatoes that store well from those that rot or sprout too quickly. She is passing this on to her daughter, but is unsure whether the skill will survive into another generation.
Gurez is a high-altitude Himalayan valley perched near the Line of Control, the heavily militarised boundary separating Indian- and Pakistani-administered Kashmir. About 80 miles (125km) from Srinagar, the valley remains cut off each winter when snow closes Razdan pass, its main road link, which sits at roughly 3,600 metres.
It is home to the Dard-Shin people, an Indigenous community who speak Shina and have a culture that is distinct from Kashmiri, with community links across the border in Gilgit-Baltistan, administered by Pakistan.
Potatoes account for about 45% of Gurez’s cultivated area, according to a 2019 study by the Indian Council of Agricultural Research’s National Bureau of Plant Genetic Resources (ICAR-NBPGR), a government body that studies and conserves India’s crop diversity. Yet the genetic diversity of the valley’s potatoes has not been systematically documented.
Dr Sheikh M Sultan, a senior scientist based at ICAR-NBPGR’s Srinagar station, surveyed the valley and later struggled to find some of the varieties he had once encountered. “When I first visited, I saw many varieties,” he says. “Later, I could hardly locate even one sample of some. The loss of genetic diversity is tremendous.”
Sultan says migration, improved roads and changing lifestyles have contributed to the decline. As traditional farming disappears, so does knowledge about selecting, cultivating and preserving local varieties.
“When people stop producing their own seeds and start relying entirely on commercial varieties, the loss can be irreparable,” he says.
He warns that research institutions often prioritise introduced varieties over indigenous crops whose characteristics remain poorly understood. “Our indigenous varieties may possess valuable characteristics, including tolerance to cold and resistance to certain pests and diseases,” he says.
“These are resources we should be studying and improving, rather than neglecting.”
Climate breakdown is adding to the pressures on farmers across the Himalayas. People in Gurez report drier springs, reduced snowfall and water shortages, which they say have affected potato production.
Abdul Jabbar Mapnoo, 70, a farmer in Chorwan, remembers winters when deep snow covered the valley. “Every house used to have two or three khraw, each holding about five quintals – 500kg – of potatoes,” he says. “The springs are drying up, and there is less snow in winter. Potato production has fallen. I remember winters when six feet of snow would cover the valley in January or February.”
As farming becomes more difficult and markets easier to access, households have less incentive to grow their own potatoes. Varieties adapted to local conditions over generations could disappear from cultivation before researchers establish what makes them distinctive.
Dr Parveen Kumar, a scientist at the Sher-e-Kashmir University of Agricultural Sciences and Technology of Kashmir, says locally adapted varieties should not be overlooked. “Climate change is a reality, and farmers need to be aware of adaptation strategies,” he says.
Pressure on farmland poses another risk. In Gurez, where cultivable land is scarce, the Kishanganga hydroelectric project has affected land in the valley through acquisition and submergence. Among the areas affected is Badwan, a village known for its potatoes.
One potential route for preserving the varieties could be through using geographical indications – a designation granted by the UN’s Food and Agriculture Organization, and is similar to the French appellation d’origine contrôlée. It can be used on goods that have a specific origin and possess qualities or a reputation linked to this – which can help increase the market value and give them greater recognition. This, and the globally important agricultural heritage systems programme have helped areas such as the saffron-growing landscape of Pampore in Kashmir.
However, recognition alone will not preserve the varieties. They must be identified and documented before they disappear from cultivation, along with farmers’ knowledge of how to select, store and replant them.
In Chorwan, Begum unloads the last sack of potatoes into the pit and covers it, ready for another winter. Some will feed her family; the rest will be replanted in spring. Knowing which potatoes to eat and which to save as seed relies on knowledge passed down through generations.
If these varieties are not documented while they are still being cultivated, Kashmir may lose a living agricultural treasure trove before scientists can fully understand what it contains.

FIFPRO World 11: Ballon d'Or winner Harry Kane not voted by fellow professionals to be named in team of the year
Harry Kane becomes the first Ballon d'Or winner to not be named in the FIFPRO World 11 after claiming the award; England team-mate Jude Bellingham is included; seven WSL stars have made the Women's FIFPRO World 11
Monday 9 November 2026 17:15, UK
Ballon d'Or winner Harry Kane has not been named in the FIFPRO World 11.
Over 18,000 professional footballers have chosen their best men's team, with the final 11 being chosen from a group of 26 selected finalists.
Kane, who won the Ballon d'Or ahead of Real Madrid's Kylian Mbappe by one of the smallest margins in history, was among the 26 finalists but did not make the final team.
Mbappe, Manchester City's Erling Haaland, Barcelona's Lamine Yamal and Inter Miami's Lionel Messi were named in a Kane-less front four, which also excluded Cristiano Ronaldo and Michael Olise.
Kane became the first English Ballon d'Or winner last month since Michael Owen in 2001, and only the fifth in history following in the footsteps Sir Stanley Matthews, Sir Bobby Charlton, Kevin Keegan and Owen.
- From forgettable EFL loans to Ballon d'Or winner - Kane's 'Cinderella story'
- Putellas wins third Women's Ballon d'Or | How ceremony unfolded
The Bayern Munich star received just 27.6 per cent of votes of all the forwards, with Haaland marginally bettering him at 28.4 per cent. It is the first time since the award's inception in 2005 that the Ballon d'Or winner has not been selected for the XI.
Kane's international team-mate, Jude Bellingham, was named in midfield alongside Barcelona star Rodri and PSG's Vitinha.
Arsenal's David Raya was named in goal, with Pau Cubarsi, Achraf Hakimi and Nuno Mendes rounding things out in a back three.
Men's Fifpro World 11:
Goalkeeper: David Raya (Arsenal & Spain)
Defenders: Achraf Hakimi (PSG & Morocco), Pau Cubarsi (Barcelona & Spain), Nuno Mendes (PSG & Portugal)
Midfielders: Vitinha (PSG & Portugal), Rodri (Man City/Barcelona & Spain), Jude Bellingham (Real Madrid & England)
Forwards: Lamine Yamal (Barcelona & Spain), Erling Haaland (Man City & Norway), Lionel Messi (Inter Miami & Argentina), Kylian Mbappe (Real Madrid & France).
SEVEN WSL stars named in FIFPRO World 11
Seven players from the WSL have been named in the 2026 Women's FIFPRO World 11.
Over 6,500 women's footballers from 64 countries voted for their team of the year, which also included five of Sarina Wiegman's Lionesses.
Lucy Bronze earned a record-breaking ninth appearance in the XI, and is joined by Chelsea team-mate, goalkeeper Hannah Hampton.
Manchester City's Alex Greenwood also features in a backline that sees London City Lionesses defender Mapi Leon included.
Manchester United's Ella Toone joins a midfield that includes Ballon d'Or winner Alexia Putellas and three-time recipient Aitana Bonmati. Arsenal striker Alessia Russo rounds out the WSL inclusions.
Barcelona defender Irene Paredes, forward Claudia Pina and Orlando Pride's Barbra Banda complete the XI.
Women's FIFPRO World 11:
Goalkeeper: Hannah Hampton (Chelsea & England)
Defenders: Lucy Bronze (Chelsea & England), Alex Greenwood (Man City & England), Mapi Leon (Barcelona/London City Lionesses & Spain), Irene Paredes (Barcelona & Spain)
Midfielders: Aitana Bonmati (Barcelona & Spain), Alexia Putellas (Barcelona/London City Lionesses & Spain), Ella Toone (Man Utd & England)
Forwards: Barbra Banda (Orlando Pride & Zambia), Claudia Pina (Barcelona & Spain), Alessia Russo (Arsenal & England).

5 Nintendo Switch 2 features everyone should know about
The Switch 2 has lots of little tricks to discover: some inherited from the original Switch and some new.
Chances are that you aren't taking full advantage of everything your Nintendo Switch 2 can do. It's easy to jump right into games and ignore the various settings that help your system run at its best.
The Switch 2 is a pretty direct upgrade to the original Switch — its design, OS, controllers and other aspects are refinements rather than something entirely new. That means many of the Switch 1's tips and tricks work on the newer console too, so if you're a Switch veteran you might already know where to look. But there are other easy-to-miss improvements to find, and they're unique to the newer system.
Whether it's making controls more comfortable or repurposing hardware you already have, you should know about the Switch 2's neat little features. For instance, you might have overlooked the option to share games with friends, which can save you all money. Try these features out before you jump into a game on your next session.
Locate your controllers
The Joy-Con 2 controllers are larger than the original models but still small enough to sink between the couch cushions or lose sight of underneath a blanket. Next time you can't find your controllers, your console can help. Open the Controllers page from the main menu, then hit Search for Controllers.
All compatible controllers you've paired to the system will appear; to find one, highlight it and hold L or R (or press the touchscreen). While you're holding the button, the controller will vibrate and play a sound, helping you track it down. If you can't find one, try walking around with the console to get back in range of it.
There are a few caveats here. While you can pair original Switch controllers with a Switch 2, this feature can't locate them. Third-party Switch controllers may or may not work. You can't ping a dead controller with this, and it won't find a controller that's paired with another console.
Preserve long-term battery health
Most laptops, phones and similar devices now include a feature to cap their charging at 80 percent (or similar values). This is designed to protect the health of the device's battery over several years, since keeping lithium-ion batteries at 100 percent for extended periods wears them faster than lower percentages.
Your Switch 2 can also do this: open Settings and scroll to System. About halfway down, you'll see a toggle titled Stop Charging Around 80-90%. Turn this on, and your system will limit itself when it's on the dock or otherwise charging. If you're headed on a long trip, feel free to shut this off first to fully juice up. But in general, especially if your Switch 2 sits on the dock most of the time, this is worth having on.
Speaking of charging, the System Battery (%) option next to this is appreciated, too. It will show the exact battery level instead of a general symbol.
Remap your controller buttons
While many modern games have expansive control scheme options, sometimes you can't adjust exactly what you'd like. For those cases, you're able to remap buttons at the system level. Open Settings and go to Accessibility. At the top, choose Button Mapping — if you plan to use this often, enable Button Mapping in Quick Settings and a shortcut to this tool will appear when you hold the Home button.
In this menu, you'll see each connected controller on the left side. Select one and choose Edit Controller's Mappings to show its buttons, where you're free to remap most of the inputs to anything else. For example, you could swap the ZR and ZL buttons with R and L, or move an inconvenient input to a button that's in closer reach.
The C button is of particular interest; if you don't use GameChat, you can disable the button to avoid accidental activation. Alternatively, turn it into a secondary input for another button, like a D-pad direction or pressing one of the sticks. Check the Control Stick Settings if you'd like to swap the left and right sticks or use a Joy-Con 2 vertically when a game intends you to hold it horizontally.
While you can't apply a remap to a certain game, you can save up to five profiles per controller and swap them as needed. After hitting Save, choose Save as a Preset and give it a name. When remapping is applied, you'll see a blue wrench icon at the bottom-left of the menu and anywhere else that controller icon appears. Games are not aware of remapping done this way, so if you've swapped ZR and R, for example, you'll need to press the latter when the game prompts the former.
There's one more related option at the bottom of Settings > Controllers & Accessories: Swap A and B. This simple toggle does what it says and is great if you're used to PlayStation or Xbox controllers that have the Confirm button at the bottom and Cancel on the right.
Share games with family and friends
You have options for letting others enjoy your games, thanks to Nintendo's virtual game cards. Any game loaded onto your system is playable by all other users on the console under their own profile. If you have a Nintendo family group set up, other members can borrow your games on their system for two weeks (during which time you're unable to play them).
Open the Virtual Game Cards page on the Home screen to see your collection. Choose one and hit Lend to Family Group Member, then Select a User to Lend To. To do this, you have to be physically near the other person. You can only loan three games at a time, and a borrower can only have a single game "checked out" at once. Either party can return the game early, and you're free to loan it again if desired after 14 days.
There's also the GameShare feature, where you can stream a copy of compatible games so anyone nearby with a Switch or Switch 2 can join you in multiplayer. You can also do this online using GameChat for friends with a Switch 2. Only a few titles (including Donkey Kong Bananza, Clubhouse Games and Super Mario Odyssey) are supported, but it's worth a look for a low-cost multiplayer.
Speed up your Switch 2 experience
There are a few ways to reduce slowdowns across your Switch 2 so you don't get bogged down in menus all the time. If you're the only user on your system, it's a waste of time to select your profile every time you open a game or the eShop. To avoid this, go to Settings > Users and enable Skip Selection Screen. This option won't appear if your system has multiple users.
You might also be able to minimize loading times in Switch 1 games. These can see smoother performance when playing off the dock if you visit Settings > System > Nintendo Switch Software Handling > Handheld Mode Boost. By enabling this, your Switch 2 runs original Switch titles as if they were in TV mode, which can improve their graphics or performance. As a trade-off, it will likely use more battery, and there are some control quirks (like the touchscreen not working). There's also an option to add this to Quick Settings for easier toggling.
Finally, there's a much better way to share media you create on your Switch 2. To share your screenshots and video clips much faster, open the Gallery icon on the home screen, hit the Settings cog on the left, and pick your profile. Enable Automatic Uploads and your system will upload up to 100 items, held for 30 days. Then on your phone, install the Nintendo Switch app and sign in with your Nintendo account. By tapping the same Album icon in the app, you're able to access your uploads and share them over chat apps, social media or similar.

Paddington: The Musical, which opens in 2027, has set its cast, featuring Arrested Development’s Tony Hale in his Broadway debut.
The musical will be led by Kelvin Dukes (America’s Got Talent) as Tony, Drew Gehling (Waitress) as Mr. Brown, Allison Guinn (Operation Mincemeat) as Lady Sloane and Hale (Veep) as Mr. Curry.
Arti Shah, who originated the role of Paddington on the West End, will reprise on Broadway, with James Hameed also returning as Paddington’s voice and remote puppetry.
The cast of the musical also includes J. Quinton Johnson (Hamilton) as Grant, Leslie Rodriguez Kritzer (The Fantasticks) as Millicent Clyde, Zonya Love (The Color Purple) as Tanya, Jessie Mueller (Waitress) as Mrs. Brown, Serena Parrish (Don’t Say Good Luck) as Judy Brown, Karen Ziemba (Contact) as Mrs. Bird and Chip Zien (Into the Woods original Broadway cast) as Mr. Gruber.
Watch on Deadline
Paddington: The Musical will begin previews on Tuesday, March 30, 2027, at Broadway’s Al Hirschfeld Theatre ahead of its opening night on Sunday, April 18, 2027.
Based on A Bear Called Paddington, written by Michael Bond and the film Paddington, the musical features music and lyrics by Tom Fletcher, a book by Jessica Swale, and direction by Luke Sheppard.
	In Paddington: The Musical, a small, lost bear from Peru arrives in London in search of a place to call home. A chance encounter with the Browns leads him into an unexpected world of adventure, where kindness has the power to change lives and strangers can become family. But London isn’t all afternoon tea and friendly faces—and even the seemingly happiest of families can have cracks beneath
the surface. So, when a mysterious and vengeful villain sets her sights on Paddington, the Browns embark on a thrilling rescue mission, realizing they need this special bear as much as he needs them.

Democrats won big on issues like immigration. But ICE still has the money
In the days leading up to the midterm elections, hundreds of people left their "I voted" stickers on a memorial for Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, a Houston man killed by federal immigration agents earlier this year.
"The fact that people were thinking of my dad and thinking of other immigrants — that just means the world to me," said Ronaldo Salgado, Salgado Araujo's son, told NPR.
Those votes resulted in a seismic political shift in Texas: for the first time, a Latina, Democrat Gina Hinojosa, will be governor. Texans also elected the state's first Democratic U.S. senator in nearly 40 years, and the Texas House of Representatives flipped.
"Unfortunately, Texas has become like the epicenter of ICE enforcement and like gross violence against immigrants," Ronaldo Salgado said. "Well, the voters have spoken — incoming lawmakers now have a duty to listen to us."
The political fallout
Immigration policy was one of the top issues on voters' minds this election, according to exit polling. Artemio Muñiz of the Texas Federation of Hispanic Republicans, told NPR "with these anti-immigrant-type policies, I think the Hispanic community got fed up."
That seems more true than ever in the counties along the U.S.-Mexico border, which flipped Democratic after supporting Trump in 2024.
"I think the message is clear from the Texas Hispanic community that the only acceptable or effective Hispanic outreach from the Republican Party in Texas is one that includes a reasonable solution for immigration," Muñiz said, suggesting the solution should include secured borders and a legal pathway for undocumented immigrants who have been in the U.S. for decades.
In Texas, Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa is facing calls to end the state's partnership with ICE.
"That's something that can happen on day one," said César Espinosa, the executive director of the Houston-based advocacy organization FIEL. He said his group would also like to see Hinojosa and the Texas legislature to push for driver licenses for undocumented immigrants. Already, Houston's mayor is reducing his police department's cooperation with ICE.
Nationwide, immigration advocates say they want to see ICE defunded, or severely restricted.
"We demand that the incoming Congress hold ICE accountable", says Murad Awawdeh of the New York Immigrant Coalition.
What could the new Congress actually do?
Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., who is set to become the next chair of the House oversight committee, had two words of advice for Republicans on Election Day: "Lawyer up."
Garcia has promised to look into several issues, including ICE accountability.
ICE is the highest funded federal law enforcement agency in the U.S. Congress essentially gave immigration enforcement a blank check in 2025 and in 2026 they awarded ICE and Customs and Border Patrol around $240 billion.
It's enough funds to run the mass deportation operation for the remainder of Trump's term.
Congress could claw back that money. And lawmakers are already eyeing more stringent oversight.
"We have to rein ICE in because its illegal, out-of-control activities (have) killed individuals … assaulted individuals … have incarcerated individuals," said Rep. Bennie Thompson, D-Miss., who is likely to chair the House Homeland Security Committee. "That system has to have accountability for the men and women who work in it."
He said he'd like to legally require policies, like requiring the use of body-worn cameras for federal immigration agents and banning them from wearing face coverings.
The major hurdle is President Trump: following the midterm election results the President said he would welcome the nickname "Mr. Veto."
Another possible indication of how the administration will be seeing immigration enforcement moving forward came Friday, a few days after the midterm elections. White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller was promoted to chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles. Miller's central project in government has been immigration control and mass deportations. Miller is considered the architect of the first Trump administration's child separation policy, and as NPR reported, was deeply involved in the project of turning large warehouses into immigration detention centers.
Naureen Shah at the ACLU says she thinks one of the most powerful things that could happen to change ICE behavior is Congressional oversight via subpoenas.
"ICE has to be afraid," she said. "They have to be afraid of losing their funding, they have to be afraid of being subpoenaed and asked extremely hard questions before a live audience of the American people."
The Trump Administration vows that "Deportations will continue".
The day after the Midterm elections, Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin posted a three-word tweet : "Deportations will continue."
Vice President JD Vance took to X to share his thoughts on the Republican Party's big loss. He said he believes it is due to voter's concerns over the economy, inflation and the war with Iran. He left immigration enforcement off that list.
He did, however, say he is open to changing enforcement tactics by focusing more on businesses that hire undocumented workers. But he said immigration amnesty is not the solution.
Shah of the ACLU says she believes ICE enforcement and the current state of the economy are inextricably linked. "What's really clear is that the stories of life becoming harder for everyday Americans are actually also stories about ICE's impact. People are afraid to take their kids to school, afraid to go to work. It impacts our schools, our teachers. It impacts the labor force when people aren't showing up for their jobs. So Democrats have an opportunity through their oversight device to tell a story about how to make everyday life more affordable for all Americans."
Could we see more oversight on ICE detention facilities?
The Trump administration has spent billions of dollars to expand ICE detention facilities — many of which have faced criticism and protest over dire conditions. There have been a record number of deaths in detention since the start of Trump's second term.
The day after mid-term election results the two major private detention center companies that contract for ICE, CoreCivic and the GEO Group , had their quarterly investor calls.
The main question asked by investors at the CoreCivic call was: how will the result of the midterms affect ICE operations?
CoreCivic President Lucibeth Mayberry optimistically, pointing out that "[ICE] have again began increasing enforcement activity. They have the secure funding to do so." But then she offered a word of advice to ICE about purchasing new detention centers: "we would urge the ICE administration to move quickly."

Adding another layer to the ongoing shareholder dispute at BharatPe-backed Unity Small Finance Bank (SFB), the Delhi High Court (HC) has rejected an appeal filed by the bank against an interim order. The interim order restrains Unity SFB from placing a proposed capital restructuring resolution before its board without prior written consent from BharatPe parent Resilient Innovations (RIPL) and Centrum Financial Services. The order, passed by a bench Justices C Hari Shankar and Vinod Kumar on November 5, restrains Unity SFB from tabling, discussing or approving 'Agenda Item 18' at its board meeting without prior written consent from RIPL and Centrum Financial Services. The HC granted BharatPe the interim relief pertaining to the case earlier this year in July The dispute stems from a Shareholders’ Agreement (SHA) signed between Unity Bank, RIPL and Centrum in October 2021, following their partnership to establish Unity SFB. The agreement features certain ‘Reserved Matters’ that would require prior written consent from representatives of both RIPL and Centrum. These include changes to the bank’s capital structure and amendments to its constitutional documents. Agenda Item 18 proposed increasing Unity SFB’s authorised share capital from ₹4,000 Cr to ₹4,900 Cr by creating an additional 90 Cr preference shares of ₹10 each. The proposal also involved amending the bank’s Memorandum of Association (MoA) to facilitate the issuance of these shares. RIPL opposed the proposal, arguing that the proposed capital restructuring could dilute its shareholding in Unity SFB from 49% to 21%. It contended that the resolution fell under the SHA's Reserved Matters and therefore required prior written consent from both RIPL and Centrum. Welcoming the decision, BharatPe said the ruling reaffirmed the shareholder rights and governance framework agreed upon when the joint venture was established in 2021. “The board must ensure that the bank complies with the court’s directions in letter and spirit. We expect the board to exercise independent judgment, free from undue influence, and act in the interests of the bank and all its stakeholders, including minority shareholders,” a BharatPe spokesperson said. The company also called on Unity’s board to respect the governance processes agreed upon at the time of the bank's inception and honour its contractual obligations under the SHA. It said the agreed framework should not be set aside to favour one shareholder group over another. Unity Small Bank, on the other hand, declined to comment on the matter. “The discussions are solely between the bank's promoter and a financial investor. The bank remains operationally unaffected, and continues to serve its customers and stakeholders as usual,” the bank told Inc42. The proposal also involved amending Clause V of the bank’s Memorandum of Association (MOA) to reflect the revised authorised capital. While the bank acknowledged in its board agenda that the proposed capital increase was a ‘Reserved Matter’ under the SHA and sought RIPL and Centrum’s approval, it also proposed taking the resolution up for board discussion and approval. RIPL opposed the move, arguing that a clause of the SHA expressly prohibits even discussing a Reserved Matter at a board meeting without prior written consent from both shareholders. It also relied on Clause 8, which bars the bank from taking decisions or actions on Reserved Matters without the requisite consent. On the financial front, Unity SFB has seen significant growth since commencing operations in November 2021. In Q4 FY25, its operating revenue surged 123% YoY to ₹977 Cr, while net profit increased 83% to ₹264 Cr. For the full FY25, the bank reported revenue of ₹2,837 Cr and net profit of ₹482 Cr. Notably, the financial results for FY26 are yet to be disclosed. On the other hand, BharatPe's FY26 operating revenue increased by 11% YoY to ₹1,862 Cr, adjusted EBITDA profit rose 20% to ₹146 Cr as per a report by ANI. The company is yet to file its annual report for the fiscal. Meanwhile, BharatPe's parent RIPL, which holds a 49% stake in Unity SFB, was reportedly exploring a stake sale in January 2025. The company was looking to offload up to 25% of its stake in the bank to raise around $800 Mn. The proposed sale was also linked to regulatory requirements mandating BharatPe to bring down its shareholding in the bank to 10% within eight years of its commencement of operations, by 2029. The company is yet to pare its stake.

A security researcher has found more than 100 serious vulnerabilities in publicly available UK government code, putting sensitive data at risk as a result of poor cyber hygiene.
The UK government has defaulted to openly publishing code it produces with public money for around a decade because it’s transparent, and making it easier for code to be reused is cost-efficient. This includes within the Department of Health and Social Care, and the Home Office, as well as local authorities.
But funding squeezes have left departments neglecting maintenance and improvement of their technology estate. While ControlPlane security researcher Chris Nesbitt-Smith found the vulnerabilities using Claude’s Opus and Sonnet AI models, he says that he used consumer-grade models on a laptop and that many of the issues could have been caught by a routine IT health check. “None of this is the level of sophistication that general media is worried about in terms of cyber attacks,” he tells WIRED. “It’s all daft stuff.”
In the most serious case he identified, the Planning Inspectorate, which handles land-use matters across England, had failed to fully remove a login after it accidentally committed them to public repository GitHub. The fact the credentials gave such wide access—and seemingly didn’t expire—compounded with the agency’s accidental publication of them, “made it particularly dangerous for them.”
The complete Microsoft Entra ID would have given “god-tier” read and write access to all SharePoint sites and private employee OneDrive accounts, according to Nesbitt-Smith, including HR records. It also would have given access to sensitive libraries which safeguard evidence under legal hold for statutory planning inquiries and appeals, according to the security researcher who found it. “The option for ransomwaring them, for encrypting all the data, or just stealing all the data, was abundantly there,” Nesbitt-Smith says.
A spokesperson for the Planning Inspectorate told WIRED its cyber monitoring tools immediately detected Nesbitt-Smith’s activity in August and that it had already been handling this as a cyber incident when ControlPlane made contact. The agency identified and fixed this vulnerability within 20 minutes of the report and verified that no data breach occurred. “We have reviewed and strengthened our systems and processes to prevent this type of issue recurring and we are grateful for the researcher’s work and for alerting us to it,” they told WIRED.
The Planning Inspectorate issue “isn’t about open source but internal housekeeping when using public tools,” Amanda Brock, chief executive officer of nonprofit industry group OpenUK. “That data was exposed because of a failure not to follow good process,” she adds. “That’s not an open source security issue.”
In around two-thirds of the 349 public sector codebases across 33 organizations Nesbitt-Smith scanned, he said he found vulnerabilities. Several of these were found in the Department of Education’s code, including in a procurement service used by schools, in a teacher application service containing personal details, qualifications, employment history and identity documents, and England’s main register of government-funded training providers and apprenticeships. He also found a vulnerability in a Scottish Government open data portal which would have allowed any visitor to read administrative account information and to change site configuration. The organizations have since dealt with the issues.
Recently, there have been arguments for public sector departments to stop publishing source code in the open, now that AI has accelerated vulnerability discovery. The NHS reportedly ordered technology teams to transition away from open source code in May amid security concerns about the impact of AI models.
Doing this without immediately fixing the underlying issues would be the “worst case scenario,” according to Nesbitt-Smith, as it prevents researchers like him from finding them, and it’s likely that an adversary has already mirrored these repositories and so will maintain access to them. “Unless you’re going to go and fix all of the problems, if anything, you’re probably drawing more attention to it by closing it,” says Nesbitt-Smith, “because you’re like, ‘Here be dragons over this space. Don’t look here though, please.’”

In November 2026, a screenshot (archived) circulated online that social media users claimed authentically showed a Truth Social post by U.S. President Donald Trump accusing Democrats of using "WITCHCRAFT AND SATANISM" to win the 2026 midterm elections.
For example, one version of the screenshot on Threads read:
I was told not to say this but we all know the truth, The Democrats and lunatic left have engaged in WITCHCRAFT AND SATANISM to interfere in our elections on a spiritual level!!
America is ONE NATION UNDER GOD and we WILL FIGHT these results!
President DONALD J TRUMP
The screenshot also circulated on Facebook and X (archived). Snopes readers wrote in, asking if the alleged post was real.
The post was fake. A search of the term "WITCHCRAFT AND SATANISM" on Trump's Truth, a site that archives the president's Truth Social posts, returned no results.
Additionally, the screenshot of the fake post listed the date as "11/4/2026." Real Truth Social posts use the date format "Nov 04, 2026." Therefore, the screenshot did not come from Truth Social.
We contacted the White House Press Office for additional confirmation that Trump did not write or publish the post in question and await a reply.
Trump reportedly told the New York Times on Nov. 3 that he was "absolutely willing" to accept the results of the election. By contrast, the fake post claimed Trump would "fight" the results.
Trump reportedly told the Times he would "look forward" to working with the incoming Democrats.
Democrats wrested power from Republicans in both the House and Senate in the 2026 midterm elections. The 120th Congress, which will include the winners from November's election, will be sworn in in January 2027.
For further reading, follow Snopes' coverage of the 2026 U.S. elections.

Krakow shooting suspect has died in hospital, police say
- Published
A gunman suspected of killing six people in Krakow has died in hospital, Polish police say.
The 24-year-old, who ministers said was apparently inspired by "far-right ideologies", was injured after opening fire in central Krakow, the second largest city in Poland, on Saturday.
Armed officers raced to the scene and engaged in a gunfight with the suspect, who was shot within three minutes of the attack beginning, preventing a further massacre, officials said.
Krakow police said the suspected gunman died early on Monday morning.
After the shooting, which began shortly before 15:00 local time (14:00 GMT) in Krakow's busy Main Market Square, police identified the attacker as a 24-year-old Polish man but did not confirm his name.
In the hours after the shooting, a minister has said early investigations indicate he was inspired by "far-right ideologies". The minister also described him as an "ultra-nationalist" without giving further details.
Six people - four women and two men - are confirmed to have been killed in the attack.
Four victims are Polish, while a British national and an Austrian woman were also killed.
Poland's Prime Minister Donald Tusk said three bodies - two women and one man - were found at the gunman's house when it was searched after the attack.
On Sunday, Polish police confirmed those three victims had been identified as the alleged gunman's 53-year-old father, 52-year-old mother and his sister, who was 21 years old.
Polish media has reported the suspect had a firearms permit and may have obtained the weapons from his family home.
Sixteen people, including five foreigners, two police officers and the attacker, were taken to hospital. The interior ministry later said they were from Austria, Britain, Germany, Portugal and Russia.
In the wake of the shooting, Poland declared the country would enter two days of national mourning.
After travelling to Krakow, Tusk said: "Until now in Poland we haven't had such drastic cases of terrorism...that's what we have to call this cruel attack on people's lives here in Krakow."
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he was "shocked and saddened by the appalling shooting in Kraków".
"My thoughts are with the families of those who have lost their lives, everyone injured and all those affected by this senseless violence. The United Kingdom stands in solidarity with the people of Poland," he added.
