President Donald Trump is sticking by Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.
At an impromptu White House press conference on Monday with Dana White, Trump said he had checked in on the exec earlier that day to see how he was doing.
On Sunday, Huang admitted to having an extramarital affair, and Nvidia's board of directors said it was opening an investigation into whether the CEO was the "target of a foreign intelligence effort."
Trump said that on a phone call Monday, he asked Huang directly about the allegations that the woman was a spy.
"He said he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy," Trump told reporters at the White House. "I asked him that question. 'Did you have any idea that she was a spy?' Said, 'I had no idea that she was a spy,' and I really believe him."
Trump also praised Huang and said he felt "very confident that he'll be in good shape."
Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The New York Times has reported that US intelligence officials believe the woman at the center of the scandal, Alice Huang, was recruited to gather information about Nvidia for the Chinese government.
The scandal has led to speculation about whether Huang will maintain his role as CEO of Nvidia.

A truck carrying goods across India spends several days or even weeks on the road, but it’s not just the vehicle that needs to keep moving. In fact, the technology watching and powering India’s trucking industry never stops, regardless of how slow or fast the journey is, or indeed whether it is the slow sales months or the peak festive season. It is this technology that has made life easier over the years, for those reliant on India’s trucking system for delivery of parcels and goods. The transformation seen in the past decade has lifted businesses and startups in retail, ecommerce and logistics sectors. The problem was manifold before technology changed things: Operators have to find loads for their vehicles, negotiate freight rates, make toll payments, track fuel consumption, monitor fleets and arrange financing. For an industry as fragmented as India’s trucking market, these everyday tasks can add to the cost and complexity of running a fleet. It was this problem that BlackBuck set out to address when it was founded in 2015. The company began as a marketplace connecting truck operators with businesses looking to transport goods. Over the years, it expanded beyond load discovery to build a wider digital platform for truck operators, bringing payments, fleet tracking, freight services and vehicle financing under one umbrella. Today, its offerings span five business lines — payments, telematics, loads classifieds, superloads and vehicle financing. While payments and telematics form its core businesses, the other three are classified as growth businesses. What The Q2 Numbers Show The expansion has translated into higher revenue. In Q2 FY27, BlackBuck reported consolidated revenue from operations of ₹235.33 Cr, up 55.7% YoY from ₹151.14 Cr. Its net profit rose 41.8% to ₹41.4 Cr from ₹29.2 Cr in the year-ago quarter. Total income, including other income, increased 51.4% to ₹253.15 Cr. But the growth is not coming from its established businesses alone. Revenue from its core Payments and Telematics businesses grew 31% to ₹161.39 Cr, while its growth businesses grew 166% to ₹73.94 Cr. However, faster growth has its own cost. Total expenses rose 64% YoY to ₹210.3 Cr during the quarter, with management attributing the increase primarily to customer acquisition across core categories and stepped-up investments in SuperLoads. Meanwhile, EBITDA stood at ₹50.61 Cr and adjusted EBITDA at ₹55.04 Cr. During the Q2 earnings call, CEO Rajesh Yabaji said upfront acquisition costs can weigh on EBITDA even as the company expects to recover them over the lifetime of a customer. The company’s adjusted EBITDA grew at a slower 29% to ₹55.04 Cr. “Wherever we see opportunities, we are expanding and gaining more market share. So, as and when there are spurts in customer acquisition, EBITDA suppresses in that particular quarter,” Yabaji said. Clearly, there is a balancing act at the centre of BlackBuck’s business model. Its established businesses continue to generate operating cash flows, but the company is using that headroom to scale newer offerings. The question is whether these newer businesses can build sustainable economics without diluting the profitability of the core platform. To understand that, first, let’s decode how BlackBuck makes money. BlackBuck’s Core: Monetising Trucking While Payments and Telematics form its core businesses, BlackBuck has other verticals that contribute to its topline, including Loads Classifieds, SuperLoads and Vehicle Finance. These make up its newer businesses that leverage the core, and will play a role in BlackBuck’s future growth. But for now, the core is what sustains the trucking company. BlackBuck earns through commissions, subscriptions, service fees and interest income, depending on the service being offered. Its payments business is built around two major use cases — tolling and fuel purchases. Through its platform, truck operators can buy and manage FASTags, make toll payments and access fuel cards. BlackBuck earns commissions from banks for distributing and managing FASTags and from oil marketing companies (OMCs) for fuel card distribution and management. It also collects service fees for FASTag issuance, replacement, activation and recharge transactions. Meanwhile, the telematics segment takes the relationship beyond the toll booth. The business offers GPS-enabled vehicle tracking, fuel sensors and dashcams, with customers paying for devices and related services through subscriptions. BlackBuck recognises this revenue over the contract period rather than booking the entire amount when a device is sold. This explains why strong device sales do not immediately translate into an equivalent jump in reported revenue. Most of the revenue acceleration for Telematics device sales in the previous quarter came from state-level AIS mandates. Newer offerings such as fuel sensors and dashcams contributed a smaller share, with dashcams still being piloted. On The Periphery BlackBuck’s pitch is to become more than a platform that helps truck operators pay tolls. It wants to be part of several decisions they make while running their businesses. It is built around getting a truck operator to return to the platform for more of the services needed to keep a truck running. The catch is that each additional service also brings its own costs, execution challenges, and pressure on the bottom line. The aforementioned newer business segments take BlackBuck further into the freight and financing value chain. Loads Classifieds is a subscription-led marketplace where shippers post freight requirements and truck operators discover available loads. SuperLoads goes beyond listing loads. It offers managed freight services, matching shippers with truck operators and facilitating truck placements. BlackBuck earns service income from these transactions, while truck hiring charges add to the cost of running the business. Lastly, vehicle finance rounds out the offering by helping truck operators access loans to buy used commercial vehicles or raise finance against vehicles they already own. BlackBuck works mostly through lending partners, which managed around ₹600 Cr of assets on the platform at the time of its Q4 FY26 results, while its own book stood at roughly ₹60 Cr. It earns through fees and interest income. It earns through fees and interest income associated with the financing activity. The lending business is claimed to be on track to achieve EBITDA break-even in FY27, supported by growth in assets under management on a relatively steady cost base. The traction across these businesses is reflected in their combined performance. Revenue from BlackBuck’s growth businesses increased 266% to ₹126.51 Cr in FY26. In Q2 FY27, the combined revenue stood at ₹73.94 Cr, up 166% YoY. What Goes Into Running The Truck Business The expanding revenue portfolio also comes with a wider cost base. Running a payments platform and selling telematics subscriptions is one thing, but managing freight transactions and facilitating truck placements brings an additional layer of operational expenses. The company has to spend on people, technology, customer acquisition and, in the case of SuperLoads, truck hiring as well. Manpower services emerged as the largest named individual expense head at ₹153.3 Cr, compared with ₹118 Cr a year earlier. This was followed by truck hiring charges which is a new cost head for the company from FY26. The distinction between manpower services and employee benefits is worth noting. Employee benefits expense of ₹160.2 Cr covers the cost of BlackBuck’s employees, including salaries, bonuses, provident fund contributions, ESOP expenses, gratuity and staff welfare. Manpower services, reported separately under other expenses at ₹153.3 Cr, capture costs associated with outsourced and contract manpower. Meanwhile, truck hiring charges are particularly interesting in the context of SuperLoads, one of the newer businesses the company has launched to bulk up its customer lifetime value. Unlike a classifieds platform that primarily monetises access to listings, a managed freight business has to coordinate truck availability and placements. That creates a different cost equation. But BlackBuck does not disclose how much of the ₹74 Cr was specifically attributable to SuperLoads. The pressure to invest to grow will continue till the end of FY27. During the Q2 earnings call, management said higher customer acquisition spending across core categories and stepped-up investments in SuperLoads contributed to the rise in expenses. Management also pointed to improving productivity in SuperLoads’ older markets through AI-led matchmaking, which it believes can help improve unit economics as the business expands. That is the bet BlackBuck is making: spend more to get truck operators and shippers onto the platform, then earn more from each customer through multiple services. But customer acquisition only works as a growth lever if the additional transactions eventually generate enough revenue to cover the cost of acquiring and serving them. For now, the company is still building out that equation. The Core Pays For The Growth BlackBuck’s core businesses are still generating cash, but like many other listed tech companies these days, the company is choosing to reinvest a larger share of that headroom into customer acquisition and newer offerings. The idea is to boost the customer lifetime value and the engagement opportunities. This is beginning to show up in its operating leverage. CEO Yabaji said the core business historically delivered operating leverage of 70-85%, and at times 100%. In Q2 FY27, this had moderated to around 50% as the company stepped up upfront spending on acquiring customers. “The nature of the core business continues to be a strong operating cash flow machine for the company. We are giving its due investments wherever needed, and we are seeing in a lot of niches a strong uptick in customer acquisition and revenue growth,” he added. The lower operating leverage suggests that a larger share of the business’s earnings is being absorbed by the cost of acquiring customers and scaling newer offerings, rather than flowing through as incremental profit. While the core continues to generate cash, its growth drivers are shifting. Telematics is gaining traction, but the tolling business has not seen a corresponding improvement in monetisation. BlackBuck’s next phase of growth rests on Loads Classifieds, SuperLoads and Vehicle Finance. While all three address different parts of the trucking value chain, they also represent a move beyond the company’s relatively established payments and telematics operations. However, BlackBuck does not disclose revenue or profitability separately for Loads Classifieds, SuperLoads and Vehicle Finance. This makes it difficult to assess which business is driving the growth, how much each is costing to scale, or whether one is closer to profitability than the others. For now, the numbers establish that these offerings are gaining traction. But growth alone will not determine whether they strengthen BlackBuck’s business model. The real test will be whether they can generate sustainable returns without relying indefinitely on the core.

The young politicians with African roots making history in the US midterms
- Published
"JD [Vance], habibi (my love)".
It was an unlikely greeting to hear at a Democratic Party victory rally after the US midterm elections.
Abdul El-Sayed, 42, born to Egyptian immigrant parents, playfully addressed Vice-President JD Vance, who had campaigned against him but will now swear him into office in January as Michigan's new Senator.
The US-born Democrat spent much of his campaign fending off attacks from conservative media and President Donald Trump, who accused him of supporting the Muslim Brotherhood. El-Sayed rejected the allegations.
"My name is Abdul Rahman Mohammed El-Sayed," he said in an Egyptian Arabic accent to the cheering crowd at his victory rally. His Arabic Muslim name was a target for many of his opponents. He is set to become the first Muslim senator.
El-Sayed ran a social media-first campaign, with TikTok edits showing him speaking directly to young voters, tapping into Gen Z humour, and sporting friendship bracelets.
The former public health administrator's campaign centred on a progressive agenda, including Medicare for All, affordable housing and curbing corporate influence in politics. He has also been a vocal critic of US military aid to Israel.
But El-Sayed was not alone. From an Ethiopian-born Gen Z congresswoman to candidates with Nigerian heritage, several other politicians with African roots won in this year's midterms.
The elections, held halfway through a president's four-year term, decide who represents Americans in Congress, as well as in thousands of state and local offices.
At 29, Melat Kiros became the first Gen Z woman elected to the US Congress.
Born in Ethiopia, she arrived in the US as a baby and grew up in Denver. She had never held elected office before defeating a 15-term incumbent in Colorado's 1st District in the Democrat primary before winning a landslide in Tuesday's election.
Kiros, like El-Sayed, campaigned on issues that have become central to young progressive voters: the cost of living, universal childcare and Medicare for All.
Endorsed by the Democratic Socialists of America, she has also called for abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement and ending US military aid to Israel.
Her outspoken criticism of Israel's war in Gaza has attracted controversy. Kiros has said her criticism is directed at the Israeli state, not Jewish people.
She was fired from a top New York law firm in 2023 after she refused to take down an open letter to dozens of law firms who had urged law school deans to crack down on antisemitism on campuses as students engaged in pro-Palestinian protests.
Kiros condemned antisemitism, but warned the law firms, including the one she worked for, against conflating "such bigotry with the geo-political question of Israel's legitimacy".
She said she started thinking more seriously about politics in general after being fired.
Adrian Boafo, meanwhile, a second-generation Ghanaian-American, will represent Maryland's 5th Congressional District after succeeding veteran Congressman Steny Hoyer, who retired after a political career spanning more than four decades.
The 32-year-old was born in Virginia and raised in Prince George's County, Maryland. His parents immigrated to the US from Ghana.
Boafo's route to Congress began in local politics. He served on the Bowie City Council before becoming a Maryland state delegate in 2023. He also worked for Hoyer before eventually winning the race to replace him.
His campaign focused on the cost of living, childcare and protecting federal workers, a major issue in a district close to Washington DC and home to thousands of government employees.
In his victory statement, Boafo said representing his constituents had "never felt more urgent", pointing to federal job cuts, rising costs and the Trump administration's immigration crackdown.
Among those returning to Congress is Somali-born Ilhan Omar, 44, who won a fifth term despite an ongoing federal investigation.
Federal agents searched her Washington home in October as part of an investigation into her immigration paperwork. Omar has denied wrongdoing and has not been charged with a crime.
First elected to Congress in 2018, Omar became the first Somali-American and one of the first Muslim women to serve in the chamber. She has also been a frequent target of President Trump, who has repeatedly criticised her and other Somali immigrants.
Trump has previously used derogatory language to describe some African countries, including Somalia. In October, his Yemeni-born adviser Amer Ghalib said the president would refrain from using such language.
Others made their breakthroughs in state and local politics.
Junior Ezeonu was born in Nigeria and moved to the US as a young child. By 27, he had already become Grand Prairie's youngest city council member before winning a seat in the Texas State House.
Then there is Carol Kazeem, 34, a Pennsylvania state legislator of Nigerian heritage who has retained her seat at District 159. At least four candidates with Nigerian heritage won in the 3 November midterms.
For some young Africans watching from across the Atlantic, these victories have offered a glimpse of what a new generation of voters could achieve at home.
On social media, users have shared the election results as a source of inspiration, particularly in Nigeria and Kenya, where major elections are due in 2027.

The Maharashtra Food and Drug Administration (FDA) seized drugs and cosmetics worth ₹34.51 lakh, cancelled 122 licences and suspended 422 others following enforcement action across the State in October 2026, according to a press note issued by the department on Thursday (November 5, 2026).
The FDA conducted 1,986 inspections of drug manufacturing, sales and other regulated establishments during the month and issued 674 notices. Of these, 1,694 inspections were conducted at drug sales establishments and 292 at manufacturing and other regulated establishments. The department cancelled 105 licences and suspended 367 licences of sales establishments, while 17 licences were cancelled and 55 suspended in the manufacturing and other categories.
The department also carried out 11 search and seizure operations involving alleged violations related to the manufacture, storage and sale of drugs and cosmetics. Two FIRs were registered, and four persons were arrested under the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act in connection with the illegal sale of narcotic drugs.
Among the major seizures, FDA officials recovered allopathic drugs worth ₹22.03 lakh from the premises of Phoenix Medicorp in Nagpur on October 7. According to the department, the establishment had stored drugs at unlicensed premises despite surrendering its licences.
In Mumbai, FDA officials seized spurious drugs identified as Empirime tablets and Cardiurex 2 ml, worth ₹1.01 lakh, from INHS Asvini in Colaba on October 29, according to the department.
In separate operations in Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar on October 14 and 25, officials seized 199 Nitrosun 10 tablets containing Nitrazepam. Four persons were arrested in connection with their alleged illegal sale.
The FDA also seized cosmetic soaps worth ₹4.05 lakh from Vedas Herbals Mahila Gruh Udyog in Baramati, Pune district, on October 14, for alleged manufacturing without a licence. In Vasai East, officials seized raw materials, packaging materials and machinery worth ₹1.83 lakh from G.B. Cosmetics on October 10 in connection with alleged unlicensed manufacture and sale of nail polish.
The Konkan division recorded the highest number of inspections in October at 556, followed by Pune with 375 and Greater Mumbai with 322. Konkan also accounted for the highest number of regulatory actions at 156, followed by Greater Mumbai with 105 and Pune with 77.
Between April 1 and October 31, the FDA conducted 7,950 inspections across Maharashtra, issued 2,888 notices, cancelled 555 licences and suspended 2,074 licences. The department recorded 2,629 regulatory actions, comprising licence cancellations and suspensions, during the seven-month period.
The FDA urged citizens to report instances of illegal drug manufacturing or sales, as well as suspected substandard drugs, medical devices and cosmetics, to its commissioner’s office or the nearest district office.

"The race is too hard for women. They are simply not tough enough to do it."
Those are the words of Lazarus Lake, race director of the Barkley Marathons - one of the world's hardest ultramarathons which to date, of the approximate 1,000 people who have started, only 20 have ever completed.
Speaking in 2015 and daring for someone to prove him wrong, it took nine years until a British ultra-runner did just that.
Completing the extreme 100-mile course with just one minute 39 seconds to spare of the 60-hour cut-off, Jasmin Paris from Midlothian made history and cemented her name in the ultra-running history books.
But now, increasingly, she is not alone.
Last summer, there was a female one-two for the first time in the gruelling Montane Summer Spine Race from Derbyshire to Scotland. Rachel Entrekin set a new course record and became the first woman to win the Cocodona 250 in Arizona in May, while last month Sophie Woods smashed the overall record by six days to complete the Via Alpina.
It appears female runners are no longer just taking part in ultra-endurance events, they are competing with their male counterparts, breaking records and in some cases, winning races outright.
All of this has prompted suggestions that they are perhaps better suited to these kinds of challenges.
But is there any scientific proof? Do women really have any physiological or psychological advantages in endurance exercise (anything that takes more than six hours)? And if so, could we see more of these records fall in the future?
In running distances up to the marathon, there is on average a 10-12% performance gap between males and females.
Men are generally stronger and built with a bigger aerobic engine.
But as the distance increases, those physical advantages appear to become less relevant and the gap starts to narrow.
The "gender pace gap" diminishes to 0.25% in 100-mile races, according to a study of more than 20 years of amateur ultra-race data conducted by RunRepeat, in collaboration with the International Association of Ultrarunners,
Anything further than 195 miles and women have the potential to be faster.
So why might this be the case?
For Professor Andy Jones, an expert in endurance performance at the University of Exeter, there are three potential physiological explanations why women could perform better over longer distances or durations.
Fat metabolism – women have higher fat stores and burn it more efficiently, giving them a steady energy source for longer.
Muscles – women have more oxygen-efficient muscle fibres, known as "slow twitch", that are better suited for endurance activities.
Fatigue resistance – women retain more strength over hours of endurance exercise.
However, Jones, who played a key role in Eliud Kipchoge's sub two-hour marathon challenge in 2019, is keen to point out that the science in this area is "behind".
"There isn't as much hard evidence as there would be for shorter distances, which have been studied for a long time in quite some detail," he adds.
That is a view shared by Dr Richard Burden, co-lead of female athlete health and performance at the UK Sports Institute, who feels a lot more information needs to be gathered before conclusions can be made.
"At the moment we are speculating … there are definitely some physiological adaptations that you see more in women than men that are favourable for ultra-type events. But those need to be better established and more studies would need to be done."
Physiology, however, only gets you so far. The realities of ultra-endurance exercise - multi-day events, sleep deprivation, extreme terrain and conditions, to name but a few – mean the journey to the finish line is as much mental as it is physical.
And for Sophie Woods, this is where women have the edge.
"It's not necessarily about being the fastest person at the start," she says. "It is about preparation, it is about mental strength and being able to continue to persevere when things go wrong."
During the New Zealand runner's record-breaking run of the Via Alpina, she was forced to expect the unexpected – from disruption caused by wildfires that made her route longer and more dangerous to swarms of horseflies.
"I was so tired and there were so many of them and I wanted to have a complete meltdown and just cry, but I couldn't because if I stopped moving, they started biting me," she says.
"I think women are really good at adapting and continuing and just knowing that once we start something, you've just got to keep moving until you get to the finish."
That view is echoed by Yngvild Kaspersen, who last month became the first woman to win the prestigious Ultra-Trail Mont Blanc CCC race in the Alps twice. She credits her victory to the "mental game" she puts herself through in training.
The Norwegian, who balances life as a professional runner with her job as a GP, also believes female ultra-runners are so strong because camaraderie in the community is unrivalled.
"We're competitors but we're also motivating each other, inspiring each other, pushing each other to do better in the races," she says. "If you see the podiums for the women this year [at UTMB], how close we are and how we're running together out there - that's very special and I'm very proud to be a part of that community and that group of women."
So can we explain why women might be more resilient?
Sports dietitian Renee McGregor, who specialises in athlete nutrition and hormonal health, believes the answer comes from the female body itself.
"The moment women step into puberty, we are dealing with a fluctuating hormonal system," she says. "We never ever give ourselves credit for that, it's just an accepted part of being female. But actually, it is an endurance in itself and I think that's probably where a big part of our resilience comes from."
McGregor, an ultra-runner herself, points to research that suggests female runners display more disciplined and even pacing strategies than men in distance races, maximising on what she terms the female "brain bank".
"I don't think women go into these races without a lot of thought and contingency planning," McGregor adds.
"For example, if you've been through a pregnancy and you've dealt with nausea, if you've had a baby and dealt with the lack of sleep or if you've gone through fertility treatment, you have to go through so much discomfort, but you know you can get through it. And I think it's that knowledge of 'I can get through this, I can find a solution'."
One of the biggest reasons why we cannot talk with any certainty about the potential physiological and psychological advantages that women may have in this field is because participation numbers are low, with women making up roughly only 20% of those on ultramarathon start lines.
Research by SheRACES, a network set up by British ultra-runner Sophie Power to correct gender disparities in running, suggests the reasons for this range from societal perceptions around women's abilities, to concerns around the time needed for training, or access to the right support at the events themselves.
Slowly but surely, however, things are starting to change.
Earlier this year, a trail race in New Zealand became the first UTMB World Series event to achieve a 50:50 gender split, while a leading UK race provider has launched a new initiative to target gender parity at its events.
And now, according to Dr Burden, society is talking about the limits of human performance in a different way too.
"Historically, the majority of the time it [the limits of the human] will be established from male models or male sports," he says. "Now we're starting to break it up into the limits of male performance and the limits of female performance and that's a distinction that needs to be made … but to make better comparisons, we would need more women taking part in ultra events."

When it comes to participation, visibility is key.
Kaspersen describes Rachel Entrekin's historic victory at Cocodona 250, one of the most demanding ultramarathons in the world, as an "inspiration" among the elites to "dare to try".
And at the amateur level, there are those like Emily Fairs, a 22-year-old ultra-runner who documents the realities of her training and races on social media as part of her mission to get more women of all ages on start lines.
"When it comes to endurance training, there are so many components that come into it and that we are fearful of but by seeing another woman do it you think 'right, if she can do it, if she has the tools, she has the knowledge, she has the ability to do all these crazy difficult challenges, then so do I. I'm no different to her. She's no different to me'," says Fairs.
Fairs says she has received thousands of messages from women about how her content has encouraged them to lace up their trainers, and believes recent trends of female success in ultra-running are just the start.
"When the proportion is so low, we have no clue what women are capable of. We're starting to see more women get faster and enter the sport and push themselves and break records. So, who knows where we'll be 10-15 years later down the line?"

Indian security personnel carrying batons and shields and accompanied by riot control vehicles surrounded the site of a planned opposition protest in Delhi on Sunday that is set to demand the resignation of the country’s election chief over a controversial revision of voter lists.
Authorities warned of traffic diversions ahead of the protest march and rally that will be led by Congress party leader Rahul Gandhi. The opposition says it expects hundreds of thousands of people to participate in what it says will be a major challenge to the prime minister, Narendra Modi, and his Bharatiya Janata party (BJP).
Opposition parties, student organisations and the youth-led Cockroach Janta party have held near-daily demonstrations since last month demanding that the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, step down over the voter list revision that critics say favours the BJP.
The Election Commission has denied favouring any party and said wrongly deleted voters can re-enrol, while the BJP has accused rivals of trying to undermine democracy by wrongly questioning legitimate electoral processes.
Analysts say the youth protests, and growing support for the opposition, form the worst crisis for Modi since he came to power in 2014. But his government remains stable and the next general election is not due until 2029.
The opposition parties have announced they will hold a nearly 1.5km march on Sunday from central Delhi to the Ramlila Maidan, a ground that is the designated site for their protest rally.
Visuals from news agency ANI showed riot control vehicles and dozens of security personnel armed with batons and shields outside the rally venue, where announcements were being made urging people to ensure smooth traffic movement and cooperate with police officials.
Delhi traffic police said a “large gathering” was expected at the venue, and traffic regulations and diversions would be implemented “as required”.
“People have started coming to participate in this rally ... we have ensured proper arrangements at the venue, and arrangements are also planned on the route of the march that will happen in a few hours from now,” senior police officer Rohit Rajbir told ANI.
The protests demanding Kumar’s resignation erupted after the Indian Express newspaper reported in September that his two deputies had raised several concerns internally about voter list revisions, registration procedures and digital systems.
The change, which began last year, removed over 130 million names from voter lists, including 28 million who died, 63 million who relocated and 30 million who could not be traced.
Opposition parties allege the deletions disproportionately affect Muslim voters and other minorities, who are unlikely to support the Hindu nationalist ruling party – allegations the poll panel and BJP reject.

A water security assessment project is being planned for the Kochi Corporation to strengthen the city’s water resilience.
The multipronged project, being developed by Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Palakkad, will address issues, including water scarcity and pollution, besides focussing on canal rejuvenation, sewage management, and flood mitigation. The project, which will be implemented with technical support from the Kerala Water Authority (KWA), is expected to be completed in six months.
Once completed, the project is expected to provide a comprehensive framework to guide the planning and implementation of water security projects in the city, said Athira P., associate professor, Department of Civil Engineering, IIT Palakkad.
‘Multidimensional assessment’
“Different parts of Kochi face specific issues, be it frequently interrupted water supply, flooding, pollution or an increase in the reporting of water-borne diseases. Water security in a region is assessed based on aspects such as water quality and quantity, water-related disasters and ecological factors. A multidimensional assessment is being planned,” said Ms. Athira.
The findings will be compiled into a dynamic model designed to help administrators, incorporating projections for the coming years. These projections will help identify the interventions required over the next 10 to 15 years, as climate and land-use patterns are expected to change in the city.
“The data will help identify the specific issues affecting different divisions of the Corporation. This will help formulate projects more effectively and identify the interventions required,” said Ms. Athira.
“Such an assessment assumes significance as several parts of the city face challenges such as pollution, water scarcity and saltwater intrusion,” the sources added.

On today’s episode of Variety‘s “Strictly Business” podcast, digital news entrepreneur Roland Martin discusses the growth of his “Roland Martin Unfiltered” program and how it gained momentum during the buildup to this last week’s historic midterm elections.
Martin’s daily political news and commentary roundtable program went on a barnstorming tour over the three weeks leading up to Election Day on Nov. 3. The show targeted key areas in the South and Southeast where the protection of voting rights, affordability, the relentless GOP attack on DEI and other issues had already fired up voters.
“Twelve cities in fifteen days. It was Little Rock, Arkansas. Fairfax, Virginia. Lansing, Michigan. We came home for a day. Then it was like Indianapolis, Atlanta and then we were in Jackson, Mississippi, Baton Rouge, Louisiana, Miami Gardens, West Palm Beach, Tallahassee, Florida. Back to Atlanta and Lithonia, Georgia again. Baton Rouge. then. Arlington, Texas. Dallas, Texas. Houston, Texas. Fort Bend County. And then came home two days before the election,” Martin says.
“It was absolutely crazy. the first week I had our 35-foot bus on the road. And then that second week I had that and the Sprinter [van] on the road. And we were flying into a city, doing the show, go to the hotel, put all of our suitcases in the Sprinter and then would just pack overnight clothes. They would drive to the next city overnight. We would then fly to the next city. Uber to the hotel, check in. Go set up. Do the show. Repeat, rinse, repeat. I was a show host, a producer, a travel agent, a logistical coordinator. It was crazy.”
Martin, an alumnus of CNN, TV One and Tom Joyner’s radio program, says the tour reflected the freedom and flexibility offered by working in digital media. And it all has the potential to reach viewers in a different way than a traditional news program.
“What’s so different from linear is that you’re really touching viewers. You’re really communicating with them. I’m not spending three, four, five, six minutes on a segment. The leader of a Kenyan doomsday sect has been sentenced to 200 years in prison for the murders of 190 children and one adult in one of the world’s worst cult disasters in recent history.
The sentence, comprising 100 years for murder by starvation and 100 years by direct homicide, came two weeks after the court in Kenya’s coastal city of Mombasa found the cult leader guilty of the crimes.
Prosecutors said Paul Mackenzie and his Good News International church ran a Christian doomsday sect whose members were ordered to starve themselves and their children to death to go to heaven before the world ended.
His accomplices threatened and beat victims to ensure they followed his orders. The emaciated bodies were found scattered in shallow graves and dumped in latrines. Some had been buried alive.
Mackenzie was arrested in 2023 after police received a tipoff, and weeks later authorities began uncovering bodies in shallow graves in the Shakahola forest near the coast in south-eastern Kenya.
In total, more than 400 bodies have been recovered. Many were severely decomposed and only 26 could be identified.
Mackenzie denied murder charges, saying he did not force the victims to starve, but the court rejected that argument.
The Shakahola tragedy has gripped Kenya since the discovery of mass graves in the forest more than three years ago.
It raised questions about how Mackenzie was able to continue operating despite being on the radar of the authorities since 2017, when police searched his premises.
In 2019, authorities shut down Mackenzie’s church and he relocated to the Shakahola forest, police said.
The case has also led to calls for tougher oversight of churches and other religious organisations in a country where religious faith plays a prominent role in public life.
Mackenzie, a former taxi driver, forbade cult members from sending their children to school and from going to hospital when they were ill, describing such institutions as satanic.
Cult members lived in makeshift homes of polythene sheeting and thatch that Mackenzie divided into areas with biblical names such as Jerusalem and Judea.
The plight of his followers began to emerge in March 2023, when a man told police his brother and wife had starved their children to death in the forest on Mackenzie’s orders.
Mackenzie was arrested but released on bail, after which relatives said he brought forward the date on which he told his followers the world would end. Police rearrested him and started combing through the forest more systematically and began exhuming mass graves.
Last month’s judgment covered 191 deaths while investigations into more than 200 other deaths are continuing.
Justice Diana Kavedza-Mochache said in a hearing lasting more than eight hours that in some cases children were isolated and denied food while their parents watched.
Mackenzie faces other charges over the forest deaths, including those of terrorism, which he has denied.
Prosecutors said that while he was in detention he also directed the deaths of 52 people in Kwa Binzaro village, about 18 miles from Shakahola. Mackenzie has pleaded not guilty in that case.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is embroiled in a spying scandal. Could the AI chipmaker survive without him?
Analysts say change at the top would be a big shakeup, but company would go on
Jensen Huang, the leather-jacket-wearing and autograph-signing co-founder and CEO of Nvidia, has made himself a seemingly inseparable part of the AI chipmaker.
But now that an investigation is underway into whether Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort, that tight control at the company's helm is creating worries about whether he could actually be replaced, if such a move were deemed necessary.
The investigation comes after the New York Times reported late last week that Huang had a close romantic relationship with Alice Huang, a Chinese tech executive who was spying on behalf of China. It's unclear when he met the executive of Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed, but the two were photographed together in 2024.
Nvidia's board said Sunday it had no reason to believe that state or company secrets were compromised, but was undertaking an independent investigation in light of the reports. U.S. House Republican committee leaders have also called on Huang to sit for a briefing on his relationship with the woman.
In a message to his staff, Huang admitted to having an affair and apologized to his family and colleagues for breaking their trust.
"I am fully committed to Nvidia and will work to earn back your confidence," he wrote.
Huang will stay on as CEO while the investigation takes place. But if the board were to oust him, or if he changed course and stepped down, tech analysts like Dan Ives say finding someone to take his place would be nearly impossible.
"In my opinion, Jensen is a one of one," said Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co., a New York-based modern merchant bank. "Nvidia is here because of Jensen."
'The king of tech'
Nvidia began as a graphics card maker in 1993 until company leaders — Huang in particular — realized that its graphics processor units could power more than just games. The company pivoted to making chips for supercomputers in the early 2010s, betting on an artificial intelligence boom that wouldn't come for many years.
An early partnership with OpenAI led to a long-term relationship with the ChatGPT creator, which still relies on Nvidia's chips to power its technology today. Amazon, Meta, Google and virtually every other company building AI tools rely on the chipmaker's hardware to power their systems.
Worth about $4.5 trillion US today, Nvidia is the second most valuable company in the world, and invaluable to the AI ecosystem as a whole, according to Ives.
- Nvidia probes whether CEO Jensen Huang targeted by foreign intelligence as he admits affair
- Can AI be regulated? Why experts say government intervention is needed — but could be tricky
From his place atop the massive company, Huang became something of a rock star, routinely signing fan autographs at public appearances. One of his signature leather jackets sold for more than $1 million at an auction earlier this year.
"He's gotten to the point where he's sort of like the king of tech. Everybody listens to what Jensen has to say," said Bob O'Donnell, president and chief analyst at Technalysis Research.
Outside of his own company, Huang has also championed the AI buildout, financially backing companies like cloud computing company CoreWeave and Anthropic, maker of the Claude chatbot. He has also dismissed fears about an AI bubble and challenged apocalyptic warnings about the technology's existential threat to humanity, and has forged a close relationship with U.S. President Donald Trump.
Ives says the loss of Huang's advocacy would be a major hit to the industry if he had to step away.
Meanwhile, within the company, Huang created an unusually flat chain of command, with many employees reporting directly to him rather than to high-level executives. On a podcast earlier this year, Huang said as many as 60 people reported to him directly.
The company's site lists only a handful of high-ranking executives aside from Huang.
Two of Huang's children are also on staff at the company — his son Spencer is director of product for robotics, while his daughter Madison is senior director of product marketing.
No clear successor
With Huang having held control at Nvidia for so long, analysts say there is no clear successor.
"There's no one person or two people or three people that could replace Jensen. And that's a scary thing for investors, given this … black-eye moment that we're seeing," Ives said.
If Huang were forced to step down, Ives worries Nvidia would never fully recover from the loss of his leadership, given his integral role in the company's growth.
But others say with a firm as big as Nvidia, there are others who could take on the top job.
"You don't create a company that large by yourself, right? It's just not possible. There's a huge team of very strong, smart, capable people," O'Donnell said.
While he agrees that Huang's loss would be massive, he says the company's technology roadmap — used to plan the next few years — is already laid out, making any potential successor's job easier.
O'Donnell expects Nvidia is on track to keep its leadership position among chipmakers for now, and doesn't expect a shakeup at the top would change that.
Furthermore, with the board saying it has confidence in Huang, O'Donnell says he doesn't expect those members would try to oust him.
Still, if Huang does stay on as CEO, his grip on the company likely won't be so tight going forward, O'Donnell says, as other high-ranking executives are likely to take centre stage as spokespeople and dealmakers at least some of the time.
"It's hard to replace an iconic figure who just lights up a room," he said. But "if the board is smart, and I'm sure they are, they recognize they're going to have to address this so people can regain confidence in the company."

After knife-edge vote, New Zealand parties put off coalitions talks
- Published
Who will form New Zealand's next government remains uncertain after the country's national election on Saturday, with final results not due for another couple of weeks.
It's the tightest vote that the country has seen in years, with the incumbent National Party and opposition Labour Party neck-and-neck in terms of party vote share.
In terms of seats, a National-led conservative coalition, which includes the Act Party and NZ First, are projected to win a combined 67 seats - giving them a narrow one-seat majority.
As questions about other coalitions swirl, party leaders are remaining tight-lipped, saying they would wait for the final results before formal discussions.
Major parties on both sides of the political aisle were "likely dissatisfied with their campaigns", Max Rashbrooke, adjunct senior research fellow at the Victoria University of Wellington, told the BBC.
The opposition Labour Party, led by Chris Hipkins, ran an election campaign that "seems to have inspired few voters", despite going up against Christopher Luxon, a "historically unpopular prime minister", Rashbrooke said.
On the other hand, he added, the incumbent National Party also "failed to spark enthusiasm" even though it "should have been safe" given the country hasn't seen a one-term government in more than 50 years.
The election dealt a huge blow to National with the loss of some of its most senior lawmakers, including Finance Minister Nicola Willis, Justice Minister Paul Goldsmith, Transport Minister Chris Bishop and House Speaker Gerry Brownlee.
Act Party leader David Seymour has expressed interest in the finance minister portfolio, telling news outlet Stuff that National must recognise the voters' message and let its coalition partners play a bigger role.
"The government barely survived, it must now put its best foot forward in every step," he said.
The big winners of election night were "the more radical minor parties", Rashbrooke said.
The left-leaning Greens and the right-wing libertarian Act Party both saw new highs this election, while the Opportunity Party, a fledgling centrist party, scored a breakout victory. Having previously failed three times at getting into Parliament, it's now projected to get seven seats.
Opportunity's incoming lawmakers, including leader Qiulae Wong, arrived at New Zealand's parliament on Monday morning, for the start of what Wong said would be a week of "induction stuff".
Opportunity, which has rejected traditional political divisions, has said it's open to forming a coalition with either major party.
Whichever coalition they join, though, they would "really need to be comfortable with the overall direction the government is going in", Wong told reporters on Monday.
Wong said that although she has received calls of congratulations from Labour's Hipkins and the Greens' Chlöe Swarbrick, they have not had any discussions about coalitions.
Luxon, who had previously ruled out working with Opportunity, told public broadcaster RNZ on Monday that he wanted to talk to Wong "shortly".
Counting is still underway for nearly 400,000 "special votes", which includes those from overseas voters and people outside of their electorate.
These make up 14% of total votes, and are likely to be important in the final count.
"They tend to lean left, as voters casting special votes tend to be younger and more likely to be renters - and therefore more likely to be living outside their electorate," senior politics lecturer Claire Timperley told the BBC on election night.
"The overseas vote might be more likely than usual to be disaffected by the current coalition, given we've seen increasing numbers of New Zealanders moving overseas as a result of cost-of-living challenges."
Faced with a stagnating economy and challenging job market, a record number of Kiwis are moving overseas in search of better career opportunities. More than 114,000 people migrated out of the country in the year leading up to August.
Young people the BBC spoke to ahead of the election said they were "tired" and "cynical" about the future - part of what polling shows is a general grim mood across the country.
"In New Zealand as elsewhere, politics is splintering. But which parties ultimately benefit remains unclear for now," said Rashbrooke.
Final election results are expected on 27 November, with the official confirmation of MPs set for 3 December.

The Trump coalition is shattered - what will Republicans do now?
- Published
Republicans are in soul-searching mode after the coalition that powered Donald Trump to three straight presidential nominations imploded in spectacular fashion in the 2026 midterms.
The stunning election defeat immediately raised questions about the party's future post-Trump.
But there are no easy answers as Republicans face the choice of doubling down on Trumpism or trying to chart a new path forward in his final years in office.
The depth of the problem was captured by outgoing Florida Governor Ron DeSantis, who called the midterms "close to an extinction-level event for Republicans".
Others struck a more optimistic tone. Vice-President JD Vance, who blamed the midterm results on public anger over the war with Iran, argued the party could turn things around. Nevertheless Vance acknowledged the fallout will be messy.
"There will be a lot of infighting and arguing over what happened and why," Vance said.
The wide range of reactions on the right highlights deep fault lines in the party that formed around Trump's improbable rise to the presidency in 2016 and never really went away.
It's too early to tell which faction will win out. But while Republicans are still licking their wounds, the intraparty battle Vance predicted is already under way.
The party must decide whether it will be "centred on one figure, one guy, or on a wider set of ideas like conservatism that can win outside the deepest red places," Rina Shah, a Republican strategist, told the BBC.
Critics on the right - the "Never Trumpers" who opposed his first White House campaign - are pushing for a return to the Republican Party's pre-Trump roots, citing the historic losses around the country on election night.
But simply turning back the clock on Trump will be extremely difficult if not impossible to do.
The party has been wholly transformed during Trump's decade-long reign. Most Republicans have shifted to the right on domestic issues like immigration, and rejected the interventionist foreign policy of the George W Bush era that led to the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan.
In Congress, the more moderate establishment wing of the party that disliked Trump from the start has almost entirely disappeared, replaced by conservative Trump backers who echo his nativism and populist rhetoric.
That trend continued this year, as old-guard Republicans like John Cornyn in Texas and Maine's Susan Collins, both of whom clashed with Trump over the years, were voted out of office.
Three days after the election Trump appointed Stephen Miller as his new White House chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles.
The move signalled Trump has no plans to moderate his policies or message in his remaining years in office. Miller, who had been serving as the president's chief domestic policy adviser, is a longtime Trump aide known for his hardline immigration policies.
- With Stephen Miller pick, Trump readies for a battle 
  - Published1 day ago
- How America voted in maps and charts 
  - Published1 day ago
One of the architects of the Make America Great Again (Maga) movement, Steve Bannon, predicted a "civil war" in the party after the midterms.
Afterwards, he blamed the Republicans' defeat on the economy and "foreign wars". "I don't think we implemented the Maga programme," he said, calling on Trump to double down on mass deportations.
But other Republican strategists said the midterms were a wake up call for Make America Great Again (Maga) loyalists who want Trump's political movement to outlast his presidency.
"There's still plenty of Maga voters out there who have supported Donald Trump through thick and thin," said Whit Ayres, a Republican strategist.
"But there is also a significant portion of the Republican Party that's non-Maga, and that's a majority now."
Should Republican hopefuls distance themselves from Trump?
The party lost control of the House and Senate, as well as governorships and state legislatures in red states like Texas and Kansas where Democrats had been shut out of power for decades - and where Trump won by double digits when he was on the ballot.
The stunning upsets underscored the fickle nature of political coalitions.
Trump expanded the Republican base in 2024, increasing support with Latinos and younger voters among other key groups. Republicans hailed the gains as a sign of future strength for the party.
Just two years later, the party lost ground with nearly every critical voting bloc. According to a New York Times analysis of voter data, Latino support for Democratic candidates increased by 29 percentage points from 2024-26. Support from young voters 18-29 years old increased by 33 points.
The swings reflected polling ahead of the midterms that found widespread disapproval with Trump's handling of the economy, immigration and the war with Iran.
Democrats also capitalised on a public perception that the Trump family and administration is rife with self-dealing and corruption. The president's focus on the White House ballroom and other Washington construction projects also contributed to a sense among voters that he was more focused on his legacy than addressing affordability issues.
It's a sentiment shared by Benjamin Shrader, the leader of the Young Republicans in Austin, who was still shell-shocked when he spoke to the BBC in Texas the morning after his party was almost wiped out in the state by a Democratic "blue tsunami".
Shrader said Trump was still a "force of nature" when asked to reflect on how the president had used his first public appearance after the results to show off the White House ballroom project.
He hesitated before adding: "I would focus on issues that are not ballrooms, that are not renaming things. I would focus on what matters."
The evidence in the immediate aftermath of the midterms suggests that Republicans could benefit by distancing themselves from Trump ahead of 2028.
'Vance was the favourite - now the race is wide open'
Vance tried to thread the needle with his midterm assessment blaming the Iran war and calling for a return to "America First." It was a nuanced critique that broke with Trump on an unpopular war, but embraced a broader political brand that remains popular with the Maga base.
Trump's next moves on Iran will be watched closely by the party for their 2028 implications. An escalation would risk fuelling the concerns voiced by Vance and other "America First" proponents.
In his postmortem statement on X, Vance also echoed the growing calls on the right to reexamine US support for Israel. But he also signalled an openness to making some immigration enforcement changes. That clashes with Miller, a Vance ally who has speared the administration's second-term immigration agenda.
Party strategists said the midterm drubbing complicated Vance's path to the nomination.
"Before this midterm, JD Vance was the odds-on favourite to win the Republican nomination in 2028. After this midterm, the nomination battle is completely wide open," Ayres said.
Potential Trump successors have some time to consider their options, but they'll have to make up their minds relatively soon. Any 2028 presidential hopefuls will face pressure to announce White House bids in the next few months. Some could launch campaigns before the end of the year.
Vance's election analysis was widely interpreted as an unofficial signal of his plans to run. It will likely be a crowded primary field.
Other rumoured White House contenders include Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Senator Ted Cruz of Texas, Florida Governor DeSantis, former US ambassador to the United Nations Nikki Haley and former New Jersey Governor Chris Christie, to name a few.
In the next election cycle, Republican presidential and congressional candidates alike will have tough decisions to make on key issues of the day, from US support for Israel to tariffs to the AI boom.
Trump's power may be diminished as he enters the final two years of his second term, but he'll still have the loudest voice in the party over the next two years. It's unclear whether he will get deeply involved in the process or take a hands-off approach.
Trump has praised Vance and Rubio at different times, but typically deflects questions about who he'd like to see succeed him.
His endorsement will loom as the biggest wildcard in the 2028 Republican primary race.
"It remains to be seen who will jump into that race," Ayres said.
"But I think it's going to be a lot larger and more diverse than we anticipated before the midterm election."

A Royal Caribbean employee has been found by two Newport Beach fishermen treading water 20 miles off the California coast.
The cruise ship worker was rescued Friday after being spotted by Sean Norton and Grant Garrett, who had been fishing for marlin that morning.
"I'm like, 'Yeah, it's a human being. Stop the boat. Let's get all of our lines in,’” Garrett recalled in an interview with CBS Los Angeles.
The employee, whose name has not been revealed, told the fishermen he was a pianist on Royal Caribbean’s 14-deck Ovation of the Seas ship.
Norton said he and Grant lifted the man, adding that the pianist was “in total shock.”
"The only thing he said to me was, 'Thank you. I thought I was gonna die,'" Norton said.
Once the man was safely out of the water, the fishermen put out an emergency call, and Newport Beach lifeguards responded.
Local authorities believe the man may have gone overboard roughly nine hours before he was found.
"It was approximately 15 to 20 miles offshore, pretty much in the middle of the ocean,” Newport Beach Lifeguard Battalion Chief Adam Yacenda told CBS LA.
A spokesperson for Royal Caribbean acknowledged the incident, telling The Independent, “We are providing support and assistance to our crew member during this difficult time. To respect the privacy of our employee, we have no additional details to share."
The rescue occurred during a particularly strong El Niño this fall that is keeping the Pacific Ocean warm off the coast of California.
"You have this crazy super El Niño year. This guy was in the water for probably 10 hours, but the water's 76 degrees. A different year — no way he makes it,” Norton said.
The Coast Guard confirmed to The Independent that a “conscious individual” was rescued from the water. The man was reportedly hospitalized but is in stable condition, the Coast Guard said, adding that the incident is under investigation.
The Independent has reached out to the Newport Beach Fire Department for comment.

She lost her sight - now she is fighting to make history for Africa
- Published
Rukayat Taiwo Suleimon only took up sambo this year, but the Nigerian has already secured her place in the history of the martial art.
The sport shares strong roots with judo and wrestling, combining techniques such as hip and leg throws to take opponents to the mat, where they can be pinned.
Originally developed by the Soviet Union's Red Army in the 1920s, it was officially recognised as a combat sport by USSR officials in 1938.
Competing at the 2026 World Sambo Cup in Armenia, Suleimon defeated Uzbekistan's Charos Ortikova in the final of the women's 54kg category to claim victory on her international debut.
It was the first time that women with visual impairments had been included at the competition.
"Being the first female blind sambist in the world to win the gold medal makes me great," the 32-year-old told BBC Sport Africa.
"This is my first time in sambo and God crowned my efforts."
Suleimon's achievement was part of a breakthrough moment for African women in the sport. She and compatriot Elizabeth Aseso, who competed in the 59kg category, were among the pioneering sambists representing the continent in Yerevan.
For Suleimon, her gold medal is a reward for the hard work over many years which has seen her move from athletics to judo and now to the top of the international sambo podium.
"I really benefit a lot from sports and, despite my blindness, I achieve a lot," she said.
"If I [were] not blind, I don't think I would be at this level. I believe I will achieve even more."
From darkness to double glory
Suleimon's journey to becoming a champion has been marked by hardship and a determination to rebuild her life.
After failed surgeries she lost her sight in 2009 because of glaucoma, an eye condition that damages the optic nerve and can lead to permanent loss of vision.
The change in her circumstances affected her relationships, leaving her feeling isolated at a time when she needed support the most.
"People looked down on me. I would just stay indoors and cry," she explained.
"So many friends left me. They stopped communicating with me."
Her life began to take a different direction after she attended a vocational training centre for blind people in Lagos.
Through a friend, she was introduced to a para-athletics coach who helped her discover her potential in sport.
Since 2011, Suleimon has won more than 20 national medals across sprint events (alongside guide runner Stephen Oyelakin), discus and shot put.
She then began practicing judo and sambo.
"Since I [started] sports I have seen that where there is life, there is hope," she said.
"What sighted people can do, a blind person can do even better.
"I'm proud of myself because it's not easy to be a champion in athletics and in sambo. I don't want to lose the glory."
Her achievements have also become a source of pride for her family. Her twin sister Ganiyat Kehinde Suleimon says her sibling's disability has never defined her worth.
"She is someone we are all proud of. She is now a champion," Ganiyat told BBC Sport Africa.
"Her disability did not make her a liability to us."
For Nigerian sambo coach Olugbenga Adekahunsi, Suleimon's performance in Yerevan offered a glimpse of what she can accomplish with the right support and continued development.
"I see a lot of quality in her because she is very strong and the confidence is there," he told BBC Sport Africa.
"I believe she will become a great sambist."
'No support' for para-athletes
Suleimon says the recognition she has earned internationally has not been matched by adequate "support" at home.
However, her victory is the latest milestone in Nigeria's growing presence in the discipline.
Two years ago Samuel Oladele Kekere became the first blind African to compete at the World Sambo Championships in Kazakhstan, and Sodiq Ajibade followed that with a bronze medal at last year's edition in Kyrgyzstan.
"Despite making Nigeria and the whole of Africa proud, there is nothing to show for it," Suleimon said.
Her concerns reflect wider complaints from Nigerian para-athletes about limited funding, inadequate specialist facilities and insufficient institutional backing, despite their achievements.
Sherif Hammed, vice-president of the Sambo Association of Nigeria, says a lack of resources can prevent talented athletes from reaching their full potential.
"When athletes do not have facilities to train, they cannot compete at the world level," he said.
"It is quite disheartening and heartbreaking.
"People with disabilities, particularly visually impaired athletes, sometimes feel that because of their challenges, they have no purpose in life."
For Suleimon, a Lagos State judo champion, the journey to training is also an issue. Travelling across the city and covering transport costs make maintaining a demanding schedule difficult.
"I leave home at 5.30am to make it to training on time," she explained.
"It takes a lot of money and sacrifice."
Suleimon was unable to follow up her World Cup success at the World Sambo Championships in Tashkent, Uzbekistan, where blind women were again scheduled to compete for the first time.
Beaten in Friday's opening round by Moldova's Ina Cernei, she still hopes her exploits on the global stage can inspire others.
"I want to encourage my fellow blind Africans to believe they can do it," said Suleimon. "And I want to make my country proud again."

This is not the first time that Trump has said the Iran war is "militarily" over, but the circumstances for him are different now.
The president has hinted at de-escalation in Iran after a bruising set of midterm election results for the Republicans last week, which senior figures including Vice-President JD Vance blamed on the Iran war.
Ahead of the midterms, Trump had said US forces conducted what he described as "minor strikes" on an Iranian island in the Strait of Hormuz. However, in an interview with 60 Minutes that aired on Sunday, the president said that he did not currently see "any reason" to escalate the conflict.
Responding to a question over why he would not officially declare an end to the war, Trump said that some of the Gulf allies could still face Iranian aggression.
"We have some great allies there and we have to make sure they're not hurt," he said, suggesting that the US naval blockade on Iranian ports was helping to make the region more secure.
Global oil prices, which have fallen sharply since the midterms, dipped further after Trump's comments.
On Tuesday afternoon in Asia, Brent crude was more than 1% lower at $91.50 (£52) while US-traded was down by 1.2% at $85.82.
Trump hosted Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdul Rahman Al Thani in the Oval Office earlier on Monday, saying they had an "excellent conversation" about negotiations to end the war.
In a post on X, the Qatari leader said he held "positive discussions" with Trump and Vance on "reaching a deal and bringing peace to the region".
Efforts to broker a peace between Washington and Tehran have largely been held indirectly through mediators since the war first broke out following joint US-Israeli strikes in February.
Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates are among the US's Gulf allies that have been hit by Iranian strikes over the course of the war, in addition to the threat of strikes that have led to major air travel disruptions in the region.
Post-election recriminations over the US war in Iran are already placing pressure on members of the Trump administration.
Republican congressman Thomas Massie launched a strong attack against Trump's Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth on Monday over the war in Iran, requesting a vote in the House of Representatives to impeach him.
Trump has backed Hegseth, who says he is "not worried" about the looming impeachment threats, calling Massie's effort a "sham".
While the move is unlikely to succeed with Republicans still in control of Congress until January, Democrats have expressed willingness to impeach Hegseth once the new session begins and they have control of both the House and the Senate.
