As the results of the 2026 U.S. midterm elections rolled in, President Donald Trump — known for his frequent and brash social media posts — remained relatively muted, attributing the Democratic Party's sweeping victories to the fact that he himself wasn't on voters' ballots.
"I wasn't on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE! Thank you for your attention to this matter. President DONALD J. TRUMP," he posted to Truth Social, his social media platform, on election night.
But according to alleged screenshots some users shared on social media, Trump posted again later, ranting about how the voters had "failed" him and that there would be consequences to face as a result.
(X user @camolNFT)
The full text of Trump's supposed post read as follows:
THIS IS YOUR PRESIDENT SPEAKING. You read that right. YOUR PRESIDENT.
But since the woke mind doesn't want that, there's gonna be some changes around here. You failed me. There's consequences since you are an enemy of the greatest president to ever live.
American Crypto? Cancelled.
Super Intelligence? Cancelled.
Stimulus checks? Cancelled.
Epstein file releases? Cancelled.
Working to get gas prices lower? Cancelled.
Hope you like cancel culture. It seems like the liberal IDIOTS do. Why would you disrespect the greatest man to ever live. My son Barron came to my room upset. He is scared because he is a white man. Every white man should be scared. God bless some of you. PRESIDENT DONALD J FREEDOM TRUMP
Snopes readers asked us to investigate the legitimacy of the images being shared.
We found the supposed screenshots were fake.
Although the profile photo and handle matched Trump's real Truth Social account, the screenshot cut out the timestamp and engagement metrics. While legitimate screenshots of Truth Social posts do sometimes leave out that information (here's an example from an official Trump campaign account), omitting it for no apparent reason makes the post more difficult to verify. As a result we needed to look for additional information.
Searching Trump's Truth Social account turned up no results. We also checked multiple websites that archive the president's posts, even if they are deleted. Nothing matched there, either, confirming he never made such a post.
Additionally, Snopes frequently checks claims about fake Truth Social posts from the president, and as a result, we are very familiar with the his written voice — and we can check his word usage against archives of his real posts. While this fake post makes some effort to mimic his tone, it falls flat in a few spots. For example, Trump has not used the word "gonna" in a single post in 2026, while he has written "going to" dozens of times.
For further reading, we also fact-checked whether an image truly showed Trump fainting in response to the midterm results.

Quick Answer
To optimize WhatsApp privacy, hide your Last Seen, Online status, profile info, and status sharing under Settings > Privacy. Turn off read receipts, silence unknown callers, restrict group invites, disable link previews, and enable disappearing messages, passkeys, two-step verification, biometric locks, and end-to-end encrypted backups.
I don’t need to specifically tell you about WhatsApp’s popularity. It has billions of users worldwide, and it is the go-to messaging app for many people. Thanks to the network effect, most popular messaging apps haven’t replaced WhatsApp, even with better features and privacy.
One of the biggest reasons most people use WhatsApp, besides the fact that their friends or family are already on it, is that it is free to use. And since Meta owns it, free usually comes with a caveat. And that’s your data and how Meta tracks your WhatsApp chats. Although your chats are encrypted and Meta openly says it won’t use your data for advertising, you can talk to a friend on WhatsApp and still see relevant ads on other Meta platforms like Instagram instantly. Don’t you believe me? Just try it once.
Fortunately, WhatsApp also offers various privacy settings to keep your conversations private, prevent scams, and more. In this ultimate guide, we’ll cover all the privacy settings you need to enable on WhatsApp for maximum privacy. This guide includes all the methods, and I update it frequently and make changes if the features or flow change. Bookmark this page and revisit it anytime to keep your WhatsApp privacy settings up to date.
Table of Contents
WhatsApp Privacy Settings You Should Enable
Hide your Last Seen and Online status
If you care about your privacy and don’t want your people to know when you were online and when you last used the app, WhatsApp allows you to hide the last seen and online status completely
By default, WhatsApp shows the exact time when you last used the app and shows users when you are actually using the app
While these two features let others know when you use WhatsApp, they can also be a downside, especially if others are expecting an immediate reply when they see you online
Fortunately, WhatsApp lets you disable your last seen and completely hide your status. It also gives you more flexibility by letting you hide these from specific contacts, from your contacts, or disable them entirely for everyone.
Here is how to hide your last seen and online status on WhatsApp:
Open WhatsApp on your Android or iPhone and tap the You tab in the bottom-right corner, then tap Privacy.
Now scroll down and, under Who can see your personal info, tap Last seen and online. To hide it from everyone, select Nobody. To show it only to my contacts, select My contacts; to show it only to specific contacts, tap My contacts except.
Hide your profile photo, About, and Links from strangers
Like Last Seen and online status, WhatsApp also shows your profile picture and About to contacts. This also applies to contacts you have outside your network.
Fortunately, like Last Seen and Online Status, WhatsApp also lets you hide your profile photo and About info from strangers, specific contacts, or no one.
How to hide your profile and About from strangers
Open WhatsApp and tap on your profile picture in the bottom right corner of the screen, then tap on Privacy, and then tap on the Profile Picture option
Now you can hide your profile picture, About, and links. To hide it from everyone, set it to Nobody.
If you want to share with all your contacts, select My contacts. To share your profile picture only with specific contacts, tap My contacts except and select the contacts you want to hide your profile picture, About, and links from.
Control who can see and reshare your Status
WhatsApp’s status feature is slowly turning into Instagram Stories. You can now also reshare statuses on WhatsApp. However, unlike Last Seen, this feature is disabled by default.
If you accidentally enabled it and don’t want others to share your status, you can turn off sharing in the status privacy settings. From there, you can also turn off Facebook Stories and Instagram Stories to prevent your WhatsApp status from being shared on other platforms.
How to turn off status sharing on WhatsApp?
Open WhatsApp and tap on your profile picture, and from here tap on the privacy option
Scroll down, tap Status, then turn off Allow sharing and set your status to be visible only to my contacts. You can also remove specific people by setting up exceptions for contacts, or you can share only with specific contacts. From the bottom, also disable Facebook Stories and Instagram Stories to prevent your status from automatically sharing to Facebook and Instagram Stories.
Turn off read receipts
Even if you hide your online status and last seen on WhatsApp, read receipts can still show blue checkmarks when you read their messages. However, if you don’t want them to know you have read their messages and feel pressured to reply instantly, or if you want better privacy and to balance work and personal WhatsApp chats, you can disable read receipts.
Remember, if you disable it, you also cannot see whether they have read your messages. WhatsApp only shows grey ticks even if you read their messages.
Here is how to turn off read receipts on WhatsApp
Open WhatsApp and tap on your profile picture. Scroll down and tap Privacy. Scroll down again and turn off Read Receipts.
Stop strangers from adding you to groups
Another feature that WhatsApp turns on by default is the ability to let your contacts add you to any groups. This includes the number you have temporarily shared with users you don’t know, and once you add it to the group, your number will be shared with everyone in that group, which is a total privacy nightmare.
Fortunately, WhatsApp allows you to stop random people from adding you to groups.
How to stop people from adding you to random groups
Open WhatsApp and tap on your profile picture, then tap on the privacy option
Scroll down and tap on Groups, then select who can add you to groups. However, WhatsApp doesn’t let you set nobody as an option, but you can still do it by selecting My contacts except and selecting all contacts.
Silence calls from unknown numbers
Since WhatsApp primarily requires your phone number to create an account, once your number is exposed, anyone can contact you on WhatsApp. This is why many of us often receive spam business calls.
However, you can silence unknown calls so that you won’t get notified of random spam calls.
How to silence unknown callers on WhatsApp
To do that, open WhatsApp, tap on your profile picture, and tap on the privacy option
Now scroll down, tap on Calls, and enable the Silence unknown callers option
Make new chats disappear automatically
WhatsApp now supports disappearing messages, which deletes chats from both the sender and receiver after a set time. WhatsApp allows you to enable disappearing messages for individual chats or for the entire WhatsApp for up to 90 days
This is especially useful if you don’t want the other person to save your chats.
Since WhatsApp keeps your messages forever even if you delete your own copy, the other person’s phone still has everything.
When you turn on disappearing messages, WhatsApp also prevents the other person from taking a screenshot and reminds you when they try to save a specific chat.
How to enable disappearing messages on WhatsApp?
Open WhatsApp, tap your profile picture, then tap Privacy. From here, tap on Default message timer and select how many days you want to set for WhatsApp. You can select up to 90 days or even 24 hours.
If you want to turn on disappearing messages for individual chats, open the new chat and tap on the three-dot menu on the top right corner of the screen, select disappearing messages, and select the timer
Keep WhatsApp photos out of your gallery
By default, WhatsApp saves all photos you receive to your media gallery, including sensitive and personal ones. Even if you lock WhatsApp, anyone can see the photos you received by opening your phone gallery. This also uses your data to automatically download them and increases your storage usage.
WhatsApp allows you to turn off automatic media download and also lets you stop showing media directly from your photos app
How to stop WhatsApp from automatically saving media
First, you can turn off automatic media downloads. To do that, open WhatsApp and tap your profile picture in the bottom-right corner, then scroll down and tap Storage and data.
From there, scroll down and tap Media auto-download, then select all three: when you are using mobile data, when you are connected to Wi-Fi, and when roaming. Then disable all download options, including photos, audio, video, and documents. This prevents files from auto-downloading on Wi-Fi, mobile data, or while roaming.
How to stop WhatsApp from showing media in your device gallery
Open WhatsApp, tap your profile picture, scroll down, tap Chats, then under Chat settings, disable Media visibility.
Turn on two-step verification with a password
WhatsApp also supports two-step verification to prevent your account from getting hacked. While WhatsApp sends a six-digit SMS code for verification, someone with access to that code can log in to your WhatsApp account. However, you can set a second verification method, such as a password, to prevent anyone from accessing your WhatsApp.
Here is how having two-factor authentication adds better security for your WhatsApp account.
Here is how to set two-step verification with a password on WhatsApp
First, open your profile picture in the bottom right corner of the screen, tap on account option, and tap on Password
Now create a new password. Tap Create password and create a new password.
Once you add two-factor authentication, remember to add a recovery email. This is especially useful if you lose your network; your email acts as a secondary verification method, where WhatsApp sends a code to your email instead of sending a verification SMS.
Create a passkey for phishing-proof login
WhatsApp also added support for passkeys; if you’re not sure what a passkey is, we have explained it in a detailed guide.
Passkeys use your fingerprint or Face ID for authentication instead of depending on SMS or passwords. Setting up passkeys lets you log in to your WhatsApp account using your device ID, which is unique to you.
But it also comes with downsides: if someone else has registered a Face ID or fingerprint, they can also log in to your WhatsApp account, so keep note of it.
How to enable passkeys for your WhatsApp account
To enable passkeys, open WhatsApp and tap your profile picture in the bottom-right corner, then tap Account. From here, under the Login and Security section, tap on Passkeys. Then follow the on-screen instructions to create a passkey.
Turn on security notifications
Next, enable security notifications on your WhatsApp account so WhatsApp notifies you if someone switches phones, reinstalls WhatsApp, or changes linked devices. This could also mean someone else accessed their WhatsApp account and signed in on a new device. Turn on security notifications and confirm with the other person why the security key changed.
How to enable security notifications on WhatsApp
To do that, open WhatsApp on your phone. Tap your profile picture in the bottom-right corner of the screen, then tap Account. Scroll down, tap Security notifications, and turn on the option that says Show security notifications on this device.
Check linked devices and log out unknown sessions
WhatsApp lets you link and use your account on multiple devices. However, this could also mean someone could link your account to their device without you knowing. So, if you are suspicious about your account activity, you can check linked devices and sign out of any you don’t recognize.
How to check linked devices and log out of unknown devices on your WhatsApp account
Lock WhatsApp with your Biometrics
WhatsApp includes a native app lock feature that lets you lock it with your fingerprint or a pattern. WhatsApp also lets you lock immediately or after a set time. WhatsApp also recently rolled out a new feature to lock WhatsApp Web chats. So, I have made a detailed guide on how to lock WhatsApp on WhatsApp Web. How to lock your WhatsApp account with your fingerprint or Face ID
Lock and hide your most private chats
WhatsApp also lets you lock individual chats, not just the app. This way, you can lock or hide your most private chats. Here is how.
However, Locked Chat uses your device’s biometrics to lock chats. And if you cannot unlock the chat for any reason, you cannot get those messages back. Your only option is to clear the messages and unlock the chat, which you can do by going to Settings > Privacy, tapping Chat Lock, and tapping Clear Chat Lock. To lock the chats, follow the guide below.
Open WhatsApp on your device and, if you want to lock multiple chats on the home screen, select the chats you want to lock, tap the three-dot menu, and tap Lock chat. You can also do it for individual chats right here only.
Turn on Advanced chat privacy for sensitive chats
While disappearing messages remove your chat after a set period, you can turn on Advanced Chat Privacy for chats with sensitive content. This stops the other user from sharing or exporting your chats, and the media used in the chat won’t be saved in that person’s gallery. It also blocks the new Meta AI used in the chat itself.
Here is how to turn on Advanced Chat Privacy on WhatsApp
Hide your IP address in calls
WhatsApp also supports voice calls. Direct calls can connect your phone to another person’s phone, which can reveal your IP address and, in turn, your location. However, WhatsApp allows you to hide your IP during calls. Here is how.
How to protect your IP address in calls
Open WhatsApp and tap your profile picture in the bottom-right corner of the screen, then tap Privacy. Then scroll down, tap on Advanced, and enable the option that says ” Protect IP address in calls.
Disable link previews
WhatsApp also supports link previews, which show a preview of the website content. However, to do that, your phone connects to your website and sends a request from your IP address.
So it can easily reveal your phone’s IP address to the website, along with your location. You can also turn off link previews, which prevents those fancy images websites use for spam calls.
How to disable link previews on WhatsApp?
Open WhatsApp and tap your profile picture in the bottom-right corner of the screen. Scroll down and tap on Privacy. From here, scroll down again, tap Advanced, and enable Disable link previews.
Block floods of messages from unknown accounts
WhatsApp also introduced a new feature that blocks messages from unknown accounts. It blocks unknown accounts that send you high volumes of messages, which is especially useful if you receive frequent spam texts or your WhatsApp is being bombed with multiple messages.
How to block a flood of messages from unknown accounts
Open WhatsApp and tap your profile picture in the bottom-right corner of the screen. Tap Privacy, then tap Advanced again, and turn on the option that says Block unknown account messages.
Encrypt your chat backup
WhatsApp relies on Google Drive for your WhatsApp backup and iCloud on iPhone. However, by default, your chat backup isn’t encrypted.
You can turn on end-to-end encrypted backup with a passkey, password, or 64-digit key so third-party servers, including Google, can’t read your backup.
Here is how to encrypt your chat backup on WhatsApp
Open WhatsApp and tap your profile picture in the bottom-right corner of the screen, then tap Chats. From here, scroll down and tap Chat backup, then scroll down again and tap End-to-end encrypted backup.
Here, you can turn it on and then use your passkey. Remember, you’ll need this passkey whenever you back up your WhatsApp with this data. You can also use a password or a 64-digit key.
Limit what Meta AI can do with your data
Like any other app, Meta also offers AI features that let you summarise and read messages and also chat with Meta AI. However, because these AI chatbots can’t use your data publicly, Meta uses Private Processing features, which it says process your data privately for those AI features.
However, both of the AI features, including Private Processing features and web search, where Meta AI can search the web based on your queries, are turned off by default. If you turn them on, you can turn them off by default to prevent Meta AI from using your data, even though it is processed privately.

Reserve a username to keep your number private
Recently, WhatsApp introduced usernames on the platform, so instead of your phone number, you can create and share a username and let others contact you through it.
However, your phone number still verifies your account, but for better privacy, you don’t need to reveal it when sharing your WhatsApp account with others. In an aside in the New York Times Cooking video I watched recently, where Melissa Clark made her lemony white bean soup with turkey and greens, the food reporter and recipe columnist invited viewers to leave a comment telling her what they do with the kale stems. It highlighted this sweet, funny relationship between a media brand’s personalities and its audience, a warm-casual vibe.
I am not among the multitudes in the Cooking section's commenter army, but a few days later I was very surprised to see some of them in open revolt. I was even more surprised to see why: In an iOS-only beta, the Times is now using AI to allow subscribers to modify recipes.
Below the article announcing the change on October 23, commenters loudly aired their grievances, threatening to cancel subscriptions, asking who wanted this, and how to turn it off.
After four days and 172 almost exclusively angry comments, commenting for the story was turned off.
The Times doesn't share Cooking's subscriber numbers, but NYT executive communications director Jordan Cohen said the site and app were visited 514 million times in 2025, and its YouTube channel has over 1.4 million subscribers. Reading over the section's AI plans and thinking about how many bungled attempts I'd seen to mush technology into places where it doesn't need to be in the kitchen, I guessed that I would side with the commenters. Then I tried the new AI feature, and found that it worked surprisingly well.
My writing for WIRED over the past decade has shown me again and again that adding tech to a kitchen product is risky at best. I've repeatedly watched companies try and fail: Bluetooth connections for all the appliances, apps that lean too heavily on crummy recipes, toasters with optical sensors or touchscreens that still couldn't toast particularly well. Just about anything that was part of the "smart kitchen" tended not to be very smart at all.
Developing dependable, delicious recipes is hard, expensive work that can require a whole staff. Yet skimping can hurt the brand. Two notable companies with a deep bench—The New York Times Cooking and America's Test Kitchen—are cooking content makers. Recipes, which is to say delicious, high-quality, tested recipes, are what they do.
Since AI is often a lousy chef, giving it a role in the presentation of NYT's gold mine of content is a big risk.
Earlier this year, the Times allowed AI to help with a recipe-scaling feature (modifying ingredient quantities so "serves 4" turns into "serves 6") and converting from imperial measurements to metric—cups, tablespoons, and Fahrenheit to grams, milliliters, and Celsius. Now, in the iOS-only beta, a "customize this recipe" field appears just above the ingredient list.
If you want to make banana bread but tell it you don't have a loaf pan, it'll ask you what kind of pans you do have, then modify the recipe to suit. All the changes throughout the recipe are noted in a visible red-orange text. Over several days of testing, I saw how you can do relatively simple things like swap ground pork for ground beef, or make more complicated demands like asking it to tailor things to your dietary needs. The modifications it makes are very visible throughout the recipe. If you ask it for something too out there—like turning Eric Kim's gochujang buttered noodles into a cookie—it gives you a "hard redirect" and points you to a better-suited recipe, which in this case is Kim's gochujang caramel cookies.
"We put a lot of effort into trying to tell you when not to do something if it's no longer in the spirit of the recipe," says Camilla Velasquez, the general manager of NYT Cooking.
For its recommendations, the LLM looks at the recipe itself, the Times’ ingredient substitution guide, user comments, and then what it calls AI "drawing on our expertise," in that order. Velasquez says the AI should be a helper, not the main act, noting, "You shouldn't be chatting with it."
She explains that when the Times built the AI functionality, recipe editors helped create the original rule set, then evaluated how it worked at the end.
When I ask what this means for the jobs of 60 editors, writers, video journalists, and other employees—the team that creates the recipes people use and curates the vibe readers relate to—Velasquez stresses that NYT Cooking has been "hiring more than ever" and that it has "zero intention of publishing fewer recipes."
So far, she says people are mainly using it for ingredient and equipment substitutions, along with adjusting recipes for dietary needs. "Some people use the chatbot to scale, or they'll scale to match an ingredient," giving the example of someone who had only one cup of oil for a recipe that needed more.
As a food writer whose career has taken some substantial turns due to AI recently, I wouldn't say I've been clamoring for this, but I find the Times’ measured approach works pretty well.
I started testing it out by making chicken and dumplings using a five-star Alison Roman recipe with more than 6,000 ratings. I asked the AI tool to swap out bone-in, skin-on chicken thighs for boneless, skinless breasts. It thought about it for a moment—"simmering" in AI Cooking patois—and then offered up "Chicken Breast and Dumplings," with the "breast" in the title rendered in the red-orange color that indicates a modification. Just below the title, it said it was "Joseph's version made with AI. Not tested or endorsed by the original recipe's creators." Along with those visible changes, I could also toggle back and forth between my version and the original.
Once I started cooking, things went smoothly. I'm a recipe follower, not an improviser, and the Times’ recipes are easy to follow. The modifications were too. I was also impressed by how the app flagged that the chicken breast simmering time would be reduced because it cooks faster than thighs, and since they don't render as much fat as skin-on thighs do, it added some butter to the roux. These changes were incorporated into the right places in the recipe.
It all made sense except for one bit. It suggested the shredded, cooked breast go back into the pot for about another 30 minutes while the sauce thickens and the dumplings cook. I saw this coming and, well, I wasn't going to do that to my dinner. I put a handful of shredded meat in as directed so I could see what happened and reserved the rest. The shredded bits that were in for that extra half hour weren’t bad per se, but their texture was notably less succulent than what I'd reserved and way less than thighs would be.
This was the largest issue I encountered in all of my testing. If I had been the creator of the Times' original recipe, I'm not sure how I'd feel about the option to use a breast instead of thighs, which is not unheard of, but not very common in classic chicken and dumpling recipes. Perhaps it's something that could be fine-tuned or simply not offered as an option.
From there, it was fairly smooth sailing. I had it turn a Francis Lam roasted mushroom and broccoli grain bowl into a roasted mushroom, cauliflower, and squash grain bowl. The crucifer crisscross was an easy one-to-one, but I also told it to add a pound of delicata squash. It had me slice the squash into half moons so everything would finish at the same time, then upped the total amount of olive oil. Lam's poetic voice was preserved in both versions of the recipe, telling you to heat the olive oil "until it slips around the pan like water" before adding beaten eggs for festive dish-topping egg ribbons. My buddy Dave had come by for cribbage night, and this made for an enjoyable, healthy, pregame dinner before he went on to skunk me twice.
I'd been curious how it would handle batters, and it capably transformed Yewande Komolafe’s Toasted Sesame and Scallion Waffles into a yeasted version, which, unlike the original, gets an overnight in the fridge, letting the active dry yeast get bubbly and add an appealing tang.
A friend suggested Colu Henry's pasta and chickpea stew. I swapped canned diced tomatoes I had in my pantry for whole, and asked it to "add more vegetables." It gave options in line with the recipe—carrots, celery, onion, zucchini, mushrooms, and extra greens—then put what I chose into the right spots throughout the procedure so everything went in at the right time. It made for a healthy, hearty dinner.
Having been to the Portland Fermentation Festival recently and wanting guidance on incorporating a few extra ingredients, particularly garlic, into my sauerkraut, I used the AI to modify Lidey Heuck's original, saying "add carrots, garlic, and kale," which it suggested grating, thin slicing, and mincing, respectively, all in the right-feeling proportions. It also added more salt, since I was making more kraut. The big jar is sitting next to me as I type, and while it's several days from being ready, a sniff test tells me it's on its way to being a good batch.
Finally, I turned Sue Li's peanut noodles with spicy tofu into peanut udon with tofu, whitefish, and cucumber. I started by asking it to make the original less spicy, add veggies, and "keep the tofu," but add some good-looking rockfish I found at the grocery store. Impressively, since the fish was an add-on, it had me cook it, then set it aside and wipe out the pan (!) before cooking the tofu. Since I swapped udon for the original bucatini, it customized the noodle-cooking guidance, too.
It seems pretty natural that the Cooking section ran into some resistance when launching this feature. The NYT employs some of the best recipe creators in the business. Using AI to help us make substitutions is helpful, and the way the app integrates those changes into the recipes is impressive, but this tinkering with the original is essentially a subtractive process. How many of us are going to make substitutions and land on something better than Melissa Clark, Yewande Komolafe, or Francis Lam set out to make by design?
Instead, it's saving us a trip to the store, or helping us use something we have on hand, or making it gluten-free, serving as a good and rare example of how you can use technology to make a product incrementally better.
It also sounds like the commenters’ concerns have been heard. Velasquez let me know right away when we spoke that people will be able to hide the AI feature in the app if they want. The Times is also keeping the whole thing in iOS-only beta for now, and not saying when it would be available on other platforms.
That bond that you can see between the Cooking team and its users is a pretty sweet thing. Deep down, I'm guessing the upset Cooking commenters felt worried they were going to lose some of that human connection. I hope it never goes away.

The National Stock Exchange (NSE) on November 9 announced plans for a new headquarters in Mumbai, with renowned architect Hafeez Contractor set to design the proposed building. In a post on X, the exchange said the new headquarters would be located in Bandra Kurla Complex (BKC) and would represent a new addition to Mumbai's skyline. The proposed structure aims to symbolise innovation, ambition and India's growing stature in global financial markets. The building will come up on plots C-81 and C-82 in BKC's G Block, covering approximately 10,995 square metres. The Mumbai Metropolitan Region Development Authority (MMRDA) has allotted the land to NSE on an 80-year lease. An architectural video released alongside the announcement offers a glimpse of the proposed building's exterior and interiors. The design features a distinctive angular structure, a large blue globe displaying the NSE logo near the entrance, a glass-fronted facade and landscaped outdoor areas. It also includes separate drop-off zones for visitors and staff. The proposed interiors feature a spacious main reception area, a public atrium and an experience centre with open spaces, multiple levels and greenery. The visualisation also showcases a dedicated listing hall with a large display screen, arranged seating and a central presentation area. Other proposed facilities include office workstations with large windows and a market surveillance room equipped with multiple screens and monitoring desks. The video also offers a glimpse of open corridors, reception spaces and areas designed for visitors and employees. Regarded by The New York Times as "The Man Who Draws India", Hafeez Contractor is a Mumbai-based architect and urbanist known for his work across India's residential, commercial and public infrastructure landscape. He founded Architect Hafeez Contractor (AHC) in 1982 and has since led the firm into a team of more than 600 professionals. Its portfolio spans residential townships, business parks, educational campuses, hospitals, sports stadiums and several public projects. Contractor's architectural approach focuses on addressing India's infrastructure requirements while aspiring to meet global standards. His work includes several prominent developments, such as DY Patil Stadium in Navi Mumbai, DLF Cyber City in Gurugram and Hiranandani Gardens in Powai, Mumbai. His residential projects across the country have also influenced the aspirations of India's growing middle class, particularly through the promotion of high-rise living and gated-community housing as defining features of urban development. Beyond architecture, Contractor's work has also influenced housing and urban policy in India. His collaboration with Shiv Shahi Punarvasan Prakalp Ltd. (SSPPL) helped establish a policy model that offered free housing to slum dwellers through developer incentives. This approach contributed to landmark high-rise developments in Mumbai, including the Imperial Towers, standing at 253 metres, and Minerva Towers, at 300 metres, according to his official website, Hafeez Contractor. Contractor's contributions to architecture have earned him two honorary doctorates: a Doctorate in Architecture in 2012 from Jawaharlal Nehru Architecture and Fine Arts University, Hyderabad, and a Doctorate in Housing in 2014 from Rai University, Ahmedabad. He has received more than 75 national and international awards, including the CWAB Architect of the Year award between 2006 and 2013 and the A+D Hall of Fame for the Decade Award. He has also been featured twice in India Today's Most Powerful Indians list over the last decade. His work across residential, commercial, educational and hospitality projects has earned him several awards. In 2016, Contractor was conferred the Padma Bhushan, one of India's highest civilian honours, in recognition of his contribution to architecture. Contractor pursued his Master's degree at Columbia University in New York, US, between 1976 and 1977. Before that, he completed his Bachelor's degree at the Academy of Architecture in Mumbai, where he studied from 1969 to 1976. His early education was at Boys Town School in Nashik, where he studied between 1957 and 1968. His academic qualifications and professional achievements include: Padma Bhushan: India's civilian honour for distinguished service of a high order, awarded in 2016. Doctorate in Housing (Honoris Causa): Rai University, Ahmedabad, 2014. Doctorate in Architecture (Honoris Causa): Jawaharlal Nehru Architecture and Fine Arts University, Hyderabad, 2012. Mamata All India Trinamool Congress MLA Paresh Ram Das was arrested on Monday (November 9, 2026) from Kolkata’s Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose International Airport. Police said there were several charges against the Canning Paschim MLA including extortion and rape.
According to police sources, the Special Operations Group (SOG) of Baruipur district police began tracking the MLA after receiving information that he was heading to Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose International Airport. Mr. Das had defeated his nearest rival, BJP candidate from Canning Paschim by a margin of over 40,000 votes.
The team subsequently contacted the Bidhannagar Police Commissionerate, following which the MLA was arrested. Mr. Das is among the handful of MLAs that have remained with former Chief Minister Mamata Banerjee.
Mamata AITC spokesperson Kunal Ghosh said that as he was with the rebel camp, the police were inactive but when the MLA pledged his alliance to Ms. Banerjee, he was arrested. Recently, the MLA has put a post of social media, stating “Alvida Canning. We will meet again”.
Several leaders of the Trinamool Congress have been arrested after the BJP came to power in May 2026, which includes five former Ministers, including Bishnupur MLA Dilip Mondal. The list of former Ministers who are behind bars includes Sujit Bose, Indranil Sen, Ujjwal Biswas and Udayan Guha.
The Mamata Banerjee loyalists claim that leaders, MLAs and former Ministers who have joined the rebel camp led by Ritabrata Banerjee are being given a reprieve by the police while those still having allegiance to the former Chief Minister are being arrested.

అమెరికాలోని న్యూయార్క్ ఎయిర్పోర్ట్లో ఇమ్మిగ్రేషన్ అధికారులకు ఒక మహిళ పట్టుబడిందని, ఆమె తన దేశం పేరు “టొరెంజో” అని చెప్పిందని, అసలు ఉనికిలో లేని ఈ దేశం పేరుతోనే ఆమె పాస్పోర్ట్ కూడా కలిగి ఉందని పేర్కొంటూ ఒక వీడియో సోషల్ మీడియాలో ప్రచారమవుతోంది. దీంట్లో ఎంత నిజముందో ఇప్పుడు చూద్దాం.
క్లెయిమ్: న్యూయార్క్ ఎయిర్పోర్ట్లో ప్రపంచంలో ఉనికిలోనే లేని “టొరెంజో” అనే దేశం నుండి వచ్చిన ఒక ప్రయాణికురాలిని చూపుతున్న వీడియో.
ఫాక్ట్: ఈ ప్రచారం పూర్తిగా కల్పితం, అసలు ఇలాంటి ఘటన జరిగినట్లు ఆధారాలు లేవు. వైరల్ వీడియో వాస్తవానికి 2004లో ప్రసారమైన ‘ఎయిర్లైన్’ అనే అమెరికన్ రియాలిటీ టీవీ సిరీస్లోని ఒక దృశ్యం. ఫుటేజ్లో లాస్ ఏంజెలెస్కు ప్రయాణించిన ఒక అరబిక్ మాట్లాడే వృద్ధురాలిని చూపించారు తప్ప, “టొరెంజో” అనే ప్రస్తావన ఎక్కడా లేదు. కావున, పోస్టులో చేయబడిన క్లెయిమ్ తప్పు.
ముందుగా, ఈ విషయం గురించి ఇంటర్నెట్లో వెతకగా, ఇటువంటి ఘటన జరిగినట్లు ఎటువంటి విశ్వసనీయ వార్తా కథనాలు లభించలేదు. ఇక వైరల్ వీడియోలోని దృశ్యాలను రివర్స్ ఇమేజ్ సెర్చ్ చేయగా, దీనికి సంబంధించిన పూర్తి వీడియోను (ఆర్కైవ్ 1, ఆర్కైవ్ 2) A&E యూట్యూబ్ ఛానెల్లో 08 నవంబర్ 2024న “Airline: Best Full Episodes of 2024 MARATHON | A&E” అనే శీర్షికతో అప్లోడ్ చేసినట్లు గుర్తించాము.ప్రస్తుతం ఈ వీడియో ప్రైవేట్ చేయబడింది.
దీని గురించి మరింత పరిశోధించగా, ఈ వైరల్ వీడియో వాస్తవానికి 2004-2005 మధ్య A&Eలో ప్రసారమైన ‘ఎయిర్లైన్’ అనే అమెరికన్ రియాలిటీ టీవీ సిరీస్లోని ఒక దృశ్యమని తేలింది. ఇది ప్రయాణికులతో సౌత్వెస్ట్ ఎయిర్లైన్స్ సిబ్బంది జరిపే రోజువారీ సంభాషణలను చూపుతుంది. వైరల్ వీడియోలో ఉన్న దృశ్యాలు, ఈ యూట్యూబ్ వీడియోలోని మొదటి ఎపిసోడ్లో 22వ నిమిషం వద్ద ప్రారంభమవుతాయి. ఈ దృశ్యాలు బాల్టిమోర్ నుండి లాస్ ఏంజెలెస్కు ప్రయాణించిన, ఆంగ్లం రాని ఒక వృద్ధురాలిని చూపుతాయి.
ఈ వీడియోలో, ఆమె పాస్పోర్ట్ ఇంగ్లీషులో లేదని గమనించిన ఒక ఎయిర్లైన్ ఉద్యోగి, “సౌదీ అరేబియా, వాళ్ళు అరబిక్ మాట్లాడతారు కదా?” అని చెబుతూ ఆమెను అరబిక్ మాట్లాడే వ్యక్తిగా గుర్తిస్తారు. ఇందులో ఎక్కడా కూడా “టొరెంజో” అనే ప్రదేశం ప్రస్తావనే లేదు. ఆ తర్వాత సిబ్బంది ఆమెను అరబిక్ మాట్లాడే మరో ఉద్యోగితో మాట్లాడిస్తారు, చివరకు ఆమెను తీసుకెళ్లడానికి ఆమె మేనల్లుడు ఎయిర్పోర్ట్కు వస్తారు.
దీన్ని బట్టి, వైరల్ వీడియోలో చెప్పిన విషయాలు నిజం కాదని, వాస్తవానికి ఆ ఫుటేజ్ ఒక టెలివిజన్ సిరీస్కు చెందినదని నిర్ధారించవచ్చు.
చివరిగా, ఉనికిలో లేని “టొరెంజో” దేశం నుండి ఒక మహిళ వచ్చిందంటూ, ఒక అమెరికన్ టెలివిజన్ సిరీస్కు చెందిన దృశ్యాలను తప్పుగా ప్రచారం చేస్తున్నారు.

Mamaearth parent Honasa Consumer reported a consolidated net profit of ₹73.2 Cr in Q2 FY27, up 86.7% YoY, while operating revenue grew 35.9% to ₹731.2 Cr
Revenue growth outpaced the increase in expenses, lifting profitability from the year-ago quarter, although both profit and revenue declined sequentially
Total expenses increased 29.1% YoY to ₹652.4 Cr. Sequentially, expenditure declined 1% from ₹659.3 Cr
Mamaearth parent Honasa Consumer reported an 86.7% increase in its consolidated net profit to ₹73.2 Cr in the September quarter (Q2 FY27) from ₹39.2 Cr in the year-ago period.
The beauty and personal care company’s operating revenue rose 35.9% to ₹731.2 Cr from ₹538.1 Cr in Q2 FY26.
Sequentially, net profit declined 19% from ₹90.4 Cr, while operating revenue fell 3.3% from ₹755.9 Cr.
Honasa’s profit growth outpaced revenue growth on an annual basis, with total expenses increasing at a slower pace than its top line. Total expenses increased 29.1% to ₹652.4 Cr during the quarter from ₹505.5 Cr. Sequentially, expenditure declined 1% from ₹659.3 Cr. (The story will be updated soon)

3-year-old girl allegedly sexually assaulted in Goa; manhunt launched to trace culprit
Police have registered a case after a three-year-old girl was allegedly sexually assaulted in a dilapidated Mapusa building. CCTV footage is being examined.
Published on: Nov 9, 2026, 13:30:57 IST
PTI
Prefer HTon Google

An unidentified person allegedly sexually assaulted a three-year-old girl at a dilapidated building in North Goa district, police said on Monday.
The child was found crying on Sunday evening outside the building near a taxi stand in Mapusa, 9 km from Panaji. A passerby noticed the child and rushed to help her, following which locals alerted the police.
The victim was initially rushed to the Mapusa District Hospital in a critical condition and later shifted to the Goa Medical College and Hospital for further treatment, a police spokesperson said.
The girl's family sells balloons, and she had accompanied them to the Mapusa market for Diwali, a police official said. Superintendent of Police (North) Rahul Gupta, who rushed to the spot late Sunday evening, said efforts were underway to trace the culprit. The victim's condition was stable, he said. The Mapusa police have registered a case and are examining CCTV footage from the area to identify and trace the culprit, officials said.

After Michigan voters elected Democrat Abdul El-Sayed as senator in November 2026, a claim (archived) circulated online that he had failed the background check required for classified Senate briefings.
One X user named Jonathan Gregory who shared the claim wrote that El-Sayed's alleged failure would exclude him from some meetings as a senator. The user wrote:
Abdul El Sayed has failed the background check required for classified Senate briefings. The denial blocks him from any session that involves sensitive national security information. Officials who conduct the clearances reported that the review did not meet the standards necessary for access to restricted materials. The failure leaves open the question of what specific issues prevented approval.
Senators who receive classified briefings must clear the same process before they can attend. El Sayed's rejection means he cannot participate in those meetings. The decision places him outside the normal flow of information that other members receive. Americans who expect every senator to qualify for the same briefings now see one individual excluded by the clearance system.
(@TrumpNews_Baby, accessed via X)
The claim also circulated on Facebook (archived). Snopes readers contacted us to verify whether it was true.
The claim was false. El-Sayed could not have "failed" a background check "required for classified Senate briefings" because no such background check exists.
Congress members, including senators, are not required to pass a background check to gain security clearance and access classified material, according to a Congressional Research Service "Frequently Asked Questions" report about security clearances from 2023.
The U.S. Constitution, which lays out the requirements for senators, does not include a requirement for them to pass a background check to access classified information. According to Constitution Annotated, the Library of Congress' legal analysis and interpretation of the Constitution, the document has never allowed for changes to the requirements for a senator because that would undermine the legislative branch's investigative powers.
Additionally, federal law exempts members of Congress, including senators, from legislation that governs background checks and security clearances.
The false rumor may have originated as satire. Snopes previously linked another false claim about election fraud to Jonathan Gregory, who shared the first instance of the rumor about El-Sayed that we identified on X. Gregory labels himself as a comedian on his Facebook page, though his Instagram and X accounts don't display such a label. None of Gregory's profiles specifically mention the word "satire," though he has previously used the term near the very end of some of his posts — potentially as a way of hinting at the truth about his content.
We've published fact checks about other matters originating from Gregory's social media accounts, all of which involved false claims.
We contacted El-Sayed's campaign to ask if he had ever applied for, been granted or denied government security clearance before becoming a senator-elect. We also asked the national intelligence director's office whether it had ever granted or denied security clearance to El-Sayed in the past. We await replies to our questions.
Congress investigative powers allow members access to classified information
Members of Congress are implicitly allowed to access classified information because the U.S. Constitution gives the legislative branch investigative powers to inform laws and ensure they are being carried out. In practice, carrying out these investigations can mean that members of Congress need to access classified material, and the Information Security Oversight Office, which is responsible for the policy and oversight of the U.S. government's security classification system, wrote in 2001 that this is generally allowed (PDF Page 66).
It is important to note, however, that though El-Sayed and any other member of Congress bypass the normal procedure for getting security clearance, that does not give them unlimited access to classified information.
For example, the ISOO wrote in 2001 that though members of Congress were exempt from background checks and filling out the government's classified information nondisclosure agreement, they were not exempt from the "'need-to-know' requirement" (PDF Page 66).
For example, the office wrote (PDF Page 66) that members of Congress, "are not inherently authorized to receive all classified information, but agencies provide access as is necessary for Congress to perform its legislative functions."
Subject to election certification by state officials, the 120th Congress, which will include El-Sayed as one of two senators from Michigan, will be sworn in on Jan. 3, 2027.
For further reading, Snopes frequently investigates rumors relating to El-Sayed.

A promising new medicine against heart disease fails unexpectedly
For stories on the science of healthy living, subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.
An experimental drug doctors hoped would be the next big advance in preventing heart attacks and strokes failed a crucial test, researchers reported Saturday.
The medicine, which reduces levels of a particle in the blood associated with heart attacks and strokes, didn't protect volunteers in a closely watched study.
"I was shocked. I had high hopes for success," says Steven Nissen, a cardiologist at the Cleveland Clinic who led the study. "Cardiovascular disease is still the leading cause of death in developed countries. And so we really were hoping to find additional therapies that would reduce risk."
The research aimed to help people who seem to do everything right. They keep their cholesterol and blood pressure low, eat well, maintain a healthy weight, and exercise regularly. But many still suffer heart attacks and strokes.
"That sort of patient we see very frequently, and we were really doing our best to try to find a way to help those patients," Nissen says.
Many of these patients have elevated blood levels of a cholesterol-carrying protein called lipoprotein(a) or Lp(a), which has long been thought to increase the risk for heart disease.
"About 20% of the global population have elevated levels. And that's about a billion people. So it's a common disorder," Nissen says.
Researchers have been searching for a drug to lower Lp(a)
Until recently, doctors didn't have any drugs that could lower Lp(a) levels. But several drug companies have developed experimental new medications in recent years that can slash elevated Lp(a).
So Nissen and his colleagues gave 8,350 adults who already had heart disease either a placebo or a drug called pelacarsen, which cuts Lp(a).
The drug did suppress Lp(a) levels by about 78%, the researchers showed. But after five years, that drop didn't translate into saving people from suffering cardiovascular complications.
"Very disappointing, terribly disappointing," says Nissen, who presented the first details about the study at an American Heart Association meeting in Chicago Saturday and published more specifics in the New England Journal of Medicine and the NEJM Evidence.
Drugmaker Novartis, which sponsored the study, announced last month that the study results hadn't met its goals but without releasing specifics.
In a statement, Novartis said the study "provides meaningful evidence" about the relationship between Lp(a) and heart disease and may "help inform future approaches to cardiovascular management." "Progress in science depends on pursuing challenging questions and studies [like the pelacarsen study] play a crucial role in moving the field forward, even if the results are not what we had hoped for," the company said.
What went wrong?
The failure of the drug to help patients is stunning because so many scientists, doctors and drug companies hoped Lp(a)-lowering drugs would provide the next major weapon in the fight against cardiovascular disease, which kills more than 900,000 Americans each year.
"I think it's a big deal because the expectation was so high that this would end up being positive," says Harlan Krumholz, a Yale University cardiologist. "And so it was really jarring to see this."
Researchers are scratching their heads about what went wrong.
It could turn out that high Lp(a) doesn't actually cause heart attacks and strokes, but instead is a marker for something else that increases the risk.
There could be other reasons for why the study failed.
"Maybe you need to treat longer. You may need to treat earlier, before people have advanced hardening of the arteries," says Roger Blumenthal, a cardiologist at Johns Hopkins University.
Another possibility is that Lp(a)-lowering drugs may only help people with higher Lp(a) levels.
"Maybe a higher Lp(a) should have been required for entry into the trial," says David Maron, a Stanford University cardiologist who serves as the president of the American Society for Preventive Cardiology.
The pelacarsen study could also have failed because Lp(a)-lowering drugs may only benefit people whose blood pressure and bad cholesterol weren't as well controlled, several experts said.
Another explanation could be that there's something about pelacarsen, the experimental drug, that doesn't produce a benefit.
It's possible other Lp(a)-lowering drugs might.
Several other drugmakers, including Amgen and Eli Lilly, are testing other experimental Lp(a)-lowering drugs. The results of those trials are expected to become available over the next few years.
"The take-home message is the story's not over," says Karol Watson, a cardiologist at the University of California, Los Angeles. "It's kind of just starting."

‘Diwali is Diwali, Eid is Eid’: BJP slams Mallikarjun Kharge over festival remark
The row stems from Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge’s choice of words when he extended his Diwali greetings to people on Saturday
The Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) on Monday launched a sharp attack on the Congress leadership, accusing party president Mallikarjun Kharge of appeasement politics and of hurting Hindu sentiments by calling Diwali the “Eid of happiness”.
The row stems from Kharge’s remarks when he extended his Diwali greetings to people on Saturday, saying this is a major festival celebrated by everyone across the country as it is a “khushiyon ka Eid” that lasts for a long time.
“Diwali is Diwali, and Eid is Eid. Why is it that when it comes to Diwali which has its own sanctity, tradition and identity, you choose to call it Eid while extending greetings to Hindus?” said BJP national spokesperson Gaurav Bhatia on Monday, alleging that the Congress sought to dilute the identity of Hindu festivals.
Union minister Giriraj Singh said this wasn’t a one-off remark and linked Kharge’s remarks to the Congress leader of Opposition Rahul Gandhi and his family.
Congress leader Pawan Khera said Eid was often used as a metaphor for joy.
Hitting back at the BJP, Khera said, “Does anybody in the BJP have a dictionary in their house? I am sure they don’t. But they have a mobile. Can they Google what Eid means? Eid means ‘tyohar’, Diwali ka ‘tyohar’, Holi ka ‘tyohar’ - that’s what he means.”
Congress leader Rashid Alvi made the same point. “Clearly, when it comes to expressing joy, Eid is often used as a metaphor, much like how, when someone reappears after a long absence, people ask, ‘Kya tum Eid ka chand ho gaye ho?’ Eid is synonymous with joy,” he said.
Bhatia said Kharge’s choice of words reflected the Congress leadership’s broader approach towards Hindu religious traditions. “This is the DNA of the Congress party. First, indulging in blatant appeasement of the Muslim community and second, hurting the sentiments of the Hindu community,” he said.
The BJP spokesperson also took issue with Alvi’s reference to air quality, alleging that Congress leaders selectively raised pollution concerns around Diwali while failing to speak about other forms of pollution. “Discrimination and selective outrage are precisely what these people indulge in,” Bhatia added.
Accusing the Congress of following a selective definition of secularism, Bhatia said, “The Congress party’s definition of secularism is to silence the majority. You have to silence the majority and surrender to the radicals.”

Claude Code is leaking sensitive information on public GitHub instances thanks to a partial oversight in the way its settings files are handled. That’s the finding of AI security researchers at Apiiro, who discovered thousands of secrets, including database passwords, API tokens, and root logins, amid Claude Code settings files embedded in GitHub repositories.
The leak stems from the way Claude Code handles user approval for automated shell commands. When a user chooses the “Yes, and don’t ask again” option to approve running a command, that choice gets stored as part of a rule in the local “.claude/settings.local.json” file on the user’s computer. That rule is sometimes coded as a pattern, but the command itself is often written to that settings file as is, including any sensitive information that may be embedded within it.
This isn’t really a significant security issue if the settings file stays on the user’s local machine (assuming that machine doesn’t become compromised itself, of course). And Anthropic notes in its Claude Code documentation that this particular settings file gets added to the developer’s global .gitignore list, which usually prevents it from being shared publicly.
But that .gitignore setting isn’t reflected at the repo level, meaning the sensitive file can be uploaded accidentally if a repo is cloned to another machine or a folder becomes a repo later, for instance. In many cases, Claude Code itself will commit changes to the settings file without the user’s input, Apiiro writes.
Apiiro’s researchers found over 100,000 cases where Claude Code’s local settings file had been uploaded to a public GitHub repository. Of these, only about 1,100 from 63 different organizations contained secrets such as public API tokens, database passwords, or private keys. Even after these files are discovered and removed from a repository, the secrets can persist in forks of the original project if a GitHub user isn’t careful.

A man in his 20s showed up to a UK hospital with the hilt of a knife sticking out of his face. The 15 mm-wide blade hidden within went completely through his right eye and through his brain, with the tip of the blade hitting the top of his skull.
Despite the ghastly injury, the man was alive and conscious when he arrived. He could still talk and move all four limbs. His doctors described him as being in a state of agitation. On the Glasgow Coma Scale, he scored a 12 (E3 V4 M5), indicating a “moderate” brain injury, just one point above “mild.” He could open his left eye when told, but otherwise kept it closed (E3 score); he could talk and answer questions, but was confused (V4); and he intentionally moved away when pressure was applied to his body (M5).
In a report published Friday in BMJ Case Report, his doctors said they were concerned that in his confused, agitated state he may try to pull the knife out on his own. So, they swiftly sedated and intubated him. They put him on prophylactic treatments for bacterial infections, including tetanus. Then they used images to see what was going on in his head.
“Pull-and-see”
The blade was entirely through the right eye socket and eyeball. It traversed the left frontal and temporal lobes of his brain, passing through in front of—and without apparently injuring—the corpus callosum, which connects the two sides of the brain and is full of nerve fibers. The blade also missed the left internal capsule, which holds another bundle of nerve fibers.
In terms of damage to major blood vessels, doctors found that the blade was close to the left internal carotid artery, a major blood vessel, but didn’t seem to have damaged it. Doctors did find, however, that a branch of the middle cerebral artery looked to be indented by the knife.
After consulting with various medical specialties, the man’s doctors moved to emergency neurosurgery. They opted to remove part of his skull to directly see into the brain, but used a conservative “pull-and-see” method to slide the blade out rather than invasively excavate it. After it was out, the doctors saw no signs of significant hemorrhaging. The brain wound was cleaned and drained before surgeons patched up his skull. His right eye, however, couldn’t be saved. Given its extensive damage, it was removed.

US President Donald Trump on Monday (local time) said that the Iran war is "effectively over" militarily, but added that he would maintain the "status quo" of economically isolating Tehran, including through a naval blockade and a newly announced initiative to sever its overland trade routes. He made these remarks at a press briefing alongside UFC CEO Dana White, the New York Post reported. The US President said, "Iran, militarily, is effectively over. We're just keeping it the status quo. And we're doing that really at the behest of countries that are their neighbors. It’s got 301% inflation. It’s got problems like you don’t even want to think about.” Quoting Trump, CBS News reported, "Look, Iran, I hope we're going to be able to make a deal with them." He added, "But nothing's going to happen. And if we have to, we'll take it very seriously. We are so loaded." Continuing his warning, Trump said that the US was "fully locked and loaded with the best equipment ever made" if the situation were to change. However, he added, "We don't think there's going to be any reason to use it, however." The US President, who has renewed threats of fresh strikes against Iran in recent weeks, has reportedly deferred a decision to attack the country following a conversation with Qatari Prime Minister Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani. This came after he announced the new "Operation Iron Gate" to sever Tehran's land connections with other countries. Trump said, "Qatar, Saudi Arabia, UAE, Bahrain, Kuwait, and others would prefer the status quo that we remain as is. In other words, a continuation of the greatest naval blockade in the history of our country, probably in the history of the world,” in addition to Operation Iron Gate. He added, "So you have land and sea, total lockdown. I’ve agreed that Iran cannot have, and everybody’s agreed, Iran will never have a nuclear weapon, and that’s a non-negotiable point. They understand that. They accept that. They don’t admit that they accept it, and they will tell you that they don’t accept it, but they accept it 100%." Trump's remarks signalling restraint towards Iran also appeared to ease concerns in the oil market, with crude prices falling sharply in post-settlement trading, Reuters reported. Brent crude futures extended their losses in post-settlement trading on Monday, falling by more than $7 a barrel to their lowest level since late August. The decline came after Trump played down the possibility of fresh military strikes against Iran. Brent crude ended the session $5.75 lower, down 5.85%, at $92.57 a barrel. It continued to slide after settlement and was last trading more than $7 below its previous close. US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude futures settled at $86.85 a barrel, down $3.98, or 4.38%. The US benchmark also extended its decline after settlement, falling by more than $5. Brent crude had already dropped 16% last week, marking its sharpest weekly decline since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic. However, it remains to be seen whether the two sides will be able to negotiate an agreement to end the war or whether Trump will order fresh strikes. Eli Lilly’s GLP-1 pill Foundayo helped alleviate sleep apnea in two late-stage studies, but it doesn’t appear as effective as Lilly’s injectable drug Zepbound.
In a one-year trial of patients who weren’t receiving PAP therapy, a form of ventilation, those on Foundayo saw a reduction of 17.8 “events” per hour on the apnea-hypopnea index (AHI), a measure of the number of times breathing stops and becomes restricted while sleeping. One killed in Indonesia helicopter crash during firefighting operation
- Published
One person has died after a helicopter crashed into a river in Indonesia during a mission to fight wildfires in South Kalimantan.
An Indonesian crew member was killed, while two others on board - an Australian and New Zealander - were "found safe" and taken to hospital for treatment, according to Indonesia's disaster mitigation agency.
Investigations into the accident are ongoing, the agency said on Sunday, adding that it could continue its firefighting operations.
For months, parts of Indonesia have been battling wildfires that have shrouded large swathes of South East Asia in toxic haze. The blazes in forests and peatlands are fuelled by a dry season that has been exacerbated by El Niño.
Videos posted by Indonesia's disaster authorities and circulating on social media show the helicopter hovering over the river with a helicopter bucket - a collapsible container typically used to douse water over fires - before it nosedives into the water.
Other videos show rescuers later reaching the partially submerged helicopter by boat.
The fallen chopper, a Super Puma H-225, was owned by a company that disaster authorities had contracted for the firefighting operations, a disaster official told AFP.
The incident comes days after another helicopter crashed in central Kalimantan during a firefighting operation, killing three crew members.
The military said on Saturday that they had managed to retrieve the helicopter's blackbox, which would help their investigations into the cause of the crash.
Despite intensive firefighting efforts, the wildfires in Indonesia this year have been especially difficult to tame due to drought conditions exacerbated by a stronger El Niño.
The raging wildfires sent toxic smog blanketing cities in Indonesia, turning the air amber and triggering a surge in respiratory illnesses in cities across the islands of Kalimantan and Sumatra.
The haze also drifted to neighbouring Malaysia and Singapore, where it has triggered public health concerns.
Foreign governments have sent assistance to help with firefighting efforts, including Australia, which has deployed aircraft and 20 personnel including pilots and paramedics.

The Union Health Ministry has proposed amendments to the Drugs Rules, 1945, to immediately suspend the manufacturing licences of drugs declared Not of Standard Quality (NSQ) on specified critical quality parameters.
The government said on Wednesday (November 4, 2026) that the proposed amendments seek to enable prompt regulatory intervention upon detection of substandard medicines, prevent their continued manufacture and distribution, and strengthen the mechanism for ensuring compliance with prescribed quality standards, in the interest of patient safety and public health.
Under the existing provisions of the Drugs Rules, 1945, suspension or cancellation of a manufacturing licence is preceded by the prescribed regulatory procedure, including issuance of a show-cause notice. This may result in a time gap between the declaration of a drug as NSQ and the initiation of regulatory action. During this period, the drug may remain in circulation, posing potential risks to public health and making effective recall more challenging.
To address this regulatory concern, the Ministry has proposed a provision for immediate suspension of the manufacturing licence of the drug by the Central Licensing Approving Authority or the State Licensing Authority upon receipt of a government analyst’s report declaring the drug as NSQ with respect to assay, dissolution, related substances, impurities or sterility.
“These parameters are critical to determining the quality of medicines. The proposed provision aims to ensure that instances of non-compliance involving these specified parameters are met with prompt regulatory action, thereby minimising potential risks to patients,’’ the Ministry said.
The proposed amendment provides for mandatory corrective measures before revocation of the suspension. The suspension shall continue until the manufacturer undertakes an effective root cause analysis to identify the reasons for the quality failure and implements appropriate Corrective and Preventive Action (CAPA) to the satisfaction of the licensing authority.
Suspension can be revoked after the requisite corrective and preventive measures are implemented and then verified by the licensing authority. This mechanism will ensure that identified quality deficiencies are adequately addressed and necessary safeguards are put in place to prevent their recurrence.
“To further strengthen regulatory coordination and facilitate timely action, consequential amendments have also been proposed to Form 13, relating to the test report of the Government Analyst. Under the proposed mechanism, the Government Analyst’s report would be endorsed to the Drugs Controller General of India (DCGI), the concerned State/UT Licensing Authority under whose jurisdiction the manufacturing site is located, as well as the manufacturer and marketer of the concerned drug,’’ the government said.
It added that the proposed arrangement is aimed at ensuring timely communication of NSQ findings to the relevant authorities and stakeholders, thereby facilitating coordinated regulatory action and strengthening accountability across the drug manufacturing and marketing chain.
The proposed amendments follow deliberations at the 65th meeting of the Drugs Consultative Committee, held on December 20, 2024, and recommendations of the 92nd meeting of the Drugs Technical Advisory Board, held on April 24, 2025.
The amendments are expected to strengthen post-marketing regulatory surveillance, facilitate timely action against substandard medicines, promote greater accountability among manufacturers and marketers, and reinforce public confidence in the quality of medicines available in the country.
The draft amendments have been notified for public consultation, inviting objections and suggestions from stakeholders and members of the public within 30 days from the date on which copies of the Gazette of India containing the draft rules are made available to the public.

(Bloomberg) -- Haitian officials said they had killed a major gang leader in the capital as private mercenaries and at least 2,000 El Salvadoran troops join the fight to regain control of the troubled Caribbean nation. 
In a joint operation with other forces, Haiti’s National Police said they had attacked a gang stronghold in Cité Soleil and fatally wounded the leader of the “Boston” gang, Mathias Saintil, who died at a local hospital.
“One less gang leader,” Interim Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-Aimé wrote on X. “The gangs won’t be getting any sleep.”
Haiti’s gang crisis has drawn an array of international support, including the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force and a private military company run by Erik Prince, a former US Navy SEAL and founder of Blackwater. Prince suggested it was his contractors, known as the Task Force, and who work as a division within the national police, or HNP, that were responsible for the gang leader’s death. 
“Hail to the HNP Task Force,” he wrote on X in response to the Prime Minister’s message. “Nice shot.”
Haiti’s powerful gangs — which at some points have controlled more than 90% of the capital and forced more than 1.5 million people to flee their homes — are coming under increased pressure. 
Last month, after four El Salvadoran soldiers disappeared in Haiti and were presumed kidnapped, President Nayib Bukele began sending thousands of troops to the country and has vowed to crush the “wicked” gangs. 
On Wednesday he posted videos of El Salvadoran soldiers patrolling largely empty streets in Haiti. “It looks like the gangs don’t want to fight us,” he wrote on X.
Also last week, one of Haiti’s largest and most notorious gang leaders, Wilson Joseph of the 400 Marozo group, asked for the United Nations to establish peace talks.

At least 34 dead after Europe-bound migrant boat sinks off Senegal
- Published
At least 34 people have died after a boat carrying migrants sank off the coast of Senegal, the Senegalese Press Agency (APS) reports, citing an official source.
The Interior ministry said one person had been rescued, but the number of people still missing was yet to be established.
The small wooden boat capsized between the capital, Dakar and the northern city of Saint-Louis, as it headed towards Spain's Canary Islands.
Spanish migrant rights group Walking Borders recorded 635 deaths on the Atlantic route to the Canary Islands between January and May 2026, the highest toll among the routes it monitors.
Saliou Diouf, founder of Senegalese migrant aid group Boza Fii, told AFP that all the bodies recovered so far were Senegalese. The nationalities of other people on board was yet to be established, as search operations continued.
President Bassirou Diomaye Faye has expressed his condolences to the victims' families and urged Senegalese nationals not risk their lives on the dangerous sea crossings.
In a statement posted on X, he pledged to intensify efforts to dismantle the networks organising the journeys.
"We will relentlessly continue the fight against those who organise these crossings and the work that gives our young people reasons to hope here," he said.
The tragedy comes amid renewed concerns over the dangers facing migrant attempting to reach Europe by sea.
Walking Borders estimates that about 21 people died for every 100 who reached the Canary Islands during the period it monitored.
Senegalese authorities said they had intercepted another boat, on Friday, carrying 142 migrants attempting to reach Spain.
Those on board included 23 women, two babies and two other children. Police said the group comprised nationals of Senegal, Gambia, Guinea-Bissau, Guinea and Nigeria.
Meanwhile, a state of emergency was declared on the Spanish island of El Hierro on Saturday following a surge in migrant arrivals.
More than 3,300 people have reached the island in about 30 boats since the beginning of November, according to local authorities.
The Canary Islands have become a major entry point into Europe for migrants and refugees making the dangerous Atlantic crossing from West Africa.
The route has grown in prominence amid tighter controls and increased cooperation between European countries and North African states, which may have diverted some journeys away from the central Mediterranean.
Limited employment opportunities, family pressures and established migration networks are among the factors driving people to leave Senegal, according to the International Organization for Migration (IOM).
For many young people, the prospect of finding work and earning more abroad remains a powerful incentive, despite the risks of crossing the Atlantic in overcrowded boat.
Nearly one in four young people in Senegal was unemployed in the second quarter of 2026, according to the country's statistics agency.
The figure highlights the challenge facing President Faye's government as it seeks to create jobs for a predominantly young population that overwhelmingly voted for him in the 2024 elections.
In a statement on Sunday, Senegal's interior ministry said it would continue efforts to combat people-smuggling networks, including by strengthening cooperation with neighbouring countries.

Germans wrestle with what to do with Hitler's destroyed Eagle's Nest retreat
- Published
Perched on a ridge high up in the spectacular scenery of the German Alps lie the burned-out ruins of a mountain house called The Eagle's Nest, which is now at the heart of an intense debate about Germany's Nazi past.
Known in German as Kehlsteinhaus, the retreat was built by the Nazis in 1938, and frequented by Adolf Hitler and other high-ranking Nazis and their guests. After World War Two it was classified as a historical monument recalling the Nazi era.
Last month it was gutted by fire in a suspected arson attack, and some believe it should be completely destroyed, the site returned to nature and all memory of its Nazi past forgotten.
But others want it either partially or completely rebuilt, wary of the risk of turning it into a site for Neo-Nazi pilgrimage at a time when Germany is witnessing the resurgence of the far-right.
Germany has an "everlasting responsibility to communicate, to deal with our Nazi past", said Isabel Heinemann, professor of contemporary history at Munich's Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität (LMU).
But rebuilding the site completely, she warned, would mean putting "highly ideologised or highly ideological architecture" back in place.
Before it was burned down during the evening of 23 October, the Eagle's Nest had been a popular tourist attraction, owned by the state of Bavaria and operating for many years as a restaurant.
Visitors would take a bus and then ride the original brass and mirror-panelled lift through the mountain to the Kehlsteinhaus to savour the magnificent views above the town of Berchtesgaden.
Once there, they could eat sausages in the beer garden on the Obersalzberg at 1,834m (6,017ft) above sea level, overlooking the Alps.
Unlike Hitler's nearby summer residence, the Berghof, which was bombed in World War Two and demolished in 1952, the Eagle's Nest survived the war.
Tens of thousands of tourists visited each season, providing an important source of income to the region.
In the 1990s, amid concerns that the site did not do enough to confront the crimes of the Nazi past, a museum, the Obersalzberg Documentation Centre, was opened close by.
Around 15 years ago, a photo exhibit was opened in the Kehlsteinhaus about its history.
Although the Eagle's Nest itself was "largely destroyed" by the fire, according to police, the documentation centre survived unscathed.
The authorities have not commented on a possible motive, but a 33-year-old man with a history of mental illness has been detained in a secure psychiatric hospital on suspicion of arson.
- Man arrested after fire at Hitler's mountaintop Eagle's Nest retreat 
  - Published24 October
Some feel this is the moment to allow the site to fade into history.
"It's been torched now. It's been destroyed. I think they should just clear away the rubble and leave the mountain as it should be in its natural state," said Prof Sir Richard J. Evans, a specialist in Nazi Germany at the University of Cambridge.
That has happened with "quite a few other Nazi sites", he argued, including the bunker in Berlin where Hitler killed himself: "The bunker was filled in with concrete and a children's playground put on the top of it on the ground."
The Kehlsteinhaus was just "a Nazi vanity project" since romanticised by the name Eagle's Nest, he said.
But Bavaria's authorities take a different view about the site's future.
Both the state's interior minister, Joachim Herrmann, and its minister for the arts, Markus Blume, have spoken out in favour of rebuilding the Kehlsteinhaus.
"We can hardly leave a ruin standing there," Herrmann said.
Sven Keller, head of the Obersalzberg Documentation Centre, believes it is important not to leave the site in ruins, as that could encourage Neo-Nazi pilgrims, who would be able to hike up there completely undisturbed.
"We have quite some experience at Obersalzberg with what happens if we clear those sites. Hitler's Berghof was demolished in the 1950s, and in our experience, this does not remove such sites from the mental maps of people," he told the BBC's Today programme.
Nor does he believe "a one-on-one reconstruction" of the site is possible, and Blume has made clear on Bavarian radio that "it should not and must not cost the taxpayer anything".
Herrmann said they would look for a sensible solution in consultation with historians, given the historically complex circumstances surrounding the building.
Heinemann, who also heads the Leibniz Institute for Contemporary History, believes full-scale reconstruction should be "out of the question".
"I rather think we can document the state left by the fire and also document the historical remains of the Kehlsteinhaus, and then reconstruct parts in a modern design, to make clear the different layers of time that can be seen in this building," she told the BBC.
Germany and Austria have long struggled to deal with the fraught legacy of buildings and sites connected to the Nazi era.
With the recent rise of the far-right AfD and the Austrian Freedom Party, the debate over Erinnerungskultur (Culture of Remembrance) has taken on a new urgency.
A row broke out recently in Germany when AfD and conservative CDU councillors in a town in Saxony decided to ban "stumbling stones" memorials - embedded small brass plaques in the streets - to victims of the Nazis.
In Austria over the summer, a police station was opened in the house where Hitler was born in Braunau am Inn. It followed years of controversy about how the house should be used.
The Austrian government said the police presence would help prevent neo-Nazi pilgrims.
But others had wanted the house to become a centre of responsibility, actively confronting the Nazi past.
As one resident of Braunau am Inn told me, it was a delicate balance between how much to remember and how much to forget.
