When I was growing up, one of my favorite things to hear from an adult was that I was smart. It made me feel special — like I was capable of doing things that other people weren’t.
Why animals are smarter than we think
Who gets to be sentient?
In hindsight, that pride came with baggage: pressure to do well academically, and a sense of competition that wasn’t always necessary. Like many, I grew out of it. But many people in power still have a preoccupation with intelligence and conventional ways of measuring it.
Now, though, the way that we think about intelligence and markers of it, such as IQ, are shifting in important ways. David Robson, the author of The Intelligence Trap: Why Smart People Make Dumb Mistakes, says that traditional markers like IQ are not the only factors when considering how smart someone is. “There’s practical intelligence, which is much more about how good you are at planning projects and executing those projects,” he explains. He even says that people with high IQs tend to be more susceptible to things like confirmation bias.
Philosopher Jeff Sebo goes further, arguing that even focusing our discussion of intelligence on people is too narrow. He’s the author of the book The Moral Circle: Who Matters, What Matters, and Why, and he says that making humans the bar for intelligence is a mistake. “Intelligence in general is the ability to process information and solve problems and adapt to the environment,” he told Vox. Animals’ brains “might not look exactly like ours, but they can help animals solve problems and navigate their environments and adapt to their situations really effectively.”
So what does animal intelligence actually look like? And what can we learn from it? We answer that and more on this week’s episode of Explain It to Me, Vox’s weekly call-in podcast.
Below is an excerpt of my conversation with Sebo, edited for length and clarity. You can listen to the full episode on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, or wherever you get your podcasts. If you’d like to submit a question, send an email to askvox@vox.com or call 1-800-618-8545.
What is it about one animal’s intelligence that makes us want to protect it versus another animal that can end up on our dinner table? I think of dogs versus cows and pigs or dolphins versus fish.
There are many factors that shape how much empathy we have for non-human animals of various kinds. Are they cute and do they look like us? Do they remind us of ourselves? What role do we assign them in our lives?
We have more empathy by default for animals who play companion roles in our lives as opposed to animals who play commodity roles in our lives. This is why we can often have much more empathy for some animals over others, even if they display the same markers of sentience and the same markers of intelligence.
What’s a discovery about an animal’s mind that might surprise people? That might make us think of that animal differently than we maybe do?
There are really interesting studies showing that bees are capable of play behaviors. You can go online and see a video of a bee rolling a wooden ball around in a way that displays all the hallmarks of play activity. This is done seemingly for the pure joy of rolling a wooden ball around.
Likewise, there are studies showing that animals like insects have remarkable capacities for perception and learning and memory and adaptive, flexible decision-making and communication with each other. Animals that we might have written off as simple, as mechanistic, are in fact incredibly complex, seemingly sensitive, seemingly intelligent. I think that has allowed people to have a little bit more empathy for some of these animals than they otherwise might.
How much of what we call animal intelligence is actually just animals doing the things that people happen to be good at? What kind of abilities are we overlooking when we think of animals and intelligence?
We do tend to look for markers of intelligence that we associate with human intelligence and that can sometimes lead us to overlook markers of specifically non-human intelligence. This can happen in so many different ways.
For example, for many years, the gold standard for self-awareness tests was a mirror self-recognition test. You would put a mark on the forehead of an animal and place them in front of a mirror and see if they notice the mark and if they try to remove the mark and that can signal a certain kind of self-awareness.
It took us a long time to appreciate that this might not be the best way to test self-awareness in many animals for a variety of reasons. Many animals are not primarily visual, so we might need to think about how to perform this kind of test with their sensory modalities. Also, many animals might not particularly care about whether they have a mark on their forehead, so we should probably not treat an attempt to remove that mark as a standard for self-awareness.
We hear that pigs are intelligent or that octopuses could solve puzzles and we think, “Oh wow, we should be treating these creatures better.” I wonder, is there a problem with that argument? Because what happens to the animals that just never impress us?
I think that learning more about animal intelligence and challenging our preconceived notions about animals is good, but I think it would be a mistake to treat a certain level of intelligence — and especially a certain level of human-like intelligence — as a necessary condition for moral consideration.
That might lead us to extend respect and kindness to elephants and chimpanzees and other relatively human-like animals while neglecting the other animals who are conscious and sentient, capable of feelings and emotions, and that have forms of agency and decision-making, even if it might not look like ours.
I think that bar should be lower and should at the very least include consciousness and sentience.
This is making me realize that I may not be clear on what it means to be sentient. How do we know if an animal’s sentient or not?
This is very difficult to know for sure, because sentience is the capacity for positive and negative experiences like pleasure, pain, happiness, and suffering. The only experiences that any of us can directly experience are our own.
With non-human animals, we can collect behavioral evidence, internal evidence, developmental evolutionary evidence. For example, behaviorally, we can ask, “Do they nurse their own wounds? Do they respond to analgesics and antidepressants the way that we do?” And then developmentally, evolutionarily, we can ask, “In their ancestral environments, did they face pressures that they could overcome if they developed the ability to experience pleasure, pain, happiness, and suffering?” None of this is proof, none of it establishes certainty, but when we find a lot of this evidence in an animal, that at least increases the probability.
In terms of ethics and policy, what matters is we should not wait for certainty that someone can suffer before taking basic steps to address welfare risks for them. If there is at least a realistic possibility that someone can suffer based on the evidence, then we should take reasonable proportionate steps to mitigate welfare risks for them when we make decisions that affect them.
I personally don’t think of plants as sentient, but one of the things I love about my monstera is whenever it’s moved around in my apartment, it turns itself towards the sun. Does it make sense to call them intelligent when they do things like that?
At least in a certain broad sense, I think that it does. Plants are remarkably sophisticated. Many plants have capacities for perception, for collecting information from the environment, for learning and memory, for retaining some information, for communication, sending signals to other nearby plants, and even for adaptive decision-making, for growing toward things that are good for them and away from things that are bad for them.
Now, this might not mean that plants are sentient, but whether or not it feels like anything to be a plant, they might still be agentic and intelligent in the sense of being able to process some information, being able to adapt to their environment in some ways. I think that can be worth acknowledging.
What would that change about our world and how it functions?
I think that if we seriously considered non-human sentience and welfare, then it would have transformative implications for how we live, but ones that could be very good for humanity as well.
Consider how we relate to food and consider how we relate to wildlife. On the food side, industrial animal agriculture is a leading driver of animal suffering, but then it is also a leading driver of public health and environmental risks for humans. It creates more antibiotic resistance, more disease outbreaks, more extreme weather events via climate change, more biodiversity loss via deforestation.
Similarly, we build an infrastructure primarily for humans, and that can lead to a lot of unnecessary conflict with wildlife. Wildlife can die because they fly into buildings or fly into cars or are trapped in light pollution or trapped in parks with no exit for them if there is a flood or a fire.
If we simply considered their interests when building our infrastructure, then we might be able to build an infrastructure that can be good for human and non-human residents at the same time. But it does require considering human and non-human interests together when making decisions that affect everybody.

With temperatures dropping, the holidays approaching, and relatives preparing to invade the sanctity of our homes, November is the perfect time to find a little peace and quiet in front of the TV.
Fortunately, this month’s lineup of must-watch shows offers plenty of excuses to escape, including a dramatization of one of the biggest scandals in cryptocurrency history, a return to the dystopian world of Blade Runner, and a dark comedy about desperate parents who turn to surveillance technology to find their missing daughter.
There’s also a return to Middle-earth, a deadly game of international espionage, and a mysterious archaeological discovery that sets off a globe-trotting conspiracy. Plus, we're revisiting two groundbreaking television series that helped shape our fascination with government secrets, surveillance, and conspiracy theories.
As always, we’re not just chasing the biggest names or the shows everyone is already talking about (as much as we do enjoy The Gilded Age). Instead, these picks reflect the kinds of stories WIRED covers every day, from technology and science to politics and culture, and the unexpected ways they often intersect.
Whether you’re in the mood for a mind-bending sci-fi thriller, a twisty international conspiracy, or a classic worth rediscovering, these are the TV shows worth making time for this month.
Black Doves
Ben Whishaw (Q in Daniel Craig’s Bond movies) is one of the finest actors working today, even if his name isn’t quite as recognizable as it should be. Fortunately, Black Doves gives him plenty of opportunities to remind us why.
The deliciously twisty British spy thriller stars Keira Knightley as Helen Webb, a seemingly ordinary wife and mother who just happens to be secretly passing government intelligence to a shadowy organization known as the Black Doves. Whishaw plays Sam, her longtime friend and a professional assassin who gets pulled back into her dangerous double life. Then there’s the always-brilliant Sarah Lancashire (Happy Valley) as Helen’s formidable handler, Mrs. Reed.
Season 2, which arrived November 5, raises the stakes considerably as Helen’s husband prepares to become Britain’s prime minister, putting her at the very heart of government. It’s a wickedly entertaining mix of political intrigue, espionage, dark humor, and double-crosses, with a stellar cast that makes even the most murderous characters hard to resist.
The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power
If you thought things were looking bleak in Middle-earth at the end of Season 2, just wait. Amazon's spectacularly ambitious—and wildly expensive—prequel to J.R.R. Tolkien’s The Lord of the Rings returns for a third season, picking up five years after the fall of Eregion. Sauron (Charlie Vickers) has been busy building his armies and conquering much of Middle-earth, leaving the Elves, Dwarves, Men, and Wizards scrambling to stop him. Meanwhile, the Dark Lord is working on his most dangerous creation yet: the One Ring.
The new season promises plenty of political intrigue, epic battles, and the kind of jaw-dropping fantasy world-building that makes the series such a visual feast. Even if you know where Tolkien’s story ultimately leads, watching the pieces fall into place is half the fun. The first four episodes arrive November 11, with the remaining four rolling out over the following two weeks.
The Altruists
Remember when cryptocurrency was going to change the world? For a while, Sam Bankman-Fried seemed poised to make that happen. The young entrepreneur became a billionaire seemingly overnight as the founder of FTX, a cryptocurrency exchange that promised to revolutionize finance. Then it all came crashing down in spectacular fashion, exposing an $8 billion fraud that landed Bankman-Fried in prison for 25 years.
The Altruists dramatizes that astonishing rise and fall, with Anthony Boyle (Say Nothing) playing Bankman-Fried and Julia Garner (Ozark) portraying Caroline Ellison (no relation to Larry Ellison), his on-again, off-again girlfriend and the CEO of his trading firm, Alameda Research. Inspired by reporting from New York magazine, the eight-part limited series explores how two young idealists who embraced the philosophy of effective altruism—using wealth and resources to do the most good—became central figures in one of the biggest financial scandals in recent history. All eight episodes premiere November 19.
Dig
If Amy Poehler and Mike Schur taught us anything with Parks and Recreation, it’s that even the most mundane workplace can be a breeding ground for brilliant comedy. Their latest collaboration takes that idea to an archaeological dig in Greece.
Based on Kate Myers’ 2023 novel Excavations, the 10-episode comedy stars Poehler as Elise, an ambitious archaeologist who has spent years waiting for her boss (Hugh Laurie) to retire so she can take over the operation. When she and three fellow excavators (Geraldine Viswanathan, Antonia Thomas, and Fina Strazza) uncover a mysterious artifact that could rewrite history, they make the questionable decision to keep it secret. Naturally, things spiral out of control, drawing the women into an international conspiracy that threatens their careers—and possibly much more. With a cast that also includes What We Do in the Shadows’s Kayvan Novak (aka Nandor the Relentless), Dig delivers an entertaining mix of workplace comedy, historical mystery, and archaeological intrigue. All 10 episodes premiere November 23.
Blade Runner 2099
More than 40 years after Ridley Scott’s Blade Runner first introduced audiences to a dystopian Los Angeles, where synthetic humans are almost indistinguishable from the real thing, the franchise is still daring to ask science fiction’s most unsettling question. In this case: What makes us human?
Set 50 years after the events of Denis Villeneuve’s excellent Blade Runner 2049, this eight-part limited series stars Hunter Schafer (Euphoria) as Cora, a fugitive who assumes the identity of a Blade Runner, a special operative tasked with hunting down rogue Replicants. She’s forced to team up with Olwen (Michelle Yeoh), a Replicant whose days are numbered, to track down another fugitive whose secret could unravel the very foundations of their society. With artificial intelligence advancing at a dizzying pace in the real world, the franchise’s questions about consciousness, identity, and the increasingly blurry line between humans and machines feel more relevant than ever. All eight episodes arrive November 25.
Where’s Wanda?
How far would you go to find your missing child? For Dedo (Axel Stein) and Carlotta Klatt (Heike Makatsch), the answer is: very far. And well beyond the boundaries of what’s legal. When their teenage daughter, Wanda (Lea Drinda), disappears without a trace, the desperate German couple takes matters into their own hands, enlisting their tech-savvy son to help them secretly install surveillance equipment throughout their seemingly sleepy suburban neighborhood. What they discover is that practically everyone has something to hide.
The delightfully dark German-language comedy blends a missing-person mystery with a surprisingly sharp examination of privacy, voyeurism, and just how easily technology can turn ordinary people into amateur spies. The eight-episode second season premiered October 21, with new episodes arriving weekly through December 9.
The X-Files
The truth is still out there. More than three decades after The X-Files premiered, Chris Carter's groundbreaking sci-fi series remains one of television’s most addictive explorations of government conspiracies, alien encounters, and things that go bump in the night (or creepily squeeze through air vents). It also made pop culture icons of David Duchovny and Gillian Anderson as FBI agents Fox Mulder, a true believer in the paranormal, and Dana Scully, a scientist and skeptic whose job was ostensibly to debunk his theories. Anderson’s character also helped to inspire a whole generation of women in STEM, a phenomenon known as “The Scully Effect.”
The pair’s chemistry, and seemingly endless will-they-or-won’t-they relationship, helped sustain the show through 11 seasons (including a two-season revival beginning in 2016), two movies, and countless monsters of the week. With Ryan Coogler’s (Sinners, Black Panther) reboot, starring Danielle Deadwyler and Himesh Patel, recently receiving a series order at Hulu, now seems like the perfect time to revisit the original.
24
Twenty-five years ago this November, Kiefer Sutherland introduced the world to Jack Bauer, a counterterrorism agent who could save the country from almost certain destruction in a single day—but never seemed able to find five minutes to use the bathroom. Premiering just two months after 9/11, 24 became a defining television series of the post-9/11 era, with its real-time format, ticking digital clock, and seemingly endless cliff-hangers making it nearly impossible to watch just one episode.
Each season follows Bauer through a particularly hellish day as he races to thwart terrorist plots, uncover government conspiracies, and navigate an increasingly murky moral landscape. The Emmy-winning thriller also gave us one of television’s most recognizable phone ringtones (courtesy of the fictional Counter Terrorist Unit) and some truly bonkers subplots—including a memorable Season 2 encounter between Bauer’s daughter, Kim (Elisha Cuthbert), and a cougar. Yes, a cougar. Some of the show’s politics and attitudes toward torture haven’t aged particularly well, but its influence on modern action television is undeniable. All nine seasons are available to stream.
Time
This acclaimed British prison drama anthology explores the lives of inmates and correctional officers, with each season tackling a different part of the criminal justice system. The first season starred Game of Thrones’ Sean Bean as a guilt-ridden prisoner and Adolescence’s Stephen Graham as a morally conflicted prison officer, while the second shifted to a women’s prison, with Thirteenth Doctor Jodie Whittaker and The Last of Us’s Bella Ramsey leading the cast.
The third installment stars Doctor Who icon David Tennant as a veteran officer at a juvenile detention facility, where a violent incident raises questions about accountability, rehabilitation, and the psychological toll of incarcerating teenagers. Siobhan Finneran (Downton Abbey) returns as a prison chaplain, the only character to appear in all three seasons.

Why has Caf abandoned plans to hold Afcon every four years?
- Published
After a shock announcement 10 months ago that the Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) would be held every four years, the governing body of football on the continent has reversed course.
The Confederation of African Football (Caf) will instead retain the tournament's traditional biennial staging, with its president Patrice Motsepe saying the U-turn was based on "advancing, protecting and promoting" the interests of the African game.
The first indication that the frequency of Afcon was being reconsidered came at Caf's strategy conference in Cape Verde earlier this month.
Questions are now being asked about the decision-making process and what this means for the future of African football.
Why was the planned change controversial?
Afcon has predominantly been held every two years since its first edition in 1957, barring two three-year gaps in the 1960s and one year between the 2012 and 2013 tournaments.
On the eve of the 2025 finals in Morocco, Motsepe announced all that would change from 2028.
The South African said the shift to a four-year cycle was, in part, to help the global calendar "be significantly more synchronised and harmonised".
In recent years Afcon has been staged midway through the European club season, leading to recurring disputes over the release of African players.
Fifa general secretary Mattias Grafstrom was sitting aside Motsepe when the plan was announced, and critics highlighted that the scheduling change favoured football's world governing body more than the African game.
"I think the general sentiment around the continent has been that the two-year cycle has served the continent very well," Football Association of Zambia (Faz) official Sydney Mungala told the BBC.
"The idea of pushing it to a four-year cycle was a bit of a surprise, maybe a concern, to the bulk of the African federations."
- Afcon to return to two-year cycle after Caf U-turn 
  - Published21 hours ago
- Afcon to be held every four years from 2028 
  - Published20 December 2025
What were the benefits of the switch?
Afcon has developed into Caf's biggest revenue generator, with a profit of $114m (£85m) forecast for Afcon 2025, up from $75m (£56m) for the previous finals in Ivory Coast.
In its stead, an annual Africa Nations League involving all 54 countries on the continent was proposed. Motsepe described the ambition as creating a "world-class competition every year".
The idea was to move beyond Caf's heavy reliance on Afcon and develop a more sustainable commercial model which could support football development.
Yet the last time an ambitious alternative competition took place in Africa, it failed to deliver on its financial promise and was quickly ditched.
The Africa Super League, announced by Caf in 2022 to revolutionise continental club competition, and with projected annual revenues of $200m (£149m), was discontinued after just one edition.
Motsepe later acknowledged that commercial deals fell short of expectations.
"We didn't proceed as quickly because the partners that were giving us money were not giving us the deals we thought we would be happy with," he said.
Why the U-turn on Afcon?
The decision to move to a four-year cycle was taken at a meeting of Caf's executive committee last December - without being tabled at a general assembly where all member nations are represented.
"These kinds of decisions should be put to the general assembly, they should be debated and discussed for months at a time," Algerian journalist Maher Mezahi told the BBC.
"Afcon is the locomotive by which Caf funds all of its other competitions."
Caf subsequently asked its 54 associations to express a preference between proceeding with the four-year format or retaining the original schedule, and the executive committee eventually voted to restore the status quo.
Motsepe said the decision was in the "best interest of African football" and would contribute to the development and growth of the sport.
He also admitted misgivings about the new Nations League, with concerns it would require "several years" before it could make "the substantial financial and football development contributions" to help the continental game be "self-supporting".
How does Fifa fit in?
Fifa president Gianni Infantino first publicly proposed holding Afcon every four years in February 2020, an idea Motsepe rejected after he was elected as Caf president 13 months later.
That has not stopped the South African cultivating a close relationship with his counterpart and Infantino's drive to expand the Fifa World Cup to 48 teams - and in the process increase African representation at the tournament - has won him backing across the continent.
Yet the Swiss' position has been under threat since his plan to sell stakes in Fifa's competitions was leaked in July.
Since then Infantino has been busy shoring up his power base ahead of his re-election bid, including at Caf's strategy meeting this month.
"He came to Cape Verde to generate support, And, by and large, Africa gave him that support," Mezahi said.
"But I think they did that in a quid pro quo - they gave him the support in return for some concessions.
"And I think the main concession was the return of the Africa Cup of Nations [to a two-year cycle].
"It shows that Africa is willing to assert its influence and look after its interests, even in the face of the global game's interest."
- Infantino says he is backed by 'vast majority' 
  - Published6 days ago
- Does Africa still back Infantino as Fifa president? 
  - Published6 August
Why is Afcon revenue so important?
Afcon is Caf's financial lifeline, accounting for a substantial share of the governing body's income.
Morocco 2025 was projected to generate $192m (£143m), representing 66% of Caf's total revenue from competitions across men's, women's and age-group football.
For many FAs, Afcon's importance extends far beyond the tournament because they cannot always rely on consistent government or corporate investment.
"We have 11 [Zambian] national teams and only two are partly sponsored by government," Faz official Mungala said.
"The rest have to be supported from the FA's coffers. We actually fund some of these programmes from the support that we get from Caf and Fifa."
What about upcoming Afcons?
The 2027 Afcon is scheduled to be held in Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda from 19 June to 17 July next year.
Yet, on a visit to East Africa in September, Motsepe called for a "heightened sense of urgency" in order to make sure stadiums and supporting infrastructure are ready on time.
The next Afcon will be held just one year later in 2028 - a decision Caf made when planning for the switch to a four-year cycle and which it as has decided to stick with.
An announcement on where and exactly when the finals will be held is yet to be made.
Subsequent tournaments will be held in 2031 and 2033 to avoid clashes with the World Cup.
The proposed kick-off date for the Africa Nations League, meanwhile, is September 2029.
Motsepe's latest statement suggests the new competition will also be held every two years - rather than annually as he initially announced last December – but that begs the question of how space will be found for the fixtures to be played in an Afcon year from 2031 onwards.
While debate continues around the game's congested calendar, Caf's U-turn on scheduling has at least protected the tradition of Africa's biggest sporting showcase.
It also exposes, however, the challenge of finding a workable financial model which benefits African football as well as the demands of the global game.

Can New Zealand's new government win over disillusioned voters?
- Published
New Zealand voted in a new government as fog choked the capital, Wellington, on Saturday - and the mood was as palpable as the grey weather.
"It's pretty flat," 21-year-old Imogen Vlutger says. "There's this kind of apathy and a bit of dread."
"Tired. I think we're all tired," Symone, 28, admits.
"I didn't even vote," one man in his 40s sheepishly confessed. He couldn't bring himself to tick any of the boxes, he explained, declining to chat further.
"Wellington's a bit of a bubble," another voter says, expressing a caveat I heard often, before describing feeling disillusioned.
But polling shows this is a pervasive sentiment across the country: the national mood is low and faith in politics is even lower.
More than half the country no longer sees it as a land of opportunity, a recent study found, while a similar portion fears that the future looks even worse.
Many Kiwis feel the economy is in ruins, there are no jobs, the cost of living has become sky high, the sense of community that used to be a source of national pride is breaking down and there's no sense of genuine progress on policy solutions.
A record number of them are abandoning ship in search of brighter futures elsewhere.
Saturday's election also saw a record number of voters desert the two major parties, giving neither a clear mandate.
But it brought new highs for parties across the spectrum: the left-leaning Greens, the right-wing libertarian Act Party and the centrist Opportunity Party – the latter of which had never won a seat in parliament before but could now hold the balance of power with seven.
"You have voted to change New Zealand politics for good," the party's ecstatic leader Quilae Wong told Kiwis on election night. "I personally came into this because I was frustrated at the slow pace of change."
It will likely be weeks before we know exactly who will make up the governing coalition and what deals have been made to form it.
But this is only the first of many challenges facing whoever is the next prime minister of a country at a crossroads.
A perfect storm
New Zealand hasn't always felt like this.
For a long time, the country was viewed as a land of milk and honey – literally – for those who worked hard, with its people ranking amongst the most positive in the world.
A satisfying career, access to quality healthcare, and a close network of family and friends – which research suggests are the three most important building blocks of a happy life – were all there for the taking, University of Auckland Prof Robert MacCulloch says.
"The lifestyle was good," the world-leader in the study of happiness economics tells the BBC. "You weren't the highest paid, but you could get by nicely."
Not anymore.
Many who spoke to the BBC said the country's decline accelerated into a dive during the Covid pandemic.
Unemployment is now at an 11-year high and rising. For Kiwis aged under 24, things haven't been this bad in three decades: jobs are so scarce that one in three either cannot get enough work or have none at all.
Michael Dawson says he did everything he thought he was supposed to: finished school, studied a trade and obtained a qualification, and has applied for dozens of jobs.
But it's been a year now and the job market is so dire he hasn't had a single interview.
"It has sucked. A lot... I'm somewhat cynical with the way I think [about the future] now," the 20-year-old says.
Zainab Ali, chief executive of support service Youth Inspire, has never seen demand so high, with waitlists for its employment aid workshops stretching into the hundreds.
The young people who do make it through their doors on the outskirts of Wellington are disheartened.
"The things we used to hear from everyone's grumpy uncle around the Christmas table sometimes, our young people are now starting to give us that same feedback: like, 'What's the point?'"
Meanwhile, household electricity bills have jumped drastically, partly driven by global supply shocks. New Zealand remains one of the least affordable places on Earth to rent or buy a home. High inflation means every dollar is having to stretch further.
The island nation produces enough food to feed its population eight times over, but about a quarter of adults are skipping meals because the price of groceries – set by a supermarket duopoly – is among the highest in the developed world.
And the headlines are full of healthcare crises: long waiting lists, chronic understaffing, crumbling health infrastructure and climbing costs for patients. Few stories have captured the state of the system like the death of a man who collapsed in an emergency department toilet after a nine-hour wait in July.
"There's a segment of the population that are facing real material hardship... and then there's another segment of New Zealanders that are quite anxious that they could be next," political scientist Luke Oldfield, from Victoria University of Wellington, says.
Increasingly polarised public debate – around topics like Māori rights and the Treaty of Waitangi, healthcare for LGBT+ people and immigration – have added to the mental load for many in those communities.
"There's been a few groups feeling like they're being used as a political football," Dr Lara Greaves, who studies Indigenous politics, says.
This perfect storm is driving about 180 people to leave the country every day – a record-breaking exodus that is dividing families, shrinking communities and draining talent pools.
Siblings Sam and Emily tell the BBC that they love New Zealand but find it hard to keep finding reasons to stay. Their friends are leaving en masse and even their parents have considered moving to Australia.
"It's not just that you're being rewarded for going to Australia, it's that you're kind of actively being punished for staying here," Sam says.
There are still large parts of the country that feel differently, though.
At the nation's largest livestock saleyard in the town of Fielding, where farmers from all over the island have gathered, Stu Morton says the last year was the best he's had in his 30-year career.
The agriculture industry - which makes up about 3% of New Zealand's GDP - was struggling under the previous Labour government's emissions reductions scheme, he adds, but has turned a corner under the National Party.
He believes the rest of the economy will follow suit.
"We've been through those times where you're questioning 'Where's the future?'
"What helps is having a stable government... [and] it comes down to a positive attitude - appreciating that what you've got is actually okay."
How did we get here?
Many of these issues affecting New Zealand are global trends - and it's undeniable that Kiwis' standard of living is better than many others.
But these issues are having a corrosive impact on its national identity.
"It leads to a crisis of confidence about what New Zealand is and where it's going," Helen Clark, who was prime minister from 1999 to 2008, tells the BBC.
Her foundation surveys New Zealanders every year about social cohesion, and its most recent report found Kiwis - in particular young poeple - feel far more isolated than they did a generation ago, attitudes towards multiculturalism are souring and the population is becoming less hopeful.
Faith in institutions and leaders has taken an alarming turn: only two out of five New Zealanders trust the government to do the right thing, while less than half of the country trusts the courts.
"There's a feeling that, really, there's no-one who cares," Clark says.
The transformation former Labour prime minister Jacinda Ardern promised on issues like healthcare and housing when she was elected in 2017 never eventuated. Many other achievements - for example world leading smoking reforms, emissions reduction policies or Maori language initiatives - have been wound back by her successors.
Her legacy is dominated by polarising Covid decisions, as is Chris Hipkins', who was health minister before his eight months in the top job after Ardern's resignation.
The National Party came to power in 2023 promising to "get our country back on track" and rebuild the economy.
"You'd have to say they've had very limited success," political commentator Grant Duncan says. "And the Luxon government can only blame the previous government for so long."
National delivered the education overhaul it pledged, but the biggest moment of their tenure was the massive hikoi – protest march – led by Māori over their coalition partner's unpopular bill to redefine the Treaty of Waitangi. And then came the two leadership challenges Christopher Luxon fought off in the past six months.
There's a sense Labour had too much ambition, much of it costly and unfulfilled, while National doesn't have enough, having spent much of its time and effort wrangling their own flank.
Both governments say their plans for the country were stymied by crises out of their control – such as Covid, the Iran war and US trade antagonism.
But Duncan says that's not cutting it with voters. He's never seen the country quite like this before: "Neither of the parties has been able to field a really strong, inspiring leader. Both of them have a track record of disappointing results."
No matter who ends up taking the top job, Sam says he's not convinced much will change.
"It does just feel stale... a lot of the population probably feels like we could do a bit better," he says. With a wry smile, he adds: "I don't think it helps that they're two white guys named Chris."

France blames Iran for supermarket fridge cyberattack
Hundreds of French supermarket fridges were hacked in early October

France has laid the blame on Iran's Revolutionary Guards for a wave of cyberattacks that put commercial refrigerators and freezers out of action across the country last month.
The hacks that struck hundreds of French supermarkets in early October were among the most disruptive cyberattacks of the Iran war that began in February, a conflict that has been marked by scattered incidents of alleged digital disruption.
These have included hacks against the Los Angeles transit system in March, against US water treatment plants in July and against ships bound for the United States in August.
French officials made the accusation on Monday, while at the same time warning that Iran would face consequences.
Jean-Noël Barrot, the French Foreign Minister, said the Iranian ambassador had been summoned to France's foreign ministry. He also threatened further EU sanctions against Iran.
The French announcement came just minutes after Reuters reported that investigators privately suspected Iran of being behind the attacks.
Iran's mission to the United Nations did not return messages seeking comment. Iran routinely denies carrying out malicious cyber operations.
The 11 October cyberattack appeared to have been easy to pull off, cybersecurity experts previously told Reuters.
The firm behind many of the stricken units said that several were obsolete or were running outdated firmware, which could have made it easy for hackers to break in.
The effects were still dramatic. Some refrigerators had the temperature turned up so high they caught fire.
In the hours after the hack, supermarket employees carted boxes full of perished meat and melted ice cream into giant trash containers.
The attack's total costs could add up to tens of millions of euros nationwide, one French supermarket owner estimated.
The October hacks were followed this month by a second wave of hacking that hit more than 100 establishments across Europe and even affected refrigerators used by French blood banks, prompting employees there to have to move some of the blood to different cold storage units.
The seemingly straightforward nature of the refrigerator hacks – and their repetition across multiple countries – prompted speculation about who might be responsible amid ongoing concerns over Russia's suspected sabotage campaign in Europe, the war between the US and Iran and the global rise of AI-powered cyberattacks.
US refrigerator hacks
The sabotage of European supermarket fridges was preceded by at least one similar incident in the United States.
In August, refrigerators in at least half a dozen military commissaries went out of commission.
Pentagon investigators are treating the malfunctions as a suspected cyberattack and are working with French officials to get to the bottom of what happened, Reuters reported last month.
Reuters could not independently establish whether there was any link between the refrigeration incidents at US military bases in August, the hacking campaign in France and the more recent wave of refrigeration hacks that struck Europe.
A person familiar with the matter said that the Pentagon considers Iran a suspect in the August commissary hacks but that the investigation is still in progress.
Reuters could not establish how the military made its determination or whether it was also looking into other suspects. That the US military considers Iran a suspect in the commissary sabotage campaign was first reported last month by news website Nextgov.
The Pentagon said on Monday that it is "aware of speculation regarding a potential cyber incident" but that military investigators were on the case and it could not offer further comment for security reasons.

On wild Cumberland Island, a land swap proposal stirs controversy
CUMBERLAND ISLAND, Ga.— Wild horses, feral hogs and deer roam free on this 18-mile barrier island, one of the largest and most ecologically diverse along the Atlantic coast. The landscape includes salt marshes, maritime forests, and an expansive stretch of pristine, untouched beach only accessible to the public by ferry.
Since 1972, the National Park Service has managed Cumberland Island National Seashore, including roughly 9,800 acres of wilderness designated by an act of Congress which stated that "the seashore shall be permanently preserved in its primitive state."
But there's more on this island than federally protected wilderness. Visitors also can find Native-American relics, remnants of Spanish missions, the ruins of ante-bellum plantations, and opulent homes built by the wealthy Gilded Age industrialist Thomas Carnegie and his wife Lucy, who had 9 children.
Descendants of the Carnegies still live or vacation here on private property, and the park service has proposed a land swap with them that would allow for new construction. That possibility is creating tension between the many stakeholders who all have differing views of what it means to preserve the island they hold dear.
Park superintendent Melissa Trenchik has been defending the plan, giving media tours to an area under a grove of huge live oak trees on Cumberland's west side, which overlooks an expansive salt marsh and Naval Submarine Base Kings Bay on the horizon.
It is currently parkland, which under the proposal would be handed over to two branches of Carnegie descendants for the construction of up to eight new private homes.
"They obviously want to be with this incredible view," Trenchik told Georgia Public Broadcasting's Jillian Magtoto, as they stood on the edge of a maritime forest looking out over the Cumberland Sound.
The idea, Trenchik said, is to consolidate private ownership on the west side of the island, so the park can better interpret natural and cultural resources on the Atlantic beachside of Cumberland, including sensitive coastal and wilderness areas where the government could then prohibit development. The park service received more than 12,500 public comments on the proposal.
"Right now, if we do nothing, development is possible," she said of the private land the park service seeks to acquire.
Trenchik said the eight new "modest" homes would be subject to permanent conservation limits and could not exceed 35 feet in height. Critics, however, say the 15,000-square footage allowance, including driveway and outbuildings, is anything but modest.
"We're swapping for McMansions," said Joseph Manning, an attorney with Defenders of Wildlife, a Washington D.C. based conservation group fighting the deal.
Manning sees what's happening on Cumberland as the latest attempt by the Trump Administration to privatize public lands, pointing to other attention-grabbing headlines about a baseball park in Grand Teton, a land exchange in Yosemite, and repeated shrinkage of Bears Ears National Monument.
"Possibly the universal theme among all of these parks and refuges land exchanges that we're seeing is that they are not being done to expand public access," Manning said. "They're being done to benefit a particular special interest or just a handful of individuals or families, as is the case at Cumberland Island."
Barclay McFadden is a great-great-grandson of Thomas Carnegie, the brother of Pittsburgh steel magnate Andrew Carnegie.
"The hysteria about mansions and the Gilded Age and all that is so unfounded," McFadden said. "We love our island."
McFadden, who is involved in one of the land deals, said he's hurt by the way the debate over the land swap paints his family as modern-day robber barons without taking into account their history on the island.
"Five generations have been buried there. We have a family cemetery. It's still there. That's where I'll go," he said. "For our children and our grandchildren, it's a sacred place."
The land swap will allow them to build homes for those younger generations, McFadden said.
"We have been wonderful stewards of the island, and we have taken care of the island," he said, pointing out that his grandmother's generation had the opportunity to sell their property to developers in the 1970's. "They protected the island from turning into a golf course."
His cousin Jamie Ferguson, who is not directly involved in the current land swap proposal, said he trusts the Carnegie descendants' legacy of protecting what's special here. He jointly co-owns (with about 40 others) a Carnegie mansion here, now operated as a bed and breakfast – the Greyfield Inn.
"It's kind of like a live oak family tree - it's really widespread," said Ferguson, the family's unofficial historian. "The common thread we have though is this place."
He said his grandmother was adamant that the land remain in the family, even when other Carnegie descendants donated property to the National Park Service.
One advantage Ferguson sees to the land swap is greater visitor access to what he calls the "most important historical monument on Cumberland," a site known simply as The Chimneys. The remnants of about two dozen brick and tabby chimneys are lined up in rows under Spanish moss draped oak trees. It's where enslaved workers lived on an old sea island cotton plantation that pre-dated the Carnegies.
Ferguson points out the National Park Service is tasked with not just preserving the island's natural history, but also its cultural history.
"Like it or not, we're part of that cultural history," said Ferguson. "And I don't mean that in a bad way. I mean, I believe that we're a part of that cultural history, and that comes with some responsibility too."
There are a few other private homes on Cumberland that are not owned by Carnegie descendants. Naturalist Carol Rucksdeschel lives in one of them. After living on the island for more than 50 years, she's still excited each day at what she discovers.
"God look at that - that's so beautiful," she said one recent day, spotting a pair of wood storks descending into the marsh grass.
At 85, Ruckdeschel still surveys Cumberland Island every Friday morning, combing the beaches looking for stranded sea turtles and new nests. The ecologist has emerged as one of the main voices opposing the land swap, which she worries is the "first nose under the tent" towards greater development on the island.
"This plan to me is a real affront to the American people, but it's also an insult to the Park Service," Ruckdeschel said. "It's not what they're supposed to be doing. They're supposed to be protecting this place."
She's also not happy that the park service plans to double daily visitation to Cumberland, up to 700 visitors a day.
Ruckdeschel, who is involved with the conservation group Wild Cumberland, said she's friends with Carnegie descendants and acknowledges their love for the island. Still, she said, more homes and more people will disturb what the island should be – a pure primitive wilderness where nature overtakes what humans have left behind.
"It's stepping into its climax stage, which is terribly exciting," Ruckdeschel said of the rewilded maritime forest she's witnessed take over old plantation cotton fields.
"And that's what I would have loved to have seen the whole island do," she said. "And then people die out, places go back to nature and that's it."

Quick Answer
You can edit Instagram Reels on Mac using Claude AI and the free Instagram Edits app. Install Claude Code, enable the app’s MCP automation server, and connect both. Then use simple text prompts to create projects, arrange clips, add transitions, titles, and effects, and export finished Reels in 4K.
The wait is over. The Instagram Edits app is finally available on desktop, but only on macOS, as of this guide. Instagram Edits is my go-to app not just for editing Instagram Reels, but also a reliable free video editor with all the features and a simple design.
Although the app is designed for creators and competes with CapCut, it has been limited to Android and iOS so far. But a few months ago, Instagram announced a desktop version, and now it is finally here. Right now, the app is only available on macOS, with Windows and other platforms coming in future releases.
I have been using the app for the past couple of days. It is very similar to the mobile app and is also free to use, but it also features an MCP connection, which you can use to connect to any of your AI subscriptions, such as Claude, Codex, and Muse, and let AI edit your videos.
The desktop interface is slightly different and can be complex for beginners. It took me a while to get used to it, but I have created a detailed guide to get started.
I also created a guide on how to connect your MCP, like Claude, to Instagram Edits to edit your videos, and it covers everything about this feature, including common setup errors. This guide is for beginners, so each step is comprehensive and detailed.
Table of Contents
How to Connect Claude AI to Instagram Edits and Edit Reels on Mac
Before connecting your Instagram Edits app to the MCP server, ensure you have the following pre-requirements:
- A Mac with an Apple chip (M1 or newer) on macOS 15.1 or later. Currently, the Instagram Edits desktop app is only available for macOS, with Windows and Linux versions coming soon, but there is no expected release date yet.
- Download and install the Instagram Edits app from here
- A paid AI subscription for any model; you can also use the free AI model.
Part 1: Get Claude Code
Step 1: Open Terminal and type the command: claude –version, and press Return. If you see a version number, it means Claude Code is already installed on your device. You can skip to Part 2 to continue setup.
If you see something like zsh: command not found: claude, it means Claude Code is not installed on your device, or Terminal can not find it yet. Follow the next steps to install Claude Code on your Mac.
Install Claude Code: To install Claude Code, use the official Anthropic installer. To do that, open Terminal on your Mac and paste this command: curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash
Wait a few minutes, and then you will see a ” Claude Code successfully installed message in your terminal.
Check the setup notes below. If you see something like installation exists but ~/.local/bin is not in your PATH, it means the terminal still can’t find Claude Code yet.
Now follow the next two steps. If you don’t see such a note, you can quit the terminal, reopen it, and use this command to confirm that Claude Code has been successfully installed on your device: confirm claude –version. If you see a Claude version, it’s installed on your device. Then continue with part two.
Next, paste this command into the terminal and press Enter: echo ‘export PATH=”$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH”‘ >> ~/.zshrc
Next, paste this: source ~/.zshrc, and press Enter. Now type claude –version and press Enter. You will see the Claude version number. This means Claude Code is successfully installed on your device in the terminal
Part 2: Turn on Claude access in Edits
Next, you need to let Claude access your Instagram edits apps. First, ensure the Instagram edits app is installed on your Mac. If not, you can use the official download link here. Once installed, follow the steps below:
Step 1: Open the app on your Mac and sign in with your account. On the home screen, you will go directly to the Projects tab.
Step 2: Next, you can tap on your profile picture in the top right corner of the screen or click on the edit option in the menu bar at the top of the screen and then click on the settings
Step 3: Next, tap on the automation from the sidebar
Step 4: By default, automation is turned off. Now, from the automation settings, turn on the toggle that says Enable Automation Server.
Step 5: Under the Connect an AI Client section, click the copy icon next to the Claude code. This will copy the connection command with your access token. Remember, don’t share this command with others. In this case, I am using Claude code. If you are using Codex, tap the copy button next to Codex. The same goes for Muse.
You can also connect any AI model. Since it is a standard MCP server, any AI app can connect to the MCP server over HTTPS and can control edits.
Remember to replace <TOKEN> with the Access token from Edits > Settings > Automation, and keep Edits open with the automation server turned on
For Google Gemini CLI:
npm install -g @google/gemini-cli
gemini mcp add –transport http –scope user –header “Authorization: Bearer <TOKEN>” edits http://127.0.0.1:19501/mcp
For Qwen:
npm install -g @qwen-code/qwen-code
qwen mcp add –transport http –scope user –header “Authorization: Bearer <TOKEN>” edits http://127.0.0.1:19501/mcp
For DeepSeek, Grok, Mistral, Kimi, GLM, and most others, we can use OpenCode
curl -fsSL https://opencode.ai/install | bash
{
“$schema”: “https://opencode.ai/config.json”,
“mcp”: {
“servers”: {
“edits”: {
“type”: “remote”,
“url”: “http://127.0.0.1:19501/mcp”,
“oauth”: false,
“headers”: { “Authorization”: “Bearer <TOKEN>” }
}
}
}
}
Part 3: Connect Claude Code to Edits
Next, let’s connect Claude Code (or any AI model) to edits. Remember that you can only do this once.
Step 1: Now, paste the command you copied from the previous section into the terminal. You will see: Added HTTP MCP server metapilot-native
Step 2: Next, for Claude, paste this command: claude mcp get metapilot-native and press Enter. Under status, if you see Connected, it worked. If it says Failed to connect, ensure the edits app is running and follow the previous steps carefully.
For other models, follow these:
| App (models) | Connect command | Check it worked | 
| Claude Code (Claude) | claude mcp add –transport http –scope user metapilot-native http://127.0.0.1:19501/mcp –header “Authorization: Bearer <TOKEN>” | claude mcp get metapilot-native | 
| Gemini CLI (Gemini) | gemini mcp add –transport http –scope user –header “Authorization: Bearer <TOKEN>” edits http://127.0.0.1:19501/mcp | gemini mcp list | 
| Qwen Code (Qwen) | qwen mcp add –transport http –scope user –header “Authorization: Bearer <TOKEN>” edits http://127.0.0.1:19501/mcp | qwen mcp list | 
| Codex (OpenAI GPT) | echo ‘export EDITS_TOKEN=”<TOKEN>”‘ >> ~/.zshrc && source ~/.zshrc && codex mcp add edits –url http://127.0.0.1:19501/mcp –bearer-token-env-var EDITS_TOKEN | Run codex, then type /mcp | 
| OpenCode (DeepSeek, Grok, Mistral, Kimi, GLM and more) | No command. Paste the opencode.jsonc block from my last message into the folder you run OpenCode in. | opencode mcp list | 
| LM Studio (local Llama, Gemma, Qwen, DeepSeek R1) | No command. Program tab, then Install, then Edit mcp.json, and paste the JSON block. | Look at the Program tab | 
| Cursor (any model it offers) | No command. Paste the same JSON into ~/.cursor/mcp.json. | Cursor Settings, then MCP | 
Part 4: Start Claude Code
Now go to the folder where the videos are saved to edit them using Instagram edits. I recommend that you store all the videos in the Movies folder so it is easy to access in the future. In this case, I stored all my files in the Movies folder on my Mac. Now, once you have access to the folder, follow the steps below.
Step 1: To use Claude, go to the folder using the CD command. For example: cd ~/Downloads or cd ~/Movies. In my case, cd ~/Movies. Next, once you are in the folder, Type Cluade and press Return.
Step 2: Claude will ask whether you trust the folder you provided. Use the down arrow and select I trust this folder, and press Enter. It asks only once, and once you give permission, you can store all future videos in this folder for edits.
Step 3: To check, you can type /mcp and press Enter. It lists the apps Claude Code is connected to. metapilot-native with a green tick means Claude can control Edits.
Step 4: Go to the metapilot-native option and press Enter to see more details. You can use the down or up arrow to navigate between the options.
Part 5: Make your first Reel with Claude
Now let’s use Claude to create my first reel. In this case, I asked Claude to edit a 50-second coffee reel from five clips. In your case, you can store all the clips in the folder. First, test the connection again. Once done, follow the steps below.
To test the connection, go to your folder and type list my Instagram edits projects and press Enter. You will see metabolist native and the table of all your edit projects.
Step 2 : Now you can ask Claude to make edits for the Instagram reel video. You can manually create a new project, add clips, and point Claude to the project title and edit your videos, or you can ask Claude to create a project, add clips, and edit your first reel. I recommend giving Claude the full location of your clips and the title.
Step 3: That’s it. Claude will now create a new project and add Sunclips. You can open the Instagram Edits app to see the changes.
Step 4: Once you’ve loaded the clips, you can ask Claude to add transitions between them and also add titles, sound effects, and much more. In this case, I’m asking Claude to add the title “Morning Coffee” in big white text for two seconds and then add smooth transitions between the clips.
Step 5: Once you’ve made the edits, you can also ask Claude Core to export the clips in 4K, and it does it for you.
Step 6: Once the video is exported, Claude notifies you of the length, format, and size. You can open the same folder to see the clip. Claude also notifies you where the clip is stored and its title.
Let AI Handle Your Video Editing
This is how to connect Claude code using Instagram Edits MCP. For now, the Instagram Edits app is only available on macOS, and you can connect any AI model to make edits.
Since Claude requires a subscription, you can try a free AI model if you have one. You can also run any free AI model locally and ask it to edit, but the quality may vary and may not be as good as frontend models.
Since this guide focuses entirely on Claude Code, we are also creating a separate guide on how to connect other free AI models, including Google Gemini (which comes with a free Jio AI offer), DeepSeek, and other models.
If you have any issues while connecting Claude Code, let me know. If you prefer a video guide, we have also created one that you can check out above.

It's hard to imagine Nvidia without Jensen Huang — and the CEO has repeatedly discussed his intention to work for as long as possible.
Now, the question of succession has come into sharp focus this week as Huang admitted to having an affair, and Nvidia's board announced it's investigating whether Huang was the target of a "foreign intelligence effort."
If Huang steps down from his role, analysts and former employees floated several potential successors, including vice president Ian Buck and chief financial officer Colette Kress. Huang's two children, Madison and Spencer, also work at Nvidia, raising questions about whether leadership could remain in the family.
Nvidia told Business Insider in a statement on Sunday that "Jensen is committed to continuing to lead Nvidia as CEO without interruption." Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment for this story.
Huang would be hard to replace, said Brad Gastwirth, the global head of research at Circular Technology. While Huang doesn't have controlling voting power, he owns about 3.6% of Nvidia and would likely "have considerable input into succession unless the investigation uncovers serious wrongdoing," Gastwirth said.
"Jensen's combination of technical expertise, strategic vision, and industry relationships is nearly impossible to replicate," he said.
Inside Nvidia's succession dilemma
Nvidia has not publicly designated a number two, and Huang is known for keeping an unusually flat leadership structure with roughly 60 direct reports.
"That works beautifully while he's in the seat, but it means nobody has been groomed, tested, or publicly positioned as the heir," said Daniel Newman, CEO of The Futurum Group.
One former employee said Madison Huang, who works as senior director of product marketing for physical AI, has been asserting greater authority across Nvidia's businesses, which they believe could be an effort to position herself for a larger leadership role.
Gil Luria, an analyst at DA Davidson, said Kress is the company's only other highly visible executive and could take over as interim CEO if Huang stepped aside.
Kress has worked at Nvidia for 13 years, and prior to that, she held finance roles at Cisco and Microsoft.
Since Kress lacks the engineering background that has been central to Huang's leadership, another possible long-term replacement is Ian Buck, a longtime executive who helped develop CUDA, the chip software that has become central to Nvidia's dominance in AI.
Buck heads Nvidia's data center and computing businesses, and he has worked at Nvidia for 22 years.
"He's already running the group that is generating virtually all the revenues," the former employee said, referring to Nvidia's data center business.
A second former employee cited the importance of Nvidia's distinctive culture in promoting a current executive as a successor.
"Ideally it has to be someone from the company who's lived the values and the culture," they said.
Could Nvidia look to an outsider?
Some observers have floated executives from other major technology companies as potential successors, including Google Cloud CEO Thomas Kurian and Amazon Web Services CEO Matt Garman.
Both oversee enormous cloud computing businesses that invest heavily in AI infrastructure and work closely with Nvidia, giving them firsthand knowledge of the customers and technologies driving its growth.
While Huang's departure appears unlikely for now, Gastwirth said losing him under the current circumstances could seriously hurt Nvidia.
"I think it would be one of the worst things that could happen to Nvidia," he said. "The company would continue operating, but I would question whether it could maintain the same pace of innovation and execution."

No clear winner in New Zealand election, as leaders prepare for weeks of talks
WELLINGTON, New Zealand — New Zealanders will wait for weeks to discover who will lead the country after Saturday's election failed to deliver a decisive win for the right or the left, leaving fraught negotiations for a wafer-thin governing majority the only apparent path to victory for either side.
The tightest vote in years delivered a stinging rebuke to the major parties which have long dominated New Zealand politics, Christopher Luxon's center-right National party and center-left Labour led by Chris Hipkins, as voters threw more support behind minor parties on the ideological flanks than before. On Saturday's numbers, minor parties would enter negotiations for a governing deal with leverage to extract deeper policy concessions from a weakened National or Labour.
The near-deadlock was partly produced because voters, apparently weary of New Zealand's economic woes and apathetic about both Luxon and Hipkins, chose to propel a new entrant group to Parliament for the first time in years. Opportunity, led by 38-year-old business consultant and political newcomer Qiulae Wong, is unaligned with either bloc and Wong has said she could work with either side to form a government.
Wong's pledges of evidence-based centrism and an end to partisan bickering had on Saturday's results secured seven seats for Opportunity — enough to frustrate both left and right in a simple path to power. It was a staggering ascension for a party that made three failed attempts at Parliament before Wong became leader less than a year ago.
The conservative bloc has a simpler route to victory, but results could change
Other winners were harder to identify and on Sunday, "who won the election 2026" was the top trending Google search in New Zealand. So unclear was the result that parties won't begin negotiations to form a government until final tallies are released on Nov. 27, confirming the exact number of seats they've won.
With 2.8 million ballots counted on election night, the conservative incumbent government led by Luxon's National party appeared close to the slimmest possible return to power — by just one seat. However, Luxon didn't claim victory, instead striking a note of cautious optimism that he could negotiate a second term in power.
Speaking to reporters Sunday, Luxon blamed public dissatisfaction on global shocks which have buffeted New Zealand's trade-based economy, noting that other incumbent governments worldwide have faced voters' rancor over living costs.
Yet his opponent Hipkins, who was turfed from office in 2023 largely over discontent about the same economic issues, didn't appear to benefit on Saturday. The left-wing bloc appeared to fall short of a majority but was still hopeful it could triumph — though that seemed a more remote prospect.
Electoral officials were due on Sunday to begin counting nearly 400,000 so-called special votes, including from New Zealanders who live abroad, a process expected to take three weeks.
Those ballots have historically granted an additional seat or two in Parliament to left-wing parties, which could snatch the current razor-thin majority from the right, although such an outcome would likely leave the left struggling to form a majority too. If a government can't be formed, New Zealand could face a fresh vote.
Incumbent Luxon urges people to 'calm down' and enjoy a break from politics
"I think everyone's over politics so let's all have a bit of a break for the next three weeks," Luxon told reporters on Sunday. He will lead a caretaker government until an outcome is reached.
Luxon suggested that National had a viable path to power and boasted that it had secured more seats in Parliament than any other group. However, Saturday night was bleak for his party.
Several of National's most senior lawmakers would exit politics on results so far, including the ministers of finance and defense, the speaker of parliament, and the attorney general. With the party's traditional governing partners winning increased support, Luxon faces a more strident list of policy demands to secure their backing.
Libertarian ACT won 13 seats and populist New Zealand First won 12. Both are led by canny veteran politicians, and detractors of Luxon, a former business executive who entered politics in 2020, said his dealings with them in the three years since he took office had highlighted his political inexperience.
The vote was a slap for both major parties
New Zealanders don't vote for prime ministers. Instead they cast two votes, one for their preferred party and another for the candidate they want as their local representative.
The country has one house of Parliament and no states, so the central government holds ultimate sway over New Zealand's direction. Governments in the South Pacific nation of 5.6 million people are elected every three years.
National won just 29.21% of the preferred party vote as of Sunday, a collapse of its previous result, and secured its 42 seats entirely by winning local constituency races. Luxon, who unusually faced two separateconfidence votes among his own lawmakers this year, further slumped in popularity as leader close to election day.
However, Labour also won just 29.36% of the party vote, a result that appeared to suggest a second election defeat for career politician Hipkins. Despite winning about the same party vote percentage as National, Labour has secured only 36 seats on numbers so far because they won fewer local races.
Minor parties on the left saw bolstered support. The environmentally-focused Greens won 16 seats and Indigenous rights group Te Pāti Māori secured five.
The total number of seats in New Zealand's Parliament changes due to quirks in how seat allocations are calculated. There would currently be 131 lawmakers elected, with 66 seats required for a majority.
Luxon's conservative bloc would currently hold 67, a razor-thin margin likely to discomfit a leader managing a three-way government with two emboldened minor parties. However, the left bloc held only 57 seats before the historically left-leaning special votes were counted.
Even if the final tally boosted the left bloc's seats slightly, Hipkins would apparently need support from newcomer Wong to govern.
Before the election, Luxon repeatedly ruled out negotiating with Wong. He sidestepped questions on Sunday about whether his vanishingly slim lead had changed his mind.

A hands-off way to maintain your sourdough starter so it’s ready when you need it. Ensures no missed or forgotten feedings. Small enough to fit unobtrusively on most countertops. All variables are customizable.
TIRED
No temperature control. Mixing cycle is loud and can be startling. Calibration is fiddly, especially if you frequently switch between flour types.
Like many people, I enjoy baking my own bread—especially this time of year. I baked sourdough on and off for nearly a decade, even having a recipe tested for a James Beard-winning bread cookbook, but I’m not proud to admit it’s been over a year since I baked a proper sourdough loaf.
As a full-time working parent, maintaining a sourdough starter sometimes feels like bringing home another pet. (You know, the kind your child swears they will care for before abandoning all tasks after three days.) You can certainly keep your starter in the fridge for around a week between bakes, but reviving it may take a day or two of feedings, and let’s be real, Will you remember to do this every week? Even the pet snake my son begged for only needs feeding every other week.
It is for people like me that King Arthur Baking Company and FirstBuild, GE Appliances’ product development lab, created the Sourdough Sidekick, a gizmo that automatically feeds and maintains a sourdough starter for you. We wrote about the Sourdough Sidekick when it was first announced in 2025, and now, after trying it for three weeks, I can say that my sourdough-baking dry spell has finally come to an end, perhaps even permanently.
The Sidekick is a Mr. Coffee-sized appliance with a built-in water reservoir, flour hopper, and glass crock with a stirring-paddle lid. I deal with an awful lot of apps in my job, and the Sidekick uses GE’s generic SmartHQ for GE appliances, which isn’t specific to this device and seemed optional. I admit I couldn’t be bothered with an unnecessary app, so I didn’t download it.
Instead, I followed the directions in the included Quick Start Guide booklet, which indicated that I simply needed to fill the water reservoir and flour hopper, set the current day and time (and the day and time I wanted the starter to be ready—you can choose up to seven days ahead; I chose seven), add a little bit of existing starter, and press “Auto Mode.” Almost immediately, a torrent of flour released from the hopper and began mixing into my seed starter with the stirring paddle. (King Arthur recommends keeping a portion of your starter in the fridge in case things go wrong, and I second this suggestion.)
Oddly, no water was dispensed in this process, so post-mixing, my starter was now in the form of an under-hydrated ball. Over the next few days, it became a larger, drier ball until I finally decided to remove the crock to add a couple of tablespoons of water; as I did, I noticed the reservoir was still at its maximum fill line.
I decided I should probably download the app, where I noticed the Sidekick indicated it needed a firmware update. After the update, the Sidekick began dispensing water during mixing, but I realized I really should have followed the instructions in the main instruction booklet, which calls for using a scale to properly calibrate the amounts of water and flour the machine dispenses.
Theoretically, you should only have to do this once, which is good because it’s an irritatingly lengthy and fiddly process. However, my next attempt (remember when I mentioned saving some starter in the fridge?) went much better, properly dispensing 30 grams each of water and flour each day and initiating a stirring cycle every two hours. It starts with a loud beep, then the paddle begins a loud mechanical whir, and for the first few days this can be quite startling, especially if you’re in the same room when it happens.
Photograph: Kat Merck
You can bypass the every-two-hours stirring cycle via the onboard controls, but since the stirring’s purpose is to knock down the starter’s volume and reincorporate any unconsumed flour, I kept it on. (For what it’s worth, I did think the paddle, an update from the Sidekick’s first design, did a pretty good job of incorporating all of the flour and water each time it mixed.)
Note that, in part due to the regular mixing and the lack of discard (Auto Mode will prompt you to discard after a week, while Ratio and Custom modes, detailed below, will have discard reminders), your finished starter in the Sidekick may not look as traditionally puffy or bubbly as you may be used to. You can disable stirring, or you can go on scent—it should smell tangy and indisputably fermented. As the many online Sidekick adherents often say, “Trust the process.” Some online users recommended adding a few teaspoons of more nutritionally dense rye flour to the (presumably all-purpose) flour in the hopper, which is supposed to supercharge the starter’s growth, but I admit I didn’t notice much of a difference in appearance, smell, or performance between an all-purpose starter and a rye-boosted starter.
Boules made with end-of-week starter maintained via the Sourdough Sidekick
Photograph: Kat Merck
Loaf and Learn
Other than enabling firmware updates, the app does little beyond displaying the machine’s current settings and sending a push notification when the starter is finished. You can’t adjust settings or control the machine from it, but the most recent firmware update supports power-loss recovery up to 12 hours, which I tested and found successful after my husband tripped a breaker one day. The display shows the ambient temperature, but unlike other starter-babysitting gadgets like the Goldie or Brod & Taylor’s Sourdough Home, the Sourdough Sidekick has no way to adjust the starter’s temperature, which could be an issue if your house or kitchen runs cold. It does, however, offer “temperature-aware” feedings in Auto Mode, adjusting amounts based on detected room temperature.
Screenshot: Kat Merck
In addition to Auto Mode, there’s Ratio Mode (where you can indicate starter-flour-water feedings by ratio—1:1:1, 1:1:2, et al.) and Custom Mode, which is what I ended up using the most, as I like to switch between flour types for different kinds of bread—you can dictate the exact flour and water quantities, as well as timing of the feeding (once a day, or even twice a day). In a typical week, the crock was about two-thirds full by the end, with more than 400 grams of starter—enough for two boules and a sandwich loaf with some seed left over for the next batch—ready to use right out of the crock.
The resulting bread turned out no differently than it had with traditionally maintained starter. If you’re unable to bake at that time, you can just discard most of the starter, leaving some “seed” behind for the next batch, or keep it in the refrigerator for a few days before reviving it the traditional way. (The crock comes with a metal lid for this purpose.)
If you’re only baking one loaf, you’ll have excess, but you can use the discard in recipes or give it away. Just note that if you intend to make a starter with a different flour, like whole wheat or full rye, you will need to calibrate the machine again as you did at the beginning. All removable components are top-rack dishwasher safe.
The Sourdough Sidekick is one of the most compelling kitchen-tech gifts I’ve ever seen for someone who bakes a lot or is interested in sourdough baking but intimidated by the process of keeping a starter. (The Sidekick also includes directions for making your own starter right in the machine.) Is it a necessary device? Of course not—especially since it costs about $175 more than a spoon and a Mason jar. But I can tell you I wouldn’t have baked bread this year without it.
