Past White House adviser Raj Panjabi has written a playbook for 'living room' crises
Dr. Raj Panjabi's new book has a simple title: Safer: A Playbook.
Yes, a playbook like the kind sports managers use to firm up a winning strategy. But playbooks aren't just for games.
"In the intensive care unit, we have a playbook when someone's heart stops beating," And when he was a White House health adviser during the COVID emergency, he says, "In the Situation Room, we had a playbook for pandemic preparedness."
Then there was his own family's situation — at age 1, his daughter was diagnosed with heart failure.
That experience inspired Panjabi to write a different kind of playbook. "I was frustrated that we didn't have a playbook for crises that appear in our own living room."
What he wrote is actually three books in one: The story of how he and his wife addressed their daughter's life-threatening condition; an exploration of public health issues that beset the globe – and straightforward advice for anyone with a living-room crisis. The book's chapter titles telegraph his philosophy: "Turn Denial Into Action." "Don't Go It Alone." "Get Ready to Pivot." "Embrace Uncertainty."
Panjabi was born to Indian parents in Liberia; his family immigrated to the United States when he was 9. He became a physician and went on to found the award-winning humanitarian group Last Mile Health, which employs community workers to bring health information to people in remote areas.
We interviewed Raj Panjabi at NPR headquarters on October 30. He had just flown in from meetings in Boston, wearing a sharp-looking sports jacket he'd bought at the airport — because his mother, who sells men's clothing, is a tough critic of his fashion choices.
So one thing that happens in a crisis — and that a playbook can help address — is denial. You and your wife both dismissed early concerns about your daughter — thinking at first that her extremely low weight was because she was a picky eater.
I was wrought with the guilt of being a dad and missing this illness — and being a doctor and missing this illness in my own daughter. I thought it was a character flaw. What I learned is that it's not. Denial is the first stage of almost every crisis. It could be a medical emergency, like in the case of my daughter. It could be job loss, that layoff you never thought would affect you.
And what I learned in researching the book — it turns out we have a hard time detecting slow moving threats until they reach a tipping point.
Psychologists call it normalcy bias — the idea that tomorrow will look a lot like yesterday. Until, of course, it doesn't. The good news is that there are ways we can overcome that.
Such as …
In the case of a slow-moving crisis like my daughter's illness, the very first thing you might do is set an if/then threshold. If I see a warning sign, I will act in X or Y way.
Your daughter is 9 now and has recovered. How do you deal with any lingering uncertainty about her heart health?
Every couple of years, she goes to the cardiologist and she gets an ultrasound of the heart. The trigger we're looking for is whether the heart's ability to squeeze is at a normal level or not. We'll see that well before we see any major heart failure. Allowing a trigger to do the monitoring for you allows you to feel some agency and allows you to control what you can control.
Health crises can be very personal — but also societal. In the United States, measles — eradicated 36 years ago, is back because parents are opting not to vaccinate their kids. What's the playbook for talking to those parents?
It's much easier to ask a blame-oriented question when someone's not protecting themselves or their community, such as "Why aren't you following the guidelines?"
And you say in a family crisis or a crisis like the measles outbreak, it's important to ask a different kind of question to move ahead.
When you meet face-to-face, you ask not a blame-oriented question but a barrier-oriented question. What's in the way of you following the guidelines? And that starts to open up potential barriers that you can solve for.
Such as …
Often you start to hear some practical barriers — I can't take time off work because I work multiple shifts in a day. I can't find enough money to get a bus ticket to come to the clinic to get a vaccine.
You may also hear, "I heard that this vaccine might lead to a side effect." Or, you know, in parts of the world I've worked in, people assume vaccines can lead to sterility or infertility.
What I've found Is in almost every scenario, if you meet face-to-face, if you ask a barrier- oriented question not a blame-oriented question, you start to understand people's beliefs and their behaviors. And you don't have to change someone's beliefs for their behaviors to be more protective.
You stress that a bond of trust is essential in this type of situation.
One of the most important messages, as we have measles spreading in many parts of the country, is to ask: Where is trust still present? And what I found again and again is it's not in Washington. It comes from your local faith leader, your local physician, your local healthcare provider, your local school. It turns out even in polling now, 80 to 90% of Americans still trust their healthcare provider. I argue in the book that our greatest protection is connection. If we build those relationships before a crisis, we're more likely to weather it.
Arguably we are experiencing an artificial intelligence crisis now. Is it good … or will it doom us? You currently do work involving AI. What's your take?
I do medical research now with scientists who are using AI to develop the next medicine to defeat cancer or the next vaccine to stop a supervirus. The same tools we're using in our labs can be used by a terrorist to design a virus and make it more capable of evading our vaccines, [of] unleashing a super virus on humanity.
How do you address that dichotomy?
Psychologists have come up [a strategy] with when we face tremendous uncertainty — draw a circle on a piece of paper. Outside of that circle are actions you can't control, such as whether or not a terrorist tomorrow decides they're going to use this or not. But within the circle, I can control whether or not the scientists I work with are minimizing the risks of the way they use AI so that we can maximize its benefit for humanity.
And there is a simple point to keep in mind. You have to grow a virus in a lab. You have to have DNA to do it. AI has not yet been able to dissolve the barrier between the screen and the freezer, as it were. But that doesn't give us permission to relax. We should be setting those warning signs, articulating them now and acting before that barrier gets dissolved.
I had to laugh at a note in your book's closing comments. You mention making "legendary" peanut butter and jelly sandwiches to woo your wife-to-be. What made them legendary?
I had been rejected about three or four times by this young woman named Amisha Raja when I was a freshman at Chapel Hill. And I was a terrible cook. So I made peanut butter and jelly sandwiches, took her out for a lunch, surprised her. It was our first date. I don't think the peanut butter and jelly sandwiches had a whole lot to do with her deciding to go on that date, but I'm grateful she did. Because 25 years later and then some were still together.
What's your jelly of choice?
Oh, I am a big, big strawberry jam guy. And you gotta layer so it's two thirds jelly, one third peanut butter.
That's … sweet!

Food Safety and Standards Authority of India has seized 3,280 tonnes of 'banned and non-compliant' food products worth ₹82 crore during its nationwide inspection drive, which began on September 1 to check adulteration during the festive season.

England make massive step up in Australia victory
- Published
In his latest BBC Sport column, England World Cup winner Matt Dawson reflects on an impressive 45-22 win for Steve Borthwick's side against Australia in the Nations Championship on Sunday.
Beating Australia with their record points tally against the Wallabies was a very positive way for England to start the autumn series, given the break they have had and how the beginning of the year went.
England were very accurate, very disciplined, creative and genuinely did not give Australia a sniff.
Before the game, I was expecting Australia to provide much more of a stern test. Some people might be a bit too critical of Australia, saying they did not turn up, but I think it edges more towards how well England played than how average Australia were.
I am not saying by any stretch that it was the perfect performance but, all in all, it was a massive step up from the Six Nations and even from the Nations Championship games in the summer.
Intensity, accuracy and discipline in abundance
A couple of days before the Australia game, Jamie George said the England team had been galvanised by a newspaper article which claimed the end of their summer tour had been marked by player unrest over head coach Borthwick's leadership.
When you are inside those international camps, you are very deliberate in staying tight and not letting anybody in in whatever way, shape or form, therefore you become very sensitive to any kind of criticism.
There is a reason for doing that - it draws you together and allows you to create a bit more determination and drive to be successful.
You could see England's intensity, their accuracy and their discipline. All the things that have maybe been highlighted over the past nine months as things England have been lacking, there was an abundance of all of it.
As much as it is easy to try to pick holes in England because it is England, sometimes you have got to pat people on the back and say they got it right.
The opposition was dangerous with good individual players, but from the off England's tactics were spot on. Their decision-making was controlled and they looked like a very well-drilled side.
- England swat aside Wallabies to back up Borthwick 
  - Published14 hours ago
- Feyi-Waboso burns bright as England energy endorses Borthwick 
  - Published11 hours ago
How England might unlock the best of Slade
England's back three of George Furbank, Tommy Freeman and Immanuel Feyi-Waboso caused plenty of problems for Australia, but I think you have to include Fin Smith and Henry Slade in that as well.
Potentially, there is something in that backline that may allow us to see the Slade we see for Exeter that we have not seen as much for England.
Having the likes of Feyi-Waboso, Freeman and Furbank around Slade and them understanding the sorts of positions he can get them into - there might be some long-term benefits to that.
Feyi-Waboso is X-factor, there is no question about that. For his early disallowed try, he shifted his weight and beat someone with that pace - I do not think there are many people in the world who could do that.
When you have got players like him who can do that regularly, all of a sudden you are getting momentum.
There was a massive difference in ruck speed and in momentum; England were getting lined up defensively and pushing Australia back, whereas when you have got players like Feyi-Waboso and Ben Earl, and then when Henry Pollock comes on as well, you have got plenty of players who can break the line in traffic and it makes attacking that much easier.
Fin Smith is leading the team, he looks like he is a general and in control of the game.
He has got a safe pair of hands and communication from Seb Atkinson, he has got vision from Slade and then a back three that if you give them half a chance, they are going to bust the line, create opportunities and probably finish.
There were bits of Sunday's game where if New Zealand were doing it, everybody would be ranting and raving about how complete some of those tries were.
Pollock's flexibility a fantastic weapon
Feyi-Waboso's injury meant Pollock came off the bench to play in an unfamiliar position on the wing and he ended up scoring two of England's seven tries.
He did very well considering he was on for a whole half. Going forward, what is the difference having Pollock there? He has got a winger's speed, the step, great hands, the power and the bulk that other wingers do not have and he is going to be a handful for the opposition.
Defensively, he was tested a couple of times and that is inevitable, but to have that flexibility on the bench allows England to have that six-two split because you have got a player who can now pretty much cover so many positions.
As great as it was, and I am sure he absolutely loved it, unfortunately he is probably inking himself in to be quite a significant bench player moving forward, which is not really what I think he would like to be labelled as.
Selfishly, from an England point of view, it is a fantastic weapon to have.
The whole bench did really well and made a difference. It goes all the way back to selection, something Borthwick has previously come under fire for a little bit.
It does not mean that just because he has got one right, the autumn is going to go swimmingly well, but from the off the selection has been right, the gameplan was a bit more expansive than I thought it was going to be and they absolutely nailed the execution.
Will England back it up against Japan?
Tactically, I loved the balance of the England performance; a really dominant set-piece, driving mauls and in-your-face defence.
England have maybe always been like that but have lacked the discipline to go with it.
Against Australia, they proved they have the capability to be disciplined and maintain concentration - and I want to see that over the next three weeks.
Can they, under more pressure - because they are going to face more pressure, particularly against New Zealand - still maintain that discipline and decision-making?
They have got the assets to overpower Japan, but can they do it by giving away fewer than 10 penalties? Can they do it by having 15 people on the pitch for 80 minutes?
All of the little things they have been after, can they do them against a team they should beat comfortably?
If they can, then when they go into the New Zealand game with it all to play for and when they are really testing themselves, they are going to have huge momentum.
Matt Dawson was speaking to BBC Sport's Phil Cartwright.

The safety reason TSA might ask you to turn on your phone
CBP can take this a step further and search your phone.
You may have heard about Transportation Security Administration (TSA) agents asking someone to turn their smartphone on while going through security at an airport and think this is something new — but it isn't. This ruling about turning on devices before boarding has been in place since 2014. Back then, the TSA implemented a new rule requiring travelers coming from overseas to turn on their electronic devices, including phones, to prove they're actually functioning. If the device does not have power, you might be subjected to additional screening. This is for the safety of all passengers because phones can be used as detonators, jamming devices or to store bomb components.
You already need to place large electronics, like a laptop or tablet, in a separate bin to go through the scanner. And though it likely doesn't happen too often, an agent might ask you to power something on, including your phone. If the device turns on, this is all the TSA agent should need to see and you can move forward. This confirms that the device hasn't been tampered with to be used for another purpose beyond its intended one.
CBP has different rules
If an officer were to engage in a lengthier search without reasonable suspicion, this is where things get murky. Technically, border agents can run a manual search of your phone. These searches have been deemed by the Fourth Circuit as routine and a reasonable action under the Fourth Amendment, which is what protects you against unreasonable search and seizure without a warrant.
For international travelers, US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) can ask to look through your phone since this falls under the border search exception. CBP can detain your phone for what is considered to be a "brief, reasonable time" if they feel the need to conduct a routine inspection, per the CBP Directive. But without a warrant or reasonable suspicion, they can only do a basic inspection, where they look at things like text messages and app activity. With reasonable suspicion, they can do a thorough inspection, which involves downloading the contents onto another device.
A proposal from late 2025 even aims to allow CBP to request five-year social media history from travelers entering from certain regions before they are permitted into the US, though this remains a proposal and is not actually law yet.
Keep your phone powered up
Given that both TSA and border agents can ask you to power on your phone, you'll want to make sure your electronics don't die when you travel. Place your phone in the security bin, and if you're asked to turn it on, power the device up or light up the screen and unlock it to show that it's a functioning phone.
All that said, most travelers will never experience this. Provided your phone's battery is powered up, there shouldn't be any issues. But if you are asked to turn the phone on, TSA agents are well within their rights to require that you do so. If you're traveling internationally, you could run into murkier situations with CBP. But as far as TSA goes, all they want to know is that the phone isn't a dummy device being used for another reason and really is a working mobile phone.

The Best Touchscreen Gloves
Featured in this article
The obvious way to keep Jack Frost from nipping at your fingers is to slip on a pair of toasty touchscreen gloves. People have been wearing gloves for centuries, with the shift from mittens to individually wrapped fingers the biggest upgrade in all that time. But traditional gloves don’t play nicely with our smartphones. Sure, you could stab uselessly at the touchscreen before slipping your glove off to use your phone. But wouldn’t you rather snag a good pair of touchscreen gloves?
All these gloves have some material or fingertip technology that works with touchscreens, but some are better than others. I tested each pair in this guide with my phone—I answered calls, browsed the web, and sent text messages—and also considered comfort, grip, and warmth, using them in 30- to 40-degree Fahrenheit weather. These are my favorites.
Updated January 2026: We've added heated gloves from Venustas, streamlined our picks, and updated our suggested settings.
Adjust Your Phone’s Settings
Before diving in, I strongly recommend you increase the sensitivity of your phone’s touchscreen. Here’s how:
On an Android phone: Go to Settings, Display and touch, Touch sensitivity, and toggle on Increased sensitivity. These settings may vary slightly on different Android phones.
On an iPhone: Go to Settings, Accessibility, Touch, and tap Haptic Touch or 3D & Haptic Touch and select Fast. You should also consider tweaking some of the settings in Settings, Accessibility, Touch, and Touch Accommodations.
Other Touchscreen Gloves We Tested
Some of the touchscreen gloves we tried fell short of a recommendation for one reason or another.
Verloop Twist Knit Touchscreen Gloves for $35: Gloves don’t have to be gray, as these vibrant, eye-catching, fun color combinations prove. I tested the Twist Knit Touchscreen Gloves in magenta and cobalt, and they proved an instant hit with my daughter. The tips of the thumb, index finger, and middle finger are touchscreen-friendly. She found it easy to swipe around and even type with some practice, but you need a snug fit to type at speed and use your thumbs. These gloves are cozy, with ribbed cuffs, and they are machine washable but not waterproof.
Black Diamond Lightweight Screentap Gloves for $35: Thin gloves can maintain your dexterity but still provide some warmth. There’s a suede patch on the palm that acts as great padding for when you hold an umbrella or steering wheel. It’s easy to use the touchscreen with my thumb, so these are great for one-handed use, and I can type at close to normal speed. These gloves also have an elasticated wrist for a snug fit and a plastic clip for joining them together when they're off, so you never lose one. They’re not especially warm, and they feel a little slippery.
Canada Goose Mixed Media Gloves for $175: Slipping on these gloves feels heavenly because the brushed inner lining is incredibly comfortable. They are warm too, with a soft shell and leather exterior. Sadly, the touchscreen performance is disappointing. You can type with any finger or your thumb, but it takes more determination than with other gloves on our list. I became fairly capable with my thumb after some practice, but using my index finger was hit-and-miss, with touches frequently not registering.
Marks and Spencer Knitted Gloves for $20 or £10: A gift from my in-laws, these knitted gloves from reliable UK retailer Marks and Spencer are pretty good. They keep your hands cozy but also have special touchscreen pads on the index finger and thumb tips. I can swipe, tap, and type reasonably well with these gloves on.
Graphene-X All Rounder Bio-X Gloves for $119: With a classy look, high-tech graphene material on the back, and plant-based bio leather on the palm and fingers, these gloves are certainly unique. They're comfy too, but they completely failed to keep my hands warm. The touchscreen material works, and I had no trouble tapping and swiping, but the joins and squared-off shape on the fingertips made it almost impossible to type accurately.
Trendoux Winter Gloves for $12: These affordable gloves have tips on the index fingers and thumbs that work with touchscreens, but the seams on the inside make them tricky to type with and a little uncomfortable. They are slim, so not especially warm, but the finish is smooth and water-resistant, with rubbery anti-slip dots on the palm and other fingers. I like the clip for snapping them together when you take them off.
Try These Instead
Maybe you already have non-touchscreen gloves you love, or you simply don't fancy any of our picks. There are a couple of alternatives worth considering:
A stylus: It may seem old school, but a stylus allows you to use your phone accurately without taking your gloves off and will work with any smartphone or gloves. The Bargains Depot 2-in-1 Stylus ($9) worked well in our testing.
A handwarmer: If you brave the cold gloveless or use one of our thinner picks above, you might want to have a rechargeable handwarmer waiting in your pocket. My favorite is the VQ Rechargeable 10,000-mAh Power Bank Hand Warmer (£30), but it's only available in the UK. Folks in the US can find a ton of similar options on Amazon.

Shopian, Nov 9: Firm apple prices during the ongoing harvesting season have improved market sentiment across south Kashmir, with traders reporting increased customer footfall and a pickup in sales after months of subdued business activity.
Markets in Shopian, Pulwama and other apple-producing districts had remained relatively quiet for over a year, as traders struggled with low customer turnout and sluggish sales.
Shopkeepers attributed the slowdown largely to poor returns from the apple industry, which remains a major pillar of the region’s economy. Damage to the crop, partly caused by disruptions and closures of the national highway and erratic weather conditions, had affected growers’ earnings and, consequently, their spending capacity.
However, firm prices this season have brought some relief to orchardists, with the improvement gradually reflecting in commercial activity across the region.
“The good apple prices have had a positive impact on the overall market,” said Tariq Ahmad, a shopkeeper in Batapora, Shopian.
He said customers had started returning to shops, while restaurants, eateries, ready-made garment stores and other commercial establishments were witnessing better business.
“Markets are bustling with customers again. There is a noticeable difference in the number of people visiting shops compared to the previous season,” he said.
Traders dealing in different goods said the improvement was visible across several market segments and was not confined to any particular category of business.
Mushtaq Ahmad, who deals in ready-made garments and woollens in Pulwama, said business had picked up in recent weeks.
“People are spending more freely than they were earlier. When growers receive better returns for their produce, it has a positive effect on other businesses as well,” he said.
He said the improvement in purchasing activity was particularly encouraging for small shopkeepers, who had endured prolonged periods of sluggish sales.
Traders said the apple economy directly influences the purchasing power of households across south Kashmir, where a large section of the population depends on horticulture and related activities for its livelihood.
Despite crop damage caused by multiple spells of hailstorms during the season, apple prices have remained firm, providing some relief to growers.
Mohammad Ashraf Wani, president of Fruit MandiShopian, said A-grade apples were selling at Rs 1,300 to Rs 1,500 per box.
“Despite the damage caused by hailstorms, the prices have remained encouraging. This has provided some relief to growers and helped sustain activity in the fruit trade,” he said.
He said better prices benefited not only orchardists but also thousands of people engaged in transportation, packaging, grading, loading and other activities linked to the horticulture sector.
Shopkeepers said the business improvement was a welcome development after a prolonged period of uncertainty. For small traders, the return of customers to markets is an encouraging sign that better returns from the apple sector are gradually translating into economic activity beyond orchards and fruit mandis.

The African National Congress is on course to suffer a bruising defeat in South Africa’s local elections, with the once dominant party of Nelson Mandela falling to under a third of the vote nationally with more than 80% of ballots counted.
Wednesday’s fragmented vote marks another stage in the decline of the ANC, which has led national governments since the end of white minority apartheid rule in 1994. High unemployment, crime, corruption and poor local service delivery have all contributed to voters turning away from the party.
The former liberation movement is projected to lose its status as the biggest party in the two most populous provinces, Gauteng and KwaZulu-Natal, as parties began coalition negotiations behind closed doors. The final results are expected to be announced on Sunday.
The ANC was on 31.8% of the vote nationally, almost 14 percentage points below its 2021 local election result. The centre-right, white-led Democratic Alliance (DA) had 24.1% of the vote, while the uMkhonto weSizwe (MK) party of the former ANC president Jacob Zuma was on 9.3%.
Turnout also rose in Wednesday’s poll. The election commission estimated that 54.5% of registered voters cast their ballot, up from 46% five years ago.
The final shape of coalitions in some of the country’s biggest cities remained unclear with the final votes still being counted. Senior figures in key parties said they would talk with almost anyone, while keeping negotiating strategies under wraps.
In Johannesburg, South Africa’s commercial capital and biggest city, with 4.8 million people, voters have had to contend with regular water and power cuts, uncollected rubbish and potholes. The municipality, which has seen 10 changes of mayor in the last decade amid unstable coalitions, has admitted to a 220bn rand (£9.9bn) infrastructure spending backlog.
With just over half of votes counted in Johannesburg, the DA was leading with 40%, having run an energetic campaign under Helen Zille, a 75-year-old former Cape Town mayor. The ANC, which leads the current coalition, was in second place on 17.5%. ActionSA, a rightwing party led by Herman Mashaba, was on 15.5%. Mashaba has pledged never to work with Zille, whom he calls “racist”, something she vehemently denies.
Many of the ANC’s township strongholds have yet to report full results. The Council for Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR), a respected thinktank, has projected the DA will finish with 34%, the ANC 20% and ActionSA 16.8%.
Coalitions in Gauteng’s three city municipalities are often negotiated together. The DA is leading in all three.
The MK party, led by 84-year-old Zuma as he continues to weather and deny numerous corruption allegations, is expected to displace the ANC as the largest party in KwaZulu-Natal. Founded in 2023, it mixes socially conservative Zulu nationalism with pledges to redistribute land and wealth from white to black South Africans.
With half of votes counted in eThekwini municipality, which contains Durban, the MK had 41%, meaning other parties could form a coalition to keep it out of power. Meanwhile, the DA is projected to maintain its majority in Cape Town, despite growing middle-class anger over rising housing costs.
Voters choose a local councillor and a party, with seats allocated via proportional representation. Councillors will then have two weeks to elect mayors and form municipal governments.

Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister N Chandrababu Naidu on Monday called for the scrapping of high-value currency notes in India. According to Naidu, currency notes of  ₹500 denomination should be crapped and only notes of  ₹100 and  ₹200 denominations should be retained.
The Andhra CM also claimed that he had made same demand in his digital currency report to Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Chandrababu Naidu.
What Chandrababu Naidu said
“I will keep speaking on this. The notes of  ₹500,  ₹1,000 and Rs. 2,000 should be scrapped. Only notes of  ₹100 and  ₹200 should be retained,” he said.
Explaining the logic, the Telugu Desam Party (TDP) supremo said curbing high-value cash and promoting digital transactions can help tackle corruption.
“If technology is perfect, wealth creation and poverty alleviation are not difficult,” he said.
10th anniversary of demonetisation
Naidu’s comments came a day after the 10th anniversary of demonetisation announced by Prime Minister Modi, who, in a late-evening address to the nation, announced that high-value currency notes of  ₹500 and  ₹1,000 would cease to be legal tender.

The government had outlined several objectives behind the decision, including flushing out black money, eliminating fake Indian currency notes, curbing the financing of terrorism and left-wing extremism, bringing the informal economy into the formal sector, expanding the tax base and employment, and promoting digital payments to make India a less-cash economy, according to the Ministry of Finance.

Rwanda's army team removed from Africa league after US sanctions, NBA says
- Published
The National Basketball Association (NBA) says it removed Rwanda's army team from its African league because of US sanctions imposed on the country in March.
The NBA had previously said the Rwandan army-funded Armée Patriotique Rwandaise (APR) club would not participate in the 2026 Basketball Africa League (BAL).
However this is the first time the NBA has revealed the reasons behind the APR's removal.
The association was responding to complaints by two US senators, who sent a letter asking them to reconsider their partnership with the Rwandan team. The US placed sanctions on the Rwandan army, accusing it of fuelling the conflict in the Democratic Republic of Congo in March.
The senators said the NBA risked "becoming complicit in sportswashing by accepting money from a Rwandan government that systematically abuses human rights".
Last week, the US also imposed sanctions on Rwanda's defence ministry over its support for the M23 rebel group which has seized control of large parts of eastern DR Congo. Rwanda denies backing the rebels despite overwhelming evidence.
Rwanda is an official BAL partner and pays the league to host its finals at the 10,000-seat BK Arena in the capital, Kigali.
The BBC has asked Rwanda for comment.

In the letter to the NBA dated 23 October, Democratic Senator Jeffrey Merkley and Republican counterpart Marsha Blackburn gave the association until 2 November to give a written response regarding its continued partnership with Rwanda.
"What is the NBA red line for accepting money from foreign governments that commit human rights abuses?" the senators asked.
Among other queries, they also questioned how the association could "reconcile its continued partnership with Rwanda with its purported commitment to justice".
In its response, NBA deputy commissioner Mark Tatum said the Rwandan team "had been withdrawn" from the BAL following the sanctions imposed earlier in the year, American sports website ESPN reports.
The NBA said the APR basketball club would remain barred while the US sanctions are in place.
The APR is one of Rwanda's top basketball teams and represented the country in the BAL in 2024 and 2025, when it came third. It was replaced by the RSSB Tigers this year.
The BAL is a pan-African basketball league established and co-organised by the NBA and the basketball's world governing body Fiba.
It is a professional league featuring 12 club teams from across the continent.
Rwanda has hosted all but one of the league's final and playoff matches since the inaugural match in 2021.
The NBA reportedly receives millions of dollars annually from the country for the marketing and partnership rights.
DR Congo has repeatedly condemned Rwanda's high-profile international sports deals, including with the NBA, European football clubs and Formula 1, asking them to end their campaigns.
It argues that these help Rwanda clean up its global image, while the conflict continues in eastern DR Congo.

In sports, a “dead rubber” is a match that takes place after the outcome of the series or championship has already been decided. The people in charge hate this*—if you wrap up a title two-thirds of the way through a season, the viewers evaporate, as there’s nothing left at stake. But anyone who decided to skip this year’s Brazilian Grand Prix this past weekend missed one of the year’s most entertaining races, as a combination of a mixed-up starting order, some very fast drivers at the back, and a wet track that dried and then saw rain again resulted in action aplenty.
A peculiarity of F1 is that even if you manage to win a championship, there’s no guarantee you’ll be in a position to defend it. Take McLaren’s Lando Norris, who took the crown in 2025 after a nail-biting fight with his teammate Oscar Piastri and Red Bull’s Max Verstappen. Sadly for Lando, McLaren did not start this year in a position to win races, and even with several upgrades, the team has produced a car that is still very tricky to drive. But this weekend in Brazil, Norris demonstrated the form that earned him the number 1.
Rain on Saturday during qualifying helped jumble the usual running order. It was heavy enough that drivers used the wet weather tire with deep treads, which usually generates so much spray that visibility disappears and running has to be suspended. But with fewer cars on track in the later knockout qualifying sessions, this was not a problem for once. More disruption came from grid penalties for Verstappen and Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton, both of whom needed to use extra power unit components outside of the season’s allowance.
Everyone’s mixed up
Norris claimed pole, with this year’s new champion, Kimi Antonelli, alongside in his Mercedes. Row two was filled with the unusual sight of Liam Lawson’s Racing Bull and Nico Hulkenberg’s Audi, followed by Red Bull’s Isack Hadjar and Oliver Bearman’s Haas. Next was George Russell in the other Mercedes, then the even more unusual sight of Fernando Alonso’s Aston Martin, normally found much farther back. One could say the same about William’s Alex Albon, who qualified ninth ahead of the second McLaren of Oscar Piastri.

Health intel-sharing group warns industry in wake of cyberattack on French blood bank
In a new security bulletin, the information sharing and analysis center devoted to the healthcare industry, Health ISAC, alerted members to a recent wave of cyberattacks targeting refrigeration controllers — including one incident that affected a major French blood bank.
"This alert is issued for situational awareness, highlighting how recent operational technology (OT) attacks against specific refrigeration brands directly intersect with emerging threats to the health sector," reads the bulletin seen by NPR. Operational technology refers to the machines that control physical processes in the real world, from cooling systems to water pumps.
Cyberattacks on grocery stores and food processing plants everywhere from Europe and Israel to U.S. military bases have drawn headlines in recent months, particularly as attacks have resulted in spoiled food, fires, broken machinery, and major business disruptions. Attackers are clearly aware of the vulnerability of these systems and are taking advantage.
However, until news broke that the French blood bank, known as the French Blood Establishment, had also been targeted, there was less public attention focused on the potential consequences of refrigeration controllers failing in other industries, particularly healthcare, where lifesaving implements like blood and vaccines often require finely tuned temperature-controlled environments to remain viable.
"This incident underscores a stark operational reality: cybersecurity in healthcare is fundamentally about patient safety," wrote Errol Weiss, the chief security officer at Health ISAC in an email to NPR. "When threat actors manipulate operational technology like cold-chain storage and refrigeration units holding donor blood, plasma, or critical therapies, they aren't merely stealing data or locking down administrative files, they are directly endangering the physical resources required to sustain human life."
On Thursday, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, the FBI, the Department of Health and Human Services, and the U.S. Department of Agriculture published their own fact sheet about threats to industrial refrigeration and cold chain monitoring systems, tools they identify as critical to multiple industries from healthcare to chemical production, food and agriculture, and transportation.
The FBI Cyber Branch Operations director, Brett Leatherman, said the bureau is tracking bad actors targeting these systems "across critical infrastructure sectors globally, putting inventory and equipment at risk."
"Industrial refrigeration and cold-chain monitoring systems protect food, medicine, and other temperature-sensitive products, making them attractive targets for malicious cyber actors," Leatherman said.
Iran, Russia and the search for the culprits
The French blood bank confirmed in a press release Tuesday that one of its vendors used in cold storage rooms was targeted by malicious cyber activity, resulting in the defrost and temperature thresholds being raised dangerously high. The French Blood Establishment ultimately managed to detect the suspicious activity in time to rescue blood samples.
It remains unclear who is responsible for the global attacks on refrigeration controllers, and whether it's multiple actors or groups.
Iran has been linked to at least one incident in Israel earlier in the spring, though that breach involved a lot more sophistication and malicious activity. Investigators probing the disruptions at U.S. military bases are also considering Iran as the potential culprit.
Meanwhile, two pro-Russian hacking groups, NoName057(16) and Z-Pentest Alliance, belatedly released videos and posted on Telegram claiming responsibility for the attacks across Europe, publishing a sample of alleged hacked credentials that would've allowed them to access equipment including machines made by the Danish company Danfoss and the American company Copeland. Those machines can monitor and control temperature and other functions. The hacking groups have some history of targeting refrigeration controllers and other operational technology. However, it's unclear if the recent wave of attacks on refrigerators and freezers across Europe even required stolen credentials to execute, a factor that has led some cybersecurity experts to be skeptical of their claims.
Even so, it will require more evidence like access logs, configuration changes, and connections between maintenance accounts on the controllers to make any clear assessments, explained Tom Hegel, who leads threat intelligence research at cybersecurity firm SentinelOne.
"Russian-aligned actors are a credible hypothesis because there is a credible precedent, including the refrigeration-related attack DOJ attributed to CyberArmyofRussia_Reborn and NoName's history of politically motivated disruption. But that is only the context, not the missing evidentiary link to these European incidents," Hegel told NPR.
"It's important to note that such Russian threat actors often seek attention and claim to cause incidents even when false," he continued.
Regardless of who's responsible, the incident highlights how these nearly ubiquitous tools used to remotely manage critical systems are vulnerable to attack in several different ways.
For one, thousands of the refrigeration controllers in France alone were exposed to the open internet with almost no protection put in place before unidentified hackers went after them in October. Afterward, experts were still tracking hundreds of devices left unprotected. That's just a fraction of the tens of thousands of exposed operational devices online, many of them embedded in critical infrastructure.
Additionally, many of the major remote management systems used in refrigerators and freezers have security vulnerabilities. After alerting the companies to the problems, cybersecurity firm Claroty published research on vulnerabilities in multiple major refrigeration controllers, including those made by both the American manufacturer Copeland and by Danfoss.
While some of those vulnerabilities have been discovered and the vendors have designed patches to seal the hole, the problems don't stop there.
Experts warn it's difficult to patch operational technology because doing so often requires shutting systems down. In industries like healthcare, even minutes of downtime create extreme risk for patient safety. And for some aging models, it's impossible to patch, because the vendor is no longer offering updates — and companies can't afford to spring for a new model.
Sometimes, executives don't even know what machines are on their networks.
Additionally, for many companies, vendors that work with them demand remote access to systems like refrigeration controllers to regularly service them. It's often a requirement in the contract companies sign.
"Industrial chillers operate under vendor contracts that mandate persistent remote access," explained Nic Adams, CEO of 0rcus, a U.S. offensive security firm. "These commercial agreements leave national food and medical supplies defenseless against basic credential abuse."
Finally, hackers are now using AI to find these vulnerabilities faster than ever, and AI is also helping them to better understand the complex machines and the processes they control. Bad actors a world away no longer need to understand individual languages or industries, or even the physics involved to disrupt operations. In recent weeks, cyber incident responders tell NPR they're seeing a massive spike in attacks that are at least in part carried out by AI agents.
The good news is that a lot of these attacks, even if they incorporate AI, are not particularly sophisticated, novel, or stealthy.
Weiss of Health ISAC tells NPR there are basic steps the healthcare industry can take to prevent being a victim of these opportunistic attacks.
That process "begins" by "eliminating public internet exposure," wrote Weiss, then "enforcing strict network segmentation" in order to isolate refrigeration systems "from standard enterprise and guest networks" and finally adding on safeguards "that software overrides cannot bypass" like "hard-wired mechanical cutoffs" and "independent thermal alarms."
In the Health ISAC alert, the industry is urged to separate not just refrigeration controllers from hospital IT systems, but also medical gas monitors, for one, and train staff onsite on how to take physical manual control of machines in an emergency.
Finally, the alert urges hospitals to have offline backups of their systems.
Store managers on the frontlines
Sharing intelligence about these kinds of cyberattacks can help other potential victims avoid disaster.
While Estonian grocery stores were targeted in the most recent wave of attacks, many of those store managers were on high alert thanks to warnings issued by Estonia's Information Systems Authority, RIA. "When one Selver store was attacked on 2 November, the attackers managed to change the refrigeration system's temperature setting to +50°C. However, the service provider reacted quickly and prevented significant damage," said Annika Müür, a spokesperson for RIA. "So while we can't say that Estonia managed to prevent the attacks entirely, I think this case is a good example of the importance of monitoring threats internationally, acting on early warnings and working closely with businesses to minimise the impact."
Weiss of Health ISAC also urged companies across sectors that are being targeted by this recent wave of attacks to share information to help others defend themselves.
"The attack highlights why timely, trusted information sharing across borders and sectors is our strongest collective defense," he wrote.
"Rapid intelligence sharing allows hospitals and health facilities globally to recognize emerging attack patterns, verify vendor exposure, and harden critical infrastructure before threat actors can cause physical harm."

Inside the French drug gangs recruiting children to kill
- Published
Warning: Strong language and descriptions of sexual violence
Although she had just bought hashish from a drug dealer, the woman decided to call the police.
It was because, along with the illegal drugs, she had been handed a note by the young seller during their brief meeting on a Marseille housing estate in 2022.
"We're being held captive and need help. We are 15-years-old," it read.
The teenage dealer, a French court heard earlier this year, was one of two boys being held by a gang which they had both initially approached looking for paid work - albeit illegal.
One boy had been tasked with handling money, the other worked streets around the Frais-Vallon estate. Soon though, bosses had accused them of being responsible for "shortfalls" in takings.
What followed were regular beatings, the court was told, and being forced to dance naked in front of a camera as a form of blackmail. One of the boys was also raped.
Hours after the woman was passed the note, the two teenagers had tried to escape from a second-storey window, injuring themselves in the process. One managed to get away, while the other was caught, beaten and stabbed, but survived.
Arrests were made. Photos on the phone of one of the boys' alleged torturers showed several other young men in a similarly distressed condition. Six men have since been handed hefty sentences for what happened to the two teenagers.
The boys' story highlights the grip that drug gangs hold over parts of France's second city.
While the blend of Mediterranean culture, street art and hip-hop scene has made Marseille a popular tourist destination - beyond the city centre, it is another story.
After months of trying, a BBC team managed to enter this dangerous world - centred on deprived streets and high-rise housing estates in the port city, which police do not enter lightly.
We found an environment where ruthless gangs lure vulnerable young people with promises of easy money, but end up trapping them in a world of drug dealing, brutality and exploitation.
We saw how gangs use social media to recruit hitmen and spoke to several young men caught up in the violence. From prison, one gang member accused of involvement in several murders explained how his "cold-bloodedness" had helped him rise through the ranks.
The city's most powerful gang, DZ Mafia, emerged victorious from a bloody turf war and is now one of the most feared criminal organisations in France.
DZ is the official internet country code for Algeria, where one of the gang's founders, a French-Algerian called Mehdi Laribi, was detained earlier this year under a French arrest warrant.
The criminal outfit rose to prominence in 2023, when it became the first French gang to capitalise on its notoriety by releasing video statements - using social media to market itself as a brand - says the head of the country's anti-drug trafficking unit, Dimitri Zoulas.
Its most recent statement came in July, when the mayor of a nearby town had to be placed in police protection, after intelligence suggested he was in danger of being targeted by the group.
In an online video, six masked men dressed in black stood behind a table - as one of them read a statement denying DZ Mafia's involvement.
France's expanding illegal drugs market - which has seen a surge in cocaine imports alongside high volumes of cannabis and synthetic drugs - has also helped the gang grow rapidly.
The number of cocaine users in France is expected soon to reach two million, says Zoulas, up from 600,000 in 2017. Drug smuggling across France generates €7bn (£5.9bn) a year, involving 200,000 people, he adds.
Many of those distributing the drugs are children and the authorities say the number of minors caught up in trafficking is increasing. During 2025, more than 10,000 children were involved in some way, according to official figures.
DZ Mafia is a prime example. To reach more customers, it needs more gang members - more children.
We have found it is now recruiting young people from across France - not just to sell drugs, but to carry out kidnap, torture and murder.
They are a generation seen as easy to corrupt, but also expendable, by the kingpins who typically control them from prison or overseas.
And, as police and judges warn, once these children enter Marseille's underworld, it is very hard to get them out.
Few know the human cost of Marseille's gangs like mother Karine Brouillard - who lives at the other end of France, almost as far from the Mediterranean coast as you can get.
Her son, Hugo, first ran away aged 15 - from his home in a village in the Nord department - after an argument with his family. He was picked up by police three days later, almost 1,000km (600 miles) away in Marseille, with money and cannabis on him. He was taken home.
But several years later, in 2023, Hugo planned to return south, telling his parents he had secured a holiday job at a restaurant near Marseille.
"He gave regular updates," Karine remembers. "He called me, everything was going well."
Three weeks later, a doctor called. Karine says she will never forget his words: "Your son arrived last night. He took a bullet to the head."
Police believe Hugo was brought for medical help from a gang-controlled area and suspect he was involved with one.
That area was Quartier Nord.
Our best way into Quartier Nord, where DZ Mafia wields power, is with the help of resident Fadella Ouidef, a 41-year-old mother-of-four who gives us a tour.
Thirty-seven seconds after entering one housing estate, we find ourselves cornered.
Car horns sound the moment Fadella's Peugeot passes a gang checkpoint - the teenagers manning the post immediately spot our camera. "Wait, stop filming," Fadella warns, as a grey 4x4 forces us to the side of the road.
"I'm making a report for my housing association," she tells the inquisitive driver. He eventually agrees to let us leave if we stop filming.
It is unnerving to see a non-police vehicle move so assertively and a relief to watch it leave.
"Lately, the gangs have been very aggressive," explains Fadella. "What we simply try to do is make sure our young people understand what's happening is wrong."
Fadella speaks to a wider fear among local families: that their children are enticed by huge sums of money to take a criminal path that robs them of their innocence.
Money is what led one young man to spend his teenage years with DZ Mafia.
In order for our interviewees to speak freely, or because of safety concerns, we have agreed to protect their identities.
Camil tells us he worked up the gang's ranks to "running security" in one area it controls.
The now 20-year-old, who claims to have left the group, is highly suspicious of our presence, but agrees to tell us how the gang recruits young members.
"They know how to get inside your head. Whatever you want, they give to you," he says. This can range from nice cars and spacious apartments, to drugs and prostitutes, he explains.
"You feel loyalty because of what they give you. You'll stay until the very end, until either death or prison."
Camil also gives a sobering assessment of what happens if the gang identifies a weakness in a recruit: "They'll exploit it. You're their bitch, it's over."
DZ Mafia member, Adam - not his real name - tells us he was part of a DZ Mafia hit squad when we speak to him in a Snapchat video call.
He is currently in prison awaiting trial, after being implicated in several murders.
"People noticed my determination, my cold-bloodedness and, without wanting to, I climbed up the ladder of the gang," says Adam. "It became my place, I had to roll with it."
During the chat, he agrees the killings he has been charged with were "quite shocking".
"Attempts in broad daylight, in traffic jams… it can range from going to hit a guy, slap him to taking him in front of his mother and burning him up in a car. I think I have good composure, I handle it fairly well."
We challenge Adam on whether he feels regret when carrying out such acts of brutality.
He says he is "feeling in-part guilty" but claims to have no regrets.
"If I hadn't done all of this, there are other people who would have done that in my place, and so on. I am just another brick in the wall," he says.
Like so many teenagers from Marseille, he knew large sums of money could be earned quickly in drug trafficking. Now in his twenties, he admits the environment he entered was a "trap".
At a so-called deal point in a social housing estate - sealed off and controlled by DZ Mafia - price lists for cocaine, hashish and marijuana are graffitied on a wall.
The estate acts as a natural fortress for drug dealers. With one major road in and out, they can control the flow of customers and see if the police are coming.
It is not uncommon for the sound of automatic gunfire to fill the night air in these areas.
After months of negotiations, a deal-point manager from a rival gang agrees to meet us where he works.
We enter the estate early in the morning, the birdsong and children walking to school providing a stark contrast to the industrial-scale criminal operation that takes place here.
"Joe" says he was making €3,000 (£2,500) a month when he was 13. Now he says that has risen to between €5,000 and €10,000 a month.
He seems to see his life path as pre-ordained, albeit a lucrative one.
We ask Joe if he thinks about the lives lost because of the violence carried out by his gang, but the 23-year-old has also long made peace with the pain and destruction drug trafficking can cause.
"It destroys people, but we all make our own choices," he shrugs.
The work that Joe's gang and DZ Mafia are doing represents a threat to national security, says Zoulas, of the anti-drug trafficking unit.
There are road accidents, as well as family violence, depressions, suicides and more than 700 overdoses each year, he says, "and it distorts the economy".
"We are heading towards a potential systemic breakdown of the criminal justice system."
Police have had success in Marseille and other cities against drug gangs.
Criminal operations are being frustrated, more kingpins arrested and drugs seized.
Since 2024, about 1,000 individuals associated with DZ Mafia have been arrested, and 600 incarcerated, police say.
But overall, it is a battle that is becoming more arduous, rather than easier.
As gangs seek to widen their operations, or replace members who have been arrested or killed, social media has become a potent recruitment tool - especially since the Covid pandemic, when many street-drug sales jumped online.
On social media, we found countless posts advertising jobs in Marseille for aspiring drivers, couriers and hitmen, often with glamourised AI-generated images.
Nets are also being cast wider, as it becomes harder to entice young people locally because they know more about what might happen to them.
The ads can reach teenagers in most corners of France - including Paris, Nantes and Lille - and serve as a powerful pull to Marseille, and the Quartier Nord, police say.
Online advertising has also changed the typical profile of someone who would join a gang's ranks, say law enforcement officials.
Now, it is often someone without a criminal past, but who has exploitable vulnerabilities, like having a difficult family life.
"These people are recruited by unscrupulous sponsors who send them into the lion's den," explains Thibaut Fontaine, the head of France's anti-organised-crime unit.
Their lack of criminal experience, he says, makes them easier to arrest quickly.
Karine still has no idea why her son, Hugo, was shot.
Asked what she would say to gang leaders recruiting children and young men in Marseille, she says: "They destroy families. Little sisters, little brothers, grandparents. But then, I don't think those people have a heart, really."
The restaurant where her son said he was going to work did exist, but staﬀ there told Karine they had never recruited anyone called Hugo.
The reason for his death almost certainly lies within Marseille's Quartier Nord.

The Telangana government has expanded cancer treatment services to all 33 districts in the State, with day-care cancer centres providing chemotherapy locally to reduce the need for patients to travel to Hyderabad, Minister for Health C. Damodar Raja Narasimha said on Tuesday, November 3. The government has also initiated steps to establish Regional Cancer Centres to further strengthen cancer care infrastructure, he added.
The Minister made these remarks during a review meeting on medical services being provided to cancer patients in government hospitals.
Oncologist Dr. Nori Dattatreyudu, who also serves as the advisor to the Telangana government on preventive, curative and affordable cancer care, said 35,000 cancer cases have been registered on the dedicated cancer portal. “Declaring cancer a notifiable disease and effective use of cancer registry will help strengthen the State’s efforts in monitoring and controlling the disease,” he added.
Citing the Human Papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination programme as an example, Dr. Nori also appreciated the State’s efforts in prevention, screening and early detection of cancer. Of the 3.4 lakh eligible girls in Telangana, 2.3 lakh of them have been vaccinated against the HPV, achieving a coverage of 67%, he said.
During the meeting, officials briefed the Minister on cancer treatment facilities available at the MNJ Cancer Hospital and the Nizam’s Institute of Medical Sciences (NIMS), besides the functioning of day-care chemotherapy centres established across the State. They explained that while patients initially receive treatment at MNJ or NIMS, chemotherapy services are subsequently provided at district-level centres. Patients are also being mapped district-wise to facilitate treatment and follow-up.
The Minister directed officials to improve facilities for patients receiving chemotherapy at district centres and ensure that the services were readily available at the district headquarters. “Patients should not have to travel to Hyderabad for chemotherapy when treatment could be provided closer to their homes,” he added.

Maresca's dream start turns into nightmare as title hopes hit
- Published
Enzo Maresca left the City Ground on Saturday evening with chants of "can we play you every week?" ringing in his ears - and the Italian's dream start as Manchester City manager is rapidly turning into a nightmare.
Amid a sea of noise from the home faithful on the banks of the River Trent, the delirious Forest supporters witnessed their side produce a thrilling performance as City sunk to a third straight Premier League loss.
Maresca's leaky backline continues to make defensive blunders and once Josko Gvardiol gave the ball away for Jair Cunha to open the scoring in the sixth minute, City were on the back foot.
With Arsenal edging past Hull earlier in the day and keeping another clean sheet, City head into the international break searching for answers after a 3-1 loss and six points behind the champions.
Maresca said: "The first half we didn't match [Forest's] intensity or win duels or second balls. The first thing required in these games is intensity.
"We tried to react at 2-0 but it's too late. We scored one, probably could have scored more but in transition we concede one more. No panic. We need to understand but no panic."
Asked why the intensity was low, Maresca replied: "I need to analyse that."
The situation already looks bleak for City, but what does history show?
Should Brighton fail to beat Brentford on Sunday, Arsenal would be just the fourth side in Premier League history to have a six-point lead after 10 games, while only two teams have been so far behind as City at this stage and gone on to win the title.
One of those was Manchester United in 2002-03. The other? City themselves in 2013-14 under Manuel Pellegrini.
But Fabian Hurzeler's Brighton have the opportunity to leap up to second place and five points behind the Gunners should they beat Brentford.
There is another factor which looms large over City's campaign.
The club have lodged an appeal after being found guilty of breaking Premier League financial rules.
That process is ongoing - and it is not yet known what potential sanctions City could face.
But - even if any possible punishment does not affect this season - their title hopes are looking slimmer by the match.

It was a miserable return to the City Ground for Anderson since his £116m move to City in the summer and the midfield dynamic alongside Enzo Fernandez does not seem to be working.
The Argentine should have scored with a headed chance from close range but spent much of the game complaining in referee Sam Barrott's ear - City team-mates and supporters may be expecting more from their club record signing.
The former Chelsea player scored in the midweek Champions League win at RB Leipzig, but that is his only goal or assist in his past nine games.
Maresca needs to work out how to get the best out of Fernandez during the international break.
Stone added: "I came here tonight thinking City would win, I thought they had chances. This is a real hammer blow to them, there is something not right about the back four at the minute.
"I have never seen a City team give the ball away so much in the middle of the park."
'Big questions to ask the manager'
Rayan Cherki's stunning strike gave City hope but they could not turn it around and the numbers following the result make for grim:
- City have lost three consecutive Premier League games for the first time since a run of four in November-December 2024
- They have become the second team in English top-flight history - after Sheffield Wednesday in 1904-05 - to win their first seven games of a season and then lose their next three
- This was their first league defeat by two or more goals against a side starting the day in the relegation zone since November 2008 (a 2-0 loss to Bolton Wanderers).
Maresca was forced to chop and change his defence again, withdrawing both Gvardiol and Marc Guehi at half-time because of injuries, according to the manager.
It meant Nunes came in at right-back, with Abdukodir Khusanov moving inside, and Nico O'Reilly playing down the left.
Former Liverpool midfielder Danny Murphy told BBC Sport: "I thought City's performance was poor in terms of mentality.
"To make so make so many mistakes when you go anywhere in the Premier League, but especially to a team who are fighting for the lives, and you know they're going to come after you.
"They were sloppy with the ball, not winning duels. I would even probably go as far as saying there was probably a bit of arrogance at the start of the game from them.
"I think that there are now some big questions to ask the manager about how he gets them back on track. I think with the talent they have got, it is not going to be a big problem.
"But I think defensively, maybe sticking to the same backline for a little while is the way forward."

Measles strategy works – Now it must expand to more countries
Cape Town Measles Declaration pledges to cut measles deaths by half
At a landmark World Health Organization (WHO)/United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF) meeting in Cape Town, leading players in the fight against measles spelled out what it will take to stop 2000 children dying every day from this preventable disease. Together with UNICEF special ambassador Angelique Kidjo, they issued a call for intensified efforts and the resources necessary to ensure all children are protected against measles.
“We can do it – we’ve done it before – in Afghanistan, Angola, in countries devastated by conflict and drought and every other form of disaster,” said Carol Bellamy, Executive Director, UNICEF. “In just three years, and against great odds, we’ve cut the number of children dying from measles by almost 25%. It’s one of the most dramatic declines in disease mortality in history. But the next 25% will be harder. With the political and financial support of donors and governments around the world, we can together save many more lives.”
The “Cape Town Measles Declaration” calls on governments to take strong action against one of the world’s most vicious and prolific vaccine-preventable childhood killers – a disease which kills 745,000 children every year. We must control this disease to meet the Millennium Development targets of a 67% reduction in under-five mortality by 2015. The world leaders are well aware of the urgency. Last year, the UN General Assembly Special Session on Children set a 2005 target date to reduce measles deaths from 1999 levels by 50%. This year, the World Health Assembly, which includes 192 member states, endorsed the WHO and UNICEF measles strategy to combat the disease.
“When 30 million children are affected and 745,000 children die every year, you have to think big,” said Dr. LEE Jong-wook, Director-General of WHO. “Since the launch of the WHO-UNICEF strategy to reduce measles deaths in 2000, we have delivered measles vaccine to more than 200 million children globally. We know the strategy works. An additional half a million children are alive today because of all the partners’ efforts. But if we’re to prevent more deaths, we must do more. And we’ll need help from governments and from the international community.”
The campaign against measles has been dramatic – hundreds of thousands of children saved, the virus almost banished from the Americas and transmission cut drastically in many African countries, where the Measles Initiative Partnership has been the driving force behind the campaign. WHO and UNICEF have identified 45 countries as the highest priority for mortality-reduction strategies, accounting for 95% of global deaths from measles.
“It has been astonishing to see the results of the immunization programme in Africa,“ said Dr Mark Grabowsky, Senior Technical Officer, American Red Cross. “Now we have proof that we can reduce measles mortality even in countries torn apart by conflict, if governments are committed, communities are engaged and we have the support of donors, NGOs and volunteers. What we have accomplished so far through the Measles Initiative Partnership gives great hope for the future, and the many thousands of children we can still save.” The foundation of the measles mortality-reduction strategy is the re-invigoration of national immunization systems. At the Cape Town meeting, delegates discussed strategies with governments and policy makers for strengthening routine immunization services and making the life-saving measles vaccine available to all children as a matter of course.
”It’s not just about reducing childhood deaths today. We need to be in this for the long haul and this means a sustainable reduction in childhood deaths, which only a strong national health system can guarantee,” said Dr Stephen L. Cochi, Deputy Director, National Immunization Program, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). ”This kind of international focus and commitment gives us the opportunity to build that strength – boosting safe routine immunization services, establishing international laboratory networks and increasing surveillance to detect and respond to outbreaks.”
“Today the call to action is clear,” said Mr Nick Farrell, Senior Programme Officer, International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies. “ We have to ensure every child receives a second opportunity for measles immunization in these 45 countries, no matter how remote or marginalized, regardless of barriers of conflict, culture and poverty.
“To date we have seen tens of thousands of health workers and volunteers trek across mountains and deserts in all kinds of conditions to find these children to ensure they receive the life-saving vaccine,” said Timothy E. Wirth, President of the United Nations Foundation. “We are witnessing incredible commitment from ordinary people. They need – they deserve to be backed up by the world’s political will and financial support.”
Ms Angelique Kidjo, Special UNICEF ambassador, believes that the Cape Town Measles Declaration indicates a clear path towards a giant achievement in children’s health.
”The world has committed, to drastically reducing the devastating, pointless waste of young life,” she said. “If we reach our targets for measles, we will have taken a huge step towards keeping that promise. I believe we can get there – but only if we make it a priority to turn this declaration into action. This goal deserves all we can give. We must do whatever is necessary.”
Further information:
- Of all the vaccine-preventable diseases, measles remains the leading childhood killer. Measles is an important cause of overall under 5 childhood mortality.
- Measles affects over 30 million children. More than 745,000 die each year from measles – more than half of them in Africa.
- A safe, effective and inexpensive measles vaccine has been available for over 40 years.
- Measles accounts for an estimated 50% of vaccine-preventable deaths among children.
- One million measles deaths are already being prevented each year with existing immunization efforts. With the successful implementation of the WHO-UNICEF measles strategy (including routine immunization and periodic supplementary immunization activities), an additional 500,000 measles deaths can be prevented each year.
- Measles is a highly contagious vaccine-preventable disease caused by the measles virus. It is one of the most readily transmitted communicable diseases and probably the best known and most deadly of all childhood illnesses. Measles causes a high fever, rash, cough and can kill. It affects mostly children, but also young adults. Children usually do not die directly of measles, but from its complications such as pneumonia and diarrhea which attack their weakened immune systems.
- It costs less than a dollar to immunize a child against measles.
- A critical goal is to reduce measles mortality by 50% by 2005 (compared to 875,000 deaths in 1999).
- The WHO-UNICEF strategy to reduce measles deaths includes: achieving and maintaining high routine measles immunization coverage – ‘the first opportunity’ to infants; Providing a ‘second opportunity’ for measles immunization for all children through periodic supplementary immunization campaigns; Ensuring high quality measles surveillance is in place to detect and respond to outbreaks; and improving management of complicated cases.
- Collaborating partners include: WHO, UNICEF, the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the United Nations Foundation, humanitarian and non-governmental organizations, including the American Red Cross and the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies, governments of countries affected by measles, development banks, donor governments (e.g. Canada, Japan, the United Kingdom and the United States of America).
- The importance of developing long term immunization planning cannot be underestimated. This includes ensuring measles activities are fully integrated with other national health goals, establishing high quality surveillance, mobilizing necessary human and financial resources and planning for financial sustainability of measles mortality reduction activities.
