Anjali Sardana and Pronto entered India’s domestic services market in 2025 to solve a familiar urban problem: finding reliable house help on demand. The result was a quick commerce-style home services platform, combining technology-led recruitment, standardised training and a hyperlocal network of professionals. Pronto, which competes with Snabbit and Urban Company, says it has served more than half a million households across 11 cities. But the real story of Pronto is being developed far away from the homes and houses that its professionals visit. This is being built in Silicon Valley. Footage recorded by professionals working in thousands of homes every day is helping shape the next generation of robots. The first signs of this ambition emerged in May 2026, when Pronto was reported to be exploring ways to generate physical AI training data using footage captured during household chores. And since then Sardana and Pronto’s ambitions have solidified. In July, Pronto formalised the experiment through Verified, an opt-in premium service in which housekeepers and cleaners wear head-mounted or body-mounted cameras during visits. In October 2026, Sardana set up Provision Labs, a physical AI venture based in San Francisco, which will collect data to train and test AI systems designed to perform real-world tasks using robots and other machines. It will work with developers building physical AI models. A few days later, Provision Labs announced that it is acquiring Mumbai-based Basilisk Industries, a 2023-founded company focused on perception technologies, which help machines interpret their surroundings. Basilisk founder Shourya Watwani will lead Provision’s hardware efforts and work on its in-house post-processing models. Watwani and his team are said to have developed a 3D hand-tracking model and built the first version of a lightweight tactile glove to capture touch-related data. Given this timeline, the fact that Pronto doubled-down on its experiment after the May 2026 introduction does not seem surprising at all. The relationship between Pronto’s household data collection and Provision Labs’ operations, however, remains unclear. Inc42 asked Pronto how the two businesses work together, if at all, but the company declined to comment. The unanswered question is significant: could a network originally built to deliver household services become an acquisition channel for the data needed to train global robotics systems? Why Record Workers? The first reports around Pronto’s collection of worker data triggered a backlash over surveillance and privacy of house help professionals. To assuage some of the critics, Pronto said that customers are informed about the terms several times before recording begins, while personally identifiable information is automatically blurred or removed on the device. “The raw footage is deleted immediately after the work is done, and no one ever accesses it. For 48 hours, an anonymised, end-to-end encrypted recording is available only to the customer, who can watch it in the app to check the work. After that, we use the anonymised footage for AI training, as our terms set out,” the company told Inc42. Pronto said more than half of the professionals participating in Verified already earn over ₹40,000 a month. The company claims workers feel safer knowing there is a record of their work, but no independent studies have been conducted to validate these claims. What’s the point of all this? Unlike chatbots, which can learn from the enormous repositories of text and images available online, physical AI systems need to understand how the real world works. A robot must learn how to pick up objects, fold clothes, navigate a room, and respond when something does not go as expected. This requires large volumes of real-world, multimodal data capturing movement, spatial information and interactions with objects. Such data is considerably harder and more expensive to collect than internet-sourced text and images. ANI quoted a Goldman Sachs report estimating that general-purpose robots could require around 10 Mn hours of high-quality physical interaction data to reach production-level capabilities. The Missing Data Layer One can see the physical AI stack through four layers. The data layer captures real-world interactions, while the model layer uses this information to train vision-language-action models that translate what a robot sees into actions. The simulation layer through platforms such as NVIDIA’s Isaac Sim allow these models to be tested in virtual environments before deployment. Finally, the edge layer runs them on physical robots, with real-world feedback informing and enhancing the training process. Global technology companies such as NVIDIA, Google DeepMind, Amazon, OpenAI and Anthropic are building capabilities across the model and simulation layers of physical AI. India has some representation at the robotics and deployment end, with companies such as Addverb, CynLr and Perceptyne developing robotic systems and automation technologies. But it is the data layer that is seeing a growing crop of Indian startups, alongside global data companies building collection operations that rely heavily on India’s workforce and physical environments. Humyn Labs, EgoData, Egolab.ai, Neocambrian AI, Human Archive, and Objectways have deployed people on the ground to collect footage across household chores, but several are also working with manufacturing units and other industrial environments. Head-mounted or body-mounted cameras and sensor-equipped gloves or even full body suits have become commonplace as the next phase of robotics takes shape. For India, the opportunity has echoes of its earlier role in the AI supply chain. Over the past decade, India has become a hub for data annotation, with workers labelling images, text and audio used to train AI models. Physical AI takes that outsourcing model a step further. Indian workers’ movements, workplaces and interactions with objects are becoming the training material. Abhinav Kukreja, founder of Neocambrian AI, sees India’s large and diverse physical environments as an advantage over markets such as the US, where access to comparable real-world data is more limited. He believes the next phase of robotics will see an explosion of different embodiments and form factors. For India to participate meaningfully in this transition, it needs to control an important part of the underlying ecosystem. “I strongly felt that this layer would not be compute, architecture or algorithms, but the data layer,” he said. Y Combinator-backed Human Archive is pursuing a similar opportunity, with a model that involves home service workers, cooks, cleaners and domestic help wearing cameras inside homes and private properties. Cofounder Rushil Agarwal told Inc42 earlier that the Indian market’s appeal lies in the diversity of industries accessible within the geographical boundary and the large labour pool. This is difficult to replicate in the US. Notably, Human Archive was evaluated by Snabbit too as it looked to launch a Pronto-like data collection pilot. However, the home services company eventually dropped the proposal. Human Archive raised $8.2 Mn in a seed round led by Wing Venture Capital and NVP Capital. Pronto’s $45 Mn Series B also saw participation from Lachy Groom, cofounder of robotics model startup Physical Intelligence; Groom has also backed Provision Labs. Bengaluru-based Humyn Labs, led by former Nazara CEO Manish Agarwal, has committed $20 Mn towards expanding its data collection network. The supply side, meanwhile, is becoming more competitive. Data collection rates fell 30% between January and June this year, an industry executive told Inc42 earlier. More suppliers have since entered the market and synthetic data generation has improved rapidly. But in the long run, the demand for human-captured footage could shrink as physical AI models mature. The larger question is who captures the value and what happens to the workers. We’ll come to the latter soon, but the current situation does not give us any clarity on what this segment might look like in a few months. While Pronto says more than half of its Verified professionals earn over ₹40,000 a month, Human Archive has cited compensation in the range of $1-10 per hour for its data collection work. These disparate compensation structures highlight the lack of clarity on the economic model. One cannot draw parallels between the kind of data captured either till the industry further matures. At this point, companies are throwing a lot more money than they are willing to to attract workers who will readily collect data that can in a few years replace them. Indian manufacturers and industrial units may recruit workers, deploy cameras and collect footage, while the resulting models and intellectual property are developed and owned elsewhere. This value drain could have serious consequences on the Indian economy and the jobs landscape. For data suppliers, the challenge will be moving beyond one-off collection contracts to building differentiated datasets that command lasting value. As more and more companies come into the picture, the collection of egocentric data and first-person footage is about to become highly commodified and consumerised. The Elephant In The Room: What About The Workers? Like we mentioned, the business opportunity comes with a difficult labour question. The blunt reading of the matter is that Indian workers are training the robots that could eventually replace them. Videos circulating on social media have raised concerns about whether workers even understand why they are wearing cameras. Some workers have reported discomfort from prolonged use, which may stretch to 5-10 hours a workday, while others believe the devices are intended to monitor their productivity. Every company maintains that workers are informed about what is being captured and why. However, when collection happens through partner businesses, the responsibility for communicating this information shifts to those partners. An openDemocracy investigation, meanwhile, found that workers at two Delhi factories were asked to wear cameras supplied by Egolab.ai without being told their purpose. Such incidents raise questions about informed consent, compensation, the privacy of other people captured in recordings and ownership of the resulting data. India’s Digital Personal Data Protection Act, whose implementation is scheduled for May 2027, adds another layer of regulatory uncertainty. Speculation is that the government may regulate these services, but to what extent can it stop individuals from participating is unclear. For Sardana and Pronto, the opportunity is significantly larger than just a quick home services platform. The data from the broad range of everyday human activity by Pronto workers can fuel Provision Labs and Basilisk’s next big plays and turn them into even bigger companies than Pronto. Whether Pronto and Provision Labs will eventually work together has not been answered. But the value of Pronto’s network may very soon be the footage of what its professionals do, rather than the quality of the service itself.

At St. Joseph’s Church in Kuriachira, Thrissur, Keralam, faith and fitness go hand in hand. An open gym on the church premises is drawing parishioners of all ages to stretch, sweat and stay fit. The unusual initiative is adding a healthy new dimension to church life.
Set up in a corner of the church campus, the facility has quickly become a meeting point for fitness enthusiasts. With no fixed timings, parishioners can drop in at their convenience, with many heading to the gym after attending Holy Mass. The altar boys, numbering around 60, are among its regular users. Parents also bring their young children, while senior citizens use the basic equipment to stay active.
Roots in fitness routine of vicar
The initiative has its roots in the personal fitness routine of the church’s vicar, Fr. Frederick Eluvathingal, 69. A footballer and basketball player during his student days, he has never allowed age or a demanding schedule to come in the way of exercise.
“I have been working out for the past 51 years, ever since my days at the Papal Seminary in Pune,” he says. His fitness routine continued during his higher studies in Rome and Jerusalem and his church assignments in Australia.
When he arrived at Kuriachira more than a year ago, he began looking for a suitable space to continue his regular exercises, including push-ups and pull-ups. Parallel bars were installed first, followed by a basketball hoop. The idea gradually grew into a community gym.
“I wanted to create a space where people could develop the habit of working out. We generally do not have a strong workout culture. If people can fit in some basic exercise when they come to church, they may gradually make fitness part of their lives,” he says.
The need is particularly pressing at a time when lifestyle diseases and obesity are on the rise. The initiative also seeks to draw more youngsters into church activities and channel their energy into constructive pursuits.
The parish welcomed the proposal, and a space around a well on the church premises was chosen for the facility. The limited space available in Kuriachira meant that the gym had to be modest, but the response has been encouraging.
“Within a week of starting the gym, quite a few people began coming here. If the demand grows, we will have to think about expanding the facility,” says P.R. Wilson, one of the church trustees.
For regular user John Vazhappilly, a real estate broker who lives nearby, the gym has come as a timely help. “I have been coming here every evening for the past week. After an accident and surgery, the muscles in my leg became weak. I want to strengthen them. This is a comfortable place to exercise, with fresh air and an open campus,” he says.
‘A form of spiritual service’
The church sees the initiative as more than a fitness facility. “We want to groom a healthy generation. Many people suffer from lifestyle diseases, while youngsters often turn to private fitness centres. We felt that providing basic facilities here would benefit the community. Spirituality is also about nurturing a healthy mind and body. We consider this a form of spiritual service,” says assistant vicar Fr. Jees Akkara.
For Fr. Eluvathingal, there is another purpose. “Youngsters rarely come to church or participate in its activities these days. This is also an opportunity to bring more of them into the church community,” he says.

Christmas came early to London’s Leicester Square on Monday as Johnny Depp touched down for a red-carpet global premiere of Ebenezer in the company of director Ti West and cast including Rupert Grint, Sam Claflin, Tramell Tillman, Ellie Bamber and Robert Strong.
The red carpet was decked out with Christmas trees and artificial snow while 1950s festive classics blasted out in the backdrop, and if by magic, temperatures dropped, ending an unseasonably balmy autumn.
The chilly conditions did not deter fans who crammed into the red-carpet enclosure, most of them there for a glimpse of Depp. He did not disappoint, arriving in a timely fashion to talk to handpicked media and then walk the fan line.
Depp’s latest role as Ebenezer Scrooge is being billed as the actor’s comeback, after being left out in cold following his high-profile legal battles with ex-wife Amber Heard.
Watch on Deadline
Rumors are rife that if Ebenezer performs well, it could help green-light a reboot of the Pirates of the Caribbean franchise with Depp reprising his Captain Jack Sparrow role.
Whether this comes to pass remains to be seen but it was plain to see on Monday night that Depp was the main draw, with the public at least appearing to have moved on.
Talking to Deadline on the red carpet, West said he and Depp had bonded over a shared love of Charles Dickens’ ‘A Christmas Carol’ as well as admiration for Alastair Sim’s performance as Ebenezer Scrooge in an 1951 adaptation.
“I’ve been obsessed with it since I was little kid. I would read it every Christmas, and I was into it because it was a ghost story and then I saw the George C. Scott film when I was really little and Marley really scared me,” he said referring to Clive Donner’s 1984 version.
“I’ve had a fascination of it and a version in my head that I was waiting for someone to make that they didn’t make. What’s also cool about it is that it’s one of the rare stories that because it’s so enduring, redoing it, is part of the charm,” he said.
West said Depp had approached him about the role when he heard the production was in the works.
“He was obsessed with Scrooge since when he was a little kid also which I didn’t know and so when he found about the movie he was like, ‘Alastair Sim is a huge reason why I am even an actor.’ It was a weird cosmic thing where it was meant to be,” said West.
Depp confirmed West’s account in a public interview ahead of heading inside the cinema.
“I adored it as a child and to this day I know there is no better person to play Ebenezer Scrooge than Alastair Sim… the challenge is to find another angle,” said Depp, praising West for creating a atmosphere on set in which there was space to experiment with the role.
Not surprisingly, given West’s horror filmography, there is a gothic horror to feel to the adaptation, giving the work an extra frisson that goes beyond past big screen versions.
Ellie Bamber, who plays Ebenezer’s long lost love, that it also remains very much a family film. “It’s still very Christmassy with a hint of fright.”

Nvidia's meteoric rise in the past few years has been good news for its CEO, Jensen Huang.
The chipmaker hit a trillion-dollar valuation in 2023 and has shown few signs of slowing down amid the AI boom. In July 2025, Nvidia became the first company to crack the $4 trillion mark.
By October 2025, the company's stock price reached an all-time high, keeping Nvidia at the top spot for the world's most valuable company.
Huang, who cofounded Nvidia in 1993 and has served as its president and CEO ever since, has seen his net worth balloon as the chipmaker's market cap rises.
In 2024, he broke into Forbes' list of the top 10 richest people for the first time ever. His net worth is about $158.7 billion, according to the ranking.
Leading one of the Magnificent 7 companies, Huang has come a long way from his first job washing dishes and cleaning toilets at Denny's. However, recent questions about his relationship with a woman who, according to The New York Times, US officials believe was passing information to China may threaten his position at Nvidia.
Here's a closer look at how Huang built and spends his fortune, and how he hit his recent rough patch:
How Huang became a billionaire
As of March 2025, Huang owned roughly 3.77% of the company's outstanding shares, according to a proxy statement. He is the company's largest individual shareholder.
Before starting Nvidia, Huang worked at computer chip manufacturer LSI Logic and at semiconductor company AMD, which is today helmed by his distant cousin, Lisa Su.
How much of Nvidia Huang owns, and what is his CEO salary
Huang received a total compensation package of $49.8 million for fiscal year 2025, which included a base salary of $1.5 million, $38.8 million in stock awards, $6 million in cash bonuses, and $3.6 million in other expenses, including residential security and car and driver services.
His pay package was up 46% from the prior fiscal year, when it was $34.2 million.
Huang followed a prearranged trading plan in 2024 to sell 6 million shares by the end of the first quarter of 2025; as a result, he offloaded roughly $700 million in Nvidia shares.
How Huang compares to other tech CEOs and billionaires
Huang's total compensation for 2024 was pretty middle of the pack compared to other tech CEOs of the Mag 7 companies.
He's one of roughly 17 centibillionaires identified on the Bloomberg Billionaires Index.
At 62, Huang is older than some of his Big Tech peers, such as Meta's Mark Zuckerberg, Google's Sundar Pichai, and Amazon's Andy Jassy, but younger than others, such as Apple's Tim Cook.
How Huang spends his fortune
As far as Huang's real estate is concerned, he has owned property in California, where Nvidia is headquartered in Santa Clara, as well as in Hawaii.
He isn't known for many ostentatious splurges, but Huang's leather jacket is a staple of his wardrobe. He has worn several over the years at high-profile events, including one lizard-embossed jacket that appeared to be from Tom Ford's spring 2023 collection and retailed for $8,990.
Huang has also given some of his fortune to philanthropic causes. In 2007, he and his wife established the Jen-Hsun and Lori Huang Foundation.
They've given $50 million to Oregon State University, which subsequently named a research center for the couple, both of whom are OSU alums.
The couple donated $30 million to Stanford University, from which Huang received his master's degree, for an engineering center. They've also given $22.5 million to the California College of the Arts.
An Nvidia spokesperson declined to comment.
Jensen Huang hit a rough patch
Huang is facing questions about his relationship with Alice Huang, who has worked as an executive at Nvidia customer Megaspeed.
Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was photographed with the Nvidia CEO on various occasions, including at dinner events in Taipei.
In October 2026, The New York Times reported that US officials believed Alice Huang had been recruited to gather information about Nvidia for the Chinese government. Jensen Huang initially described their interactions as normal business dealings involving Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that rents out computing capacity.
On November 8, Jensen Huang told employees in an open letter that he had been unfaithful to his wife of more than 40 years and apologized to his family. He did not name the person with whom he had the affair.
Nvidia's board launched an independent investigation into whether he was targeted by a "foreign intelligence effort." The board said it still has confidence in his leadership and that it has no reason to believe that company secrets or national security have been compromised.

New Delhi: India is looking to export solar cells as its rapidly rising manufacturing capacity of the product, which converts sunlight into electricity and assembled into solar panels, is set to far outstrip domestic demand. In a first, the government is now in talks with several countries to find buyers for these cells, Union minister for new and renewable energy Pralhad Joshi told Mint in an interview.
This optimism comes even as India's dependence on China for cells' key inputs remains a challenge to scaling up production.
India already exports solar panels, or modules, but steep US tariffs have disrupted shipments to its largest overseas market, forcing manufacturers to look for buyers elsewhere. Export of solar cells will mark a significant shift for a country that once relied on the product's import to manufacture modules for its transition to green energy.
India's cell manufacturing capacity, currently at 50 gigawatts (GW), is expected to double to 100 GW by next year, Joshi said. But with annual domestic demand of no more than 50 GW, the country could soon face a glut, much like the one already seen in modules.
The minister said the government is already in talks with several countries for cell procurement from India at a time when the US market remains virtually shut due to high duties. Africa and Europe are among the potential export markets.
“Our manufacturing capacity is growing. Now, our cell manufacturing capacity will be 70 GW by December. In another three-four months, it will be over 100 GW. Once it is over 150 GW, we should be in a position to look at the market also…,” Joshi said.
Exports needed
Citing the excess production of solar cells, he pitched the need for export, either as cells as is or “with domestic cells we should manufacture modules and export”, adding that "if some country is ready to take the cells and manufacture the modules, we should do that."
The minister said there is global interest. "When we do things in this scale, the world also starts believing. We are already doing it (exploring the global market) for cells. Several countries want cells after seeing the success of India. We will see as we were already supplying modules to the US. Let's see what happens," he said.
Backed by domestic sourcing requirements, incentives and investments, India's solar module manufacturing capacity has grown sharply in recent years, helping the country emerge as a key supplier to the US as it looked to reduce its dependence on Chinese imports. The country has been the largest buyer of Indian solar modules, but recent anti-dumping and countervailing duties of up to 126% have forced manufacturers to halt shipments and explore alternative markets.
Considering ways to create demand
Data from the commerce and industry ministry showed that India exported $61.47 million worth solar modules to the US during April-July, way lower than $646.23 million in the year-ago period. During these four months this fiscal, most of the exports went to the US. Total exports of solar modules for the period were at $65.24 million, about one-tenth of the $668.05 million shipments in the year-ago period.
Now, with a booming cell manufacturing capacity, the government is forced to think of ways to create demand for these indigenous cells.
In a recent report, industry body the Indian Solar Manufacturers Association (Isma) said India's overall solar photovoltaic manufacturing is projected to attract about $89 billion by 2047, translating into an average investment of about $4.3 billion annually during 2027-2047. Nearly 70% of this amount is expected to flow into polysilicon, wafers and cells, it said.
The report projects that the country’s annual solar component import bill could decline from about $4.4 billion currently to zero by 2041 under the Vision 2047 pathway. India could account for 26.5% of global solar module supply by 2047, compared with around 5.9% under the current policy scenario by 2030.
Solar modules are produced by assembling cells, and the backward integration involves use of polysilicon to manufacture ingots that are used to produce wafers. These wafers are then used to manufacture the cells.
Cell conundrum
The production pathway for solar cells comes with a share of uncertainties. Although India has considerable capacity of cells to meet its domestic demand, Chinese cells are still imported, as they cost less. The freight on board (FOB) cost of Chinese cells is around ₹5 per kilowatt peak, while that of Indian cells is around ₹11.
Although the growth projections are robust, external factors may play a key role in India's plans of becoming a solar component export hub. The sector's top global player China recently proposed curbs on export of equipment for solar component manufacturing, which, if implemented may impact manufacturing of cells, wafers and ingots in India.
India is almost entirely dependent on China for wafers, ingots and polysilicon that are, in turn used to manufacture cells and eventually modules. Government has said it will bring wafers and ingots under the ambit of the Approved List of Models and Manufacturers (ALMM) framework, in a bid to develop sub-component manufacturing and indigenize the entire solar component ecosystem.
This framework requires government-backed projects to source specified equipment from approved domestic manufacturers. ALMM-I and ALMM-II cover locally-manufactured solar modules and cells, respectively, while the Approved List of Models and Manufacturers for Wind covers quality-certified turbines permitted for use in utility-scale projects.
Call on ALMM framework soon
While the frameworks for solar modules and wind turbines are operational, that for solar cells has been deferred until 31 December amid concerns over supply constraints. The minister had recently said government would soon take a call on the need to further extend implementation of the ALMM framework for cells.
Santosh Kumar Sarangi, secretary to the ministry of new and renewable energy, had on Thursday said in view of the high dependence on "certain geographies", the industry has urged government to extend its domestic manufacturing push beyond solar modules and wind turbines to include battery energy storage systems (BESS) and other critical components, seeking measures along the lines of the ALMM norms.
Although India has seen significant growth in terms of green power generation and module and cell manufacturing capacity addition in the past few years, its energy transition pathway faces several challenges, including a lag in commensurate growth in transmission capacity to evacuate the power generated, leading to generation curtailment and distress sale of excess power on the exchanges.
The lack in storage capacity has also resulted in a pile-up of unsigned power purchase agreements for about 40 GW of renewable energy capacity. Lack of storage capacities amid growing green power generation also raises concerns over grid stability, as both solar and wind are intermittent sources that could lead to instability and grid collapses.

Blockchain analysis firm Chainalysis said that hackers have obtained sensitive personal information—including names, usernames, password hashes, and live tokens—for all of its users following a breach of its network security.
The accomplishment could be a major coup for the attackers. Both Chainalysis and public sources have revealed a long list of high-profile customers, including government agencies such as the FBI, US Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency, and the US Air Force, as well as private companies such as Microsoft, Coinbase, and Barclays. It’s unclear if the data theft exposed customers to additional threats.
We regret to inform you…
Last Friday, Chainalysis said it had been the target of a cybersecurity incident in October that was similar to the hacks of other platforms during the same month. The external actor used AI agent-assisted offensive techniques to gain unauthorized access to Chainalysis systems and internal tools. An email the company sent to affected customers said some “non-sensitive customer data, such as user IDs, full names, email addresses, and organization role labels for users provisioned on our platform were accessed.” It’s not clear why the company considered such information “non-sensitive.”
In a Wednesday update, the company said that part of the “ongoing multifront cyberattack” involved an “on-path attack” that exposed a subset of customer passwords, and that the attack vector had been identified and fixed. Also known as an adversary-in-the-middle attack, on-path attacks happen when a hacker gains access to a piece of infrastructure sending traffic back and forth between two parties. Chainalysis has yet to say where the infrastructure compromise occurred and if the data obtained from it was TLS encrypted.

Delhi pollution monitors went dark as AQI surged on Diwali
DPCC data showed a peak of 3,744 and a worst-hour average of 1,480, suggesting the official AQI understated the pollution.
PM2.5 readings, which capture levels of smoke, at many of Delhi’s air monitoring stations went blank on Diwali night as they climbed towards 1,000 micrograms per cubic metre, pulling down the capital’s official air quality index (AQI) for the day after, HT’s analysis of records kept by the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) shows.
The missing hours, filled partially by on Monday evening by the Delhi Pollution Control Committee (DPCC), one of the three agencies that run the stations, show the smoke reaching a peak level of 3,744 µg/m³, more than 60 times the national 24-hour standard of 60.
CPCB did not explain the outage. A Delhi government official, who asked not to be named, acknowledged a glitch but gave no details: “The air quality monitors are giving hourly data. There were some technical glitches but all our 43 stations are giving data.”
Deep Dive
While the PM2.5 data was missing, the stations were still working. All through the night they kept sending readings for gases such as nitrogen dioxide, carbon monoxide and ozone. For the 1am hour on November 9, 38 of the 39 long-standing Delhi stations HT examined sent a nitrogen dioxide reading while 13 sent one for PM2.5. The PM2.5 readings mostly stopped just as they neared 1,000 µg/m³, and no reading in CPCB’s records for the night went past that figure.
DPCC’s release on Monday evening showed how high the missing readings had gone. Every one of the 125 station-hours missing from CPCB’s records at DPCC’s stations was above 1,000 on DPCC’s site. A station hour is one station’s reading for one hour. The readings dropped out somewhere between the stations and CPCB’s records, and the pattern points to a cut-off at about 1,000 µg/m³. Why it exists, and whether it is new, was not clear.
Also Read | AQI of 387 in India would be nearly 1,500 in US and 10 in UK. Why the range is so wide
The data gaps pulled the official figure down. Delhi’s AQI, the average of its stations’ scores over the past 24 hours, came in at 344 in CPCB’s 4pm bulletin on Monday, the day’s official reading, with the night’s worst hours missing from the stations’ averages. AQI is a composite number, capped at 500 for the official figure, that factors in readings of individual pollutants such as PM2.5.
In CPCB’s 4pm bulletins since 2015, Delhi’s air has been worse the day after Diwali than in the day before it every year. This year’s initially published figures broke that run: 344 the day after, against 369 on Diwali eve.
The late evening revision by DPCC changed how air pollution this Diwali will be recorded. Counting the readings DPCC released, HT’s estimates show, the AQI in the bulletin would have read about 360. The 9am figure, 370 as published, would have been about 384. Both estimates leave the blanks at stations run by CPCB and the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology (IITM) as they are, so both are a floor.
PM2.5 is fine dust, particles 2.5 micrometres across or smaller, and micrograms per cubic metre (µg/m³) is the unit for measuring how much of it is in the air. PM2.5 originates from burning, such as of firecrackers or paddy stubble.
The highest reading in CPCB’s records for the night was exactly 1,000.0, at Sirifort for the 15 minutes from 4.45am and at ITO for the 15 minutes from 6.15am. Last Diwali, 29 of the 39 stations recorded at least one hour averaging above 1,000, the highest 2,224 at NSIT Dwarka, according to OpenAQ’s copy of CPCB’s live feed.
Also Read | The Air We Breathe
At the worst of the night, the 1am hour, PM2.5 across the 22 stations with a full night of readings averaged 1,480 µg/m³, HT’s analysis of DPCC’s released readings shows. In CPCB’s records, where only eight of the 39 stations had a full night of readings, that hour had averaged 547.
Both figures are worked out as HT measured last Diwali: an average over the stations with a PM2.5 reading for every hour from 10pm to 6am, so that each hour is compared on one set of stations.
The released readings also show where the night was worst. Mundka recorded 3,744 µg/m³ at 2am, JNU 3,023 at 4am and NSUT’s West Campus 3,008 at 5am; Mandir Marg, Nehru Nagar and Wazirpur all went past 2,700.
Eleven of DPCC’s 30 stations went past 2,000. Where both sources had a reading, the figures matched in every hour.
Last Diwali, the worst hour of the night averaged 1,137 µg/m³ of PM2.5 across the 27 stations with a reading for every hour. This Diwali, once DPCC’s readings are counted, it averaged 1,480 across 22 stations. The two sets of stations differ, so HT also compared like with like.
Thirteen stations have a full set of readings for both nights. On those 13, this year’s worst hour averaged 1,173, against 1,017 last Diwali, about 15% higher.
The Supreme Court allowed firecrackers on Diwali only from 6am to 7am and from 8pm to 10pm, but they were burst across the city well beyond that window. PM2.5 rose steeply through the last hours of the window and stopped soon after. At North Campus, an IITM station, the 15-minute reading climbed from 291 µg/m³ at 8pm to 999 at 10pm, and the next readings were blank. Moreover, farm fire smoke and calm winds held pollution at a high level even before the city went into the festival. Diwali eve was the most polluted in a decade, HT reported on Sunday.
For this year’s Diwali analysis, HT considered the 39 stations that were also live last Diwali. Since then, 20 more have been added, including 13 in October, many of them on the outer edge of the city ,that have dragged down the city’s overall AQI, HT reported on November 6.
Across all 59 Delhi stations, 43 had a gap in PM2.5 between 10pm and 6am. Of those, 23 sent a last reading of 800 µg/m³ or more before it, and 14 of 900 or more. Stations run by all three operators went blank: CPCB, IITM and DPCC.
Between 10pm and 6am, 148, or 42%, of the 351 station-hours across the 39 long-standing stations were blank . The rate of failure was about six times the season’s baseline: on CPCB’s hourly data feed, which HT has stored since October 3, these stations had a blank in only 7% of their PM2.5 station-hours between 10pm and 6am, up to Diwali eve. .
HT had flagged a similar problem of unreliable data last year, when stations went dark. But even then, 27 of the 39 reported PM2.5 every hour from 10pm to 6am; this year, only eight did until DPCC updated the data. The DPCC update came late in the evening, meaning the 4pm bulletin -- the official record for the day -- for day the day after Diwali 2026 would not account for these emissions -- or the others from CPCB and IITM sources that remained blank.

Manoj Kumar, an analyst at the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA) who examined CPCB’s data, said many of the readings went missing as PM2.5 approached what he described as the instruments’ upper measurement limit of 1,000 µg/m³. “These observations should not simply be treated as missing when calculating hourly or daily averages or deriving AQI. Doing so could underestimate pollution levels,” he said, adding that 1,000 µg/m³ should be taken as a lower bound.
“This requires attention and transparency as one cannot completely blank out data when readings are expected to be alarming,” said Sunil Dahiya, founder and lead analyst at Envirocatalysts.
Political parties attacked the Delhi government over the readings on Monday. Aam Aadmi Party leader Saurabh Bharadwaj accused it of “AQI data fraud” in a video posted on X, alleging that the 20 new monitoring stations had been put in open, green areas and that water was being sprinkled around stations in heavily polluted localities to lower their readings.
Responses from CPCB, DPCC, IITM, the Delhi government and the Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM) were awaited at the time of going to print.

After the Democratic Party's sweeping victory in the 2026 U.S. midterm elections, a rumor spread that Time magazine had published a cover with a black-and-white photograph of Republican U.S. President Donald Trump with a sticker on his mouth that read "I Voted" and included the illustration of a U.S. flag.
The supposed magazine cover spread across social media, including on Facebook and Reddit. One X post read "TIME Magazine unveils new cover" (archived):
Several Snopes readers searched the website and emailed us seeking to confirm the claim was true.
The image is real; Time published it as the cover of its Nov. 23 issue.
The magazine's Instagram account shared the cover on Nov. 4, the day of the midterm elections (archived):
The caption read, in part (emphasis ours):
If Democrats had spent much of President Donald Trump's second term searching for a way to break his grip on Washington, voters had now handed them one. The midterms generated a blue wave that swept Republicans out of power in the House and the Senate, reversing the party's fortunes just two years after Trump's return to the White House. The results amounted to a decisive rebuke of a President whose handling of the economy, rising prices, and the war with Iran had fueled widespread discontent, and who spent the closing days of the campaign musing about candidates' anatomy and dismissing Americans' concerns over their bottom line.
Time also shared the image on its X account (archived) and its website, in a cover story analyzing the outcome of the elections (archived) and outlining the path ahead for Democrats.
The image appeared to suggest that voters in the U.S. had handed a definitive loss to Trump and his camp after two years of brash rhetoric and policies that resulted in the opposite of what his supporters believed he and his allies had promised, including an end to wars and more affordable cost of living.
According to Time, Trump has appeared on the cover of the magazine more times than anyone else.
For further reading, Snopes has verified other covers of Time, including a cover it titled "The Transgender Tipping Point" in 2014.

Skydance's top execs are thanking employees after a solid inaugural earnings report.
CEO David Ellison and co-CEO Ynon Kreiz sent an email to staffers after the Paramount side of Skydance reached its revenue goal and topped its profit projections in the third quarter — the first since the Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery mega-deal last month.
"The progress we've made is a direct result of your contributions," Ellison and Kreiz said in a post-earnings memo, which was obtained by Business Insider.
In the memo, Ellison and Kreiz reiterated their three goals:
- Establishing Skydance as the premier global content engine and the home of the world's leading storytellers
- Accelerating our integrated direct-to-consumer platform
- Optimizing our highly profitable linear TV portfolio, anchored by CBS.
The Skydance CEOs expressed confidence that their new-look company has the size and library to compete with tech-savvy giants like Netflix and Google's YouTube.
Skydance controls a slew of enviable, iconic assets, including the Warner Bros. studio, Paramount Pictures, HBO, CBS, CNN, Paramount+, HBO Max, Pluto TV, TNT, HGTV, and Comedy Central.
"We will lead in a crowded market by using our scale, assets and global reach to drive transformation and growth," Ellison and Kreiz wrote.
However, investors aren't sold on Skydance's business so far.
Despite posting a solid report, shares slid 2% in after-hours trading after initially jumping over 4%. The stock has whipsawed in recent weeks, soaring over 8.5% on Monday after falling more than 11% from pre-merger levels.
Skydance's success hinges on its ability to pay down its debt load of roughly $79 billion, a concern for some investors and analysts.
"The newly merged Skydance comes with massive debt that remains at the center of concern over the company's ability to profitably grow," Forrester media analyst Mike Proulx said in commentary ahead of Skydance's earnings report.
Ellison's company has said it plans to save $6 billion by buying WBD, and that the majority of those cost savings won't come from layoffs. Still, employees are antsy about cuts and bracing for stiff internal competition as Paramount and WBD's teams come together.
In late October, Skydance told employees to return to the office five days a week, or take a buyout offer, Business Insider has reported.
Read Ellison and Kreiz's full memo below:
Team, It's been a very busy five weeks since we closed the transaction and launched our newly combined company, Skydance. In many ways it feels like we just got started, and in others, it's hard to believe how much we've accomplished together in such a short time. This afternoon, we reported our third quarter results for legacy Paramount and shared an overview of the business, including our strategy and plans for the combined company. We wanted to follow up with all of you because the progress we've made is a direct result of your contributions. We've moved quickly to put our leadership teams in place across our three segments (Skydance Studios, Direct-to-Consumer and TV), established our organizational structure and are well on our way with integration. These are still early days, but the more we dig into the business, the more excited we are about the opportunity ahead. As we shared on day one, our strategy is built around three goals: establishing Skydance as the premier global content engine and the home of the world's leading storytellers, accelerating our integrated direct-to-consumer platform and optimizing our highly profitable linear TV portfolio, anchored by CBS. To get there, we will win in storytelling by leveraging our creative capabilities, talent relationships, production prowess and expansive library of iconic IP. We will build the most technologically capable media company, with a unified technology platform spanning streaming, live and linear that improves the user experience and drives efficiencies. We will lead in a crowded market by using our scale, assets and global reach to drive transformation and growth. And we will earn trust every day by communicating directly and transparently, backing up our words with action and following through on our commitments to the people we serve and work alongside. Underpinning all of it is our pledge to achieve at least $6 billion in annual savings and efficiencies as we bring the two companies together, and we're already seeing real results. We know there is still a lot of work ahead to position this company for long-term success. And the reason we're so optimistic about getting there is you. Everything we've done so far, and everything we hope to build, starts with our people. Whether you're telling stories, building products, reporting the news, serving our partners, supporting our productions or helping keep this great company running every day, you've embraced the pace and the change of the past several weeks with extraordinary determination and enthusiasm. We're incredibly grateful. We encourage you to review our shareholder letter for more details on the quarter. A replay of today's earnings call will be available shortly on our investor Relations site. Thank you for your effort, your commitment and your belief in what we're building. Keep up the great work! David and Ynon

Cricket Scotland said it will not schedule matches against Afghanistan outside International Cricket Council (ICC) events, citing concerns over the treatment of women and girls under the Taliban government and broader human rights issues.
“Cricket Scotland will not proactively schedule bilateral series or participate in tri-series involving Afghanistan Men unless there is a material change in the circumstances surrounding Afghanistan women’s cricket and wider human rights considerations,” Cricket Scotland said on Monday.
Women’s sport has effectively disappeared in Afghanistan since the Taliban returned to power in 2021, while access to education and employment opportunities for women has been severely curtailed.
The Taliban says it respects women’s rights in accordance with its interpretation of Islamic law and local customs and that internal matters should be addressed locally.
Scotland’s move aligns with decisions by Cricket Australia and the England and Wales Cricket Board to suspend bilateral ties with Afghanistan, which the ICC made a Full Member in 2017.
“This policy will be kept under review annually or following any significant ICC decision or material change in circumstances,” the statement added.

Scotland has not faced Afghanistan in a full international match since the 2021 T20 World Cup, but the governing body said the ACB requested training facilities in July ahead of its men’s series against Ireland.
The ACB had made another request for training facilities in Scotland in September regarding the T20 Afghanistan Premier League, it added.
Cricket Scotland also said it would continue to consider its contractual obligations to players and would issue no-objection certificates (NOCs) if the ICC gives the Afghan league official approval.
“If an NOC is issued, participation by that player/s must not be interpreted as an endorsement by Cricket Scotland of the current Afghan regime or its policies,” the statement said.

Psoriasis is an autoimmune condition that causes thick, scaly patches on the skin. However, it often remains unidentified and undiagnosed because it does not look the same on all parts of the body: it could be mistaken, for instance, for dandruff on the scalp, persistent eczema on the palms, or a fungal infection. You can’t always judge psoriasis by looking only at visible parts of the skin.
Why does this happen? Our skin isn’t the same everywhere. The thickness of the skin can vary considerably depending on the diversity of the environmental conditions that it is exposed to and the kind of treatment given to it. These factors can contribute to how psoriasis appears and feels.

If a good night’s sleep has become your holy grail, who are the knights in shining armour you will employ to reach that chalice? Most people seem to be deploying melatonin and magnesium supplements, over the counter, but the question that remains is: are they effective, and if so, at what combinations or levels?
The consensus among most sleep specialists, is that both melatonin and magnesium (glycinate) can have an ameliorative impact – in the short term. Both these supplements, however, work differently – while melatonin is a key body clock signal, magnesium helps relax the body. When and how you take both supplements makes a great deal of difference to your hours of sleep and sleep quality as well.

Nasdaq-listed traveltech major MakeMyTrip has expanded into the carpooling segment via the acquisition of a majority stake in Bengaluru-based Quick Ride for an undisclosed amount. In a statement, MakeMyTrip said that the acquisition will allow it “to establish a presence in the ride pooling segment, which is complementary to the group’s existing ground transportation portfolio.” As part of the transaction, Quick Ride’s brand and ride-pooling business have been transferred to a newly formed entity, Co Ride Mobility Private Limited, in which MakeMyTrip has acquired a majority stake. Quick Ride’s promoters will continue to lead the business. However, Quick Ride’s erstwhile electric vehicle (EV) taxi business will remain with its predecessor entity, iDisha Info Labs Pvt Ltd. Founded in 2014 by KNM Rao, Quick Ride offers a ride-sharing application that connects passengers to riders. It connects the commuters travelling in the same direction. It also offers an enterprise solution for shared mobility and counts IT companies such as Wipro, TCS, Infosys, IBM and Cognizant, among others as its clients. Its services are available in Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Chennai, Pune, Kochi, Delhi NCR, Mumbai, and Kolkata. The startup has raised over $14 Mn from investors like Sequoia, Prosus and Venture Highway. Sequoia exited the startup in 2021. MakeMyTrip's Acquisition-Led Expansion The Quick Ride acquisition is part of MakeMyTrip's broader strategy to expand its presence across adjacent travel and mobility segments through strategic investments and acquisitions. Commenting on the acquisition, MakeMyTrip group CEO Rajesh Magow said that the investment would help the company establish a presence in daily intra-city commutes while strengthening its intercity travel offerings. “As part of our expansion strategy, we have pursued selective strategic partnerships, investments and acquisitions that complement and strengthen our existing business and expand the breadth and depth of our offerings. Ride pooling gives us a presence in high-frequency daily commutes within cities, as well as intercity travel,” he added. The company plans to leverage its experience in building redBus across India and overseas markets to scale Quick Ride's ride-pooling business. In the past few years, MakeMyTrip has acquired Savaari to strengthen its car rental services, Happay in corporate travel and expense management, and Flamingo Transworld in regional group holiday packages. It has also made a strategic minority investment in visa processing platform Atlys. The development comes as MakeMyTrip looks to deepen its presence across the travel value chain, moving beyond conventional travel bookings towards a broader set of transportation and ancillary services. On the financial front, the travel tech major’s consolidated net profit for the three months ended June 30, 2026 (Q1 FY27) plunged 65% to $9.1 Mn from $25.8 Mn in the year-ago period. MakeMyTrip’s revenue grew 6% YoY to $285.6 Mn.

After protests in Arunachal Pradesh against the proposed Siang Upper Multipurpose Project (SUMP) turned violent on October 23, the state has unleashed a massive crackdown on the movement. The response has included the use of force by armed forces and law enforcement agencies, internet shutdowns, a paid PR campaign, censorship of social media content, and action against journalists and lawyers.
A 12-hour Arunachal bandh was called by local bodies and youth groups, including the Siang Indigenous Farmers Forum (SIFF), Adi Baane Kebang United and the Adi Galo Welfare Society, on October 23. The bandh was followed by large-scale arson in Pasighat, East Siang district, targeting an office of the National Hydroelectric Power Corporation (NHPC), a police station, and the homes of two MLAs and the BJP’s state president.
The proposed SUMP, with an estimated capacity of 11,200 megawatts, is planned on the Siang River across the Upper Siang and Siang districts. First proposed in 2008-09 by the UPA government, it was initially conceived as two smaller projects, with memorandums of understanding signed in 2013. On September 26, 2017, following a meeting between chief minister Pema Khandu, state delegates and NITI Aayog, the plan was changed to a single 250-metre-high dam, which would be the country’s largest in terms of installed capacity. However, stiff local resistance forced survey teams to withdraw, bringing the project to a temporary standstill.
The BJP-led governments at the Centre and in Arunachal Pradesh revived the project in 2020, following reports of China’s plan to build a dam on the Yarlung Tsangpo River, known as the Siang in India. In April 2022, the Centre directed the National Hydroelectric Power Corporation (NHPC) to conduct a pre-feasibility survey to assess the project’s technical, economic, social and environmental viability. The exercise involves geological investigations, including drilling, and identifying villages that may require relocation.
Chief minister Pema Khandu and other state representatives have maintained that the survey does not amount to a decision to build the dam. NHPC has said that preliminary topographical, geological and geophysical work is complete, but core drilling to assess rock characteristics remains on hold because of local opposition.
However, the manner in which the survey was pursued has fuelled distrust. In May 2025, Central Armed Police Forces were deployed at several locations. Police maintained that the deployment was necessary to maintain law and order and that the required clearance had been obtained months earlier.
In September 2026, the state Cabinet approved an empowered committee to oversee the survey, alongside a significant deployment of central forces. Villagers, however, fear that the survey is a precursor to the dam’s construction and have accused the government of using security forces to suppress their opposition.
Questions over consent have further deepened the mistrust. Activist and politician Tadak Nalo alleged that many consent forms cited by the government were false, with endorsements largely coming from villagers whose lives would not be directly affected by the project.
Several indigenous communities, including the Adi, Galo, Nyishi, Apatani and Idu Mishmi, inhabit the Siang valley and depend heavily on the river, not only for their agricultural practices but also for their cultural identities and religious beliefs. They call the river Ane Siang, or Mother Siang. According to independent fact-finding reports, the SUMP would completely submerge nearly 27 villages across the Upper Siang and Siang districts and displace an estimated 1.5 lakh people, almost 11% of Arunachal Pradesh’s population.
With their homes, livelihoods and cultural heritage at stake, people in the Siang valley have only intensified their resistance over the past two weeks. The BJP government’s response, however, has been one of force and intimidation rather than dialogue. It bears resemblance to the way dissent has been dealt with elsewhere under BJP rule — in Delhi, for example, against ongoing protests demanding accountability from chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.
Use of Force, Detentions and Internet Shutdown
One of the issues against which the October 23 bandh was called was the detention of anti-SUMP protesters since October 9. According to reports, The state government invoked the Arunachal Pradesh Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (APUAPA) and detained at least 10 protesters. Four of them — Adum Tayom, Omak Paron, Okut Paloh and Oson Paron, picked up from Pasighat — were reportedly held under APUAPA. Among those detained was the president of the Siang Indigenous Farmers Forum (SIFF) Youth Wing, a vocal opponent of the mega project.
The crackdown intensified after the October 23 violence. A further 69 people were arrested and four detained in connection with the violence. A total of 55 cases were reportedly filed: 26 criminal cases in Upper Siang, 21 in Siang and six in East Siang district. Arrests and detentions were also carried out under the APUAPA. Those arrested reportedly face charges relating to rioting, the torching of vehicles and the vandalism of office buildings and residential houses.
The state has also significantly increased its security deployment in the region. At least 30 companies of Central Armed Police Forces and three companies of Assam Police have been deployed, in addition to Arunachal Pradesh Police personnel. The Centre also flew in two additional companies of the Rapid Action Force (RAF).
There were also reports of police using tear gas and batons against protesters on October 23. Five women were reportedly taken to hospital after experiencing breathing difficulties. The police, meanwhile, maintained that some protesters had allegedly attempted to breach barricades and attack security personnel.
The crackdown has not been confined to Arunachal Pradesh. On October 31, a solidarity protest against the SUMP outside Arunachal Bhavan in New Delhi, organised by Youth for Change (YFC) Arunachal and Himkhand, also ended in the detention and alleged manhandling of protesters by the Delhi Police.

Protesters demanded the release of the detainees under APUAPA.
Censorship of Social Media Content
The crackdown on the anti-SUMP movement has also extended to the online space, with social media accounts of activists, journalists and news outlets being restricted or taken down. The censorship is part of a wider pattern in India, where government orders and platform restrictions have increasingly curtailed the circulation of content critical of those in power.
Tadak Nalo, founder and president of the political party Arunachal Frontier Tribal Front (AFTF), released a video statement after his Facebook account was restricted. Describing the situation in Arunachal Pradesh as “emergency-like”, he said fundamental rights, including the right to freedom of speech and expression, were being suppressed.
“My Facebook page, ‘Tadak Nalo for Revolution’, has been misused under the Information Technology Act and restricted completely within India today. If you want to view my page, you will have to go outside India. That is how they have set it up,” he said in the video.
Nalo alleged that his commentary on the SUMP was among the reasons behind the restriction. “A project this big is being built in our Arunachal, and it will cause displacement and render the indigenous inhabitants here landless. I had made some commentary on this and written some posts,” he said.
Several journalists and news pages have also reported having their Facebook pages disabled. Shaan Jijong, managing director of Upper Siang News 24*7, released a video statement saying that the outlet’s official Facebook page had been disabled. He also named two others, Ebo Mili and Katon Moyong, whose Facebook pages had allegedly been taken down.

He created a new account and published a post declaring that the censorship would not silence his opposition to the SUMP and that he had not lost his voice. However, we could not locate the new account on Facebook either, suggesting that it may have been taken down as well.
Two news reports published by Arunbhoomi News were also made unavailable for viewing in India. The outlet’s editor-in-chief, Takam Sonia, released a video statement condemning the move.
Human rights lawyer and activist Ebo Mili, whose Facebook account was also restricted, reportedly described the action as “deliberate and linked to his use of social media to raise public awareness about the project”.
The Facebook page Save Aborland and the general secretary and spokesperson of Adi Baane Kebang United, Datik Ratan, have also faced restrictions.
The Arunachal Press Club (APC) and the Arunachal Pradesh Union of Working Journalists (APUWJ) have condemned the restrictions on news reports and videos relating to the SUMP on social media platforms in India, and demanded transparency and their immediate restoration.
Targeting Arunachal Times Deputy Editor and Lawyer Defending Activists
Arunachal Pradesh Police have also moved against a journalist covering the anti-SUMP movement, seeking a search warrant against Tongam Rina, deputy editor of The Arunachal Times, in connection with the violence in Pasighat on October 23.
Police have also sought a search warrant against her lawyer, Sunny Tayeng, along with youth leader Otul Jerang, who has been arrested, and activist Tajong Talom, who was previously detained and allegedly harassed.
Rina took to X to assert that the police action would not deter her from her journalism or activism. “…I have seen enough intimidation in my life, so this isn’t something that will stop me from writing or my activism. She also criticised the move against Tayeng, pointing out that the lawyer was representing several activists, including Ebo Mili, Tajong Talom and Otul Jerang. Rina said she wanted Tayeng to be able to “focus on her practice rather than be burdened by extra work”.
The application for the search warrant, as reported by The Wire, describes Rina and the three other individuals as “accused persons”. No executive has pulled the strings in the artificial intelligence era quite like Nvidia’s CEO Jensen Huang. He parlayed the boom into incredible wealth, became a close confidant of President Donald Trump, and emerged as a prominent voice in US-China relations. That now all stands in the balance.
Over the last few days, Huang’s status as an AI titan has come under scrutiny amid an admission that he had an affair with Alice Huang, an executive at a Singapore-based company whom US intelligence services concluded was a Chinese intelligence asset.
Nvidia’s board of directors said that the company would launch an investigation into the incident. Huang, the company said, “fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it.” Huang earned $36 million last year, owned about 3.5 percent of Nvidia as of March, according to a corporate filing—which also noted that Huang is an at-will employee who can be let go anytime without severance.
How exactly the investigation shakes out, and what it means for Huang’s future at the company, remains to be seen. But the incident at least puts his position at risk, and raises questions about how the industry will respond.
“He’s the person who decides who gets the chips and who doesn't,” says David Yoffie, a professor at Harvard Business School who tracks the chip industry.
Nvidia, which Huang cofounded in 1993, controls 90 percent of the market for chips used in training frontier AI models. With those chips in short supply, Huang has the power to determine which areas of AI get a boost next. Nvidia has also bankrolled much of the AI buildout, investing billions in the very companies buying its chips, such as OpenAI and Anthropic. When Elon Musk wants to build a new data center, Yoffie says, he can put in a call to Huang.
Internally, Huang closely manages even small details at Nvidia, responds to emails from any one of its roughly 60,000 staffers, and raises his voice to get points across, according to current and former employees. He’s a regular on cable TV and at tech conferences, where he’s been trying to deflate concerns about an AI market bubble and boost the positioning of his company.
But Nvidia has no other executive anywhere close to Huang’s prominence, and no apparent potential successor. “We have no idea who would replace him,” Yoffie says. “You put someone new into that position, if you're a customer, who knows what that's going to mean.”
Ryan Fedasiuk, a senior fellow at the think tank Foundation for American Innovation, says that Huang has played such an important role—and become so close to the president—that he has become load-bearing for the entire US AI industry.
“On the one hand, Huang is irreplaceable. He built Nvidia into the juggernaut it is today, and he was the visionary behind the GPU, which has sustained the intelligence revolution,” Fedasiuk says. But he says that the company, which is indispensable to the AI industry, has to come first.
“He has to be replaceable as the CEO of the world's largest company, at $4 trillion in capex.”
Nvidia shares fell more than 4 percent on Monday, even as broader stock market indices rose.
The board’s investigation will most likely focus on whether Huang violated any company policies, Yoffie says. But the FBI could also investigate whether laws were broken, and Congress may decide to look into whether Huang’s affair influenced the US government’s policy on selling chips to China.
Nvidia didn’t immediately respond to WIRED’s request for comment.
The scandal also raises serious questions about whether China may have gained sensitive information about US AI companies and the government’s strategy on China, Fedasiuk says.
Huang’s affair appears especially damning given how outspoken he has been in recent years against calls for more aggressive technology export controls on China. His credibility on the topic could be permanently in doubt.
Both the first Trump administration and the Biden administration imposed export controls designed to limit China’s access to Nvidia’s chips, as well as technology required to mint advanced semiconductors. In his second term, however, Trump loosened these controls, giving China access to older generations of Nvidia chips; it was better to make China reliant on US technology, the argument went.
Sam Bresnick, a research fellow at Georgetown University’s Center for Security and Emerging Technology, says the Huang scandal is likely to accelerate efforts to crack down on chip exports.
“There was going to be more of an impetus to control what chips are getting sent to China anyway,” he says. “I expect there to be more scrutiny on what's going on, what's getting sent to China. I think there's also going to be more scrutiny from the Commerce Department.”

Amid rising concerns over the spread of Ebola to neighbouring countries, the Department of Health, Medical and Family Welfare, A.P., has stepped up surveillance at three airports — Bhogapuram (Visakhapatnam), Vijayawada, and Tirupati — as a precautionary measure.
According to Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, an official U.S. government website, the outbreak is spreading “substantially faster” than previous Ebola outbreaks and is now the second-largest Ebola outbreak on record.
In this connection, the Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare held a video conference on November 5, Thursday, with State governments regarding the precautionary measures to be taken. The Union government officials also reviewed the implementation of the Ebola guidelines.
A.P. Health Secretary G. Veerapandian, who took part in the conference, explained the arrangements being made in the State as part of the preparedness.
Arrangements at 5 govt. hospitals
According to a release from the department on Thursday, isolation beds at five government hospitals, medical personnel, emergency equipment have been readied. Mr. Veerapandian informed the Union government that medical teams had been deputed at three airports to screen passengers arriving from Ebola-affected countries for any symptoms. Similar arrangements are also in place at Visakhapatnam, Kakinada and Nellore ports.
A total of 46 beds, 3,288 personal protective equipment (PPE) kits, 104 sample collection kits and five ambulances had been kept ready to deal with any eventuality, he said.
Mock drill
A mock drill will be conducted on November 12 to assess preparedness at the State and district levels, he said, adding that the departments concerned would be alerted to ensure that the guidelines are followed.
The Central officials have advised that passengers arriving from Ebola-affected countries be screened for symptoms, and those who had direct contact with infected persons be placed under observation. The medical teams should verify travel history of even those who do not exhibit any symptoms, the officials said.
If any person exhibits any symptoms, they should be taken to the hospital where isolation beds have been set up, the officials told the States.
As of October 31, Democratic Republic of the Congo reported 10,467 cases and 5,103 deaths, Kenya nine cases and two deaths, Uganda 20 cases and two deaths, Nigeria one case and France one case. Overall, 10,498 confirmed cases and 5,107 deaths were reported across five countries.

Sports Personality of the Year returns - with five awards decided by public
- Published
The 2026 BBC Sports Personality of the Year show will be held on Sunday, 13 December - with five winners decided by public votes.
Clare Balding, Gabby Logan and Alex Scott will again host the programme, which will be hosted in Salford and broadcast live on BBC One, BBC iPlayer and the BBC Sport website and app from 17:45 GMT.
Five of the nine awards to be presented on the night will be decided by public vote.
The show will celebrate another great year of sport, including Team GB's most successful Winter Olympics, England's best finish at a men's Fifa World Cup since 1966, and record-breaking displays at the European Athletics Championships.
There will be two new award categories at the ceremony this year - Men's Footballer of the Year and BBC World Service Women's Footballer of the Year.
The latter has been a BBC World Service award since 2015 but will now be presented as part of the BBC Sports Personality of the Year awards for the first time. Voting - for global audiences - opens on Tuesday, 10 November.
In addition to crowning the winners of both football awards, fans will also select the winners of the World Sport Star of the Year, Team of the Year and Sports Personality of the Year award itself.
An independent panel made up of industry experts, sports broadcasters, sports journalists and former sportspeople will determine the shortlists for the Sports Personality of the Year, Team of the Year and World Sports Star awards, with the winners chosen by public votes. The independent panel will also determine the winners of Young Sports Personality of the Year and Coach of the Year.
Separate panels of football experts will provide the shortlist of contenders for Men's Footballer of the Year and Women's Footballer of the Year.
Alex Kay-Jelski - director of BBC Sport - said: "What I love about BBC Sports Personality of the Year is that it brings together all those moments that stopped us in our tracks. The goals, the medals, the upsets, the records, the stories that had us talking at work, in the pub and around the dinner table.
"And what a year we've had. This year's shortlists will be packed with athletes and teams who have achieved extraordinary things, but what's especially exciting is that audiences will have a bigger say than ever before in who takes home the trophies."
The nine award categories are:
- BBC Sports Personality of the Year
- Helen Rollason Award
- Young Sports Personality of the Year
- Coach of the Year
- Team of the Year
- Lifetime Achievement award
- Men's Footballer of the Year
- Women's Footballer of the Year
- World Sport Star of the Year
Full voting details, dates and T&Cs will be announced in due course.

A man who lost over $308,000 making sports wagers on Kalshi is suing the prediction market for violating the state of Washington’s ban on online gambling. He’s trying to turn those losses into an overall victory with a lawsuit seeking a payment of over $580,000.
Bellevue, Washington, resident Scott Bright’s “wagering occurred at a time when it was unlawful in Washington and when the Washington Attorney General had already sued KalshiEX LLC in this Court alleging precisely that,” said the gambler’s lawsuit filed on September 24 in King County Superior Court. Kalshi has since filed a motion to dismiss the lawsuit.
While state attorneys general throughout the US are trying to shut down Kalshi for allegedly violating state gambling laws, Bright’s case tests whether unsuccessful gamblers can obtain restitution from the company through individual lawsuits.
“Washington has prohibited Internet gambling since 2006. Washington has also provided, since long before that, a statutory cause of action permitting any person who loses money at illegal gambling to recover it from the proprietor for whose benefit the game was conducted,” Bright’s lawsuit said.
Even if Bright’s lawsuit fails, gamblers who lost on Kalshi could get money back through the lawsuits filed by state governments. For example, Washington’s lawsuit against the company said the attorney general “is entitled to recover all money Washingtonians have lost through Defendant Kalshi’s illegal gambling operation” under the state’s Recovery of Money Lost at Gambling Act. Washington already won a court order restricting the kinds of wagers Kalshi can offer in the state, but it took effect after Bright’s losses.
Kalshi says event contracts aren’t gambling
Kalshi wants Bright’s lawsuit to be moved to US District Court for the Western District of Washington, saying it must be tried in a federal court instead of a state one. In an October 30 motion to dismiss Bright’s case, Kalshi argued that he did not lose any money on “gambling.” Kalshi said he lost money on “event contracts,” which Kalshi says can only be regulated by the federal government.

Can Hong Kong hold its ground as Nasdaq brings Wall Street into Asian hours?
Nasdaq’s plan to trade US stocks nearly round the clock could tighten links with Asian markets, intensify investor competition, analysts say
