U.S. House Republican moves to force vote on impeaching Pete Hegseth
Secretary of War says he is happy to litigate military actions of the administration 'all day long'
Republican Rep. Thomas Massie moved Monday to force a vote to impeach Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, putting pressure on his fellow Republicans to decide whether to remove one of the Trump administration's most prominent figures following sweeping election losses.
The impeachment resolution largely focuses on the war in Iran. It also includes references to Hegseth's role in carrying out military actions in Yemen and Venezuela.
Massie said the secretary's actions amount to "high crimes and misdemeanours" and his leadership at the Pentagon "thus warrants impeachment."
A vote in the House could come by mid-week, putting pressure on Republicans — many of whom blamed their election wipeout on the Iran war — but next steps are highly uncertain.
House Speaker Mike Johnson had tried to prevent this outcome, and warned lawmakers against impeaching Hegseth while the U.S. is engaged in military actions in the Middle East.
"Impeaching a cabinet secretary right now, especially the Department of War in the middle of hostilities abroad would be a terrible, terrible look, a terrible thing for our allies and our enemies to see that," Johnson, a Republican, said as he opened the chamber.
"We don't impeach cabinet secretaries for political gain or for cheap tricks, and I think that's what this is and I think everybody knows it."
Hegseth defends actions
Speaking to reporters Monday afternoon, Massie said Hegseth has violated international norms and the U.S.'s own conventions of war in Iran.
"It's to the disadvantage and the dishonour of our country, and to the danger of our soldiers in future conflict," he said.
Hegseth said earlier Monday he's eager to litigate the military actions that he and U.S. President Donald Trump have taken against Iran, Yemen's Iranian-backed Houthi rebels and Venezuela's previous leaders.
"If you want to take issue with what we did in Epic Fury or Rough Rider or nabbing Nicolás Maduro, you're taking issue with the troops and what they accomplished, which is historic," Hegseth told reporters Monday, using the military code names for the Iran war and campaign of strikes to halt the Houthis' attacks on shipping in the Middle East.
Hegseth also announced that he would hold a rare news conference on Tuesday — his first in more than 180 days — on the impeachment threat. His last briefing was in May, and he has not held one on the Iran war, strikes on alleged drug-trafficking boats or other U.S. military actions since then.
The Pentagon chief is bearing the brunt of anger and calls for his ouster after the Iran war and its economic impact contributed to severe Republican losses in the midterm elections that cost the party control of Congress. Massie pushed forward an impeachment resolution over the objections of House Republican leadership as momentum grows to hold Hegseth accountable for the conflict.
Hegseth gave a State of the Force address at Marine Corps Base Quantico, Sept. 30, but has not held a media availablity since May. (Alex Wong/Pool/The Associated Press)
Hegseth waves off impeachment push as 'noise'
Hegseth, after giving a speech at the Naval War College in Rhode Island, brushed aside the possible impeachment push.
"There's a lot of politically motivated people who may have substantial policy disagreements, but their disagreements are with success," he told reporters. He added that "if we want to litigate" the military actions that the Trump administration has taken, "I'm happy to do it all day long."
"My team, we're not worried about the noise — it's what I told the troops, too — don't worry about the noise," he said.
Asked about U.S. Vice-President JD Vance blaming the Iran war for the massive Republican losses in the election, Hegseth noted that Trump said he would do it again, and "I agree."
He largely repeated a line that Secretary of State Marco Rubio said to reporters a day earlier: "It doesn't have to be necessarily popular, but it can be necessary."
Hegseth argued that the war was necessary because "someone had to confront the Iranian regime's pursuit of a nuclear weapon" and said "the choice was don't act and wish it away or take a bold move."
Iran has long maintained that its nuclear program is peaceful. According to the International Atomic Energy Agency, Iran has 440.9 kilograms of uranium that is enriched up to 60 per cent purity, a short, technical step from weapons-grade levels of 90 per cent.
Trump defended Hegseth to reporters on Sunday night.
"He's guilty of two things, basically winning two wars," Trump said. "I believe we saved the Middle East and Israel combined. And it's awfully hard to say let's impeach somebody who did that."
Hegseth insists 'Iran is devastated'
Hegseth reiterated that "Iran is devastated," even though the Islamic Republic has been able to keep striking military bases in the Middle East that are used by the United States, causing billions of dollars in damage, as well as commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz.
Disruptions to shipping in the waterway, where one-fifth of the world's oil passed before the war, have led to higher energy prices that hit voters' pocketbooks.
He said the next steps on the war are up to Trump, including telling Iran: "Hey, we're done, and we're going to watch your nuclear material. You better not move it."
With anger in Congress rising, Hegseth has been on a social media blitz, posting a video last week acknowledging the threat of impeachment. He said it would be "all about the politics of personal destruction" and insisted that "won't work with me. You can rest assured of that."
Since then, scores of political appointees within the Pentagon have posted images of Hegseth emblazoned with the words, "Stand. Fight. Defend the Republic." The White House also posted a video to social media that featured praise from Trump.

For three months, Suraj Kumar’s job was to feed discarded clothes into shredding machines in Panipat, an industrial city in the north Indian state of Haryana. Clothes discarded in the US, Canada and Europe arrive in the city to be torn back into fibres and spun into yarn, feeding a textile recycling industry that supplies markets across the world.
Suraj, 19, had travelled from West Bengal state to work in Panipat’s factories, following his cousins and friends who had already found jobs there. He hoped to earn enough to send money home to his parents. But in late August, an electrical short circuit in the machine propelled him into the shredding mechanism. The accident crushed both arms.
“I wish I had died rather than lost both my arms,” Suraj says. An only child, he had hoped his job in Panipat would support his parents. Instead, he fears he has become a financial burden on them. The work he had taken up to help his family has left him dependent on others, with no certainty about what his future will look like.
By some estimates, Panipat processes more than 1m tons of used clothing from across the world every year, making it one of the world’s largest textile recycling hubs. In the city’s 20,000 factories, employing about 300,000 people, discarded clothes are shredded into yarn and made into finished products, including home furnishings for brands such as H&M Home, Ikea, Primark, Tesco and Walmart.
But the fast-fashion industry, built on buying more and more clothes and wearing them less, carries a devastating cost for workers tackling its waste. Ramesh Chaudhary, an environmental activist who has worked in Panipat’s labour department, has been tracking reports of injuries and amputations across the city for the past five years. He estimates that at least one worker a day loses a limb, rising to as many as five on some days.
“Every day, we come across cases of workers injured inside factories, sometimes losing a hand or a leg, and sometimes even dying,” Chaudhary says. He gathers his information through a network of labour contractors who supply workers to factories across Panipat. But not all news of injuries reaches him, he says, suggesting the scale of the problem could be greater.
Between 17 and 24 August this year, the Guardian monitored reports from 11 private hospitals and two government hospitals in Panipat. In that period, six cases of textile workers with severe limb injuries were reported: two had lost an arm, another man lost both, one lost a hand, one lost a leg and the sixth their fingers.
Such injuries are common in Panipat’s factories, says Chaudhary, because machinery often lacks the necessary safety mechanisms. If a worker gets caught in a spinning machine, he says, cutting the power may not stop it immediately. By the time the machine comes to a halt, a worker may already have catastrophic injuries.
During numerous visits to spinning units and factories, the Guardian did not see anyone wearing any kind of safety gear. None of the workers interviewed reported having safety training.
India’s 1948 Factories Act places a duty on factory owners to protect workers’ health and safety. It requires serious workplace accidents to be reported to the authorities. But the effectiveness of safety oversight remains a concern, says Sandeep Sachdeva, co-founder of the Safe in India Foundation, which works to reduce industrial injuries.
“Factories are often audited by buyers, especially where quality and critical components are involved, and inspected by government industrial safety and health departments. Buyer audits tend to focus more on commercial requirements and product quality than on workplace safety or working conditions,” he says.
“Government inspections are selected through a central software system, but inspectors are now required to inform factories before visiting. Their role is now that of a facilitator-cum-inspector – a shift that undermines the effectiveness of inspections, particularly in factories with unsafe working conditions.”
For workers, losing a limb means losing their livelihood. Ramashankar Singh, who is in his fifties, from Chapra in Bihar, spent 18 years in Panipat’s factories before an accident last year led to him having a leg amputated.
It happened when a hot ball bearing fell on his foot. Ramashankar’s injury was first just wrapped in discarded cloth, before the factory owner sent him to a pharmacy.
The wound worsened as the infection spread. When Ramashankar approached his employer again, the owner agreed to arrange treatment and admitted him to a private hospital. By then, the infection had progressed so far that doctors had to amputate his leg above the knee.
“The factory owner said he would give me another job, possibly as a cook or a security guard at the factory,” Ramashankar says. “But that never happened.” The owner also said he would help him secure a government disability pension, but he has received no pension since the accident and relies on a prosthetic leg provided by a charitable organisation.
After so much of his life spent in a factory, Ramashankar says: “I have almost forgotten how to live without work. Much of my day now passes lying on my bed, staring at the ceiling fan.”
He also struggles with guilt that he has become a burden on his family.
India’s textile industry is the country’s second-largest source of employment after agriculture, directly employing more than 45 million people. An estimated 92% of its workforce is informally employed. In Panipat, more than 90% of workers are employed informally, says Ina Bahuguna, programme manager at the Estonia-based Reverse Resources, which monitors the city’s textile waste.
“Formal employment contracts and the social security benefits that accompany them, including pensions, are largely limited to workers in management, clerical roles and some specialised jobs, such as tailoring,” says Bahuguna.
Most workers on the factory floor lack these protections, leaving those who suffer serious injuries particularly vulnerable. Without formal employment or adequate social security coverage, they are left without employer-backed compensation, rehabilitation support or a source of income.
The Guardian asked several factory owners why they hired workers on a contractual or piece-rate basis rather than in permanent positions, and most cited the workers’ seasonal migration, saying some did not return to Panipat after travelling home.
For workers who sustain life-changing injuries, getting employers to pay for medical treatment can be a struggle. Indrapal Singh, who lost his arm in 2017, had worked in Panipat for 15 years, two and a half of those at the factory where he was injured. His hand was caught in a Chinese-made carding machine, which tore away the skin. He was given a painkilling injection but, as the infection worsened, his arm had to be amputated. The factory owner refused to pay his hospital bills.
Indrapal spent six years fighting his case through the courts, but says he received no compensation. The police told him that he had signed documents withdrawing his complaint, something Indrapal, who says he cannot read or write, disputes.
“I lost my arm, fought for six years, and in the end, all I got was a government pension of 5,700 rupees [£45]. The factory owner has faced no consequences, and the factory continues to operate as before,” he says.
Chaudhary says: “Workers have very little bargaining power when they are up against factory owners who are not only financially powerful but sometimes politically influential too. For many workers, taking them on in a legal fight is simply not an option.”
Arvind Kumar, the officer in charge at one of Panipat’s 12 police stations, says three workplace injury cases have been registered at his station so far this year. One involved the death of a worker. “Fewer than 1% of workplace injury cases reach the police and are formally registered,” he says.
Most cases, the officer says, are settled outside the formal legal system. Workers may receive a one-time payment towards medical bills, but then are generally left to manage the long-term consequences of their injuries on their own. The police rarely get involved.
For now, Suraj Kumar’’s family are grateful that the factory owner covered his hospital bills. They are not sure whether to register a police complaint.
“He [the owner] is like God to us. He is paying for our boy’s treatment,” says his mother, Sita.
Suraj struggles to imagine what comes next. “I thought that if I worked hard for two years, I could buy myself a motorcycle. I had so many things I wanted to do with my life. I never thought I would have to start by figuring out how to live without my arms.”

South Africa's ANC records worst-ever results in local elections
- Published
South Africa's ANC has recorded its worst-ever showing in local elections since Nelson Mandela led the country out of apartheid and into democracy more than 30 years ago, a result the party has called "catastrophic".
While it won the most votes of all parties in the country, the African National Congress won 30.76% of the overall vote, one third down from the 46% it gained in 2021, and a far cry from the 64.82% 20 years ago.
The story of its decline is also clear in the provinces and cities. The party won a majority in just one of the country's nine provinces, Limpopo. In 2021 it won six. It also won the most votes in just two of the eight cities, compared with six at the last local elections.
The Democratic Alliance (DA) came second in the overall vote with 24.64%, retaining majority control of the city of Cape Town. Former president Jacob Zuma's MK party came third overall with 9.76%, unseating the ANC as winner in the city of Durban, while the Economic Freedom Fighters (EFF), led by Julius Malema, once seen as a serious challenge to the ANC, came fourth with 6.22%.
"This has been a very catastrophic outcome for the ANC," said secretary-general Fikile Mbalula on Saturday. "We knew this disaster is coming, we're staring at it. As we got into elections, the cost of living of our people was too high. The middle class have turned on the ANC in big numbers."
Entering the count centre tonight, South Africa's president and leader of the ANC Cyril Ramaphosa said: "We accept the will of the people however concerning it might be, we accept that this is how the people of South Africa in our towns, in our cities, in our metros have spoken - and this is their verdict, we accept it with humility. It is a decline that is concerning, that is how I characterise it."
It's a continuing decline for the ANC, which lost majority rule in the national elections in 2024 for the first time in its history. It then had to form a coalition government with a raft of other parties in what is now known as the GNU, or government of national unity.
While the Democratic Alliance made significant gains in the cities in these local elections, its overall vote share rose marginally from 21.83% in 2021, and was below the 26.9% it gained in 2016.
Voter turnout was 52.29%, an increase from 45.9% in 2021, when elections were held during the Covid pandemic.
"This election is delivering a devastating message to the ANC", said political analyst Susan Booysen. "It's an ANC in decline at local municipal level, at the metropolitan level, and when the results are reflected provincially and nationally, we see severe declines in ANC levels of support all around."
The reason for that decline in support is largely due to poor service delivery and infrastructure across the country, from water and power to sanitation. "These are huge problems," says Booysen, "and have really been affecting the lives of ordinary people, in the suburbs, in the townships, and in very dramatic ways."
The big picture looks even more bleak for the ANC. The party will elect a new leader next year as Cyril Ramaphosa comes to end of his term. He is due to stay on as president of the country until the next national elections in 2029, but there are few candidates lined up to succeed him in either role.
- ANC under pressure to reverse South Africa decline 
  - Published4 days ago
"It is sort of the end of the liberation movement era in South Africa," said political analyst William Gumede, "and the dominance of the liberation movement since the end of apartheid. So the ANC is going to be a party that by 2029 could be the second biggest rather than the biggest party. It may actually spiral into a long period of just total infighting. This is a new era for South Africa's politics and also the ANC."
The elections also saw a significant shift in voting patterns, with the DA, traditionally known as the "white party" for attracting a largely white vote, gaining more black votes. "We're moving towards a post-racial voting pattern in South Africa," added Gumede.
South Africa now faces days of local coalition building, with the three metropolitan municipalities in the province of Gauteng, the country's powerhouse, under particular scrutiny. The ANC may even find itself shut out in the cities of Johannesburg and Pretoria.
"We are now in a coalition country," said Gumede. "Essentially, what the voters are saying is, "Well, the ANC has dominated the last three decades, they didn't use their power to change the society for the good, so we don't want the dominant parties anymore, whether at national level, provincial level, or rather now at a local level. We actually want coalitions. We want people to work together."
Parties now have 14 days from the moment results were announced to negotiate coalitions.

- Nintendo is hiring a digital archivist to preserve decades of its gaming history for "future generations."
- The archivist will organize historical records and interview longtime employees to collect more information on past games.
- The 12-month contract for the digital archivist role is based in Redmond, Washington.
Nintendo is taking steps to preserve decades of its gaming legacy. The company is looking to hire a digital archivist to organize and protect historical hardware and software records, development documents, and other important materials.
The role involves interviewing longtime employees to ensure their valuable knowledge about the company’s older projects is not lost over time. The move further highlights Nintendo’s commitment to its gaming legacy, especially since it has no plans to abandon physical games.
On the official Nintendo career page, the company has shared a job listing for a “Digital Archivist, Historical Systems” to preserve information about its older gaming platforms.
This will “ensure historical information remains discoverable, usable, and preserved for future generations,” says Nintendo in the job listing.
The listing went live in November 2026 and is an approximately 12-month contract-based job in Redmond, Washington.
The archivist will be responsible for building a searchable digital repository. This will contain historical technical records, engineering documents, and software development materials for games like Super Mario, Zelda, Pikmin, and more.
This digital repository will allow Nintendo’s engineering, development, legal, and research teams to access important information about older systems when needed.
Interestingly, the job also involves interviewing longtime Nintendo employees and industry experts to document their knowledge of past projects. This will help preserve details that may never have been formally documented. It could also prevent valuable knowledge from disappearing as experienced employees eventually retire.
Such materials could potentially be useful for remasters, remakes, or other projects involving classic games, similar to The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake. Additionally, this also shows that game preservation is not just about making older titles playable on modern consoles.
It also involves protecting development documents and other historical materials. Nintendo is not the only gaming company that is investing in these kinds of efforts. PlayStation already maintains a very detailed collection of historical materials, while Blizzard has also been working on preserving its gaming history.
For now, the job listing highlights Nintendo’s efforts to preserve the history behind its iconic games and consoles. Maybe this will enable the company to use AI to reflect on its massive game library for additional information and inspiration while working on future projects.

Two attacks in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) have killed 4 workers responding to the Ebola outbreak and injured 5 others.
The attacks occurred overnight on a shared living camp in Biakato Mines and an Ebola response coordination office in Mangina.
“We are heartbroken that people have died in the line of duty as they worked to save others,” said Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, World Health Organization Director-General. “The world has lost brave professionals.”
The dead include a member of a vaccination team, two drivers and a police officer. No WHO staff are among those killed, one staff member was injured.
“My heart goes out to the family and friends of the first responders killed in these attacks,” said Dr Matshidiso Moeti, WHO Regional Director for Africa. “We are doing everything possible to bring the injured and front-line workers in the impacted areas to safety. These constant attacks must stop. We will continue to work with the DRC Government, partners and MONUSCO to ensure the security of our staff and other health workers.”
In the last week, there were 7 cases of Ebola, down from a peak of over 120 per week in April 2019.
“Ebola was retreating. These attacks will give it force again, and more people will die as a consequence,” said Dr Tedros. “It will be tragic to see more unnecessary suffering in communities that have already suffered so much. We call on everyone who has a role to play to end this cycle of violence.”
The situation is still evolving. WHO will provide updates as new information comes in.

Erstwhile real money gaming (RMG) giant Dream11’s cofounder and CEO Harsh Jain has hinted at plans to launch a revamped version of the platform by 2026-end. In a post on social media platform X, Jain said that the “brand new Dream11” would be built by sports fans and for sports fans. He did not disclose the upcoming platform’s features, commercial model or a specific launch date. “A brand new Dream11 is launching (at the) end of Dec - by sports fans, for sports fans. Stay tuned…,” said Jain in his post. The move signals Dream11’s next phase of evolution after the ban on online real-money gaming last year disrupted the platform’s paid fantasy sports business. While the teaser points to a product overhaul, it remains unclear how substantially the new offering will differ from its existing services. This comes more than a year after the Parliament passed the Promotion and Regulation of Online Gaming Bill, 2025, which prohibited online real money games and restricted their promotion and advertising. Following the legislation, Dream11 discontinued paid contests and pivoted to a watch-along platform where users can follow gameplays of prominent content creators. It has also been exploring alternative ways to engage sports fans. Last year, parent Dream Sports forayed into the wealth tech space under Dream Money and began offering mutual funds, digital gold, fixed deposits, and loans. It later also forayed into stockbroking with DreamStreet and forayed into the SaaS space with Dream Horizon. However, it has been rethinking many of its newer bets. The startup shut down Dream Money in June this year. Dream Sports also quietly shut FanCode’s sports merchandise business earlier this year amid persistent issues with commercial viability. It also shut down its AI-powered sports performance analytics app Dream Play in June this year. Nevertheless, the startup’s portfolio still remains substantial. FanCode continues to operate as a sports streaming platform, while DreamCricket represents its push into AAA gaming. It also has its investment platform DreamStreet. Beyond the business challenges, Dream Sports is also facing GST dues of more than ₹20,000 Cr. In a blow to the company, the Supreme Court (SC), earlier this year, also upheld the tax authorities’ move to impose a 28% retrospective GST on real money online gaming companies over the full face value of bets placed through their platforms.

Packers & Bengals win in style - NFL week nine
- Published
The potential Super Bowl contenders are starting to emerge in the NFL with the regular season having reached its halfway point this weekend.
The San Francisco 49ers have the league's best record after winning on Sunday and will be joined on 7-1 by either the Buffalo Bills or Minnesota Vikings - provided they do not have a tie in Monday's game.
The Chicago Bears and Denver Broncos both ground out hard-fought wins to improve to 7-2 heading into their bye weeks.
The Cincinnati Bengals put on a show as the NFL's international series continued while the Green Bay Packers outclassed one of last season's Super Bowl teams.
Here are the top stories from week nine in the NFL.
Broncos claim NFL record
After winning at defending champions Seattle last week, Chicago looked set for another impressive victory as they charged into a 14-0 lead against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers in Sunday's primetime game.
Bears quarterback Caleb Williams then threw a career-high four interceptions before the Bucs drew level with three minutes remaining.
But Williams managed to lead the hosts into field-goal range, with Cairo Santos making a 38-yard kick as time expired to beat the Bucs 27-24 for Chicago's fourth straight win.
The Bears are now second in the NFC North, the only division in which all four teams have a winning record, but will go top if the Vikings lose to the Bills on Monday.
Denver are top of the AFC West after they scored two touchdowns in the final quarter and sacked Carolina Panthers quarterback Bryce Young with just over a minute left to clinch a 26-21 road win.
Not only did it extend the Broncos' winning run to five but was their 16th straight win in one-score games in the regular season - a new NFL record.
Bengals put on a show in Spain
Joe Burrow attended Milan fashion week this summer and modelled in Paris in 2024, but this week he visited Madrid to play his first international game.
The Cincinnati Bengals quarterback vowed to put on a show at the Bernabeu Stadium in the seventh of a record nine international games this season, and the Bengals did just that as they beat the Atlanta Falcons 34-17 to go 6-2.
After being involved in six touchdowns last week, Burrow played a part in another four in Spain. The 29-year-old completed 24 of his 29 passes for 271 yards to cement himself as a contender for his first Most Valuable Player award.
Ja'Marr Chase had a season-high 155 receiving yards as the Bengals scored more than 30 points for a fourth straight game – tying a team record.
The Bengals are now 6-2 and joint-top of the AFC North with the Pittsburgh Steelers, who they face in next Sunday's primetime game.
Their divisional rivals the Cleveland Browns lost 23-22 at the New Orleans Saints in overtime.
Packers ruin return of Patriots legends
Four-time Super Bowl winner Rob Gronkowski was inducted into the New England Patriots' hall of fame while his former team-mate Tom Brady returned to Gillette Stadium for the first time in his broadcasting career.
Yet they had to watch Green Bay quarterback Jordan Love put on a masterclass as the Packers romped to a 45-27 win against a New England team that reached last season's Super Bowl. It was the most points the Patriots had allowed at home since 1970.
Love went deep time and again, racking up 372 passing yards, three touchdown passes and a touchdown run. Wide receivers Christian Watson and Matthew Golden became the first Green Bay players to each claim more than 150 receiving yards and a touchdown in the same game since 1942.
Brady and Gronkowski are third all-time for passing yards from a quarterback-tight end duo (9,186) and Kansas City Chiefs pair Patrick Mahomes and Travis Kelce went top of that list on Sunday.
Mahomes brushed off an injury scare against the New York Jets to ensure he and Kelce surpassed Philip Rivers and Antonio Gates (9,352) to reach 9,360 during a 35-12 win for the Chiefs.
Garrett stars on Rams return
Myles Garrett and Aaron Donald finally played together for the first time as the Los Angeles Rams won 20-13 at the Washington Commanders.
After making his Rams debut in Australia in week one, Garrett needed knee surgery and Donald didn't make his return from retirement until week two.
While Donald, 35, is still waiting for his first sack of the season, Garrett claimed three and forced a fumble to help the former Super Bowl favourites clinch a third straight win.
Puka Nacua racked up 150 receiving yards and a touchdown but could join fellow wide receiver Davante Adams (hamstring) on the sidelines as he injured a knee. Nacua will have an MRI on Monday.
Although the Rams are now 5-4, their NFC West rivals the San Francisco 49ers and Seattle Seahawks both got back to winning ways.
The 49ers (7-1) won 38-17 against the Las Vegas Raiders while defending champions Seattle (5-4) beat the Arizona Cardinals 17-3.
More Colts trades before deadline?
The Indianapolis Colts have already begun a rebuild, trading away two key players during the season, and they could have more big-name departures before the trade deadline on Tuesday.
The Colts slipped to 2-7 with a 27-23 loss to the Dallas Cowboys but had already been in talks over running back Jonathan Taylor, their prized asset.
They have reportedly taken calls about quarterback Daniel Jones too, while wide receiver Josh Downs has requested a trade.
The New York Giants withdrew an offer for Taylor but head coach John Harbaugh said that "things do change" after Sunday's 19-11 win over the Philadelphia Eagles – a seventh straight loss for Philly and the Giants' first win at their divisional rivals in 13 years.

The young Somali woman changing how the world sees Mogadishu
- Published
As the sun rises over the Indian Ocean, waves lap onto the golden sands while palm fronds rustle in the cool sea breeze. Welcome to... Mogadishu.
This is the image that one young Somali woman wants the world to have of her home city - in contrast to the one of suicide attacks and young men wielding AK-47s that many people currently associate with Somalia's capital.
Sucdi Abdul Fattah Abdul Khader is among a growing number of local guides taking visitors beyond the headlines to explore Mogadishu's beauty spots, historic sites and culture.
Her favourite spot is Jazeera beach, where visitors can enjoy the sea before heading to nearby sand dunes.
"It's one of the tourist attractions where we bring our guests. It's a nice place," says the 23-year-old.
The dunes, she adds, remind some visitors of the Sahara.
But her tours are about more than scenic views. She also takes visitors to the fish market, where they discover the variety of marine life available along Somalia's extensive coastline and to parts of the city that reflect its history as a busy Indian Ocean trading centre, with the influences of both its Ottoman and Italian former rulers.
Visitors can also sample Somali food, including camel meat, samosas and traditional tea.
Sucdi says many arrive in the city with expectations shaped by years of hearing about the insecurity.
"Mostly, they are surprised by how beautiful the country is and how welcoming people are," she says.
At the fish market, she says, visitors are particularly impressed by the variety of fish species.
Guiding tours runs in Sucdi's family. Her father worked in the profession for over three decades, taking journalists, photographers and visitors from different countries around Somalia.
He introduced her to the business nearly three years ago.
"I started this job as a hobby, but it has become something that I like and am passionate about," she says.
She now works alongside her father and a team of guides, building on his experience while using social media to reach a wider audience.
She shares videos of her tours on TikTok, offering people outside Somalia a glimpse of places they may never have imagined visiting.
She is also considering producing content in English to reach audiences who do not speak Somali.
Tourism remains a relatively new field in Somalia, she says, with only a handful working as guides in Mogadishu.
The business is seasonal, but Sucdi says this year has been particularly encouraging, although numbers are still fairly low. Having five tourists a week is considered a success but she is confident that numbers will grow.
However, she says many visitors are still concerned about security.
Since the collapse of Somalia's central government in 1991, Mogadishu has endured decades of civil war, destruction and displacement. Much of the city centre was reduced to rubble, and basic services and infrastructure largely broke down.
But following the withdrawal of the Islamist militant group al-Shabab from most of the city in 2011, and the establishment of the federal government in 2012, Mogadishu has undergone a gradual transformation.
Returning members of the Somali diaspora, local entrepreneurs and investors helped fuel a construction boom, with new hotels, restaurants, businesses and residential developments reshaping the capital.
Today, Mogadishu is a growing commercial hub, although insecurity and the legacy of conflict remain part of everyday life.
About 10,000 tourists visited Somalia in 2024, a 50% increase on the previous year, according to the country's tourism department.
Many visitors ask about their safety before travelling and often encounter security checkpoints around the city.
But she says their experience on the ground is generally positive.
"What they heard from the news and everywhere else is not the same as what they see in the country," she says.
Although some question whether Mogadishu is safe enough for a young woman to be working as a tour guide, Sucdi is determined to continue.
She wants visitors to experience a Somalia that is rarely seen.
"I would want them to see the beautiful, welcoming side of Mogadishu, and not the side that they heard from the media, which is explosions and bombs," she says.
Somalia has Africa's longest mainland coastline, stretching more than 3,000km (1,860 miles) along the Indian Ocean and Gulf of Aden.
Its beaches and sand dunes sit alongside historic coastal cities such as Mogadishu, whose culture reflects centuries of Indian Ocean trade.
For some tourists, that contrast between the country's reputation and what they experience can be striking.
American travel content creator Chris Reese, who goes by the name Authentic Travelling, has visited Mogadishu twice.
His first trip, almost a year ago, was a solo visit. He enjoyed it so much that he decided to return with a group of friends, who had seen videos of his visit on social media.
"I had such a positive experience - I really enjoyed seeing the country for the first time - that I opted to bring back a group of my friends," he says.
What stands out for Chris is the city's coastal setting, its food and atmosphere.
"It is such a beautiful tropical place. I love the vibe, the weather and the food," he says.
During the group's visit, they enjoy lunch overlooking the Indian Ocean before heading out to explore the beaches and sand dunes.
"The desert is beautiful and picturesque. It is also amazing that it's barely a 30-minute drive from Mogadishu," he says.
Before his first trip, Chris says, much of what he knew about Somalia came from international news coverage.
"If you only read the news reports about Somalia, you would be scared to visit. And honestly, that's what I saw in the media before I came, mostly negative headlines."
But visiting the country challenged those perceptions.
"Coming here, on my very first trip, showed me that there is so much more to this country than what is shown in the headlines," he says.
Mihaela Patap, from Romania, loves Somalia's natural beauty.
Although she has spent only a few hours in Mogadishu, she has already visited the sand dunes and taken in the Indian Ocean coastline.
"The desert was so beautiful to see. I have also enjoyed the beach, and the ocean. It is inspiring," she says.
Having travelled to Somalia from neighbouring Ethiopia, she says she has been struck by the people's friendliness.
"I don't see anything dangerous. I feel safe and the people are warm," she says.
An experienced traveller, Mihaela says she prefers to visit new countries without having preconceived ideas.
"I travel the world to see new places, to see countries, to see the differences. I don't take a picture in my mind to compare the reality with. I'm just expecting the new to come to me," she says.
She hopes to share her experience and encourage others to visit Somalia.
"I'm going to post my pictures and say good things about what I'm experiencing. I'm going to promote it," she says.
For Sucdi, that potential is personal.
She is continuing a family profession while building a business in an industry with few women and using digital platforms to reach audiences far beyond Mogadishu.
"Somalia still has a long way to go before tourism becomes a major industry," she says.
"Through my tours, I am giving visitors an opportunity to experience its landscapes, our culture and people beyond the familiar negative headlines."
For her, every visitor is another opportunity to tell a fuller story of Mogadishu.

Kenya seizes 454kg of meth in drug crackdown

Kenyan police have seized 454kg (1,000lb) of methamphetamine worth an estimated $27m (£20m) in an operation targeting international drug trafficking networks.
Three suspects, two Tanzanians and a Ugandan, were arrested at the Kenyan coast following an intelligence-led operation involving Kenyan anti-narcotics officers and their Tanzanian counterparts.
Police said the investigations began after a key suspect was arrested in Tanzania last week and handed over to Kenyan authorities at the border.
Methamphetamine, commonly known as meth, is a harmful illegal synthetic drug that is highly addictive and can lead to severe psychosis, heart attack or stroke.
The suspect, who was allegedly linked to a separate seizure of 250 kg of suspected methamphetamine and cocaine in Tanzania, led officers to a location in Msambweni on the Kenyan coast, where the drug haul was discovered.
Police made further arrests at the site and seized two motor vehicles and a motorcycle.
The four suspects are currently in custody and due to be arraigned in court, while the recovered narcotics and the seized items are being kept as exhibits.
The police say the operation remains ongoing and urged members of the public to to share information that will help tackle drug trafficking.
Last month, Deputy President Kithure Kindiki declared illicit alcohol and drug abuse among top threats to the Kenya's future.
He warned that the government would introduce tougher laws and intensify nationwide operations to deal with the menace.
In a separate operation last month, authorities destroyed more than a tonne of methamphetamine from a consignment intercepted last year by the Kenyan navy about 630km (391 miles) off the Mombasa coast.
The Institute for Security Studies, a think-tank, has warned of a shift in East Africa's role in international drug trafficking role.
It says the region's coastline is increasingly becoming not just a transit route for drugs destined for other markets but also an entry point for manufactured drugs intended for local consumption.

Social media platform X has told the Delhi High Court that takedown notices purportedly issued by the Delhi Police against digital rights organisations Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) and Software Freedom Law Center (SFLC.in) were fake. According to a post by IFF today, X said an internal investigation found the purported police communications to be fake and that it had filed a complaint with law enforcement authorities. X’s counsel told the court that an imposter had submitted the requests in the Delhi Police’s name. “X stated that it is not likely to take any action at this stage,” IFF’s post added. The court recorded X’s statement and disposed of the organisations’ petitions, granting them liberty to approach it again if the platform takes action against their accounts. Senior advocate Akhil Sibal, representing both organisations, placed X’s transparency reports and a legal notice purportedly sent on behalf of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) on record. IFF said it had written to the RSS seeking confirmation of the legal notice’s authenticity but received no response. Separately, SFLC.in said an email seeking verification of the takedown requests had bounced back from the Delhi Police address mentioned in the communication. How The Dispute Began IFF said X forwarded two ‘Illegal Content Reports’ to it on Tuesday (November 3), submitted in the name of the Special Commissioner of Police (Crime), Delhi Police. The first, dated October 31, sought the removal of a post IFF published on October 30 and another by SFLC.in. The second, dated Monday (November 2), sought the removal of 37 posts and the withholding of the accounts of IFF, SFLC.in, and GeoBlockedIndia. The reports alleged that the posts defamed the RSS under Section 356 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS). The posts reproduced and commented on a legal notice the organisations said they had received in the RSS’s name. IFF contested the requests, arguing that its posts were protected speech under Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution. It also questioned their legal basis, saying the reports cited no complaint, FIR, Magistrate’s order, or court order. Through its counsel, IFF subsequently served a legal notice to the Delhi Police, with a copy to X, seeking withdrawal of the reports and details of the authority under which they had been submitted. It also asked X not to act on the requests pending their withdrawal or adjudication. IFF approached the Delhi High Court after receiving no official withdrawal or clarification from the Delhi Police. Platform Accountability Under Scrutiny The dispute comes amid a wider debate over content takedowns, transparency, and platforms’ responsibilities when responding to government requests. In July, former Twitter CEO Jack Dorsey claimed that the Indian government had directed GitHub to remove three URLs linked to bitchat, an open-source messaging app that enables peer-to-peer communication without internet connectivity or centralised servers. The Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre’s (I4C) reported directive gave GitHub three hours to remove or disable access to the URLs. These covered the project’s main source code repository, Android repository, and Android releases page. The agency cited concerns over anonymous communication and difficulties in lawful interception and investigations. Meanwhile, MeitY is reportedly exploring withdrawing safe harbour protection under Section 79 of the IT Act, 2000, from social media platforms. The provision limits intermediaries’ liability for third-party content, subject to prescribed conditions.

How a bank collapse left millions in limbo and toppled Paraguay's president
ASUNCIÓN, Paraguay — When Ueno Bank's services abruptly stopped working in the early hours of Tuesday morning, the consequences were immediate for the millions of Paraguayans who had come to depend on it for everyday transactions.
"People don't have any trust," said Elizabeth González, a 28-year-old barista at a café in downtown Asunción, a few blocks from Paraguay's Congress building, where protesters had begun gathering after the bank's collapse was announced Tuesday.
Earlier, one customer had walked into the café and insisted on paying in cash. He no longer trusted any bank.
"If Paraguayans themselves aren't confident right now, foreign investors will be less so," González said.
The collapse affected far more than the bank's shareholders. Ueno said it had 2.9 million customers — around 60% of Paraguay's adult population. The Central Bank said the bank had approximately 1.8 million depositors.
By Saturday, authorities said almost 1.2 million customers had received an advance payment under the state's deposit guarantee fund, but many were still waiting.
It also led to the impeachment and removal of President Santiago Peña, a close ally of President Donald Trump, and exposed a power struggle inside within the ruling Colorado Party.
The anger was palpable outside Congress on Friday, where hundreds had gathered to protest not only their inability to access their money but also what they saw as a broader failure of accountability.
"I came not because it affects me personally, but because it affects all of Paraguay," said Elodia Saveredo, a 71-year-old housewife who sells her own handicrafts online.
Batarram Caballero, a 23-year-old fifth-year biochemistry student and president of the student center at the National University of Asunción, said classmates had money frozen that they needed to cover basic expenses.
"It wasn't a lot of money, perhaps, but it was money for their bus fare. It was money for their food," she said. "To hear that and not be able to do anything because I don't have the resources to help them is very discouraging."
Ueno Bank launched as a fintech in 2021 and began operating as a bank in November 2023. Its meteoric rise to become one of the country's most important financial institutions was driven by slick marketing and a digital model based around convenience and cashback deals; customers could open accounts on their phones and were offered incentives to process payments through the platform.
Caballero believes the crisis was foretold by an intense campaign in the days before accounts were frozen.
"They were bombarding us with messages telling us to put our money there," she said. "There were also rumors about what was already on the cards."
The bank also held substantial public funds. The Social Security Institute, known as IPS, had around $355 million invested in Ueno, roughly 9% of its portfolio.
The sums involved have raised questions about how such a young bank came to hold so much public money.
Manuel Ferreira, an economist and former finance minister, told local outlet ABC Color that the collapse raised fundamental questions about how the bank managed its assets. He pointed out that, in a typical bank, shareholders provide only a small portion of the money behind its assets, while the bulk comes from customer deposits.
He also argued that marketing and discounts helped attract customers but did not create lasting assets. A bank's principal asset, he said, was its loan portfolio: money owed by borrowers.
But in the case of Ueno, many of those loans had gone to companies directly linked to the bank's controlling owners, Grupo Vásquez, including $146 million in loans made to just three companies. He described Ueno's promissory notes as being signed by the same people on both sides of some transactions.
The scandal hit Peña particularly hard because of his personal links to the bank's holding company, in which he held shares even after taking up the presidency. He also appointed Carlos Carvallo, who had led Ueno Bank, to head Paraguay's Central Bank in 2023.
In his asset declaration submitted weeks after taking up the presidency in 2023, Peña listed shares in Ueno Holding, then valued at around $845,000. Those shares represented around 1.6% of the company's paid-up capital when he later sold them in March 2025.
Prosecutors allege that, while president, he used his position to influence public agencies and state-owned entities to maintain deposits with the bank despite his connections to its parent group.
Peña resigned Thursday and was impeached and removed from office Friday. The following day, prosecutors charged him with breach of trust and administration for personal gain. He was ordered held in pretrial detention at a military facility pending the investigation. Peña has pleaded not guilty. Pedro Alliana, the country's vice president, has been sworn in as president to serve out the rest of Peña's term until August 2028.
Carvallo was also arrested and charged with breach of trust, administration for personal gain and producing false public documents. A judge ordered him held in pretrial detention at a police facility. Eight Ueno executives, including 36-year-old CEO Miguel Vásquez, were also arrested and charged.
The crisis has also put the spotlight on Horacio Cartes, a tobacco magnate and former president of Paraguay who wields considerable political and economic influence.
Cartes handpicked Peña, his former finance minister, to lead his Honor Colorado faction into the 2023 presidential election. But the relationship between the two men had become increasingly strained, apparently over Peña's efforts to establish his own power base within the party.
In September, senators aligned with Cartes sought information from the Central Bank about Ueno's transactions with related companies and its public-sector deposits.
After the bank collapsed, Cartes publicly distanced himself from Peña, releasing a public statement on Wednesday calling for an investigation and insisting there should be "no impunity for anyone." The following day, his faction backed Peña's impeachment.
The move was widely seen as a decisive withdrawal of political protection for Peña, and an opportunity for Cartes to reassert his influence.
But for those gathered outside Congress protesting, the scandal was about more than a bank collapse. It was a reckoning with Paraguay's political establishment.
For Rodrigo Piatti, a 45-year-old activist with the anti-corruption campaign group Comisión Escrache Ciudadano, the scandal would only lead to real change if the political establishment, including Cartes, were challenged.
"Everything that's wrong with Paraguay… is Horacio Cartes and his line of succession," Piatti said. "[Paraguay needs] the opposition to take power. A real opposition to take power, and for all these criminals to be put in prison. That's the dream of all Paraguayans."
The crisis has also raised questions about Paraguay's image among foreign businesspeople. Eduardo López, a 35-year-old exporter whose company operates in Paraguay and the United States, said the scandal would only worsen the lack of confidence he had already seen among American business contacts.
"We are a serious Paraguayan company, but [American businesspeople] don't trust the Paraguayan government," he said. "It's a disaster."
Nearby, Lizza Lugo, a 22-year-old student leader at the National University, expressed frustration with the status quo and said she hoped voters would bring change in the 2028 presidential election.
"The laws apply differently to those who have money and those who don't. That is the reality in Paraguay," she said. "I do hope people don't have short memories, because they forget these things very quickly."

Steven Tan walks along a narrow concourse in the Northern Leaf greenhouse in St Lawrence, Jersey, reading aloud the strains of his cannabis plants: Pink Gasoline, Moon Beam Gelato, Carbon Fibre, Gorilla Kush. Rows of plants stretch off into the distance. To the untrained eye, they look largely the same, with their distinctive jagged-edged, multi-fingered leaf shape and sticky buds like tiny pinecones.
But Tan, the CEO and director of medical cannabis manufacturer Northern Leaf, knows them intimately. “These plants are all different,” he says, stopping next to a mature Carbon Fibre specimen. “Just like humans.”
Northern Leaf is one of the largest licensed medical marijuana producers in Europe. Its 100,000-square-foot growing facility is based in Jersey, the largest of the Channel Islands, located between England and France. Previously, this greenhouse was home to Jersey tomatoes, once a famed crop on the island that came close to extinction, thanks to growing fuel costs and cheaper competition from overseas. Now, it is fitted out with all of the technology required for cultivating cannabis that meets strict regulations for medical use, which include: automated irrigation, environmental monitoring, and air purification.
Despite being just 45 square miles in size, with a population of 100,000, Jersey—which lies 14 miles off the coast of the French mainland but is a British Crown Dependency—has emerged as an unlikely player in the medical cannabis industry. Although its total exports (over 9,200 kilograms in 2025) are small compared to UK growers, this represents an enormous amount per capita, and cannabis is fast becoming one of the island’s important new industries. Jersey’s chief minister, Lyndon Farnham, has previously said that he wants Jersey to be a “centre of excellence” for medical cannabis, and for cannabis production to become a mainstay of the island’s economy.
Currently, 90 percent of Jersey’s cannabis production comes from Northern Leaf. In 2025, the company exported £8.4 million ($11.3 million) worth of medical marijuana to markets including the UK and Germany (regulations mean it is only permitted to grow for export and cannot sell to customers in Jersey). Tan has much greater ambitions. He points to another famous Jersey export, Jersey Royal potatoes. “Jersey’s potato industry did £40 million in 2025,” he said. “I am already doing a quarter of the potato industry on 5 percent of the land. On 20 percent of the land, I could create an industry worth more than the potato industry. That is where it will get interesting.”
Born in Malaysia to a Chinese dad and Irish mother, Tan, 50, wanted to become a vet, but after graduating from university in 1998, ended up developing software for Citibank. He was making good money, but his heart wasn’t in finance. What really interested him was growing weed. “I loved the science of it, the genetics, the seeds, the smells,” Tan says.
The early 2000s were the perfect time for an inquisitive young business grad to get into the cannabis business. Across the world, governments were legalizing medical marijuana and moving towards decriminalization over draconian sentencing.
Tan began bouncing around jurisdictions that were relaxing laws on cannabis, working as a consultant in California, the Netherlands, and Canada. “I started to see these legal frameworks opening up. The minute they existed, I went there,” he says.
Jersey has a somewhat unique regulatory environment. As a Crown Dependency, it has close ties to Britain, but is not a part of the UK. Crucially, it is self-governing: It can make its own laws. Jersey’s main reputation today is as a tax haven, attracting some of the world’s wealthiest individuals and companies, thanks to its lack of capital gains tax and 0 percent corporation tax for most companies. Along its coastline, next to twee beachside cafes and Nazi bunkers (the Channel Islands were the only part of the British Isles to be occupied by Hitler’s forces in World War II), you can find offices of international banks and wealth management firms catering to the super rich.
Although traditionally culturally conservative, Jersey has become something of a trailblazer on cannabis. The island legalized medical cannabis in 2019. Today, five private clinics operate on the island. The latest figures suggest that 6 percent of the population is prescribed cannabis, compared to an estimated 0.4 percent in Germany and 0.1 percent in the UK. Upon legalization, the island’s chief minister, Lyndon Farnham, laid out ambitious plans for the island to become a hub of the medical cannabis trade, repurposing the horticultural facilities and know-how from its tomato-growing glory days for this new endeavor.
Tan joined Northern Leaf as CEO in 2024, when the company was in dire straits after a failed IPO. That year, it was valued at just £3.7 million, despite having spent as much as £30 million on its weed-growing facility.
Tan nevertheless saw a lot of potential, and over the last two years has seen capacity at the site increase from 25 percent to 75 percent. He believes the £8.4 million of product the company exported last year is just the beginning.
Sarah Clover, a barrister at Kings Chambers who works on cannabis licensing in Jersey, told WIRED the island’s advantage is hard to replicate. Growers are inspected by the UK Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA), which is known for enforcing rigorous standards on quality. “Anybody buying from Jersey knows that the stuff coming out of it is absolutely gold standard, because the MHRA says it is,” she says. Permits, however, are handled by a small team on the island: “You can make an application for a permit on a Monday and get it on a Tuesday.”
Many within the Jersey medicinal cannabis industry now want to go beyond growing the raw ingredient and package it for export as a final product on the island. Northern Leaf already has the facilities to do so, but Jersey law dictates it can only export bulk amounts of raw cannabis for other companies to process and pack for distribution and sale. The company is waiting to see if Jersey will change its law. “At the minute we’re kind of on this seesaw—which way will the island go?” Clover says. “It could really take off here. Jersey could be a life sciences hub, not just for cannabis but for all sorts of pharmaceuticals.”
But running a cannabis business on a small island poses challenges, and not everyone is enthused about the idea of expansion. Tan has faced off against residents every time that the facility has expanded production. Some locals have complained that they can smell cannabis from their balconies. Others have linked the growing industry to concerns over misuse of cannabis on the island, despite the fact that all of its product is exported. Cannabis is a “contributory factor” in 22 percent of admissions to the island’s acute mental health ward, according to Jersey’s health minister.
One patient, Michael, told WIRED that he was prescribed medical cannabis for 18 months after having tried two other prescribed medications for insomnia and anxiety. “The initial assessment was simple. I had a meeting with the cannabis doctor who was pretty evangelical about its medicinal properties. They check your medical history with your GP, and within 10 days you’re good to go,” he says.
Michael was prescribed 30 grams a month of “unbelievably good” cannabis and told that if he ran out he could back and ask for more. “I stopped because it was seriously affecting my mental health [and] I have since seen a psychiatric professional who said I should never have been prescribed it given my documented mental health history,” he says.
Illegal resale of medical cannabis is also an issue, with a rise in so-called “user-dealers,” who sell their excess medical marijuana to others. Jersey Police told WIRED this “undermines the legal framework and creates opportunities for criminal supply.”
Overall, however, cannabis-related offenses have dropped since Jersey legalized medical cannabis in 2019—from 216 in 2016 to just 12, as of July 2026.
Tan is circumspect about the challenges of operating on Jersey. “Culturally, the people here are harder to convince about cannabis,” he says. “It’s an older society.” But after 25 years working in the industry, he’s used to the pushback.
“It’s a normal challenge,” he says. “And I think when anyone sits down and meets me, they understand. This isn’t a bunch of stoners growing a bit of weed in a plastic greenhouse.”
While Jersey’s medical cannabis industry grows, some people on the island want to go further. In 2024, a vote to decriminalize recreational cannabis was defeated by a single vote in the island’s parliament. When it was brought back for another vote by the island’s then health minister, it was withdrawn before it could be debated. It is expected to be brought back before the parliament in the coming months.
Some individuals on the island have decided not to wait. By exploiting a loophole in current laws, they have made Jersey one of the only places in Europe outside of Amsterdam where THC products can be purchased and consumed legally.
One morning in February 2024, Gary Tucker arrived at work, his weed shop in St Helier, Jersey, to find a dozen customs officers and the local media waiting outside. It was a raid—and not his first. The officers emptied shelves and boxes into bin bags. “They were literally running their arms down the shelves and putting everything into bags. They took everything,” Tucker, a California native and former analyst in the US Army, told WIRED.
Tucker operates outside of Jersey’s medical cannabis industry. His shop, Bailiwick Botanicals, sells products that are clearly recreational: hash cakes, gummies, and other snacks, all infused with tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), the psychoactive ingredient in cannabis that gets you high and is heavily controlled.
He’s able to do this owing to a loophole in Jersey law which allows the sale of products containing CBD—another critical ingredient in cannabis, but one that doesn’t get you high. Jersey’s law says that the amount of THC in CBD products cannot exceed 3 percent of the weight of the CBD. So, if you want to sell products with high levels of THC, you just have to boost the CBD. “It’s just a math equation,” Tucker says.
Tucker admits it isn’t an ideal situation: studies suggest that ingesting high levels of CBD can cause liver damage. But he sees that as an issue with the regulation, not his solution. “I’m just following consumer demand,” he says.
Tucker is somewhat evangelical about the properties of cannabis. In his time as a weapons trainer for the military, he struggled with the mental health impacts of hearing that recruits he had trained had been killed in action. “I needed to step back from it. It started to really affect my mind,” Tucker says.
Veterans he knew were turning to cannabis, and Tucker began buying it on the black market. “It was the only thing that helped me,” he says. ”Cannabis gave me my life back.”
Tucker currently manufactures most of his products in the US before shipping them to Sark—a smaller Channel Island best known for having no cars and also its own government—and then to Jersey. New regulations in the US, however, mean Tucker may need to change his approach.
Tucker sees Jersey as a potential export hub for THC products to Europe. He believes Jersey’s budding weed industry should push beyond medical cannabis and into the recreational market. “This isn’t just a bunch of guys in a cellar somewhere. Not only does cannabis help people, but getting it to the shelf creates jobs. From the grower to the retailer. It permeates across all industries. We’re making cosmetics. We’re making gummies. We’re making drinks,” he says.
After the 2024 raid, Bailiwick Botanicals shut its doors for two weeks, and its full stock wasn’t returned until six months later. As of June 2026, Tucker and his team are selling THC-infused fudge, chocolate, and other sweets. His newest product, THC-infused coffee beans, is selling well. The police have stayed away.
In a written statement to WIRED, Jersey’s government said that the “possibility of abuse of our limits to get round the law in other jurisdictions is a matter of concern to the Government of Jersey and we are looking at ways to address it. Work is underway to consider whether Jersey’s existing legal exemptions for CBD products require amendment.”
For his part, Tan is reluctant to be drawn on his views on the so-called “rec” (recreational) market. For now, Jersey still has harsh sentencing rules on recreational cannabis use, with the penalties for possession and possession with intent to supply remaining up to five years and 14 years in jail, respectively. The proposed (and withdrawn) law to decriminalize cannabis notes that, the way the law is currently written, someone who rolled three joints and gave one to a friend would be guilty of supply and receive a criminal record. “Without change, people will continue receiving serious criminal records for small amounts … punishments [that] can result in additional harms greater than the drug itself,” it said.
While Jersey makes its own laws, however, it may not be able to completely legalize cannabis. Jersey is a signatory to the UN Convention on drugs control via the UK, and the UK Home Office would undoubtedly have a view if the island were to set itself up as an “Amsterdam on the Sea.” In 2022, an effort by the government of Bermuda (a British Overseas Territory) to legalize recreational cannabis was blocked after the UK withheld Royal Assent from the bill.
Back at the Northern Leaf warehouse in the Jersey parish of St Lawrence, Tan is flipping the lids off large boxes and rifling through clear plastic bags packed full of cannabis.
This is all weed that will not be sold, either because there were issues with production or the THC levels were too low. Instead, it is taken to a secure area of the facility where it is locked away in a reinforced armored vault. Specialist staff with bodycams take the bags to the island’s incinerator, where it is unceremoniously burned, as required by law.
Tan regularly makes a case to the government for changes to the law and support for the cannabis industry, such as an industrial energy tariff to help with spiraling energy costs.
He has claimed that Jersey could be home to “the Monsanto of cannabis,” alluding to the agricultural giant that was acquired by pharmaceutical company Bayer in 2018 for $66 billion. He’d like to get deeper into the genetics of cannabis, form a tissue-culture lab, and “bring out strains that nobody has ever seen.”
But speaking of himself, he references a different genre of business: He’s Willy Wonka, but for weed. Thirty years ago, when Tan quit corporate finance, his father warned him that he could make a lot more money if he stayed in banking. “And you know what, he was right,” he says. “But I would not have had nearly as much fun.”

Gajju Khan is smiling as he sits in an unfinished building in the northern Indian state of Punjab in the late afternoon. The 87-year-old is hopeful that before he dies he will hear the azaan, the Muslim call to prayer, echo across his village once again when the mosque is completed.
The last time he heard it here was when he was eight years old, living with his parents in Tira Maloya, a village in Chandigarh, not far from where he lives now.
He is also excited because the mosque has been funded almost entirely by the Sikhs and Hindus living in his village of Jakhiwal, in Fatehgarh Sahib district. Even though he fondly remembers how Sikh neighbours sheltered him and his brothers when brutal sectarian violence erupted during partition in 1947, he never expected a house of worship to be rebuilt for the 18 Muslim families who remain in the village.
“This was my maternal home. My parents sent my two brothers and me here to save us from the bloodshed – they were killed back in our village,” says Khan. “Sikhs hid us from the patrols of men with sticks and burning torches.”
Khan reserves his deepest gratitude for Bibi Rajinder Kaur, 77, a Sikh villager who persuaded her grandson to donate a parcel of their farmland to build a mosque. She did so, she says, because every other faith had a place to gather, while local Muslims had none.
“There is no deed better than giving someone a place to worship,” Kaur says. “Also, it felt like we needed to appease God for the blood this land had seen. The Muslims in our village had to travel 4km [2.5 miles] to another village just to pray.”
During the partition of British India, the border severed Punjab in two, unleashing catastrophic communal blood-letting and forced migrations that virtually emptied the eastern, Indian side of the region of its Muslim population. Hundreds of village mosques were abandoned, desecrated or turned into cattle sheds and storage units.
But over the past decade, several rural Sikh and Hindu communities have quietly stepped forward to restore these places of worship. Even in villages without a Muslim population, people have invited Muslim farmhands and clerics from nearby districts to pray in these newly revived mosques.
About 50 miles fromJakhiwal, in Sangrur district’s Punawal village, Jaspal Sharma, who comes from a family of Hindu priests, donated his land for the construction of a new mosque and hosted a feast for the entire village at its inauguration in February.
Sharma, 48, says the donation was about neighbourly duty. The village has 550 households, of which just a very small proportion are Muslim.
“It’s right opposite our house, so the sound of prayers five times a day creates a lively atmosphere. We like it,” says Sharma. “And it wasn’t just us; everyone in the village, Hindus and Sikhs together, contributed what they could. Some gave money; others donated bricks and cement.”
For Sukhjinder Singh Pandher and his brother, restoring a local shrine in Malerkotla’s Umarpura village was an act of filial reverence. Their grandfather fled west Punjab during partition to settle in India.
“Nobody is treated as different here,” says Pandher, sharing a cup of tea with his Muslim neighbours on the bare floor of the restored mosque. “Eid and Gurpurab [Sikhs’ most holy festival] are celebrated by both communities with the same fervour.
“We live as one and no matter what happens in the rest of the country, the mood here is that of love and unity. Punjab’s conscience cannot tolerate cruelty against a being, irrespective of caste and religion,” he says.
Pandher points to the syncretic traditions and blending of cultures that are deeply rooted in Punjabi history, noting the popular belief that the 16th-century Sufi saint Hazrat Mian Mir was invited to lay the foundation stone of Sikhism’s holiest site, the Harmandir Sahib, or Golden Temple, in Amritsar.
Inspired by the former shahi, or chief, imam of Punjab, Maulana Habib-ur-Rehman Sani Ludhianvi, non-Muslim villagers have contributed to more than 165 such mosques in the past nine years.
“Partition tore at the natural fabric of Punjab,” says the current shahi imam, Maulana Muhammad Usman Rehmani Ludhianvi, who succeeded his father in 2021. “This state itself is an inquilab [revolution]. Online, there is immense polarisation, but on the ground in our villages, ordinary people are still choosing to protect each other.”

As Delhiites burst firecrackers well past the 10 p.m. deadline set by the Supreme Court for Deepavali night, air pollution shot up to over 50 times World Health Organisation (WHO) limits in parts of the city, official data showed.
The level of PM2.5 (a major pollutant) in Akshardham was 760.99 micrograms per cubic meter at 11 p.m. on Sunday (November 8, 2026), as per Delhi Pollution Control Committee (DPCC) data. This is about 50.73 times the WHO permissible limit of 15 micrograms per cubic meter for a 24-hour period.
Deepavali 2026: All you need to know about Supreme Court-permitted time slots, green crackers and other directives
PM2.5 (Particulate Matter 2.5) are fine inhalable particles, which can get into lungs and bloodstream and lead to a range of respiratory and other diseases.
The level of PM2.5 in Anand Vihar was 767 micrograms per cubic meter at 11 p.m. on Sunday (November 8, 2026), as per DPCC data — This is about 51.13 times the WHO permissible limit.
The level of PM2.5 in Jawaharlal Nehru Stadium was 702 micrograms per cubic meter, as per DPCC data, which is about 46.8 times the WHO permissible limit.
The overall air quality of Delhi continued to be in the “very poor” category while many parts of the city continued to reel under “severe” air quality.
Every winter, air pollution spikes in Delhi-NCR and many parts of the larger Indo-Gangetic Plains, mainly due to meteorological factors such as lower wind speeds and a drop in temperature. Also, pollution from stubble burning during October and November and bursting of firecrackers during the festive season add to existing pollution from vehicles and dust, worsening the air quality.
